Lucy Lost () is an upcoming French animated mystery historical film, directed by Olivier Clert and produced by Xilam Animation. The film's script was written by Clert and Helen Blakeman.

It is an adaptation of the 2014 children's novel Listen to the Moon by British author Michael Morpurgo, set during World War I.

==Plot==
Lucy lives with her family in a village on a small, isolated island. Her extraordinary gifts are met with rejection by the villagers. When she meets Milly, a little girl only she can see, Lucy embarks on a great adventure to uncover the secret of her mysterious powers.

The English dub of the film will be recorded in the United Kingdom. [ref: Olivier Clert’s Annecy competition title 'Lucy Lost' sells widely including Germany, Italy, Spain, China, Japan, Screen Daily]

==Production==
Marc du Pontavice first read Listen to the Moon in 2017, when he was having a drink with an artist Xilam collaborated with, and he recommended it to du Pontavice [ref: 'Lucy Lost' Producer & Director Share the Secrets of Their Magical Animated Mystery (Exclusive First Look), Animation Magazine] and that he thought the "themes of family, love and memory against a backdrop of vivid landscapes, would translate beautifully to the screen". After acquiring the rights to the book, his original idea was to adapt the novel into a 10-episode television miniseries as announced in 2019 [ref: « Lucy Lost »: découvrez le projet au Cartoon Forum !, Xilam], which was originally to be directed by Jean-Christophe Dessaint and it would be fully animated in CGI, with a final 2D rendering. [ref: Xilam finds Lucy Lost in Morpurgo book, C21Media] Helen Blakeman came on board for the script of the project then a miniseries in 2020. [ref: Xilam's 'Lucy Lost' Taps Bafta-Winning Writer Helen Blakeman (EXCLUSIVE), Variety]

Du Pontavice struggled due to its bifurcated structure, which was across two parallel narrative threads and that the crew had great difficulty adapting the story, which worked very well in the novel but was hard to translate to the screen. [ref: Xilam's Buzzy 'Lucy Lost': 'From Europe, We Can Explore a More Emotionally Driven Form of Family Storytelling', Variety] [ref: Festival d’Annecy 2026: pourquoi «Lucy Lost» d’Olivier Clert bouleverse le public, Radio France Internationale] The original budget as a miniseries was $6 million. [ref: What we're watching at MIPTV, Kidscreen] After meeting Olivier Clert in 2022, he convinced him to make it into a theatrical movie instead, by deciding that they would tell Lucy's story and by uniting the different narrative strands of the book by bringing Milly, who exists in another plot of the novel, directly into the Lucy's world, which du Pontavice really liked, where Clert developed it by creating a complete storyboard, editing it with voice acting and music, making it look like a movie. [ref: How Olivier Clert's Storyboarding Instincts Cracked Xilam's 'Impossible' 'Lucy Lost' Adaptation, Cartoon Brew] Clert joined the project later, after seeing some early visual materials at Xilam, as he was drawn to their timeless quality. Originally, he was only going to contribute as a storyboard artist, but he soon became more deeply involved in developing the story.

Site: Physics Stack Exchange
Title: Heat transfer kinetics and eutectic mixture cooling
Tags: thermodynamics, physical-chemistry, thermal-conduction

Question:
I am working on a physics research problem regarding the cooling rate and minimum achievable temperature of a room-temperature beverage chilled in an ice bath with added salt ($\text{NaCl}$) and alcohol ($\text{Ethanol}$).

My theoretical understanding so far:Freezing Point Depression:

Adding salt/alcohol lowers the freezing point of the ice-water mixture, causing rapid melting. Since melting is an endothermic process ($\Delta H_{\text{fusion}}$), the bath temperature drops significantly below $0\,\text{^\circ C}$.

Thermal Contact: Liquid salt-water-alcohol bath provides a much higher heat transfer coefficient ($h$) compared to solid ice cubes due to maximum contact surface area.

Cooling Kinetics: Chilling rate seems to follow Newton's Law of Cooling, but the bath temperature $T_{\text{bath}}(t)$ is dynamic rather than constant.

Questions I need help with:

How do I theoretically model the coupling between the melting rate of ice (latent heat absorption) and the transient temperature of the beverage?

How does the presence of ethanol alter the heat capacity ($C_p$) and viscosity of the eutectic mixture compared to pure saline solution, and how does this impact natural convection around the can?

Is there an optimal mass ratio of $\text{Ice : Salt : Ethanol}$ that maximizes both the heat removal rate ($\frac{dT}{dt}$) and the lowest achievable temperature?

Any pointers to literature, relevant thermodynamic formulas, or differential equations describing this dynamic heat exchange would be greatly appreciated!

Thank you a lot!

Title: Finite-resource cooling of qudits beyond thermodynamic length

Abstract:
Cooling a quantum system with $N$ thermal machines costs more than Landauer's bound. For swap-based collision models the excess is set by thermodynamic length, which is optimal for qubits and was suggested by numerics to be optimal in general. We show that for qudits, permutations of energy eigenstates that use several resonant transitions at once do better for every spectrum, reducing the excess by up to 83% near the ground state. To second order, coherent collisions do no better, and at infinite temperature $d_M$-level machines reduce the excess by at most a factor $d_M-1$.

Title: Short-Circuit Current Calculation in DC Shipboard Microgrid Using Operational Admittances

Abstract:
The increasing adoption of DC shipboard power systems is driven by the need to integrate energy storage systems seamlessly onboard. In this context, accurate calculation of short-circuit current transients is critical for sizing fast-acting protection devices. This paper proposes a methodology to calculate short-circuit current transients based on operational admittance modelling of network elements and power converters. The superposition principle is then applied to calculate current contributions and voltage time profiles. The methodology is validated with a detailed EMT model of a notional LVDC shipboard microgrid section consisting of an active front end, a bidirectional buck-boost converter and two special loads. Results demonstrate that the methodology accurately tracks nodal voltages and the fault current contributions dynamics up to the prospective fault current peak, thus providing a computationally efficient tool for fault analysis and protection coordination in LVDC microgrids.

state.text:
Title: Measuring Longer-Horizon Leveraged ETF Performance

Abstract:
Many investors hold leveraged exchange-traded funds (LETFs) for more than one day. Because these products reset leverage daily, their longer-horizon returns need not equal the stated leverage multiple times the underlying return. We explain this gap using a return identity that separates what we call the convexity bonus, volatility drag, and product costs. We also discuss several common ways to measure LETF performance and highlight how these measures can produce misleading assessments of how real-world LETFs perform. We propose evaluating ex-post performance using realized terminal wealth, which measures how much invested wealth grew. For ex-ante analysis, we propose using expected log returns to quantify how fast capital compounds over time. We show that estimating expected cumulative return by compounding the historical arithmetic mean can rank investments backwards, report gains for funds that lose money, suggest that infinite leverage is optimal when expected returns exceed borrowing cost, and reward temporary price fluctuations that reduce LETF wealth. We argue that even if the distribution of daily returns is known by the econometrician, expected terminal wealth is sensitive to whether the model draws days independently or draws monthly or annual blocks of daily returns and can be driven by a small number of economically infeasible payouts.

Most likely camera location

The view direction implied by the photo (valley farmland with a barn and two silos, forested ridge behind) matches the typical look-north viewpoint from the edge of South Mountain above Torbrook. The likely roadside viewpoint is around:

44.9179, -65.0025

Open directly in Google Maps:
https://maps.google.com/?q=44.9179,-65.0025

This spot is:

•  On the north escarpment of South Mountain
•   About 1–2 km south of Torbrook Mines
•   Looking north across farms in the Torbrook / Nictaux valley.

Why this location matches the photo

Clues in the picture:
•   High vantage point → consistent with the steep north-facing escarpment of South Mountain.
•   Large rectangular pasture field with a farmstead and twin silos in the middle.
•   Tree line forming a “ring of fire” around the field in fall.
•   Another forested ridge in the far distance (the opposite side of the valley).
That geometry is exactly what you see from the edge of South Mountain overlooking the Torbrook farmland.

{"text": "My BBB Autoline arbitration experience is over.  
The outcome was decidedly mixed.  I won the battle but 
lost the war.  The arbitrator found that the car was 
defective, but decided to offer a repurchase well below 
market value :(.  At the time of the hearing, average 
retail on my truck in the NADA book was $21,025, but 
the decision was for  $17,665.  I wrote a letter to the 
Council of Better Business Bureaus pointing out the 
fact that if you have an automobile that does not 
depreciate rapidly, the manufacturer has no incentive 
to deal with you.  There is no way that the 
manufacturer can loose because they can turn around and 
sell the vehicle at a profit if the consumer is awarded 
a repurchase.  The attitude of Chevrolet's 
representative at the hearing tends to support this 
point of view;  he was totally unprepared and did not 
seem to take the proceeding very seriously.

I decided to take the repurchase, even though I am 
getting totally screwed on the price.  I will not have 
to deal with continuing repairs or selling a lemon 
myself, and I have no case for a civil suit based on 
the Idaho lemon law.  I am planning to send a letter to 
my elected representatives telling them how utterly 
ridiculous the Idaho lemon law is.  The law allows for 
a "use deduction" equal to the IRS mileage allowance.  
As if Chevrolet were buying my gas and paying 
for my insurance.

Summary of the case:  In May 1992 I bought a new 3/4 ton
HD Chevrolet pickup.  Between May 1992 and December 1992 
this vehicle required repair after repair.  Systems 
that required attention included the transmission, 
heater fan, paint, suspension, and motor.  The main 
problem was the five speed manual transmission.  They 
could not install a non-defective transmission in at 
least four attempts.

So, in summary, it is possible to get a repurchase, but 
you are going to get screwed on the price, unless you 
paid too much in the first place, or if your car

state.text:
Title: Modules with unbalanced support

Abstract:
A finitely generated module has unbalanced support if its support has positive dimension but meets a top-dimensional component of the spectrum only at the closed point. We ask what homological signals are left behind by this geometry. Separating the spectrum into two wings, we prove first Tor nonvanishing for positive-depth modules and give criteria for second Tor nonvanishing. In depth zero, we obtain a structural sequence describing the finite-length torsion under a first Tor vanishing. A recent counterexample to the Peskine--Szpiro dimension inequality conjecture establishes the existence of modules of finite projective dimension and unbalanced support \cite{Ma}. We apply our framework to these modules and establish a numerical torsion--spine balance for linked Cohen--Macaulay wings. We also construct such modules over a reduced Gorenstein ring with exactly two irreducible components.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: just (non-virtually nilpotent) quotients in residually finite groups
Tags: group-theory, solvable-groups, nilpotent-groups

Question:
Question

Let $G$ be a finitely generated, residually finite group that is not virtually nilpotent. Is it always possible to find a just non-virtually nilpotent (JNVN) quotient of $G$ that is also residually finite?

Context & Motivation

Recall that a group is defined to be just non-virtually nilpotent (JNVN) if it is not virtually nilpotent, but every proper quotient is virtually nilpotent.

By applying Zorn's lemma to the set of normal subgroups $N \triangleleft G$ where $G/N$ is not virtually nilpotent, it is straightforward to show that any finitely generated group that is not virtually nilpotent admits a JNVN quotient. However, residual finiteness is generally not preserved under taking arbitrary quotients.

From Emmanuel Breuillard's work (On uniform exponential growth for solvable groups https://www.imo.universite-paris-saclay.fr/~emmanuel.breuillard/expgr8.pdf), if $G$ is a finitely generated solvable group that is not virtually nilpotent, it admits a JNVN quotient which is virtually metabelian, and hence automatically residually finite. I am particularly interested in whether a similar statement holds when $G$ is residually finite and residually solvable:

Any insights or counterexamples would be greatly appreciated!

state.text:
Title: Central limit theorems for high-dimensional ridge regression under uniform subsampling

Abstract:
We study ridge regression based on uniformly subsampled observations in high-dimensional linear models, where the number of predictors and the sample size grow proportionally. Subsampling is implemented through independent Bernoulli indicators with a common selection probability. We establish central limit theorems for linear contrasts of the ridge estimator, allowing for non-Gaussian predictors and general population covariance matrices. Under a vanishing-signal assumption, we obtain an explicit bias correction in the isotropic case and develop consistent estimators of the asymptotic variances. These results enable asymptotically valid tests for linear contrasts of the regression parameter in the isotropic setting. Our proofs exploit the resolvent representation of the ridge estimator and combine leave-one-out arguments with deterministic equivalents from random matrix theory.

Site: Law Stack Exchange
Title: Virtual dvd/blu-ray disc rental service: playing and streaming physical discs to remote users
Tags: united-states, copyright, intellectual-property, internet, entertainment-law

Question:
I'm wondering about the legality of a business idea. It would basically be a virtual dvd/blu-ray disc rental service (maybe including VHS, laser disc, etc.). The discs would not be ripped to a drive. They would be streamed, and the user could also explore the disc's extras, rewind and fast forward, pause, etc. They would basically have access to something like VLC player (a free, open source video player), running on a linux server, streamed to their device. It would basically be giving them remote control over an instance of that software.

The discs would be bought in bulk, used. Please advise if the legality would be different if commercial" copies of these discs were bought instead (though part of the idea is to take advantage of the large amounts of used discs out there). And part of the user agreement would contain a prominent warning to users that they were prohibited from further streaming the result and/or showing it in public. It would be for their private use only (including their friends/family ideally).

There would be a ton of dvd/blu-ray players hooked up in server racks to computers. These computers would stream each players' output to a single user online. The entire catalog would be presented to the users, along with the current number of available copies of each item. They would make their selection and a human or bot of some kind would physically retrieve the disc, insert it into a player, and basically verify that the disc was OK and connect that player via the software to the user. The user would have some kind of time limit in which to watch the disc.

There's a question in here from someone years ago who wanted to own and stream X copies of a disc, based off of ripping one of them. This would not be ripping. It might be slightly buffered (like a few seconds) but only if that presented no additional legal problems. Any buffer would be deleted immediately upon being seen. And it would not be "screen-shared", like another person has asked. The only party seeing the disc would be the remote party.

I'm aware of VidAngel's legal issues. This would not be breaking any encryption. It would not be ripping anything or marking anything in the work. It would basically just be connecting the output of a server's disc player via a software video player directly to a single user online. 1:1. A virtual disc rental service.

Please advise on the American legality first, Canada second if possible, and worldwide.

Would the legality be mitigated by keeping track of each work and the number of times it was rented and somehow passing on fees to the rights holders, to the studios? Or would this just require negotiating a streaming license for each work (which might make having the physical discs pointless anyway)?

Part of the idea is to be able to stream rare works that are almost impossible to find in modern streaming video services. Lots of different niches to exploit. Plenty of old movies that very few bother to carry anymore. It would not be attempting to directly compete via new releases and popular stuff carried by the big streamers necessarily.

Thank you!!

Title: Is loop invariant a combination of one (or both) of universal and existential quantification?
Tags: logic, first-order-logic, loops, loop-invariants, predicate-logic

Question:
So I have two questions:

Is loop invariant a combination of one (or both) of universal and existential quantification?

Is my loop invariant example correct?

I have been trying to self-study CS for too long now,
and the topic of loop invariant still bothers my mind.
There has to be a question, or answer, on CS StackExchange
that explicitly mentions existential quantification (or $\exists$ symbol),
universal quantification (or $\forall$ symbol),
and loop invariant in the same sentence or paragraph.
But I still cannot find it.

The Wikipedia article on Loop invariant says

loop invariants are expressed by formal predicate logic

It includes the keyword predicate logic,
but I do not see $\forall$, nor $\exists$ symbols anywhere
in that Wikipedia page.
If the answer to my question is true,
I wish that Wikipedia article had used them in some sections.
Althought it could be that the article wanted
to approach the topic
using reader-friendly natural language in English.

Question 1

I have read that Universal quantification, and Existential quantification
are under predicate logic.
So loop invariants and universal/existential quantification
must be under the same thing?
In other words,
can I express loop invariant using $\forall$, and $\exists$ symbols?

Take for example, the following Python program
for printing all natural numbers
that is even and less than or equal to 100

num_max = 100

for num in range(num_max + 1):
    if num % 2 == 0:
        print("num = {} is even".format(num))

What is the loop invariant of this?

The first sentence of the Wikipedia article says, a loop invariant is

a property of a program loop that is true before (and after) each iteration

Can I take this to mean,
a first-order logic statement using $\forall$ or $\exists$ symbols,
that is true before (and after) each iteration?

I feel like the universal quantification statement
of the form $\forall{x} (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x))$ is stronger
because it states something is true about the entire thing.

So I feel inclined to say this universal quantification statement
about the example Python program in discussion,

$$\forall{x}, x \in \mathbb{N}, x \le 100, (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x))$$

where $P(x)$ is the statement $x$ is an even number,
and $Q(x)$ is the statement $x$ is printed to the console

But since I use universal quantification (only $\forall$ symbol),
I feel that this makes it a statement
about the entire loop,
not an individual statement about an individual loop iteration?

How to make this a statement about an individual loop iteration
instead of the entire thing?
I feel that
instead of talking about the entire thing via $\forall x$,
I should talk about one specific thing via $\exists x = x_i$,
where $i \in \mathbb{N}, i \le 100$.
So for example, halfway through,
when the loop counter variable num hits $33$,
we are talking about a particular number $x$
that takes value $x_{33} = 33$.

Question 2

Can I say that,
the for loop in that Python program,
has the following loop invariant?

$$ \exists x = x_i, i \in \mathbb{N}, (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x)) $$

But now I am concerned with loop invariant definition
that says, "before (and after) each iteration".
Because before an iteration,
the Python program
has not done the if num % 2 == 0 code expression
that checks whether $x$ is an even number yet?
So that existential quantification statement
is not true yet
until it hits the end of the loop iteration?

Title: Channel State Information-Free Angle Spoofing for Differential Localization Privacy

Abstract:
This paper proposes a channel state information (CSI)-free angle spoofing strategy that remains effective even when the eavesdropper (Eve) uses differential statistics to estimate the location of the transmitter (Alice). Specifically, by designing a precoding matrix, Eve incorrectly estimates the angle differences of departure (ADoDs), thereby spoofing Alice's location. Meanwhile, the trusted user (Bob) can still infer Alice's true location with a modest amount of securely shared side information. Given the channel parameters estimated by Eve from the spoofed channel, the resulting localization bias introduced to the eavesdroppers under the spoofed geometric is analyzed. Eve's bias can be driven to infinity asymptotically in a key parameter of the precoder. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method introduces significant localization errors for Eve. When combined with a prior CSI-free spoofing strategy, further degraded performance is achieved by Eve.

Draft text:
Tapas Chakraborty is an Indian computer scientist, researcher, and deep-tech entrepreneur. [ref: Can AI fix India's land record problem? This startup believes so, The Economic Times] He is the founder of Vixplor and its automated document intelligence platform, DocXplor. [ref: DocXplor extracts medical record, speeds up process in hospitals, insurance cos, The Hindu BusinessLine] His career spans a decade in the multinational software industry, peer-reviewed computational research in bioinformatics, and the deployment of artificial intelligence tools for public sector governance and healthcare infrastructure.

== Early life and education ==
Chakraborty completed his primary and secondary schooling at the historic Hindu School, Kolkata in Kolkata. He demonstrated early academic distinction under the West Bengal state boards, securing the 34th state rank in the Madhyamik examinations in 2001, and subsequently the 63rd state rank in the Higher Secondary examinations in 2003. He was named a recipient of the National Scholarship for his performances in both board tiers. Additionally, during his Higher Secondary board exam, he was awarded a Gold Medal from the Government of West Bengal for attaining a perfect score (200 out of 200) in mathematics.

He then attended Jadavpur University, graduating with a Bachelor of Engineering (BE) degree in 2007. Following a decade in corporate technology enterprises, Chakraborty returned to academia at Jadavpur University to pursue advanced computational research.

He completed his Master of Engineering (ME) degree in 2019. His master's research specialized in audio signal processing using deep learning frameworks, culminating in his thesis titled "Speaker identification on multimodal environment using deep learning" (2019). In 2026, he was awarded a Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) in Computer Science from Jadavpur University. His doctoral work specialized in structural bioinformatics and computational biology. His dissertation, titled "Computational studies on protein protein interaction" (2026), proposed a series of deep neural network architectures introducing innovative approaches for predicting protein-protein interactions (PPI), protein self-interactions, and protein residue-residue proximity frameworks.

== Career ==
=== Enterprise technology (2007–2017) ===
After earning his engineering degree, Chakraborty spent ten years working within the enterprise software and technology consulting sectors. During this period, he held corporate engineering roles at global technology consulting firms, including IBM and PwC (PricewaterhouseCoopers), where he designed enterprise application architectures and automated software data flows.

While at IBM, Chakraborty was assigned to highly specialized corporate optimization and data analytics projects:
* Severn Trent Water (Predictive Analytics): He contributed to the data analytics and predictive framework infrastructure for the UK-based water utility company Severn Trent. His work centered on building analytical modules to identify geographical "hot spots" in water distribution networks to isolate areas requiring immediate infrastructural intervention or targeted pipeline replacements.
* Philip Morris International (Research Infrastructure): He was integrated into the specialized technological research and development infrastructure team for Philip Morris International (PMI), assisting in building backend systems mapping data flows for their IQOS electronic nicotine delivery research programs.

=== Entrepreneurship and public sector utility (2017–present) ===
In 2017, Chakraborty left the multinational technology sector to establish his deep-tech startup, Vixplor, focusing on intelligent automation and character recognition. Under Vixplor, he developed **DocXplor**, an artificial intelligence platform utilizing specialized Deep Learning models and Large Language Models (LLMs) to read, interpret, and digitize highly variable printed and handwritten text records without requiring static templates.

The platform has been deployed in several public public infrastructure and private enterprise use cases:
* Land Records Digitization: The Finance Department of the Government of West Bengal contracted the platform to process, extract, and digitize legacy handwritten municipal registries and land deed repositories, algorithmically stitching together "chain deeds" to map real estate ownership lineage across multiple decades.
* Healthcare and Insurance Automation: The platform is used by national healthcare facilities and over a dozen insurance providers to instantly extract structured digital data from handwritten medical prescriptions and clinical invoices, reducing manual data entry delays and accelerating claim pre-authorizations.

In 2026, Chakraborty presented his document intelligence platform on zee TV Zee 24 Ghanta's startup program, Tigers Pitch (Season 1), securing institutional validation and ecosystem funding.. [ref: Tigers Pitch Season 1, Zee 24 Ghanta] He has also been invited as a domain specialist on state television networks, including Doordarshan DD Bangla's flagship economic and entrepreneurship programs, to speak on sustainable scaling and AI integration bottlenecks within emerging industrial corridors. [ref: Pratyasha: 2025-er Safalya 2026-er Pratashya, DD Bangla] and [ref: BARTAMAN ARTHONOITIK ABOSTHA EBONG START-UP BUSINESS, DD Bangla]

Title: Beyond Direct Imaging: Quantum Measurement Design for Small-Target Detection in UAV Hyperspectral Sensing

Abstract:
Small mineral patches can be spectrally distinct yet difficult to detect when diffraction mixes their light with the surrounding rock. Conventional hyperspectral detectors analyze recorded intensities, leaving an opportunity to recover target evidence through the optical measurement itself. We develop a quantum-assisted framework for exploiting this opportunity in prospective unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) hyperspectral sensing. A common radiometric and diffraction model describes direct imaging and spatial-mode measurements of the same light. The theory identifies target changes that survive background fitting and explains when mode measurements retain more detection information. It quantifies losses from mode mismatch and unresolved outputs, linking the quantum benchmark to finite receiver design. A common-basis result identifies when material spectra can share a spatial measurement at fixed geometry. An adaptive receiver uses an imaging pilot to select candidate modes and combines both stages in a full-region presence test. Simulations based on measured mineral spectra and published UAV acquisition scales demonstrate gains over complete direct imaging at a shared active-exposure budget, including pilot cost and optical loss. At matched empirical 1\% region-level false alarms, detection increases from 62.95\% to 69.65\% for a representative target. Paired analysis supports gains with registration uncertainty and, separately, under controlled nonuniform backgrounds. Calibrated mode errors reveal where measurement losses weaken or reverse the benefit. These results connect background identifiability to receiver choices and their operating conditions. They provide a framework for designing spatial measurements alongside spectral channels to detect small material features.

Humankind 2 is a turn-based strategy 4X video game currently in development by Amplitude Studios. A sequel to Humankind (2021), the game will be released for Windows in 2027.

== Gameplay ==
Humankind 2 is a 4X game similar to its predecessor. Like its predecessor, players are able to select whichever civilizations to play as across six eras of human history, from the nomadic age to the modern day, ultimately deciding how their civilizations evolve over time. The game introduces a new system called First Tales, which are founding myths that affect the development of civilizations in-game. [ref: Humankind 2 Rethinks One of Its Predecessor’s Most Divisive Ideas, Which May Solve The Great Culture-Switching Debate, IGN]

Players can also choose to keep playing as the civilization they chose at the start of the game, unlike its predecessor. Every civilization also has a new culture tree, which provides bonuses related to the chosen civilization's history and culture. A new system called Adaptations is introduced. Adaptations provide bonuses depending on which biomes your cities are located in on the world map. [ref: After Civ 7 stumbled, Humankind 2 looks like it's making smart choices to pick up the 4X torch, PC Gamer]For example, a city in the desert can adopt methods to gather water and protect against the heat, while a city in the forest can specialize in hunting animals and foraging fruit. Players can also adopt advancements from other civilizations they interact with in-game. [ref: 4X strategy sequel Humankind 2 gets its first extended in-game footage, rich in era-spanning, culture-shaping, history-rewriting action, Rock, Paper, Shotgun]

== Development ==
Humankind 2 is currently being developed by Amplitude Studios. [ref: Humankind 2 Forces You To Deal With The Consequences Of Climate Change, GameSpot] It was revealed at the 2026 Gamescom Opening Night Live with a live action trailer. Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: How do existence assumptions work when solving differential equations? Do they prove solutions work? Do they use conditional or biconditional steps?
Tags: calculus, integration, ordinary-differential-equations, derivatives, algebraic-equations

Question:
When solving a differential equation (like $\frac{dy}{dx} + 3x = 5x$, or simplified to $\frac{dy}{dx}=2x$), how does the logical framework and process of solving it work in formal/rigorous mathematics? Specifically:

Initial Assumptions: Do we need to assume beforehand that $\frac{dy}{dx}$ exists (meaning $y$ is a differentiable function with respect to $x$) so we can write and manipulate the equation (like apply operations to both sides) without having undefined terms? I don’t mean that we assume a solution satisfying the equation exists, but just that $y$ is differentiable so that $\frac{dy}{dx}$ isn’t undefined in the equation and it is a real number (if $y$ is a real-valued function).

Conditional vs. Biconditional Logic for the Solution: When we solve a differential equation by integrating and manipulating terms, is the process conditional (like if we get $y=g(x)+C$ as our solution to the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)$, then the conditional statement would be: "if $y$ is differentiable, then the solution to $\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)$ must be $y=g(x)+C$") or is it biconditional (like “$y$ is differentiable if and only if the solution is $y=g(x)+C$”)? For example, what I mean is that once we reach the end solution $y(x)$, does getting that result automatically prove our initial assumption (that $y$ was differentiable) and prove our solution works, since the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says that the integral of a continuous function is differentiable (or just by looking at $y(x)$ and seeing that differentiation rules apply to it), which makes the entire chain of steps biconditional, so we don’t have to recheck our answer? And would the original assumption that $y$ is differentiable just disappear after verifying our solution $y(x)$ is differentiable and all the steps become biconditional, or would the original assumption still stay there? Or would all of this above be circular reasoning, where instead we would have to work backwards separately to verify our solution (like by differentiating our solution again to get back to the original differential equation we wanted to solve)? And is this solving process essentially the same as solving algebraic equations (where we declare the number system for the variable $x$ (same as us assuming $y$ is differentiable, so it exists as a real number), and use biconditional operations to solve for $x$ (same as us integrating to get $y$), and then making sure our solution for $x$ is within our number system domain (same as us checking if $y$ is differentiable, which it should be since we integrated to find it, which is reversible))? Because I’m not sure if after we find the solution to a differential equation, we always have to recheck it (similar to how if you solve an algebraic equation for $x$, you usually never plug it back in to recheck unless you specifically used non-biconditional operations like squaring)?

Necessity of Existence Theorems: Is an existence/uniqueness theorem actually necessary to solve simple differential equations (similar to how we need the Implicit Function Theorem to do implicit differentiation (so that the $\frac{dy}{dx}$ term exists)), or are our assumptions alone (that $y$ is differentiable) enough to solve it?

Any help would be greatly appreciated. Thank you!

Title: Beyond Smart Homes: Characterizing IoT Vulnerabilities Across Sectors, Vendors, and Products

Abstract:
The Internet of Things (IoT) has expanded beyond consumer smart homes to sectors, such as industrial systems, healthcare, and smart cities, broadening the IoT attack surface. Prior empirical work has focused on studying aggregate IoT vulnerability characteristics or specific protocols, so patching is directed by aggregate security guidance. However, if dominant weaknesses differ substantially across sectors or products, such uniform guidance misdirects the remediation effort. To address this gap, we present a fine-grained, data-driven analysis of IoT vulnerabilities using a dataset of more than 15,000 IoT specific CVEs. We design a pipeline to enrich noisy CPE (Common Platform Enumeration) metadata, normalizing vendors and products, then assigning product type and sector labels using lexical matching, fuzzy clustering, and LLM-assisted classification. We find meaningful differences in the weakness profile of IoT sectors. For example, healthcare is dominated by authentication and credential weaknesses, while automotive faces memory issues. More importantly, we find that weakness profiles are more similar across different product types from the same vendor than across the same product type built by different vendors. This suggests vendor-level factors such as shared code and development practices dominate weakness inheritance, making a vendor's disclosure history informative about its other products. Our findings suggest weakness classes should be used to prioritize remediation efforts.

Site: Law Stack Exchange
Title: Are there limits to fair use parody protections, or is all parody protected in all circumstances?
Tags: copyright, fair-use

Question:
Or did The Simpsons' Mary Poppins parody really have to be called Sherry Bobbins?

TV shows that involve parody always have a breaking-the-fourth-wall gag where the characters talk about how they had to change the name to keep from being sued. I always thought it was an annoying trope, because fair use protects parody, so legally, they don't have to change anything, as long as it's clearly in a parody context.

But the trope is so persistent, I wondered if there was any truth to it. Could The Simpsons producers really have been sued if the Mary Poppins character had been named Mary Poppins?

My guess is that it could be genuine legal advice, if not strictly necessary. Humor is subjective; parody has absolute protection, but what constitutes parody is a grey area that a litigious rights holder could exploit. Changing the name to something similar is more clearly parodic, and makes it absolutely clear that parody is the intent.

Same reason porn parodies all have "a porn parody" in the title.

Or is this more than good advice? Could something that's in a parody context be the basis of a copyright claim, if the use is not parodic enough?

Or is it just an annoying trope that has no basis in legal reality, and does not reflect real legal advice?

Site: Law Stack Exchange
Title: If an emoji renders differently on two devices due to compatibility issues, whose interpretation is valid?
Tags: united-states, contract-law, legal-terms, breach-of-contract, digital-contract

Question:
Suppose X and Y are frequent traders. Y buys X's products in mass from time to time. X sends a proposal to Y, which says that Y will buy 1000 of X's products for a million dollars. The contract states that Y is supposed to pay once the products reach Y. Y responds with a ✅ (U+2705) emoji, indicating that they accept the offer.

However, unbeknownst to Y, on X's device, the emoji was not supported because the phone was outdated. Instead of displaying the emoji, the system displayed ☒ (U+2612, Ballot Box With X), which is the default glyph it fall backs to when it receives a symbol that is missing on the device.

Therefore, X interpreted the reply as a no, found another buyer and shipped their products to a third party. Y was expecting a shipment which never came, and they recorded a huge loss because of the lack of supplies.

If the emoji was the final communication between X and Y, is it Y's fault for not replying with standard text even though it wasn't their intention for the emoji to be represented differently on the receiver's end? Does X have any responsibility to double-check Y's intentions? X is not a tech-savvy person so they took the fallback symbol at face value.

Answer A:
england-and-wales

No Contract

In England generally parties who are at cross purposes are held to have contracted on what the terms objectively mean (to a hypothetical reasonable bystander). If there is ambiguity they are held to what the terms probably mean.

But there are decided cases which appear to say that if two possible interpretations of the terms are equally likely then there is no contract. For example in NBTY Europe v Nutricia it was said (at [25]) that:

But where parties are genuinely at cross-purposes as to the subject
matter of the contract and the terms of the offer and acceptance are
so ambiguous that it is not possible to point to one or the other of
the interpretations as the more probable, the court must necessarily
hold that no contract exists

So I think the answer to the question in England would be that there is no contract.

Answer B:
Acceptance must be communicated

This is a longstanding tenant of common law contract formation. Once Y’s message reaches X, the contract is formed, irrespective of whether X has read or understood the message. Now, the requirement for communication can be waived, specific modes of communication may be specified, communication may be by conduct, and there’s also the postal rule, but none of those are relevant here.

In many jurisdictions, electronic communications have specific rules about when they have been received. In australia, each jurisdiction has an Electronic Transactions Act and we can take new-south-wales as an example. The time of receipt is dealt with in s 13A and happens at different times depending on if the electronic address has been “designated” by the recipient; in this case it’s not clear so we’ll deal with both.

If X nominated the address (email, phone number, WhatsApp, whatever), then the message is received when it “becomes capable of being retrieved” at that address. If it wasn’t nominated, then in addition, X must also have been notified that it is retrievable. Now, the courts have held that an email or text is capable of being retrieved when it’s available from X’s ISP or phone company, but links in those are not capable of being retrieved until they are actually clicked on.
[truncated]

Answer C:
canada

Interpretations of communications in the context of contract acceptance is not based on either the sender's or recipient's interpretation.

Interpretation is from the perspective of an objective observer.

See Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church of Canada St. Mary Cathedral v. Aga, 2021 SCC 22:

the test of agreement for legal purposes is whether parties have indicated to the outside world, in the form of the objective reasonable bystander, their intention to contract and the terms of such contract

Whether any particular communication would be understood by the objective reasonable observer to constitute acceptance will depend on all the circumstances, including (especially in the case of non-standard means of acceptance) the history of transacting between the two individuals.

See e.g. South West Terminal Ltd. v Achter Land, 2023 SKKB 116, affirmed on appeal 2024 SKCA 115. The court there found that in that specific context and history, a  "👍" constituted acceptance and a signature (paras. 62–63).

As for "which version is relevant," the answer is both. See Hailink Dent Removal Inc. v Kindersley Mainline Motor Products Limited, 2018 SKQB 138, paras. 22-23 (excerpting, including from internal quotations, and omitting citations):

The above question establishes that numbers are sometimes spelled out both in digits and in letters/words in statutes. Generally speaking, everything matches. What happens if there is a contradiction? For example, consider this hypothetical law:

No resident of this state shall be qualified to vote in a state election unless he has submitted his voter registration form at least thirty (3) days before the date of such election.

Does a potential voter need to submit their registration form at least thirty days before the election or may they submit later than 30 days before but before 3 days?

Title: Hydrodynamic flow in the gut hinders the fixation of beneficial mutants but accelerates their invasion

Abstract:
Gut bacteria experience a spatially structured environment with hydrodynamic flow. Using a branching-process approach, we show that beneficial mutants arising randomly upon division have a reduced fixation probability compared to the well-mixed case. The suppression factor is set by the spatial heterogeneity of mutant fate across the gut. In contrast, the invasion of mutant lineages that avoid early stochastic extinction is accelerated in the gut compared to a matched well-mixed case. Stronger advective flow decreases fixation probabilities while accelerating mutant invasion.

state.text:
Title: Spectrum of the steady-state distribution function of disordered Lindbladian fermions at large channel number

Abstract:
Free fermions coupled to particle gain and loss relax to a Gaussian steady state, in which every natural orbital has its own occupation. We find the distribution of these occupations $\varrho_{\rm st}$ for a random Hamiltonian coupled to many random gain and loss channels. Each orbital is filled and emptied at its own rates, and the Hamiltonian, moving particles across the levels during their lifetime, averages the differences between the orbitals. We show that this averaging is incomplete: the spread of the occupations decreases only as the inverse square root of the number of channels per level. At large system size the distribution depends on the grain Hamiltonian only through its density of states $ν(E)$. The spread is bounded by the baths alone: even Hamiltonians with unbounded, heavy-tailed spectra cannot widen it beyond this bound. The spread suppresses the particle-number fluctuations below their binomial value.

Title: Rational curves of submaximal quantum index

Abstract:
On a complex toric surface, oriented real rational curves tangent to the toric boundary at real points are distinguished by their value of quantum index. Using variants of usual Welschinger multiplicities, G. Mikhalkin defined enumerative invariants $W_{\tildeΔ}^κ$ that are provided by a signed count of oriented real rational curves with given quantum index $κ$ and fixed tangency points on the boundary of the positive quadrant (the tangency orders being encoded by $\tildeΔ$). We prove that, for most toric surfaces and tangency orders, the invariant $W_{\tildeΔ}^κ$ is zero in the case of the highest nonmaximal value of $κ$. This is done by enumerating tropical curves with Block--Göttsche multiplicities. Additionally, we prove that, in many situations, the lower bound, given by the absolute value $|W_{\tildeΔ}^κ|$ of $W_{\tildeΔ}^κ$, for the number of oriented real rational curves is not sharp close to the tropical limit in the case of the highest nonmaximal value of $κ$.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: Further misunderstanding when calculating moment of inertia of a torus
Tags: definite-integrals, physics

Question:
I am yet again still working on calculating the moment of inertia of a uniform-density body in the shape of a torus $\mathcal K$ of mass $M$ whose outer and inner radii are $a$ and $b$ respectively.

This is item $40.14 (\text a)$ in Schaum's Mathematical Handbook of Formulas and Tables, 1968 (item $11.14 (\text a)$ in the 3rd edition of 2009).

Context: staving off incipient senility by giving my brain exercise.

The story so far: we need to calculate:
$$\int_b^a r^3 \sqrt {(a - r) (r - b)} \, \mathrm d r$$

where $a$ and $b$ are outer and inner radii respectively of the torus.

Specifically, I am using Euler's 3rd substitution, and I am having trouble resolving the limits.

Euler's third substitution is a technique for evaluating primitives of the form:
$$R (x, \sqrt {a x^2 + b x + c} ) \, \mathrm d x$$

where $R$ is a rational function of $x$ and $\sqrt {a x^2 + b x + c}$, and $a x^2 + b x + c$ can conveniently be expressed in the form $a (x - \alpha) (x - \beta)$.

Euler's third substitution is the substitution:

$(1): \qquad \sqrt {a (x - \alpha) (x - \beta)} = (x - \alpha) t$

In this case, setting $a \gets -1$, $\alpha \gets a$, $\beta \gets b$ we find ourselves with:

$$r = \dfrac {b + a t^2} {1 + t^2}$$

$$\dfrac {\mathrm d r} {\mathrm d t} = \dfrac {2 (a - b) t} {(1 + t^2)^2}$$

and to calculate $\sqrt {(a - r) (r - b)}$ in terms of $t$ we can use $(1)$ to get:

$(2): \qquad \sqrt {(a - r) (r - b) } = \sqrt {-(r - a) (r - b) } = (r - a) t = \left({\dfrac {b + a t^2} {1 + t^2} - a}\right) t = \dfrac {(b - a) t} {1 + t^2}$

Or, by directly substituting for $r$:
[truncated]

Answer A:
Your question is somewhat trippy because $0<b<a$ but this is more of Schaum's bad choice than yours, so I will follow accordingly.

The offending radical is $\sqrt{\left(r-b\right)\left(a-r\right)}$, where your way of writing, and mine, both make it clear that in your integration region, namely $\int_b^a$, it is clear that the stuff under the radical is $\in\mathbb R^+_0$ and so the square root is the simple one, giving $\mathbb R^+_0$ output.

This is actually not always trivial. I mean, it is very possible, say, we want to use the tricks of complex analysis, and thereby explicitly choose for the square root branch cut to be taken exactly along $(b,a)$ as the real number line, and this crazy looking choice opens up the ability of swapping this integral for picking up the residues everywhere else in the complex plane, which might often be easier to do.

But, at least from the perspective of physics, you may always know in advance that your smaller root is $r=b$ and the radical becomes positive in-between the two roots.
Now, let us pick a slightly different form of the Euler substitution
$$
\begin{align}
\tag4\sqrt{\left(r-b\right)\left(a-r\right)}&=(a-r)t\\
\tag5\sqrt{\frac{r-b}{a-r}}&=t\\
\tag6\frac{a-b}{a-r}-1&=t^2\\
\frac{a-b}{1+t^2}&=a-r\qquad\text{sub into Eq. (4)}\\
\tag7r&=a-\frac{a-b}{1+t^2}=\frac{b+at^2}{1+t^2}\\
\tag8\frac{\mathrm dr}{\mathrm dt}&=2t\frac{a-b}{\left(1+t^2\right)^2}
\end  {align}
$$
There are many niceness to this choice: From Equation (7), we see that $(t,r)=(0,b)$ and $(t,r)=(+\infty,a)$ is also awarded internal self-consistency with a positive derivative in Equation (8). This means that we have never flipped the sign of the path of integration, and kept everything clearly non-negative along the way. There is then no need to fret about signs, somewhat mechanically we can directly assert that
[truncated]

Answer B:
If I understand it correctly, you are using
$$ \sqrt{(a-r) (r-b)} = (r-a)t.$$
Solving for $t$:
$$ t = \frac{\sqrt{(a-r) (r-b)}}{(r-a)} = \frac{\sqrt{(a-r) (r-b)}}{-(a-r)} = - \frac{\sqrt{ r-b}}{\sqrt{a-r}}. $$
It's best to write this way because $b \leq r \leq a$ in your problem, thus we can see clearly that $t$ must be negative:
$$ r \to a^- \implies t\to -\infty $$
$$ r \to b^+ \implies t\to 0^- $$

So the problem is that to obtain (3) you assumed the positive square-root of $t^2$ was $t$, when in fact it is $-t$:
$$ \sqrt{\frac{(a-b)^2 t^2}{(1+t^2)^2}} = \left | \frac{(a-b) t}{(1+t^2)} \right | = \frac{(a-b) (-t)}{1+t^2} = \frac{(b-a) t}{1+t^2},$$
which is the same you got with (2).

Edit

Some further details. With this (correct) substitution you get
$$ I := \int_b^a r^3 \sqrt{(a-r)(r-b)} dr = -2(a-b)^2 \int_0^{-\infty}   \frac{t^2 (b+at^2)^3}{(1+t^2)^6} dt.$$
You can flip the sign and the limits of integration:
$$ I = 2(a-b)^2 \int_{-\infty}^{0}   \frac{t^2 (b+at^2)^3}{(1+t^2)^6} dt.$$
Finally, notice the integrand is even, thus $\int_{-\infty}^0 f(t) dt = \int_0^{+\infty} f(t) dt$:
$$ I =  2(a-b)^2 \int_{0}^{+\infty}   \frac{t^2 (b+at^2)^3}{(1+t^2)^6} dt,$$
which is what you had (the errors in the limits of integration and the sign of $t$ cancelled out in the end). So you can proceed as you did to get the final answer.

Title: When History Overrides Intent: Relational Schema Lock-In in Human-LLM Interaction

Abstract:
Long-context interaction and persistent memory allow LLM assistants to develop history-grounded understandings of users. When users change direction, however, an understanding built through earlier exchanges may conflict with their current instruction. We introduce relational schema lock-in to describe cases in which an assistant grants that accumulated understanding authority to override the current instruction without user authorization for the intervention. Study 1 documents reports of AI assistants using prior interactions to question or alter requested actions. Study 2 reproduces the pattern across controlled histories and six models: models retained history-grounded positions but differed in whether and how those positions shaped task execution. In Study 3 with 360 participants, artifact substitution preserved task completion while reducing faithful enactment: 75.0% sent the AI's suspension letter, including 11 participants who reported cancellation as their final stated intent. Overt resistance reduced task completion while leaving sent artifacts faithful.

Site: Travel Stack Exchange
Title: Does Ontario offer a province-wide library card, like British Columbia’s One Card?
Tags: ontario

Question:
I have a library card from Windsor Public Library, my home public library, across the border from Detroit. I am presently traveling to eastern and northern Ontario, well beyond commuting distance from my home! I need to use the libraries in person in my Ontario destinations. Does Ontario proffer something like BC’s One Card program, a provincial “library card to access and borrow material from any participating public library in the province?”

A library card from your home public library opens the door to public libraries wherever you travel – or stay – in British Columbia.

Libraries across BC are participating in the BC OneCard program, which offers access to materials at other libraries across the region. If the library you’re visiting participates in the BC OneCard, you can obtain a free decal by showing them your valid library card along with identification with proof of your current address. Materials borrowed can be returned to that library or any other participating
OneCard library in the province, including your own public library.

Answer A:
Hamilton allows borrowing by regional systems (southwestern Ontario, west of Toronto but not going as far as Windsor/Sarnia/etc.); non-resident cards are $100/year. (I don't know if the borrowing privileges are reciprocal, i.e. whether HPL cardholders can borrow from Waterloo/Burlington/etc. etc. — seems likely, but you'd have to look it up on each library's system ... ??)

https://www.hpl.ca/librarycard

Answer B:
No, there is no such card. However there are a number of ways of using local Ontario libraries without such a card.

The first is Reciprocal Borrowing. It's the easiest, but probably least useful to you. Most libraries allow borrowing by anyone with cards from neighbouring libraries. For example Peterborough (Ontario) allows anyone with cards from Cavan Monaghan, Douro-Dummer, Kawartha Lakes, Otonabee-South Monaghan, North Kawartha, Selwyn, or Trent Lakes to use the Peterborough libraries. This may not seem a lot of use to you, but it can be if you combine it with the next approach.

The second way is Out of Town Memberships. This allows those who do not live in the area to get a library card as if they did. It usually requires the payment of a small fee. For example Peterborough charges $25 for a 3 month membership, no matter where you live. Longer memberships are available. Of course if you are travelling to many places this might involve some expense.

Site: Electronics Stack Exchange
Title: 1 gigaohm / 10 M internal Impedance and voltage
Tags: voltage, voltage-measurement, input-impedance

Question:
As part of corrosion measurements, I measure voltages formed on metals in solution using a reference electrode. As part of checking reference electrodes I need to measure the voltage at 10 MΩ and 1 GΩ internal impedance. Most manufacturers don’t easily include this information, so buying one is tricky. If I stick a 1 GΩ resistor in series with a 10 MΩ impedance resistor do I get the same effect?

Answer A:
An easy way to measure the voltage with a standard digital VOM is to use a voltage divider. If you are dealing with several hundred millivolts, and the meter goes down to .1 mV or .05 mV (many do) and has a 10 MΩ input impedance, then a 1000:1 divider will do the trick. Connect a 1m resistor in parallel with the meter, and then connect a 1 GΩ resistor between the source and the meter. Calibrate the meter and divider using a known voltage (a standard AAA cell will do, you can measure it directly to verify the voltage, usually near 1.5 V). See what the meter reads with the divider in place (on the most sensitive scale) and determine the correct multiplier to get the actual battery voltage. You now have a fairly straightforward way to measure the voltage with a 1 GΩ effective input impedance. If you need greater sensitivity, increase the parallel resistor to 2 MΩ or even 4.7 MΩ, and re-calibrate. This should give you more significant digits. And, by actually doing the calibration, you compensate for the meter's input impedance.

Answer B:
If I stick a 1gihaohm resistor in series with a 10Mohm impedance resistor do I get the same effect?

It depends what you also have in parallel to that to actually measure the voltage.

If it's a very high impedance buffer amplifier, CMOS perhaps, then you may be OK. Check its specifications for bias current.

If it's the input of a standard 10 MΩ meter, then unfortunately not. The 1 GΩ resistor will form a potential divider with it and you'll read 1/100th of the voltage.

Title: Conformal ordering: Distribution-free predictive inference for orders and ranks

Abstract:
We study distribution-free predictive inference for the ordering and ranking of multiple unobserved outcomes. Although numerous methods, such as conformal prediction, have been developed for prediction and predictive inference of unobserved outcomes, extending them to provide inference for the ordering of multiple outcomes with an interpretable guarantee is not straightforward. To this end, we develop a framework and methodology for uncertainty quantification in predictive ordering. Our approach begins by reformulating the problem of determining an ordering among multiple objects as a graph inference problem. Our method adopts a multiple-testing-inspired approach and constructs an uncertainty graph, where each edge represents a confidently inferred pairwise ordering. We develop a distribution-free procedure for constructing a consistent uncertainty graph while controlling either the family-wise error rate or the false discovery rate. Moreover, we show that the resulting graphs naturally yield risk-controlling prediction intervals for the ranks of the outcomes. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed procedure achieves the target guarantees tightly while maintaining reasonable power and prediction-interval widths.

Title: Identification through Heteroskedasticity in One Lemma: Partial Identification, an Eigenvalue Construction, and a Caution on Rank Tests

Abstract:
This teaching note unifies known results on identification through heteroskedasticity, under volatility regimes, GARCH, stochastic volatility and covariate-driven variances, in one lemma with a short linear-algebra proof. A shock is identified up to sign and labelling if and only if no other shock shares its variance path, and shocks that share a path are identified up to a rotation. The rows of the structural coefficient matrix solve one generalised eigenvalue problem that nests Rigobon's (2003) two-regime solution. Rank tests on second moments of the errors count at most linearly independent centred variance paths, not identified shocks. A simulation illustrates each point.

Title: Does the infinite product ∏(1 - λ₀/(1 + i/τ)) converge to a value strictly less than 1?
Tags: probability, convergence

Question:
I'm a non-mathematician writing an essay using a rate-based compound probability model. I've tried my best, but I have specific questions about whether the math holds.

Setup. Per-attempt catastrophe risk decays as

$$\lambda_i = \frac{\lambda_0}{1 + i/\tau}$$

with $\lambda_0$ a starting per-attempt risk and $\tau$ a "safety progress" timescale. Cumulative probability over $N$ attempts is

$$P_N = 1 - \prod_{i=0}^{N-1}\left(1 - \frac{\lambda_0}{1 + i/\tau}\right).$$

Numerical check. Cumulative probability $P_N$ at three parameter combinations:

$\lambda_0 \tau$
$N = 10^3$
$N = 10^4$
$N = 10^6$
$N = 10^9$

$0.001$
$0.0049$
$0.0067$
$0.0115$
$0.0183$

$0.1$
$0.2107$
$0.3539$
$0.6021$
$0.8006$

$1.0$
$0.9117$
$0.9886$
$0.9999$
$\approx 1$

Questions:

Is $P_N = 1 - \prod_{i=0}^{N-1}(1 - \lambda_i)$ the correct expression for cumulative catastrophe probability when each $\lambda_i$ is an independent per-attempt risk? Are there standard mistakes to watch for when using this with non-constant $\lambda_i$?

Does $P_\infty = \lim_{N \to \infty} P_N$ equal $1$, or strictly less than $1$? My intuition: $\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \lambda_i \sim \lambda_0 \tau \log(N/\tau)$ diverges (harmonically), so $\prod(1 - \lambda_i) \to 0$ and $P_\infty = 1$ — but the convergence is logarithmic, slow enough that $P_N < 0.5$ for any realistic $N$ when $\lambda_0 \tau$ is small. Is that correct?

Is there a closed-form or clean approximation for the threshold on $\lambda_0 \tau$ below which $P_N < 0.5$ holds for $N \le N_{\max}$? Back-of-envelope: roughly $\lambda_0 \tau \log(N_{\max}/\tau) < \log 2$.

Is this decaying-rate failure model standard in any field (reliability theory, aging processes, hazard analysis)? I worked it out independently but suspect it exists in the literature.

I'm happy to post the full essay & charts if useful. But I mostly want to make sure my math holds up.

Wiki: English Wikipedia
Draft: SCADS (Shipborne Containerized Air Defense System)

Draft text:
SCADS, or Shipborne Containerized Air Defense Systems, are a class of air defense systems. Typically composed of small, mobile modules of radar, command, and fire elements disguised within international standard intermodal containers, they are intended to be placed upon merchant ships being urgently pressed into military service at the outbreak of a conflict.

== Examples ==
After the conclusion of Falklands War in 1982, the British government investigated a SCAD system for their ships. The dramatic loss of the unarmed SS Atlantic Conveyer to Argentine Exocets demonstrated the need for self defense systems upon the ships of the STUFTS (Ships Taken Up From Trade) program. The British SCADS system was split between two concepts; SCADS A, which was to use a set of containers to convert the merchant ships to small anti submarine aircraft carriers (Similar to the join Anglo-American Arapaho Containerized Aircraft Handling System), and SCADS B, which would integrate vertical launch anti air and anti submarine systems, such as Seawolf and Ikara, along with ECM, chaff, and flares. [ref: SCADS A AND B - TWO VERSIONS FOR THE ASSIGNMENT OF PART OF THE LOAD TO WEAPONS SYSTEMS ON CONTAINERSHIPS, British Maritime Technology] [ref: This Containerized Missile Launcher Could Give Almost Any Ship Short-Range Air Defenses, The War Zone]

In the early 2000s, the United States Navy investigated the Affordable Weapon System, a containerized cruise missile similar to a miniaturized Tomahawk to be launched from standardized containers, however the project seems to have been cancelled during the budget cuts and cancellations of 2007-2008 as any information on the project past that point is scarce. [ref: ONR/Titan Affordable Weapon, www.designation-systems.net]

In early 2019, MBDA revealed SPIMM (Self-Protection Integrated Mistral Module), a small containerized system using their Mistral heat seeking MANPAD, which was derived from the existing SIMBAD-RC naval mounting for the missile. SPIMM is intended to be used aboard auxiliary ships. SPIMM will carry two missiles read for immediate fire, along with four more in a storage container which can be used to rearm the module. The system will be able to track and fire upon targets in any direction using 360 degree panoramic infrared cameras. Designed to fit within a 10 foot intermodal container, SPIMM only needs a place to be mounted and an electrical connection to the host ship to operate. The Mistral missile's 4 mile range limits its capabilities, however the system adds a useful layer of defense to otherwise large, undefended targets. It has the ability to be used against aerial or surface targets. MBDA is also investigating the possibility of using SPIMM in land mountings.

In October of 2020, at the Euronaval 2020 expo, Danish defense manufacturer SH Defence revealed their modular shipborne equipment system, The Cube. The Cube is intended to use more than 128 interchangeable modules to allow ships with the system to engage in air, surface, and submarine warfare, or perform other tasks such as search and rescue or delivering humanitarian aid. The system requires internal rails running through spaces within a ship to move the modules through the hull of a ship to perform their missions from various spaces. [ref: Euronaval Video: SH Defence Unveils Cutting Edge Equipment 'The Cube', Naval News] [ref: The Cube – SH Defence]

In 2023, the United States Navy test fired an RIM-174/SM-6 surface to air missile from a Mark 70 Payload Delivery System mounted on the flight deck of the Independence class littoral combat ship USS Savannah, significantly advancing the firepower of the littoral combat ships, which have been criticized for lacking in firepower. The Mark 70 system is also able to fire Tomahawk cruise missiles and Patriot PAC-3 land based surface to air missiles [ref: PAC-3 MSE launched from virtual Aegis ship hits cruise missile target, Defense News]. The Navy had previously used the Mark 70 system to fire another RIM-174/SM-6 from the unmanned vessel USV Ranger [ref: This "Ghost Fleet" Ship Firing An SM-6 Missile From A Modular Launcher Is A Glimpse Of The Future, TWZ]. The Mark 70 system is a naval variant of the US Army's Typhon Missile System, both of which are descended from the navy's Mark 41 Vertical Launch System [ref: SM-6 Missile Fired From Littoral Combat Ship, TWZ].

Title: LesionStudio: A Patient-Informed Platform for Task-Specific Optimization of Emission Tomography Reconstruction and Analysis

Abstract:
Purpose: For task-specific PET and SPECT reconstruction optimization, we developed LesionStudio, an open-source platform incorporating patient background heterogeneity, realistic lesion morphology and texture, and lesion-background interactions beyond conventional phantoms. Methods: LesionStudio, a Python framework built on PyTomography, inserts lesions into PET/SPECT data using modality-specific forward projection and stochastic background ablation. Clinical realism was evaluated by physician review of 30 inserted lesions in eight DLBCL patients from a 1,579-lesion FDG lymphoma library. Quantification and detectability were assessed in FDG PET using spherical and patient-derived lesions varying in size, LBR, and site, reconstructed with OSEM and BSREM. Results: Inserted lesions were visually indistinguishable from true disease (AUC = 0.49). OSEM improved the patient-derived quantification limit from ~3.7 mL at iteration 4 to ~2.0 mL at iteration 10, but with increased noise and edge artifacts. Weakly regularized BSREM (beta = 5) achieved a similar ~2.0 mL limit with stability, whereas stronger regularization increased under-recovery. Detectability was contrast-dependent: no lesions were detected at LBR 2:1, whereas detectable volume ranged from 0.70 to 3.63 mL at LBR 4:1 and decreased to 0.70 mL at LBR 6:1-8:1 for both OSEM and weakly regularized BSREM. Conclusion: Reconstruction settings can shift SUV metrics and detectability enough to affect interpretation, so no single protocol suits every task. OSEM required early stopping for detection and feature stability but more iterations for mean-SUV quantification, whereas weakly regularized BSREM matched both at one setting. LesionStudio (https://github.com/qurit/LesionStudio), with our public library of realistic lesions, provides a reproducible framework for task-specific optimization across radiopharmaceuticals and scanners.

Title: Coarse-Graining Optimal Transport for Rollout-Free Post-Training of Flow Matching

Abstract:
Flow matching depends critically on the coupling used to pair source and target samples. Optimal transport (OT) couplings can reduce velocity conflict and straighten trajectories; but, in practice, challenges remain: the source comes from a continuous distribution, only a finite number of target samples data are accessible, and the neural network has finite capacity. For these reasons, making the coupling more OT-like may not consistently improve sampling quality, in particular in the low number-of-function-evaluation (NFE) regime. Motivated by this, we introduce ReCouple, a controllable framework that constructs coarse-grained OT couplings, to better understand rollout-free OT-based post-training. We also consider extensions of this basic framework: ReCouple+ extends this toward the continuous-source setting by increasing source resolution, converging to semi-discrete OT in the appropriate limit; and ReCouple++ further adds spatial regularization, motivated by the observation that straight trajectories need not correspond to spatially simple velocity fields. Empirical validation demonstrates the effectiveness of these methods, and it reveals an NFE-dependent interplay between coupling optimality, neural realizability, and generation quality.

Wiki: English Wikipedia
Draft: TriTopic

Draft text:
TriTopic is an open-source method and Python library for topic modeling of text collections. It was introduced by Roman Egger in 2026. [ref: TriTopic: Tri-Modal Graph-Based Topic Modeling with Iterative Refinement and Archetypes] The method combines semantic text representations based on sentence embeddings with lexical information from tf–idf weighting and, optionally, document metadata in a single document graph. Topics are then identified through repeated graph-based community detection and consensus clustering. [ref: TriTopic – Graph-Based Topic Modeling, SmartVisions]

== Background ==
Topic modeling aims to discover recurring themes in large collections of text. Classical approaches include latent semantic analysis, non-negative matrix factorization and latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA). [ref: Applied Data Science in Tourism: Interdisciplinary Approaches, Methodologies, and Applications, Springer] More recent methods such as BERTopic and Top2Vec cluster documents based on transformer-based text embeddings. [ref: A Topic Modeling Comparison Between LDA, NMF, Top2Vec, and BERTopic to Demystify Twitter Posts, Frontiers in Sociology]

TriTopic belongs to the embedding- and graph-based approaches. Unlike probabilistic models such as LDA, it does not rely on a generative model but represents similarities between documents as a graph. The original publication motivates the method with three limitations it attributes to existing embedding-based approaches: results that vary between runs, a loss of lexical precision, and reliance on a single view of the data.

== Method ==

=== Document representations ===
Documents are first encoded with a sentence embedding model, and the dimensionality of the embeddings is reduced with UMAP. In addition, a lexical representation based on tf–idf captures the actual vocabulary used. Optionally, metadata such as source or date can be included; according to the documentation, metadata only strengthens links between documents that are already similar in content and does not create new ones.

=== Graph construction ===
The representations are fused into a weighted document graph in which documents are nodes and similarities are edges. Neighbourhoods are determined using mutual k-nearest neighbors and shared nearest neighbors, and links that appear in more than one view receive a higher weight.

=== Consensus clustering ===
Communities in the graph are detected with the Leiden algorithm. [ref: From Louvain to Leiden: guaranteeing well-connected communities, Scientific Reports] Because the result depends on random initialisation, TriTopic runs the clustering several times and builds a consensus graph in which document pairs that are frequently assigned to the same community receive stronger links. This is intended to make the results more reproducible.

=== Number of topics and refinement ===
The number of topics can be specified or determined automatically. In automatic mode, several resolution parameters are tested and compared by the coherence of the resulting keywords. The document representations are then iteratively moved towards the centre of their topic and re-clustered until consecutive partitions agree.

=== Topic representation ===
Topics are described by characteristic keywords and representative documents; keyword selection takes into account both how frequent a term is within a topic and how many of the topic's documents contain it. The publication also describes an archetype-based topic representation that considers boundary cases in addition to central documents. Unlike density-based clustering methods such as HDBSCAN, every document is assigned to a topic.

== Further features ==
The library supports partially guided topic modeling, in which known categories are supplied as seed topics while further topics can still emerge from the data. It also provides functions for analysing how topics change over time, hierarchical topic structures, and analysis tools aimed at empirical research, such as topic stability under resampling, thematic saturation and group comparisons.

Large language models are not required to form the topics. They can optionally be used after clustering to name and describe topics.

== Evaluation ==
In the original publication, TriTopic was compared with LDA, non-negative matrix factorization and BERTopic on the 20 Newsgroups, BBC News, AG News and arXiv datasets. The author reports a mean normalized mutual information (NMI) of 0.575 for TriTopic, compared with 0.513 for BERTopic, 0.416 for NMF and 0.299 for LDA. No independent comparative evaluations have been published so far.

== Applications and limitations ==
The documentation lists open-ended survey responses, interviews, customer reviews, news articles, social media posts and support tickets as typical applications, for collections ranging from a few hundred to tens of thousands of texts. It describes the method as less suitable for very short text snippets, for long documents covering many themes (which should be split into sections first) and for corpora of millions of documents.

== See also ==
* Text mining
* Natural language processing

Site: Physics Stack Exchange
Title: What does standard cosmology actually mean by "the singularity" - and can we meaningfully speak of a "pre-Big Bang epoch"?
Tags: cosmology, spacetime, time, big-bang, singularities

Question:
I understand that in standard cosmology, asking “what happened before the Big Bang” is usually dismissed as meaningless, since time itself is part of spacetime and is said to begin at the Big Bang.

However, this seems to leave an unresolved tension in how the singularity itself is treated.

On the one hand, the Big Bang singularity is often described using physical language: infinite density, infinite temperature, vanishing volume. In both pedagogical and semi-technical contexts, it is frequently spoken of as if it were a state or limit-state of the universe.

On the other hand, if time does not yet exist, it is unclear in what sense such a “state” could be said to exist at all. A physical state normally presupposes temporal applicability: something that obtains, even if only in an idealized or limiting sense.

This leads to a deeper conceptual dilemma that I don’t see clearly resolved:

• Either the singularity has some kind of physical or ontological status, in which case describing it as “non-temporal” seems problematic.

• Or the singularity has no physical status at all and merely signals a breakdown of the classical description, in which case much of the language surrounding it (state, properties, epoch) appears misleading.

My question is therefore not about “what came before,” but about what we are actually committed to when we keep the singularity in our models and explanations.

Is the Big Bang singularity meant to be taken as a physically meaningful limit, or as a purely formal boundary of applicability? And if it is only the latter, should we reconsider how confidently we speak about time, spacetime, and their “beginning” as physically well-defined concepts?

I’m trying to understand whether standard cosmology has a coherent position here, or whether the singularity marks a deeper conceptual inconsistency that is often glossed over in practice.
