Draft text:
Jordan Zietz is an entrepreneur and the co-founder and CEO of LemonLime, a San Francisco-based artificial intelligence startup. [ref: LemonLime, Y Combinator] [ref: AI Startup Apologizes for Offering Job Interviews in Exchange for Company Tattoos, The Wall Street Journal] A 2024 graduate of Stanford University, he drew criticism in July 2026 after promoting an offer of job interviews to party guests who got LemonLime tattoos. [ref: Tech CEO in hot mess over tattoo-for-job-interview tit for tat, USA Today]

Before LemonLime, Zietz gained national attention as the 44th Stanford Tree, the university's unofficial mascot, a role from which he was suspended in 2022 for displaying a banner that read "Stanford Hates Fun" on the field during a football game. [ref: ‘Stanford Hates Fun’: Students Revolt After Tree Mascot Suspension, The Wall Street Journal] [ref: Stanford student suspended from serving as Tree mascot, ESPN; Stanford Tree mascot suspended for holding 'Stanford hates fun' sign during game, CBS Sports; Stanford's beloved tree mascot suspended for antics taking place during Arizona State game, Sports Illustrated] His other prior ventures include founding GameReef and All-Star eSports League, and co-founding the social app Confetti. [ref: Jordan Zietz is solving the problem plaguing gamers nationwide, Kidpreneurs] [ref: Competing for College: South Florida high school senior creates esports league for students to earn scholarships, WSVN] [ref: A Startup Offered Job Interviews to Anyone Willing to Get Its Logo Tattooed. 7 People Took the Deal, Inc.]

== Early life and education ==
Zietz is a Florida native and attended Pine Crest School. [ref: Business Spotlight: Eau Resort & Spa managers give their best for Habitat, The Coastal Star] He studied management science and engineering at Stanford University, receiving a Bachelor of Science degree in 2024. [ref: 134th Commencement: List of Conferred Degrees and Degree Candidates, Stanford University] [ref: CEO apologizes for offering interviews to people who got tattoos of his AI company logo, San Francisco Chronicle] From 2021 to 2024, he was a member of the editorial board of The Stanford Flipside, a student satirical newspaper. [ref: Staff, The Stanford Flipside] In April 2023, he appeared as a contestant on Wheel of Fortune, representing Stanford during the show's College Week Spring Break episodes. [ref: College Week Spring Break 4]

=== Stanford Tree ===

During the 2022–23 academic year, Zietz served as the 44th Stanford Tree, the official mascot of the Leland Stanford Junior University Marching Band and the unofficial mascot of the university. [ref: Stanford Tree gets the axe, suspended until January, The Stanford Daily] [ref: Meet the sapling: Bravery and new beginnings with Emily Rodriguez ’26, the 45th Stanford Tree, The Stanford Daily]

On October 22, 2022, during the Stanford University football game against Arizona State, Zietz and three other students, including Arizona State's mascot, carried a 40-foot banner across the field which read "Stanford Hates Fun". [ref: Inside “Stanford’s War On Fun”: Tensions mount over University’s handling of social life, The Stanford Daily] The slogan referred to student complaints about the university administration's handling of social life.

Following the stunt, the band's executive committee suspended Zietz from the role. The committee said the decision concerned his use of the position "for personal benefit" and was unrelated to the banner's message.

A student-led campaign protested Zietz's suspension and the university's social-life policies at the November 5 football game against Washington State, including the creation of a petition calling for Zietz's reinstatement which attracted over 700 signatures. [ref: ‘Stanford Hates Fun’ protests campus social life restrictions during football game, The Stanford Daily]

In 2023, Zietz judged auditions for the role and selected Emily Rodriguez as his successor.

== Career ==

=== Early businesses ===
Zietz started his first business, GameReef, through a Young Entrepreneurs Academy program supported by the Boca Raton Chamber of Commerce. Abstract:

Site: Physics Stack Exchange
Title: Parametrization of a straight line in 3D for electrostatics (Zangwill problem 3.21)
Tags: electrostatics, vectors, integration

Question:
I am working on a problem from Modern Electrodynamics by Zangwill and I'm having trouble understanding why my approach does not yield the correct solution. The problem:

I attempted an approach which deviates from what the author suggests doing.

I start from the general definition of the potential:

$ \phi(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \int d^3r' \frac{\rho(\mathbf{r'})}{|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r'}|}$

Then, I use the fact that the density is nonzero only along the segment PP', and the following parametrization:

$\mathbf{r'}(s') = \mathbf{r} + \mathbf{c} + s'\mathbf{a}$

to turn the integral into:

$ \phi(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\lambda}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \int_0^1 \frac{ds'}{|\mathbf{c}+s'\mathbf{a}|}$

Then, the integral becomes:

$ \int_0^1 \frac{ds'}{\sqrt{c^2 + 2s'\mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{a} + s'^2a^2}}$

which after some steps evaluates to:

$ \ln(\frac{c - \mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{a}/a}{\sqrt{c^2+a^2+2\mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{a}} - \mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{a}/a - a})$

I have verified numerically that the expression above does not match the expected answer.

I suspect that my parametrization of $\mathbf{r'}$ is invalid, but I can't see why. I would appreciate anyone who could point out my mistake.

Title: Harborth's theorem p(5)=18 revisited

Abstract:
Let $p(n)$ be the minimum cardinality of a finite planar point set in which each point has exactly $n$ unit-distance neighbours. Harborth proved $p(5)=18$ in work presented in 1985 and published in 1987, using a detailed case analysis. We revisit the proof using convex-hull arguments, incidence counts, and elementary properties of intersections of unit circles. These tools give an alternative treatment of configurations with $14$ and $16$ points and organize the final case distinction by a common vector-sum structure. We also treat a configuration not explicitly covered by the case analysis in the online PDF copy of Harborth's paper available to us, and give an explicit justification of the six-point classification used in the argument. No result subsequent to Harborth's proof is required.

state.text:
Title: Graphical Models Induced by Irreversible Event Accumulation on Trees

Abstract:
Decomposable graphical models are usually adopted for their computational convenience rather than derived from a data-generating mechanism. We show that a special class of them arises naturally from the irreversible accumulation of events along a branching history. Each event is attached to an edge of a latent rooted tree and is inherited by everything below that edge; an observation records which events have occurred at a randomly chosen node, not necessarily a leaf. When the tree is a path, this is the cumulative coding of an ordinal variable, whose indicators form a Markov chain; in the general tree case the Markov chain is replaced by a junction tree. The conditional independence graph of the event indicators is always decomposable and, in fact, is the line graph of the tree (maximal cliques correspond to nodes where two or more edges meet and separators are the single events on the edges joining two such nodes). The graph determines the tree up to the choice of root. A connected graph arises in this way if, and only if, it is chordal, any two of its maximal cliques share at most one vertex, no vertex is in three maximal cliques, and the graph is such that any two maximal cliques share at most one vertex. This provides a simple graphical test for compatibility with the mechanism (necessary but not sufficient, as irreversibility also constrains the distribution's support). The structure breaks down if we look at just the leaves, and measurement error destroys the exact screening and leads to a denser graph rather than simply a weaker dependence. We discuss inference, provide diagnostics for departures such as recurrent events, illustrate them on some simulated data and discuss their application in the context of mutation accumulation and lineage tracing where both ancestral and descendant types are sampled together.

Title: Dual Area-Volume-of-Fluid (DAVOF): co-advecting volume and face-area fractions for a closed-form, cell-local interface normal and position on unstructured meshes

Abstract:
Geometric Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) on unstructured polyhedral meshes reconstructs the interface orientation from the volume fractions of a stencil of neighbours; on irregular cells and in the presence of wisps it degrades, and the curvature built on it drives the parasitic currents of capillary flows. We transport, consistently to the volume fraction of every cell, the wetted fraction of every face area. From the area and volume fractions, closed-form equations recover the interface normal and position of a cell, for the first time in VOF: the normal from one sum over the cell's own faces, the divergence theorem on the liquid sub-volume, and the plane's position from a second, without neighbours or iteration. Both identities are exact for a plane on hexahedral, perturbed and polyhedral cells. On a sphere and an ellipsoid the normal has the order of the face fractions, the position is second order for every state and mesh, and a quadric through one ring of recovered normals gives a converging curvature where the reference models show none. Transported with the plane clipping, the ring normal, the same identity on the union of the cell's ring, stabilises the state and carries a sphere over 3.3 diameters bounded and conservative, first order in the face fractions as the clipping law predicts, at plicRDF's position and shape errors. A preliminary transport implementation with one paraboloid per cell, its frame from the normal, its curvature tensor from the ring and its position from the volume fraction, carries the sphere bounded and conservative over the resolution ladder with face fractions of order 2.8 per period with the exact normal and 2.1 with the ring quadric's normal over N = 32 to 128. The loop has the order of the normal it is fed; a transported normal of second order is the research goal. This document is the basis on which the further development of the method is documented.

Title: Passive Identification of Unequal Phase Grid Impedances by Phase-Domain Source Cancellation

Abstract:
Passive grid impedance estimators that return a single resistance--inductance pair cannot represent a grid whose phase impedances are unequal. This paper identifies a separate pair for each phase from recorded point-of-common-coupling (PCC) voltage and current without injected perturbations. In each phase, the unknown grid-source voltage is cancelled by a periodic difference (PD) or by a second-order-generalized-integrator notch difference (SOGID), and moving-window integration (MWI) replaces the current derivative by an integral and an endpoint feature. The resulting two-parameter regression requires a period or notch-frequency estimate but no phase-locked-loop angle. A voltage-balance analysis gives the source residual left by frequency mismatch and bounds the parameter error by the ratio of this residual to the conditioning of the two features. In the unequal-phase interval (8.3--9.8~s) of a 10-s EMTP grid-forming record, SOGID-MWI attains phase-averaged R/L errors of 5.09/0.33\%; a shared value has a minimum error of 41.67\% for the phase ratio 1:0.5:2. On a 50-s constant-impedance grid-following record, the errors are 0.56/0.06\% over the 20--30-s synchronization disturbance. In a controlled 40-dB noise study, a noise-referenced update rule reduces the white-noise GFL error from 55.9/65.0\% to 12.3/11.5\%.

Title: Learning nuclear mass systematics with hybrid quantum-classical mixtures of experts

Abstract:
We introduce a mixture-of-experts framework combining sixteen hybrid quantum-classical neural networks with nucleus-dependent classical gating to learn residual corrections to the WS4 nuclear mass model. On a fixed AME2020 test set, the framework reduces the root-mean-square error from 456.22 to 179.83 keV and outperforms a parameter-matched classical counterpart. The learned corrections improve shell-gap systematics near the Sn and Pb shell closures, while analysis of the gating networks identifies shell-related descriptors as the leading inputs. For 66Ca, the model predicts Sn = 0.577 MeV and S2n = -0.252 MeV, allowing two-neutron emission while the one-neutron channel remains closed.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: Is a pull-back a contravariant functor?
Tags: differential-geometry, manifolds, smooth-manifolds, functors, pullback

Question:
I am reading through "Analysis, Manifolds and Physics", and I've gotten to page 116 where pullbacks are introduced for differentiable manifolds. They introduce the idea of the pull back of a mapping $g$ under $f$, as $f^*g=g\circ f$, and then they say we have here an example of a contravariant functor. Specifically, if $X,Y,Z$ are differentiable manifolds, $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$ are differentiable mappings, $E,F,G$ are vector spaces of functions defined on $X,Y,Z$ and:$$\begin{align}
C(X)&=E\quad C(Y)=F\quad C(Z)=G \\
C(f)&=f^*:F\to E\quad \text{by} \quad f^*h=h\circ f \\
C(g)&=g^*:G\to F\quad \text{by} \quad g^*k=k\circ g
\end{align}$$

Then C is a contravariant functor:
$$(g\circ f)^*:G\to E\quad \text{by} \quad (g\circ f)^*k=k\circ g\circ f$$.

I am confused by what exactly is being done here. It doesn't specify what $h$ and $k$ are, so I am unsure whether they are functions on the Manifolds (and if so what their codomain is ), or mappings between them. I am also unsure what $C$ is and what it does to the manifolds, and why it acts on the way it does on the mappings $f,g$. Finally, I don't get how the final result shows that $C$ is a contravariant functor, since my understanding is a contravariant functor should reverse the order of composition. Any clarification would be welcome.

Answer A:
Let's just do a special example: let $C(X) = \mathscr{C}^\infty(X)$ denote the (real) vector space of smooth functions from $f:X\to \mathbf{R}$. The claim is that we have a (contravariant) functor from the category of smooth manifolds $\mathbf{Man}_\infty$ to the category of vector spaces over $\mathbf{R}$, denoted $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathbf{R}}$, defined on objects as $X\mapsto \mathscr{C}^\infty(X)$ and on morphisms $f:X\to Y$ as $f^*:\mathscr{C}^\infty(Y)\to \mathscr{C}^\infty(X)$.

Note that this is well-defined, since if $\varphi \in \mathscr{C}^\infty(Y)$, then $f^*(\varphi) = \varphi \circ f:X\to Y\to \mathbf{R}$ and is smooth, being a composite of smooth maps. Furthermore, $f^*$ is easily shown to be linear.

To verify functoriality, you need to show that the identity $\mathrm{Id}_X$ of an object $X$ is sent to the identity on $\mathscr{C}^\infty(X)$. This is not hard, because for any function $\varphi\in \mathscr{C}^\infty(X)$, we have $\mathrm{Id}_X^*(\varphi) = \varphi \circ \mathrm{Id}_X = \varphi$.

Finally, you have to verify that given a pair of maps $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$ of manifolds and $\varphi \in \mathscr{C}^\infty(Z)$, you have $(f\circ g)^*(\varphi) = g^*(f^*(\varphi))$ – this is the contravariance condition. However, this follows from
$$
[truncated]

Answer B:
Too lengthy for a comment, but probably worth saying at this point. Denote with $ \mathsf{Mfd} $ the category of manifolds and with $ \mathsf{cAlg}(\mathbb R) $ the category of commutative algebras over the real numbers. As the previous answers said, there is a functor
$$
\mathsf{Mfd} \xrightarrow{C^\infty({-})} \mathsf{cAlg}(\mathbb R)^\mathrm{op}
$$
that acts on objects as
$$
M\mapsto C^\infty(M) = \{\text{$ f\colon M\to \mathbb R $ smooth}\}
$$
and on arrows as
$$
\bigl(M\xrightarrow{F} N\bigr)\mapsto \bigl(C^\infty(N)\xrightarrow{F^*} C^\infty(M)\bigr)
$$
i.e., as pullback.

This functor is fully-faithful! This is indeed an easy corollary of the fact that the set map
$$
\lvert M\rvert \to \mathsf{cAlg}(\mathbb R)^\mathrm{op}\bigl(\mathbb R, C^\infty(M)\bigr)
$$
from the underlying set of $ M $ to the set (duals of) of algebra homomorphisms from $ \mathbb R $ to the algebra of smooth functions on $ M $ is bijective (the so-called Milnor's exercise).

The major advantage of embedding the category of manifolds into the category of commutative algebras is the fact that the latter accommodates a far wider range of objects such that the (algebras of formal functions on) "infinitesimal points", such as the algebra of dual numbers $ \mathbb R[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2 $.
[truncated]

Answer C:
For the contravariance, observe that $(g \circ f)^* k = k \circ g \circ f = f^* (k \circ g) = f^* g^* k$. This shows that the order of composition is reversed, since $(g \circ f)^* = f^* \circ g^*$. Of course, in the end you must get back to something involving $g \circ f$, since $f \circ g$ is not well-typed.

== Vissoth Nam ==

is a Cambodian business executive and entrepreneur serving as Chief Executive Officer of AirAsia Cambodia [ref: VISSOTH NAM, AirAsia Newsroom] since its inception in 2022 [ref: Capital A to launch AirAsia Cambodia as it resumes growth, Reuters]. He previously worked in macroeconomic research for the National Bank of Cambodia and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and was named a Young Global Leader [ref: Meet the Young Global Leaders Class of 2026, World Economic Forum] by the World Economic Forum in 2026.

== Early life and education ==
Born in Phnom Penh and raised in France, Vissoth completed his higher education in Paris, studying law and economics at Université Paris-Panthéon-Assas from 2009 to 2012. He subsequently earned a Master’s degree in Management with a specialization in Global Financial Management from ESCEMBusiness School.

== Career ==

=== Economic research ===
Early in his career, Vissoth specialized in central banking and macroeconomic policy. He served as Deputy Section Chief in Economic Research at the National Bank of Cambodia (NBC), focusing on monetary policy, national financial stability, and macroeconomic indicators. He later joined the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as an economist, where he co-authored research analyzing domestic credit growth, banking sector leverage, and financial cycles in Cambodia. [ref: https://www.imf.org/-/media/Files/Countries/ResRep/BGD/2018/032018.ashx]

=== Entrepreneurship and hospitality ===
In 2017, Vissoth transitioned into the private sector, founding Sivilai Asia, a Cambodia-based investment and holding firm focused on hospitality and strategic local ventures [ref: Capital A Forms AirAsia Cambodia As Budget Carrier Seeks New Growth Markets, Forbes]. Through Sivilai Asia, he led development and management projects aimed at elevating Cambodia's regional hospitality and commercial ecosystem.

=== AirAsia Cambodia ===
In December 2022, Capital A (AirAsia Group) partnered with Sivilai Asia in a joint venture to establish AirAsia Cambodia, with Capital A holding a 51% stake and Sivilai Asia holding 49%. As Director of Sivilai Asia, Vissoth was appointed Chief Executive Officer of the new low cost airline.

Under his executive leadership, the airline navigated regulatory approvals with the State Secretariat of Civil Aviation (SSCA), securing its Air Operator Certificate (AOC) in April 2024 [ref: ]. AirAsia Cambodia launched domestic operations on 2 May 2024, connecting Phnom Penh, Siem Reap, and Sihanoukville [ref: AirAsia Cambodia Takes Off!, AirAsia Newsroom], before expanding to international regional routes [ref: AirAsia Cambodia launches first int’l flight to Kuala Lumpur] to boost tourism and economic integration within ASEAN.

=== Recognition ===

- [https://ctb.gov.kh/about-ctb Cambodia Tourism Board] (CTB): Appointed to the Board of Directors in 2026 to advise on national tourism strategy, aviation policy, and destination marketing [ref: Cambodia Tourism Board]

Title: Downlink MU-MIMO for LEO Direct-to-Device: Feasibility, Architecture, and Implementation

Abstract:
Direct-to-device connectivity from low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites is commercially available, but its throughput is limited by the satellite antenna size and by payloads that separate users only by beams and frequency reuse. This article shows that a single LEO satellite with a meter-scale array can serve hundreds of users on the same time-frequency resource through multi-user multiple-input multiple-output precoding. The number of users it can separate with a single stream each, i.e., its spatial degrees of freedom (DoF), follows from the aperture in wavelengths, the orbit altitude, and the minimum elevation angle. With minimum mean-square error (MMSE) precoding, the throughput of these users grows with the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), whereas maximum-ratio transmission becomes interference-limited. The precoder can be computed from the user positions and the satellite ephemeris and attitude, with a throughput loss of less than 0.5\% at 20~dB SNR compared with perfect channel knowledge under the 3GPP non-terrestrial channel models. The DoF also set the number of digital chains of a hybrid payload, and the functional split among satellites and ground trades inter-satellite-link and feeder-link load against on-board processing. As the satellite moves, the precoder can be updated from the known geometry every radio frame, i.e., 10~ms, while the computationally intensive user pairing can be kept for a few seconds with a throughput loss below 1\%. Finally, we keep the cell-specific signals on fixed beams while precoding the user data jointly across all cells of the satellite. For a $50\times50$ array at 600~km and a minimum elevation angle of $60^\circ$, one satellite serves 410 users at 6.1~bps/Hz on average, more than four times the throughput of fixed beams with four-color frequency reuse.

Title: Preference-Conditioned Group-Relative Policy Optimization for Terminally Constrained Multi-Objective Control

Abstract:
Multi-objective optimal control is commonly addressed by reinforcement learning with fixed scalarization weights, requiring a separate training run and constraint enforcement for each trade-off. This letter extends critic-free group-relative policy optimization to terminally constrained multi-objective control: a single preference-conditioned policy is trained over random preferences and returns a feasible approximation of the Pareto front in one run. Three structural results are established. Group normalization after scalarization preserves the prescribed preference, whereas per-objective normalization induces policy-dependent distortion; with pairwise distinct normalization scales, only single-objective preferences remain unchanged. A positive floor prevents the terminal-constraint multiplier from vanishing and renders the penalty exact when the floor exceeds a geometric multiplier. Deterministic terminal violation is bounded by expected stochastic violation plus a term depending on terminal-state curvature and action variance, so stochastic feasibility alone does not certify deterministic execution. On a heavy-duty range-extender powertrain with six stage costs and a terminal state-of-charge band, a representative training run places all 32 preference-grid solutions in band on six cycles inside and outside the training pool. Averaged over ten runs, the method yields more in-band solutions under deterministic execution than a critic-based conditioned baseline with the same terminal-constraint handling.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: Three bijections of $y=\frac{2x}{1+x^2}$ and their inverses
Tags: functions, inverse-function

Question:
The curve $y=\frac{2x}{1+x^2}$ can give rise to three bijections:
$$f_1:(-\infty,-1]\rightarrow [-1,0),\quad f_1(x)=\frac{2x}{1+x^2},$$
$$f_2:[-1,1]\rightarrow [-1,1], \quad f_2(x)=\frac{2x}{1+x^2},$$
$$f_3:[1,\infty)\rightarrow [0,1], \quad f_3(x)=\frac{2x}{1+x^2}.$$
For the given curve, we can write $$x=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{1-y^2}}{y}$$
The question is: What are their respective inverse functions?

EDIT: Finally, the answers to these questions can be presented in the following Fig., where the curve is in blue and three piece inverse function is in green, the line $y=x$ is in blue.

Answer A:
Start from $y=\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}$ and solve for $x$:

$$y x^2-2x+y=0 .$$

For $y\neq 0$ this is a quadratic in $x$ with discriminant $4-4y^2$, so for $|y|\le 1$

$$x=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{1-y^2}}{y}.$$

The two roots multiply to $1$ (product of roots $=y/y$), so one root has $|x|\ge 1$ (the "$+$" sign) and the other has $|x|\le 1$ (the "$-$" sign). Now pick the right sign on each piece:

$f_1:(-\infty,-1]\to[-1,0)$. Here $|x|\ge1$, so we need the "$+$" root:
$$f_1^{-1}(y)=\frac{1+\sqrt{1-y^2}}{y},\qquad y\in[-1,0).$$
Check: $y=-1$ gives $-1$; as $y\to0^-$ it tends to $-\infty$.

$f_2:[-1,1]\to[-1,1]$. Here $|x|\le 1$, so we need the "$-$" root, and at $y=0$ we must fill in the value $x=0$ by hand (the formula is $0/0$ there):
$$f_2^{-1}(y)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1-\sqrt{1-y^2}}{y}, & y\neq 0,\\[2mm] 0, & y=0.\end{cases}$$
This is continuous at $0$, because $\dfrac{1-\sqrt{1-y^2}}{y}=\dfrac{y}{1+\sqrt{1-y^2}}$, which is the nicer form that also works at $y=0$.
Check: $y=\tfrac12$ gives $x=\dfrac{1-\sqrt3/2}{1/2}=2-\sqrt3\approx0.268$, and $\dfrac{2(0.268)}{1+0.0718}\approx0.5$.

$f_3:[1,\infty)\to(0,1]$. Here $x\ge1$, so again the "$+$" root:
$$f_3^{-1}(y)=\frac{1+\sqrt{1-y^2}}{y},\qquad y\in(0,1].$$
Check: $y=1$ gives $1$; as $y\to0^+$ it tends to $+\infty$.

A small correction to the statement: as $x\to\infty$ we have $f_3(x)\to 0$ but never equals $0$, so the range of $f_3$ is $(0,1]$, not $[0,1]$. With codomain $[0,1]$ the map $f_3$ is not onto, so to be a true bijection the codomain should be $(0,1]$.

So $f_1^{-1}$ and $f_3^{-1}$ have the same formula (they differ only in domain, $[-1,0)$ versus $(0,1]$), while $f_2^{-1}$ uses the other sign.

Answer B:
The bijections $f_1$ and $f_3$ have distinct domains and can be merged into one.

The two inverses are naturally

$\dfrac{1-\sqrt{1-y^2}}y$ for $f_2$, and

$\dfrac{1+\sqrt{1-y^2}}y$ for $f_{1/3}$.

Or you can discriminate $1/3$ by the sign.

Title: A Characterization of Functions on the Integer Lattice That Are L-Extendable through Local Convex Extensions

Abstract:
L-extendable functions on the integer lattice are functions that admit a $\frac12$UJ-convex relaxation; that is, values can be assigned to the additional half-integral points, while keeping the original values at integer points, so that the resulting function is $\frac12$UJ-convex. Various examples of L-extendable functions and their applications are known. A general characterization of L-extendability for functions on the integer lattice, however, remains open. In this paper, we study the L-extendability of functions on the integer lattice. We first obtain a necessary condition: L-extendable functions are integrally convex. We then consider a special subclass of L-extendable functions, namely, those whose local convex extensions give L-convex relaxations. This subclass has a useful optimization property: the optimal value of the original function coincides with that of the $\frac12$UJ-convex relaxation given by its local convex extension, a property not guaranteed for general $\frac12$UJ-convex relaxations. We characterize this subclass by showing that a function is L-extendable through its local convex extension if and only if it is integrally convex and its restriction to every unit hypercube is D-convex, where D-convexity is a discrete convexity associated with reflected Freudenthal simplicial divisions. This subclass strictly contains the class of D-convex functions. We also give a combinatorial characterization of D-convex subsets of the vertices of a unit hypercube: a set $X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n$ is D-convex if and only if it is majority-closed and contains a relative opposite pair.

Site: Stats Stack Exchange
Title: In this experimental context, does the re-use of a control bias/invalidate the result?
Tags: p-value, experiment-design, control-group

Question:
I'm contributing to a paper where I am a fairly minor author. I'm concerned by the experimental design but the corresponding authors, who have decade(s) more experience in the field than I have, seem unconcerned and there's the implication that I'm being unnecessarily picky. I'm 95% sure I'm correct, but given their attitude and the fact that my remaining option is to have my name removed from the paper, I'm chasing that final 5% of sureness.

In the first experiment, knocking out a gene was shown to cause a significant increase in cell size (simple t-test). To confirm this phenomenon, they then knocked out another gene involved in the same biological process and showed the same effect (also using a t-test). They then tested another three or four genes more tangentially related to that process and saw a significant effect in some of them and not others (t tests). Due to time constraints and the fact that, at the time, they didn't know if this was going anywhere, these three experiments all compare to the same control. While they've built on this in later experiments, these three experiments are all in the paper and provide the base for the latter experiments.

This concerns me. Firstly, we know there’s a lot of variation in the experimental model over time so the control from the first experiment doesn't necessarily control for technical variations in the second two experiments. Secondly, and more importantly, in the second two experiments they compare the effects of disrupting a biological process to a "control", but that control has already been shown to have reduced growth compared to another genotype where that process is disrupted. To my mind, this invalidates any stats based on this experiment.

Their argument is that when you look at the overall results in the paper, the big picture is consistent and validates their results, and this can all be fixed with a p-value correction (in this case, Dunnett's test).

I think presenting this data in a paper needs those experiments to be repeated with the proper controls. I think a Dunnett's test would be perfect if this was a pre-designed screen comparing knockdown of a number of genes to a single control, but not in this context.

I'm wondering if I'm right, if they're right and I'm being picky, or if I'm right that it's a problem but they're right that it's a minor one?

(description)When the city commission approved the Brentwood Hills Addition plans on June 1, 1953, it created the city of Kansas City, Kansas' first subdivision in Wyandotte County established for African Americans (west of 18th street). The stakeholders formed a Land Investors Group guided by Douglass State Bank.

Dr. Charles.W. Alexander and Dr. William M. Blount, both physicians in KCK; Harold Robbins and Wendell Robbins of Robbins & Robbins Construction Company; Henry W. Sewing, President of Douglass State Bank; Earl D. Thomas, an educator and Principal at Lincoln High School, KCMO;  Isadore Gross, a real estate broker and taxicab company owner in KCMO; Ernest W. Robbins, a retired railway mail clerk;  Atty. Elmer G. Jackson; Mrs. J.A. Hibbler; widow of a physician from KCMO and Rev. Isaiah H. Henderson Sr., pastor of Eighth Street Baptist Church, came together and brought their vision to life.

In total, 54 acres was purchased from Judge Norman B. Sorter. The original boundaries of the subdivision sat between 34th and Farrow and 38th and Farrow to 34th and Bell Crossing and 38th and Oak. It consisted of 143 homes.

According to the April 16, 1954 edition of the KC Call, 1200 people attended the open house. The official dedication was held on the Sunday afternoon of April 11, 1954 in Quindaro Park. Dr. George W. Snowden and William F. McKinney, both federal officials with the Federal Housing Administration, were in attendance.

The neighborhood became a village for the families that lived there. It consisted of doctors, teachers, beauticians and small business owners. It even had its own baseball team, The Quindaro Dragons, with Mr. Harold Rucker, as the coach and a Cub Scout Troop with Mrs. Lorraine Robinson as troop leader.

Missouri submitted Interstate 635 to the American Association of State Highway Officials (AASHO) as part of its proposed Urban Route Numbering on July 31, 1958 and it was approved on November 10, 1958. Construction of I635 began in 1969. Fourteen of the Brentwood Hills homes on 34th Street were acquired which changed the landscape of the subdivision, but not the pride of the people.

Title: Affinizations and braided module categories

Abstract:
We relate affinizations of braided monoidal categories to braided module categories, allowing a twist by a braided monoidal automorphism. Our main theorem establishes a bijection between twisted braided structures on a right module category and extensions of its action to the corresponding twisted affinization. We also show that the twisted affinization is the free twisted braided module category on one object. We give explicit presentations of twisted affinizations, both as monoidal categories and as module categories, using invertible dots and reflection relations. We also describe the relation to cylinder twists and tensor-pair cylinder twists, including the naturality condition needed to obtain a braided module structure. As applications, we obtain module-category presentations of the affine Kauffman and affine oriented skein categories and an orientation-reversing twisted version of the latter. We realize the disoriented skein category as a quotient of this twisted affinization by a single additional relation.

[user] 10:57, 27 September 2026 (UTC)

----

Itavia Flight 115 was a scheduled passenger flight from Rome to Genoa, Italy. On 14 October 1960, the aircraft operating the flight crashed into the slopes of Mount Capanne near the town of Elba at 728 meters (2,388 feet), killing all 7 passengers and 4 crew members. [ref: Accident de Havilland DH-114 Heron 2 I-AOMU, Friday 14 October 1960, aviation-safety.net]

== Aircraft and crew ==
The aircraft involved was an Itavia de Havilland DH-114 Heron 2, registration I-AOMU (serial no. 14090), manufactured in 1955. [ref: ] [ref: Il disastro aereo del 1960, Mucchio Selvaggio] The flight crew consisted of captain Ennio Scipione, aged 30, first officer Francesco Cossu, aged 44, and two flight attendants, Giovanna Pertusio, aged 25, and Grazia Candeloro, aged 20.

== Accident ==
The flight took off from Rome Urbe Airport at 15:02 pm local time. At 15:19, the crew contacted the tower in Genoa, stating that they were currently flying over the city of Civitavecchia. The controller, seeing the poor weather conditions along the flight's path, offered to divert them to either Turin or Nice. There was no response to this message from the crew. Moments later, the aircraft struck the slopes of Mount Capanne at 2,388 feet, exploding and breaking up on impact and killing all 11 occupants onboard. [ref: La Stampa (1960-10-15), Editrice La Stampa S.p.A.]
== Investigation ==
The investigation found that the crew was flying according to visual flight rules instead of instrument flight rules, which was required given the poor visibility on the flight's route. Why the crew chose to fly in VFR instead of IMC is unknown.

== Lawsuit ==
A court case followed the accident, with penal charges brought forward against the flight company, and responsible personnel of Civilavia and the Urbe airport. Among them were General Romolo Abbriata (director of the civil aviation authority), Luigi Petragnani (manager of Itavia), Renato Panini (technical organizer of Itavia) and Riccardo Rubbiano-Pivawere. However, they were acquitted of all charges in both instances (1965/66). [ref: La Stampa (1966-02-11), Editrice La Stampa S.p.A.]

== Memorial ==
=== 1960 ===
At the scene of the accident, a small white marble tombstone was built and placed against a rock formation, engraved with the star of David in memory of Silvio Sciunnach, a Jewish passenger who was onboard the flight and a victim of the accident.

=== 2013 ===
On October 13, 2013, on the evening preceding the 53rd anniversary of the accident, a monument was built on the accident site. [ref: Un Monumento sul Capanne in memoria del disastro aereo di 53 anni fa, www.elbareport.it]

Heidrick & Struggles International Incorporated, commonly called Heidrick & Struggles, is an American executive search and management consulting company headquartered in Chicago, Illinois, United States, with offices in 56 offices across the Americas, Europe, Africa and Asia as of 2026. ==History==

Heidrick & Struggles was founded in 1953 in Chicago by Gardner Heidrick and John E. Struggles, both of whom were former employees of American management consulting firm Booz Allen Hamilton. [ref: Heidrick & Struggles Company Overview & News, Forbes] [ref: Headhunting: A Brief History of a Profession, Eurogalenus]

From the late 1950s through the 1960s, Heidrick & Struggles opened offices in Los Angeles, San Francisco and New York City. In 1968, the firm established its first international office in London.

In 1999, the firm completed an initial public offering (IPO) and began trading on the NASDAQ under the ticker symbol HSII. [ref: Forbes: Headaches and Struggles, Forbes] [ref: Internet Cos., CONSOL Energy, Heidrick & Struggles Plan IPOs, Bloomberg] On April 30, 1999, the IPO closed with 4.2 million shares offered at $14/share. [ref: Internet deals shrug off technology scare, Deseret News] As of 2005, the company had more than 50 offices in six continents. [ref: Headhunters and How to Use Them: A Guide for Organisations and Individuals, John Wiley & Sons]

In January 2013, Heidrick & Struggles purchased Senn Delaney Leadership Consulting Group, a Huntington Beach organizational culture advisory firm, in an all cash deal for $53.5 million. [ref: Senn Delaney bought for $53.5 million, Orange County Register]

In September 2017, Heidrick & Struggles acquired 2GET, an executive search firm in Brazil. [ref: Heidrick acquires one of largest executive search firms in Brazil, Staffing Industry Analysts (SIA)] In December 2021, the company entered into an agreement to acquire two executive search and leadership consulting companies, RosExpert in Russia and WE Partners in Ukraine and Kazakhstan. [ref: Heidrick & Struggles Enters Agreement to Acquire RosExpert in Russia and WE Partners in Ukraine and Kazakhstan, Hunt Scanlon Media]

In March 2022, the company posted global revenues of $1 billion. [ref: Heidrick & Struggles Reports 61 Percent Revenue Rise; Names Diversity Leader, Hunt Scanlon Media]

In April 2021, the company acquired Business Talent Group, an online marketplace for on-demand independent consultants. [ref: Heidrick buys Business Talent Group, entering the on-demand talent platform space, Staffing Industry Analysts (SIA)] In January 2023 Heidrick & Struggles acquired Atreus, an executive interim management firm based in Germany. In 2024, the company appointed Tom Monahan as chief executive officer. [ref: Heidrick & Struggles’ new president shares what he learned about going for a CEO job, Fortune]

In December 2025, the company agreed to be acquired by an investor group led by Advent International and Corvex Private Equity, ending 26 years as a public company. [ref: Heidrick & Struggles soars after $1.3 billion go-private deal]

== Research studies ==
Heidrick & Struggles regularly conducts studies and research focused on industry trends.

[ref: ] That same month, the company released a report on "High-End Independent Talent." It found a 151% increase in demand for interim leaders since 2021, with human resources being the top business function seeking interim leadership support. [ref: ]

In May 2026, the company’s "CEO & Board Confidence Monitor" found that of the approximately 2,000 CEOs and directors surveyed, only four out ten expressed confidence that CEO succession planning had positioned organizations properly for the future. Süleyman Gazi Erçel (February 20, 1945 – June 13, 2022) was a Turkish economist who served as 18th Governor of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey (1996-2001). [ref: Governors of the CBRT, www.tcmb.gov.tr] He previously served as Director General of the Ministry of Treasury and Finance of Turkey as well as chairman of Tütünbank. [ref: Turkish stock market: Time to clean things up, www.euromoney.com] [ref: Former Central Bank Governor Gazi Erçel has passed away., [[The Independent]

==Early life and education==
Erçel was born on February 20, 1945 in Istanbul, Turkey. [ref: Gazi Erçel, former governor of the Central Bank, has passed away., www.bankadunyasi.com] He earned his bachelor's degree from the Department of Finance and Economics of Ankara University in 1967 and his master's degree from Vanderbilt University in 1976.

==Career==
Erçel began his career in 1967 at the Turkish Ministry of Treasury and Finance where he held several roles, including Deputy Director General of the Treasury, as well as various roles in the economic research, banking and foreign exchange, IMF, and World Bank departments.

From 1982 to 1986, Erçel left the ministry to serve as Deputy Executive Director of the IMF. He returned in 1987 upon appointment as Director General of the Treasury.

In 1989, Erçel left civil service to pursue a career in the private sector. He was a board member at Yaşar Holding as well as Tütünbank, where he became chairman in 1994.

Erçel was appointed governor of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey in 1996 by the cabinet of Turkish President Süleyman Demirel. [ref: Turkey names new Central Bank governor, www.upi.com] Three weeks into his term, Erçel addressed the Institute of International Finance in Istanbul, remarking that his two primary goals as governor would be to reduce inflation and to prepare the Turkish economy for entry into the EU Customs Union. [ref: Remarks by Gazi Erçel, Governor, The Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, at the Spring Meeting of IIF, Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey]

In December of 1999, Erçel announced an IMF-backed disinflation program with a three-year horizon, aimed at tackling an inflated consumer price index, lowering real interest rates, and redistributing resources throughout the Turkish economy. [ref: Disinflation Program for the Year 2000: Implementation of Exchange Rate and Monetary Policy, Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey] In 2000, Erçel secured $7.5 billion in loans from the IMF to help replenish the central bank's reserves after growing government deficits led to a liquidity shortage. [ref: Turkey markets calmer with IMF cash to boost reserves, www.cnn.com] In response to the 2001 Turkish economic crisis, Erçel resigned as governor on moral grounds, asserting that Turkey needed a reconstituted negotiating team to establish a new IMF agreement. [ref: Turkey's sparring leaders meet, www.news.bbc.co.uk]

After leaving the Central Bank of Turkey, Erçel became a financial columnist for several Turkish newspapers and served as a lecturer on the Faculty of Economics and Administrative Sciences at Istanbul Aydın University. He died at home on June 13, 2022 at the age of 77. [ref: Gazi Erçel kimdir? Gazi Erçel neden vefat etti?, www.cnnturk.com]

Title: A note on a problem of Ma and Chen

Abstract:
Let $S=(s_1,s_2,\cdots)$ be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers. For any real number $α>0$, let $S_α=(\lfloorαs_1\rfloor,\lfloorαs_2\rfloor,\cdots)$. We prove that if $s_{n+1}\le 2s_n$ for every positive integer $n$, then there exists $0<α<1$ such that $S_α$ is strongly complete. In addition, this gives a negative answer to a problem of Ma and Chen in [Acta Arith. 203 (2022), 307--318]. We also prove that the same result is true if $s_{n+1}\le 2s_n$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

state.text:
Title: A universal gauge structure in the photon content of light-matter systems

Abstract:
After truncating the matter Hilbert space of a single-mode light-matter model, gauge transformations leave the spectrum invariant whereas the ground-state photon number is gauge dependent, hence, its meaning remains disputed. We show that this gauge dependence obeys an exact algebraic law whenever the gauge transformation acts as a displacement of the field coupled to a matter operator $G$. Namely, the ground-state photon number is a quadratic polynomial in the gauge parameter $λ$, $\langle a^{\dagger} a\rangle_λ$ $=$ $\langle a^{\dagger} a\rangle_{0}$ $+$ $Cλ$ $+$ $Qλ^2$. Here the coefficients are the correlator $C=\langle G\,p\rangle$ of $G$ and the field momentum $p$, and $Q=\langle G^2\rangle$. Its minimum over all gauges is naturally gauge-invariant, and for the quantum Rabi model it is determined by the ground-state energy alone. We show that it is strictly positive for the quantum Rabi and Dicke models with level splitting, so that a residual photon content survives in every gauge. At weak coupling the gauge of minimal photon number is the Jaynes-Cummings gauge, and for the Dicke model it remains so at all couplings in the thermodynamic limit.

Site: Law Stack Exchange
Title: Can a confession be made expressly conditional on information supplied by police during interrogation?
Tags: united-states, criminal-law, rules-of-evidence, statement

Question:
Suppose police in the US make factual assertions during an interrogation, some true, mistaken, exaggerated, or deliberately false.

The suspect later writes:

“Subject to the truth and completeness of all information provided to me by the interrogators, I accept responsibility for the following…”

The rest would otherwise look like an ordinary confession.

What is the evidentiary effect of making the police-supplied information an express condition of the confession?

For example, suppose police say that forensic evidence implicates the suspect, a witness identified them, and another suspect implicated them. The written confession expressly relies on all three claims. If one was fabricated, the confession may still be “voluntary”, but it is also conditional on a proposition the prosecution cannot prove.

Can the prosecution introduce the confession while disregarding that condition? Does the rule of completeness require the condition and relevant police representations to be considered with it? If the confession expressly depends on all information supplied during interrogation, must all those predicates be proved before the confession can support an inference of guilt?

More generally, do US confessions have any doctrine dealing with informational provenance? Corroborating that a police-supplied fact is true does not show that the suspect knew it independently.

This seems analogous to chain of custody: physical evidence is examined for both authenticity and preservation of integrity, whereas confession doctrine appears to focus mainly on whether the suspect made the statement voluntarily.

Site: Electronics Stack Exchange
Title: BCS6402 reaches 4.2 V immediately at 2 A charge — wiring resistance or setup issue?
Tags: batteries, battery-charging

Question:
I am using a BK Precision BCS6402 to charge a 1-cell 3.7 V, 10 Ah Li-ion polymer battery.

With one battery, the open-circuit voltage was about 3.747 V. At 1 A charge current, the BCS showed about 3.923 V and operated normally in CC mode. When I increased the charging current to 2 A, the BCS terminal voltage quickly rose to the 4.2 V limit, so charging stopped because Voltage Shut was set to 4.2 V.

Below is the behavior at 1A charging current,my test setup,BCS configurations

JUST AFTER CONNECTING THE BATTERY AND TURNING ON BCS:

AFTER CHARGING ON:

BATTERY TO BCS CONNECTION:

BCS CONFIGURATION:

I observed the same 2 A behavior with a second identical battery, so it does not appear to be specific to one battery.

On another identical battery, during a 1 A charging test, I measured approximately:

3.970 V at the BCS output terminals

3.855 V directly at the battery-side connection

So there was about 115 mV difference between the BCS terminals and the battery connection at 1 A.

The cable length is only about 30 cm, but the wires and inline connector are relatively small.

My question is: does this mainly indicate excessive series resistance in the wiring/connectors, or could there be another issue with the BCS6402 charging setup? Would remote sensing be appropriate here, or should I first replace the leads/connectors with lower-resistance ones?

Answer A:
There will always be voltage drops.  The key is to get them to be as low as practical.  Thicker wire will help.  Also try wiggling the wiring, especially at each connection.  Also wiggle the plug in the socket.  All of this while watching the voltage on the instrument.  The lower it goes, the better.

Real-world charging will always exhibit a small amount of resistance.  That's why a typical charging algorithm doesn't just stop when it hits the terminal voltage.  It will hold the voltage there and watch as the current decreases to some predetermined level.   I don't know anything about the BCS6402 or what its charging plan is.  You may well have alternate choices like that.  Of course with the current held to a lower level, the cell takes longer to charge.

Answer B:
If your wiring is dropping 115mV at 1A, then it will drop about 230mV at 2A. That's going to be enough to fool the charger that it's hit the maximum 4.2V when the battery is still around 3.97V.

It looks like you need thicker wiring and a plug and socket to match.

Title: Safety Verification for Voltage Control in Inverter Dominated Radial Distribution Networks under Actuator and Sensor Adversarial Attacks

Abstract:
This paper develops a safety verification framework for inverter-based radial distribution networks under sensor and actuator attacks. Each customer is equipped with a droop-based controller to regulate its voltage within a desirable bound of a reference, i.e., to achieve safety. In our setting, attacks and disturbances enter the droop-based controllers, while actuator attacks corrupt the reactive power injected into the network. Consequently, invariance of the controller state alone does not guarantee compliance with inverter capacities or customer voltage limits. To address this challenge, we derive conditions to guarantee that the reactive power state remains inside a predefined ellipsoid, while at the same time ensuring that the attacked reactive power injections and customer voltages respect predetermined operating limits that hold uniformly for the entire predefined ellipsoid. Together, these conditions guarantee safety under all admissible disturbances and state-dependent sensor and actuator attacks. Finally, we express the resulting containment condition as a linear matrix inequality (LMI) feasibility problem. A five-customer radial network based on the CIGRE benchmark corroborates our theoretical developments in simulations.

Site: Law Stack Exchange
Title: Does copyright protection differ between an original script and a TV series adapted from it, and can the copyright owners differ?
Tags: copyright, united-kingdom, intellectual-property

Question:
If a person writes an original script, and a TV series is produced based on that script, is the TV series protected as a separate copyright work from the script, such that the copyright owner(s) of the TV series can be different from the copyright owner(s) of the underlying script?

For instance, could the writer own copyright in the script (as a literary work) while the production company (and/or other contributors) own copyright in the TV series (as a film work), with the series only lawfully made via a licence/assignment of the underlying script rights?

I’m looking for the copyright position under the CDPA 1988 (ignoring any unusual contractual arrangements), and how the “underlying work vs adapted work” relationship affects ownership.

Answer A:
united-states

This question is governed by 17 USC 103. It provides that the television series receives its own separate copyright, given that the script was used "lawfully" (i.e. without violating the writer's copyright). Because most TV studios employ the production cast and crew (rather than hiring independent contractors), the TV series is a "work made for hire" and its copyright vests in the TV studio or some other corporate entity, as provided in 17 USC 201. See also the definition of "work made for hire" in 17 USC 101.

The contract might be a license or a transfer. A license gives the TV studio permission to use the script. It may or may not set limits, such as requiring the series to be produced within a specified period of time, allowing or prohibiting spinoffs and other adaptations, etc. In practice, such licenses tend to be favorable to the studio or publisher, and are usually exclusive licenses, meaning that the writer may not turn around and sign another contract with some other studio for the duration of the license. A transfer, on the other hand, gives the TV studio complete rights to the script, and lets them do whatever they wish.

There is one important limitation to both licenses and transfers, described in 17 USC 203. The author may elect to terminate a license or transfer within a five year period beginning 35 years after the license or transfer takes effect. This effectively claws back whatever rights the author may have signed away, regardless of what the contract says. The termination right (the right to terminate a license or transfer) may not be sold, given away, contractually blocked, or otherwise disposed of, except that it automatically passes to the author's surviving spouse and children upon the author's death. Works made for hire are not subject to termination rights. The purpose of termination rights is to protect authors and artists from predatory contracts.
[truncated]

Answer B:
You correct there's one extra dimension in your hypothetical. What is specified in the contract.

The writer of the original script (OS) at some moment entered an agreement (the contract) with the producers of the TV series to license the use of the OS. In this license agreement, the terms for the copyright of the derivative work (the series) and even the OS can be sold permanently, licensed for a period of time, or anything in-between so long the law permits it.

Each work has its own copyright. The writer owns copyright of the OS, while the TV producers have copyright over the audiovisual work (the series).

Most likely, the licensing contract includes exclusivity to adapt the work to a series of medium. For example, a book I sold to a publisher included exclusive rights to the book (in written and audio formats) and a comic adaptation. It didn't guarantee a comic would be made out of it (it wasn't) but it granted the publishing company exclusive rights to make it if it was ever done. The contract also specified that the copyright of the comic would be jointly owned by the publisher and me. But this could have been assigned exclusively to the publisher as well.

Without looking at the contract, it's impossible to determine how long the license and/or exclusive rights last. Or which rights are assigned.

Under section 90 of the CDPA, the owner can Transfer Ownership in full or partially, for works completed or yet to be created. The transfer must be documented in writing and signed by the lawful owner. Copyright can also be assigned by will as "personal or moveable property."

Title: Two-neighbor lattice percolation percolates in all dimensions

Abstract:
It is trivial that $1$-dimensional $2$-neighbor lattice percolation percolates. Coupier, Henry, Jahnel and Köppl proved the $2$-neighbor lattice percolation percolates in dimension 2; and then for sufficiently large dimensions, Bäumler, Jahnel, Köppl, Lodewijks, Reeves and Tóbiás showed this is still true. In this paper, we verify that the $2$-neighbor lattice percolation percolates in all dimensions $d\ge 3.$

Title: Following part of a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem for primes - why must a factor must only divide one thing of the form $x+ y \omega^j$?
Tags: number-theory, unique-factorization-domains

Question:
Let $p>3$ be prime. Let $\omega = e^{2 \pi i /p}$. Further suppose $\mathbb Z [\omega]$ is a unique factorization domain (UFD), i.e.

Let’s consider the equation $x^p + y^p = z^p$ for $x,y,z$ coprime integers, not multiples of $p$. This is, of course, a special case of Fermat’s Last Theorem, and has no solutions. I’m trying to follow part of a proof as to why.

I understand that we can factor $x^p + y^p = z^p$ as

$$(x+y)(x + y \omega)(x + y \omega^2) \dots (x + y \omega^{p-1}) = z^p.$$

One part of the proof I am trying to follow is now considering divisors of these factors on the LHS, in the number field $\mathbb Z [\omega]$. In particular, I want to show that if there is some factor $\pi$ of $x + y \omega$, it cannot be a factor of any of the other $x + y \omega^j$s. The plan of attack for this is twofold:

If $\pi$ obeys this condition, then it divides both $z$ and $yp$,

This is a contradiction.

I can see that if we assume that $\pi$ does divide both of these things, we then get $\pi$ divides $y \omega (1 - \omega^{i-1})$. Now by observing that

$$(1 - \omega) (1 - \omega^2) \dots (1 - \omega^{p-1}) = p,$$

we have that $\pi$ divides $yp$.

I’m happy with this so far, but what I’m not happy with is the next claim in the proof that $\pi$ divides $z$. Clearly $\pi$ divides the LHS so $\pi$ divides $z^p$ also. I don’t see how it follows that $\pi$ divides $z$. If $\pi$ were prime in $ \mathbb Z [\omega]$ then its surely true by unique factorization, but we may have that $\pi$ is the $p$th power of something, in which case it doesn’t follow.

If we grant that $\pi$ divides $z$, I think I see what the contradiction is, but I’m not sure. We know that $yp$ and $z$ are relatively prime, so from Bezout that $zm + ypn = 1$. $\pi$ divides the left-hand side so presumably then we’re saying $\pi$ divides $1$, so $\pi$ is a unit. The proof I’m read never assumes $\pi$ is a non-unit though, so I don’t entirely understand what’s wrong with that.

For context, this is exercise 1.17 from Daniel A. Marcus’ Number Fields.

Draft: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry

Draft text:
The Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry is a public inquiry in the United Kingdom into the implementation and operation of the Horizon accounting system, and the actions taken by Post Office Ltd and others in response to apparent financial shortfalls recorded by the system. The inquiry was established on a non-statutory basis in September 2020 and was converted into a statutory inquiry under the Inquiries Act 2005 on 1 June 2021, with Sir Wyn Williams as chair. [ref: Terms of reference, Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry]

The inquiry examined the development and operation of Horizon, the use of information generated by the system in investigations and prosecutions, the treatment of postmasters, compensation and access to justice, and the governance and oversight of the Post Office and its relationship with government. Its work was divided into seven phases. Public hearings began in February 2022 and concluded with closing submissions in December 2024. [ref: Key Documents, Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry] [ref: British Post Office scandal, Wikipedia]

The first volume of the chair's final report was published on 8 July 2025 and dealt with the human impact of the scandal and financial redress. It contained 19 recommendations. As of July 2026, five further volumes remained in preparation; Sir Wyn Williams said that these would cover the period from the development of Legacy Horizon to events after the end of the litigation brought by Alan Bates and other claimants against the Post Office. [ref: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry Report: Volume 1, Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry] [ref: Progress Update from Sir Wyn Williams, Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry]

== Background ==

The inquiry arose from the wider British Post Office scandal, in which hundreds of postmasters were prosecuted and thousands more were held financially responsible for apparent losses recorded by Horizon. The system was developed for the Post Office by Fujitsu and began to be rolled out from 1999. Postmasters had reported discrepancies in branch accounts almost from the beginning of the rollout, but the Post Office continued to rely on Horizon data in seeking to recover alleged shortfalls and, in England and Wales, in criminal prosecutions.

In 2009, Computer Weekly reported allegations that Horizon could generate erroneous information, while the Justice for Subpostmasters Alliance was formed to campaign on behalf of affected postmasters. Subsequent investigations, the group litigation brought by 555 postmasters, and judgments of the High Court and Court of Appeal established the basis for challenges to convictions and increased pressure for an independent inquiry.

Following the settlement of the group litigation in 2019 and the beginning of successful appeals against convictions, campaigners and parliamentarians called for a judge-led investigation into the causes of the scandal and the conduct of the Post Office and government.

== Establishment ==

=== Non-statutory inquiry (2020–2021) ===

On 26 February 2020, the government indicated that it would establish an independent inquiry into the Horizon scandal. On 10 June 2020, the government announced an independent review of the Post Office's Horizon IT system and the use of information generated by it in criminal trials.

The review was established as a non-statutory inquiry in September 2020 under the chairmanship of Sir Wyn Williams. It issued a call for evidence on 1 December 2020, and its first public hearing took place on 15 January 2021. Two public hearings were held during the non-statutory phase, followed by a preliminary hearing on the provisional list of issues in November 2021. [ref: Key Documents, Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry]

The original review had a narrower remit than the later statutory inquiry. In particular, it did not include the Post Office's prosecution function, the settlement reached in the group litigation, or the conduct of current or future litigation.

=== Conversion to a statutory inquiry (2021) ===

On 19 May 2021, the government announced that the inquiry would be placed on a statutory footing. It was formally converted under the Inquiries Act 2005 on 1 June 2021, giving the chair additional powers to compel witnesses and require the production of evidence.

The statutory inquiry's terms of reference required it to establish what went wrong with Horizon and the Post Office's use of information from the system; obtain relevant evidence from the Post Office, Fujitsu, government departments and UK Government Investments; assess whether changes promised by the Post Office had been delivered; and examine governance, oversight and whistleblowing arrangements.

The terms of reference also required the inquiry to take account of the findings of the High Court in Bates & Others v Post Office Ltd and the Court of Appeal in R v Hamilton and others, as well as other judgments in which convictions had been quashed.

Title: Does is_mdm_removable=false affect the 30-day provisional release for Configurator-added iPhones?
Tags: ios, mdm

Question:
I am implementing a custom MDM server for supervised iPhones using Apple Business Manager (ABM) and Automated Device Enrollment (ADE). The devices are added to ABM manually with Apple Configurator, rather than assigned by a participating reseller at purchase.

The relevant ADE profile settings generated by the server are:

{
  "is_supervised": true,
  "is_mandatory": true,
  "is_mdm_removable": false
}

The server also generates a separate configuration profile containing these settings (excerpt; UUIDs and other required metadata omitted):

<key>PayloadRemovalDisallowed</key>
<true/>
<key>PayloadContent</key>
<array>
  <dict>
    <key>PayloadType</key>
    <string>com.apple.applicationaccess</string>
    <key>allowEraseContentAndSettings</key>
    <false/>
    <key>allowUIConfigurationProfileInstallation</key>
    <false/>
  </dict>
</array>

In the implementation, that restrictions profile is sent using InstallProfile after TokenUpdate; it is not embedded in the ADE enrollment profile. I am not treating an installation command being queued as proof that the restrictions are effective on a device.

Observed behavior: during the initial 30-day period, the iPhone offers Leave Remote Management. Selecting it erases the device and releases it from management. I need to determine whether preventing that action from the first enrollment is something my MDM server can configure.

I have read Apple's documentation on Configurator-added devices and the provisional period. I understand that restricting Erase All Content and Settings is a different operation from releasing a provisional enrollment. However, the ADE Profile documentation also describes is_mdm_removable=false as preventing removal of the MDM payload through the device UI.

Does the Configurator provisional release action operate independently of is_mdm_removable=false and PayloadRemovalDisallowed=true, or is there a documented ADE/MDM setting that controls that action during the provisional period? I want to distinguish an incorrect server configuration from behavior that cannot be changed through Apple's supported MDM protocol.

To tackle the integral
$$
\int \frac{1}{(x-1) \sqrt[4]{x^3+x}} d x,
$$
we need an odd substitution
$$
t=\frac{x+1}{\sqrt[4]{x^3+x}} .
$$
Taking the fourth power of both sides yields
$$
t^4-8=\frac{x^4-4 x^3+6 x^2-4 x+1}{x^3+x}=\frac{(x-1)^4}{x^3+x}.
$$
By logarithmic differentiation, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{4 t^3}{t^4-8} d t & =\left(\frac{4}{x-1}-\frac{3 x^2+1}{x^3+x}\right) d x \\
& =\frac{(x+1)^3}{(x-1)\left(x^3+x\right)} d x \\
\Rightarrow \frac{4}{t^4-8} d t & =\frac{\left(x^3+x\right)^{3 / 4}(x+1)^3}{(x+1)^3(x-1)\left(x^3+x\right)} d x=\frac{1}{(x-1) \sqrt[4]{x^3+x}} d x
\end{aligned}
$$
Integrating both sides yields
$$
\begin{aligned}
I & =4 \int \frac{d t}{t^4-8} \\
& =\frac{4}{2 \sqrt{8}} \int\left(\frac{1}{t^2-\sqrt{8}}-\frac{1}{t^2+\sqrt{8}}\right) d t \\
& =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left[\frac{1}{2 \cdot 2^{3 / 4}} \ln \left|\frac{t-2^{3 / 4}}{t+2^{3 / 4}}\right|-\frac{1}{2^{3 / 4}} \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{t}{2^{3 / 4}}\right)\right]+C \\
& =\frac{1}{2^{9 / 4}} \ln \left|\frac{x+1-2^{3 / 4} \sqrt[4]{x^3+x}}{x+1+2^{3 / 4} \sqrt[4]{x^3+x}}\right|-\frac{1}{2^{5 / 4}} \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{x+1}{2^{3 / 4} \sqrt[4]{x^3+x}} \right)+C
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer B:
$$ I = \int \frac{dx}{(x - 1)\sqrt[4]{x^3 + x}} $$

Use the Möbius substitution

$$ x = \frac{1 + t}{1 - t}, \quad dx = \frac{2 \, dt}{(1 - t)^2} $$

and,

$$ x^3 + x = x(x^2 + 1) = \frac{2(1 + t)(1 + t^2)}{(1 - t)^3} $$

$$ I = 2^{-1/4} \int \frac{dt}{t(1 - t^4)^{1/4}} $$

Let, $u = t^4$.  $du = 4t^3 \, dt$,

$$ I = \frac{2^{-1/4}}{4} \int \frac{du}{u(1 - u)^{1/4}} $$

let,

$$ s = (1 - u)^{1/4}, \quad u = 1 - s^4, \quad du = -4s^3 \, ds $$

Then

$$ \int \frac{du}{u(1 - u)^{1/4}} = -4 \int \frac{s^2}{1 - s^4} \, ds = -2 \int \left( \frac{1}{1 - s^2} - \frac{1}{1 + s^2} \right) \, ds = 2(\arctan s - \operatorname{artanh} s) + C $$

$$ I = 2^{-5/4}(\arctan s - \operatorname{artanh} s) + C $$

$$ \boxed{\int \frac{dx}{(x - 1)\sqrt[4]{x^3 + x}} = 2^{-5/4} \left[ \arctan \left( \frac{2^{3/4}(x^3 + x)^{1/4}}{x + 1} \right) - \operatorname{artanh} \left( \frac{2^{3/4}(x^3 + x)^{1/4}}{x + 1} \right) \right] + C} $$

Title: Cryogenic Optical Characteristics of S-FPL51 and S-LAH71: Refractive index, Transmission and Thermal expansion

Abstract:
Several near-infrared instruments on upcoming extremely large telescopes use a combination of OHARA S-FPL51 and S-LAH71 glass prisms to correct for the atmospheric differential refraction. Because large parts of these instruments are contained within a vessel cooled to liquid nitrogen temperatures, the changes in optical and mechanical properties should be considered during the design phase. In this report, we provide an update to our continuing efforts to characterize the S-FPL51 and S-LAH71 glass under cryogenic conditions. These efforts include a measurement of the refractive index (293 K, 100 K and 80 K), transmission measurements (293 K, 77 K and 43 K) and a determination of the coefficient of thermal expansion (between 293 K and 45 K). We will describe the cryogenic test setups that we have used to obtain our results, and provide summarizing equations of these material properties. This characterization will prove useful for conceptual design trade-offs, mechanical interface solutions and detailed optical design for future near-infrared instrumentation on large telescopes.

Tags: effect-size, ancova, pre-post-comparison

Question:
We have conducted a study comparing two different training interventions. We used ANCOVA to analyse the data. Taking the example of countermovement jump (CMJ) test, findings indicated significant between-group difference at post-test for the CMJ (p < 0.001; η² = 0.439). Pairwise comparisons based on estimated marginal means revealed that the Group 1 achieved significantly greater post-test performance than the Group 2 (Mean Difference = 1.413 cm, p < 0.01; 95% CI [0.769, 2.057]). Significant pre- to post-test improvements were observed in both groups (Group 1: ∆ = 9.64%, d = 0.76; Group 2: ∆ = 5.48%, d = 1.09). An independent-samples t-test comparing percentage improvements indicated a significant advantage for Group 1 over Group 2 (p < 0.01). The problem now is that if you look at pairwise comparison, there is a discrepancy between the delta and d (effect size). Any idea why is that? is it related to the greater SD in Group 1 compared to Group 2? And does it make sense to keep speaking of the advantage of Group 1 over Group 2?

Title: Various ways for $\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{\cos^{-1}x}{1+x^2+x^4+x^6}dx$
Tags: integration, definite-integrals

Question:
Recently the integral in the MSE:Evaluation of $\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{\cos^{-1} x}{1+x^2+x^4}dx$
recieved a good response.

Here, we extend it to solve $$I=\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{\cos^{-1}x}{1+x^2+x^4+x^6}dx\tag{1}$$$$I=\int_{0}^{1} \frac{\cos^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}(-x)}{(1+x^2)(1+x^4)} dx=\pi\int_{0}^{1}\frac{dx}{(1+x^2)(1+x^4)}=\frac{\pi}{2} \int_0^1 \left[\frac{1}{(1+x^2)}-\frac{1-1/x^2}{x^2+1/x^2}\right]dx $$
Let $u=x+1/x\implies du=(1-1/x^2)dx$, then
$$I=\frac{\pi^2}{8}-\frac{\pi}{2}\int_{\infty}^{2} \frac{du}{u^2-2}=\frac{\pi^2}{8}+\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}\coth^{-1} \sqrt{2}.$$

What could be other ways of obtaining this integral $(1)$?

Answer A:
$$\frac 1{1+x^2+x^4+x^6}=\frac 1{(x^2+1)(x^4+1)}=$$
$$\frac{1}{2 \left(x^2+1\right)}+\frac{2 x+\sqrt{2}}{4 \sqrt{2}
   \left(x^2+\sqrt{2} x+1\right)}-\frac{2 x-\sqrt{2}}{4 \sqrt{2}
   \left(x^2-\sqrt{2} x+1\right)}$$ gives an immediate answer for the antiderivarive
$$\int \frac {dx}{1+x^2+x^4+x^6}=\frac 12\tan ^{-1}(x)+\frac{1}{4 \sqrt{2}}\log \left(-\frac{x^2+\sqrt{2}x+1}{x^2-\sqrt{2} x+1}\right) $$

Answer B:
Using the same method as here,

Since $\arcsin(x)+\arccos(x)=\frac{\pi}{2}$, we have $I=\int\limits_{-1}^{1}\frac{\cos^{-1}x}{1+x^2+x^4+x^6}dx =
\frac{\pi}{2}\int\limits_{-1}^{1}
\frac{dx}{1+x^2+x^4+x^6}-\int\limits_{-1}^{1}\frac{\arcsin x}{1+x^2+x^4+x^6}dx$.

Observing that $\frac{\arcsin x}{1+x^2+x^4+x^6}$ is an odd function (since $\arcsin x$ is odd and $1+x^2+x^4+x^6$ is even), the right integral vanishes, i.e., $\int\limits_{-1}^{1}\frac{\arcsin x}{1+x^2+x^4+x^6}dx=0$. Hence $I=\pi\int\limits_{0}^{1}\frac{dx}{1+x^2+x^4+x^6}$.

Next, $1+x^2+x^4+x^6=\frac{1-x^8}{1-x^2}$, for $|x|<1$, $\frac1{1+x^2+x^4+x^6}=\frac{1-x^2}{1-x^8}
=(1-x^2)\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty}x^{8n}$
$=\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty}(x^{8n}-x^{8n+2})$.

Hence we have,
$\begin{aligned}
I&=\pi \sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac1{8n+1}-\frac1{8n+3}\right)\
&=\frac{\pi}{8}\left[\psi\left(\frac38\right)-\psi\left(\frac18\right)\right].
\end{aligned}$

Finally, by Gauss's digamma theorem, $\psi\left(\frac38\right)-\psi\left(\frac18\right)=\pi+2\sqrt{2}\ln(1+\sqrt2)$, giving $\boxed{
\int\limits_{-1}^{1}
\frac{\cos^{-1}x}{1+x^2+x^4+x^6}dx = \frac{\pi^2}{8}
+\frac{\pi\sqrt{2}}{4}\ln(1+\sqrt2)}$

Note: From here, $\psi\left(\frac p8\right)=
-\gamma-\ln16-\frac{\pi}{2}\cot\frac{p\pi}{8}
+2\sum\limits_{n=1}^{3}\cos\frac{np\pi}{4}\ln\sin\frac{n\pi}{8}$.

Using
$\sin\frac{\pi}{8}=\frac{\sqrt{2-\sqrt2}}2,\qquad
\sin\frac{3\pi}{8}=\frac{\sqrt{2+\sqrt2}}2, \qquad \cot\frac{\pi}{8}=1+\sqrt2,\qquad
\cot\frac{3\pi}{8}=\sqrt2-1$.

$\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\psi\left(\frac18\right)
&=-\gamma-4\ln2
-\frac{\pi}{2}(1+\sqrt2)
-\sqrt2\ln(1+\sqrt2) \\
\psi\left(\frac38\right)&=-\gamma-4\ln2
-\frac{\pi}{2}(\sqrt2-1)
+\sqrt2\ln(1+\sqrt2)
\end{aligned}
}$

$\implies
\psi\left(\frac38\right)-\psi\left(\frac18\right)=\pi+2\sqrt2\ln(1+\sqrt2)
$

Title: M-PFT: Angular Margin for Calibrated Prompt-Tuning of Fine-Tuned Vision-Language Models

Abstract:
Prompt-tuning has emerged as a parameter-efficient technique for adapting large-scale vision-language models (VLMs) to downstream tasks while keeping the pre-trained weights frozen. However, prompt-tuned VLMs often suffer from a base-to-novel dual miscalibration problem, where models typically show underconfidence on base classes and overconfidence on novel classes. Current VLM calibration approaches address this dual miscalibration either separately or jointly, but lack a geometric understanding of the hyperspherical embedding space and thus fail to exploit angular discriminative properties to adjust distorted decision boundaries. To address this, we propose M-PFT, a novel angular-margin approach for prompt tuning that introduces two complementary objectives to promote class discriminability and semantic anchoring. This enlarges the angular margin by 1) minimizing the maximum cosine similarity between tunable class embeddings to reduce embedding collapse and 2) minimizing the angular distance between each tunable embedding and its corresponding zero-shot embedding to preserve semantic geometry. Extensive experiments across 9 prompt-tuning methods with various backbones on 15 diverse datasets show that our approach reduces the average calibration error on novel classes, while remaining competitive on base classes and maintaining comparable accuracy. Further analyses reveal that M-PFT effectively adjusts distorted decision boundaries induced by prompt tuning while preserving the pre-trained embedding space, improving calibration with negligible computational overhead.

Title: On $t$-designs supported by self-orthogonal codes

Abstract:
We study self-orthogonal $t$-$(v,k,λ)$ designs satisfying the condition that the codes generated by the designs are self-orthogonal codes whose codewords of minimum weight $k$ correspond to the blocks. A classification of such designs is given under the conditions that $t\geq \lfloor k/4\rfloor+1\geq2$ and $t \le 11$. This yields a classification of self-orthogonal codes of minimum weight $k$ whose codewords of minimum weight form a $t$-design under the same conditions.

state.text:
Title: Critical-level wave absorption controls chaos in a wave--mean flow system

Abstract:
Wave-mean flow interactions in stratified fluids can drive spontaneous oscillations, yet the mechanisms controlling transitions between periodic and chaotic regimes remain poorly understood. Using a minimal one-dimensional model of wave-driven mean-flow reversals motivated by the quasi-biennial oscillation (QBO), we identify two distinct mechanisms that suppress the formation of multiple extrema in the velocity profile: critical-level momentum deposition by a broad spectrum of undamped small-scale gravity waves, and wave-amplitude growth due to exponential density stratification. Although physically distinct, both mechanisms inhibit the route to chaos and reduce sensitivity to small-scale viscosity, substantially widening the region of periodic behavior in parameter space. These results identify a general internal mechanism for the stabilization of wave-driven oscillations, with direct implications for QBO-like phenomena in geophysical and astrophysical flows.

The road is classified as Main Road 184 for its entire length.

== Route ==
The Darling Causeway begins as Station Street at the intersection with the Great Western Highway at Mount Victoria, and heads north as the road changes name to the Darling Causeway as it passes the Mount Victoria railway station. The road follows a ridge in the Blue Mountains that it shares with the Blue Mountains Line, which the road parallels for its entire length. The road then terminates at an intersection with the Bells Line of Road and Chifley Road at Bell.
