= Rebel Reid =

Rebel Reid is a Māori musician, guitarist, songwriter and producer from Aotearoa New Zealand. She is known for her work with the South Auckland band Valkyrie and her solo music, including the 2023 EP Hiria. Her music draws on pop rock, blues, soul, folk and country, while her solo work incorporates te reo Māori and English. [ref: Silke Hartung, “Q & A: Catch Up With Valkyrie’s Rebel Reid”. NZ Musician.] [ref: Conor Lochrie, “On ‘Hiria’, Rebel Reid Beautifully Memorialises Her Beloved Mum”. Rolling Stone Australia/New Zealand, 9 August 2023.]

== Early life ==
Rebel Reid was born on 4 June 1987 in Auckland, New Zealand, and grew up in Papatoetoe, South Auckland, with her mother, Leia Reid, who raised her as a solo parent. She attended Papatoetoe High School.

Her mother’s influence continued to shape Reid’s music throughout her career. In 2023, she released the solo EP Hiria in memory of her late mother. The project explores love, loss and remembrance, with the song “Leia” serving as a personal musical tribute to the woman who helped shape her life.

== Career ==

=== Valkyrie ===
Reid is the guitarist and songwriter for Valkyrie, a New Zealand band associated with South Auckland. The group developed a sound combining pop rock and alternative influences with a theatrical performance style. [ref: Sam Carswell, “Vallkyrie: Stirring the Pot”. NZ Musician.]

Reid and vocalist Omer Gilroy had known each other since childhood and later reconnected to pursue music together. Valkyrie subsequently developed its live performance profile and released its debut album, Joyride, in November 2022. [ref: “Aotearoa’s Valkyrie release smash debut album JOYRIDE”. Music Managers Forum Aotearoa, November 2022.]

In October 2023, Reid was included in the lineup for Aotearoa House at SXSW Sydney, a showcase featuring 30 New Zealand artists and supported by Creative New Zealand, Te Māngai Pāho and the New Zealand Music Commission. [ref: Levi Hartnett, “Aotearoa House to Bring 30 Kiwi Artists to SXSW Sydney”. Rolling Stone Australia/New Zealand, 3 October 2023.]

=== Solo career and Hiria ===
In July 2023, Reid released her debut solo EP, Hiria, coinciding with Matariki. The three-track project was dedicated to her late mother and features the songs “Leia”, “Cry Cry Cry” and “Dancing in the Stars”. [ref: “Rebel Reid shines on debut solo EP, ‘Hiria’, in memory of her beloved mum”. Muzic.NZ, 14 July 2023.]

In an interview with Rolling Stone Australia/New Zealand, Reid discussed her mother’s influence on her musical tastes and the personal significance of making Hiria. She described the EP as a gift to her mother and to her people and culture, connecting the release to Matariki and her experience of grief.

The EP blends English and te reo Māori with musical influences including blues, country, folk, pop and rock. Reid also discussed the influence of Witi Ihimaera’s book Navigating the Stars on the songwriting process.

The release received coverage from Rolling Stone Australia/New Zealand, Te Ao Māori News and Muzic.NZ. [ref: Mārena Mane, “Māori musician Rebel Reid releases new EP, an ode to her late mother”. Te Ao Māori News, July 2023.]

=== PROMISELAND ===
Reid is developing a music project titled PROMISELAND, drawing on blues and soul influences. In an August 2026 review of a Play It Strange fundraising concert at Auckland’s Tuning Fork, music journalist Paul Marshall described the blues and soul qualities of Reid’s voice and reported that she performed a song titled “Promised Land”. The review also quoted Reid expressing her ambition to record an album at Sun Records in Memphis, Tennessee. [ref: Paul Marshall, “Play It Strange”. Write Said Paul, 26 August 2026.]

The project’s wider concept, including its planned bilingual songwriting and cinematic elements, has not yet been independently documented in the sources identified for this article.

== Musical style and influences ==
Reid’s musical influences include blues, soul, country, folk, pop and rock. In coverage of Hiria, she discussed growing up listening to artists including Elvis Presley, David Bowie, Billy Idol, Pink Floyd, Queen and Prince. She also cited film composer Hans Zimmer among the music she listened to while recording the EP.

Her work with Valkyrie combines rock and pop influences with theatrical performance, while her solo work explores more personal themes through bilingual songwriting and acoustic arrangements.

Title: A System Dynamics Model for Zero-emission Heavy Vehicle Transition in Australia

Abstract:
What would it take to accelerate the adoption of zero-emission trucks? Even if battery electric trucks become cheaper to own over their lifetime than diesel trucks, that alone is not enough. This study develops a system dynamics model of rigid and articulated truck fleets, calibrated to Australian fleets. Under current policy regimes, more than a third of the fleet still runs on diesel in 2050. Battery and fuel cell trucks become as attractive as diesel trucks only in 2031-2032, held back by slow fleet turnover and by how long operators take to trust the charging network, the most influential assumption tested in this study. Taxing diesel barely works at politically feasible levels. Charging trucks the full fuel excise lifts the zero-emission share by one percentage point; adding ten points would require a road user charge of about 5 AUD per litre, fifteen times the 2025-26 rate. A 70 AUD per tonne carbon price and a purchase subsidy covering 60% of the price premium do little better. Per percentage change in cost, operating-cost support is five to six times as effective as purchase support, yet the best single instrument adds only two percentage points. Only a combined push-pull package, which still raises fuel-tax revenue, shifts the market materially. Policy should stop relying on diesel prices and instead build operators' confidence in the network, cut operating costs and recycle road-charge revenue into infrastructure.

Title: Sample size for proportion on aggregated counts
Tags: sample-size, statistical-power, proportion

Question:
I would like to compare if the proportion of students passing an exam changed over time (both directions considered). I have only aggregated data:

In 2020, 300 students took the exam and 50 passed.
In 2025, 400 students took the exam and 55 passed.

Is there a way to calculate the power of that comparison? Or a sample size to obtain a desired power? If so, would that sample size mean increasing the amount of students is considered in the study? I am quite lost here, as we can't change the fact that one year less students took the exam.

Wiki: English Wikipedia
Draft: John R. Woznicki

Draft text:
John R. Woznicki is a literary scholar and academic administrator whose scholarly work primarily involves twentieth-century American poetry and poetics. Woznicki is the author of Ideological Content and Political Significance of Twentieth-Century American Poetry [ref: John R. Woznicki. Ideological Content and Political Significance of Twentieth-Century American Poetry. Edwin Mellen Press. 2002.] and the edited collection The New American Poetry: Fifty Years Later. [ref: John R. Woznicki ed. The New American Poetry: Fifty Years Later. Lehigh University Press. 2013.]

== Scholarship ==

Woznicki’s first monograph, Ideological Content and Political Significance of Twentieth-Century American Poetry [ref: John R. Woznicki. Ideological Content and Political Significance of Twentieth-Century American Poetry. Edwin Mellen Press. 2002,] is an interdisciplinary examination of politics and ideology in twentieth-century American poetry, drawing upon philosophy, sociology, literary criticism, and cultural studies. It examines the work of Ezra Pound, Charles Olson and the L=A=N=G=U=A=G=E poets, with particular attention to totalitarianism, utopian thought, and political consciousness.

He then edited a collection of essays and wrote the introductory chapter for The New American Poetry: Fifty Years Later, [ref: John R. Woznicki ed. The New American Poetry: Fifty Years Later. Lehigh University Press. 2013,] a collection of scholarly essays reassessing Donald Allen’s influential 1960 anthology The New American Poetry 1945–1960. [ref: Donald Allen ed. The New American Poetry 1945–1960. Grove Press. 1960.] Woznicki’s collection considers the anthology's formation, its modernist antecedents, poets and movements represented in it, and its subsequent literary and cultural influence. A paperback edition was subsequently published in 2015. [ref: John R. Woznicki ed. The New American Poetry: Fifty Years Later. Lehigh University Press. 2015.]

== Reception ==

Orchid Tierney reviewed Woznicki’s volume in the Journal of Modern Literature. [ref: Orchid Tierney. “Back to the Future of Poetry? A Review of The New American Poetry: Fifty Years Later." Journal of Modern Literature, vol. 40, no. 1, 2016, pp. 164–168. DOI:10.2979/jmodelite.40.1.09.]  Tierney characterizes the collection more broadly as an investigation of tradition-building and the reasons Allen's anthology remained relevant to poets, readers, and scholars of innovative writing.

Choice Reviews recommended The New American Poetry: Fifty Years Later. The review discusses aspects of the legacy of Allen’s anthology, including women poets, the British avant-garde, the long poem, and Language poetry. [ref: John. R Woznicki.The New American Poetry: Fifty Years Later. Bloomsbury Book Page. Bloomsbury Publishing. https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/new-american-poetry-9781611462142/.]

Patrick James Dunagan reviewed The New American Poetry: Fifty Years Later in the journal Your Impossible Voice. [ref: Patrick James Dunagan. Review: The New American Poetry: Fifty Years Later, edited by John R. Woznicki. Your Impossible Voice. ISSN #2327-381X. https://yourimpossiblevoice.com/review-new-american-poetry-fifty-years-later-john-r-woznicki-ed/.] Dunagan considers Woznicki’s introductory argument and the volume's attempt to move critical discussion beyond the original construction of Allen's anthology toward questions concerning its reception, cultural influence, and continuing relationship to contemporary poetry.

In discussing Donald Allen and the historical significance of The New American Poetry, Stephanie Anderson directs readers to scholarship concerning Allen's anthology and includes Woznicki's collection alongside work by Alan Golding and Stephan Delbos. [ref: Stephanie Anderson. “‘It's Only Vanity if It's Not Good’: Daisy Aldan and Women Midcentury Small Press Publishers.” Post45, 2024.]

In his book titled The New American Poetry and Cold War Nationalism, Delbos identifies Woznicki’s volume in his discussion of prior scholarship on Allen’s anthology, citing essays from the collection throughout his study. Delbos engages Woznicki’s own interpretation of Charles Olson. In the chapter “This Thing Is Most National: Nationalism and Assimilation in The New American Poetry,” Delbos discusses Woznicki's interpretation of correspondence from Olson as revealing Olson's conception of his American poetic identity in relation to the European cosmopolitan tradition associated with figures such as Ezra Pound and T. S. Eliot. Delbos argues that the passage can be taken further by examining the nationalism underlying Olson's position. [ref: Stephan Delbos.The New American Poetry and Cold War Nationalism. Modern and Contemporary Poetry and Poetics series. Palgrave Macmillan, 2021. p. 135.]

Site: Physics Stack Exchange
Title: Transport properties along reciprocal lattice vectors in non-orthogonal unit cells — physical direction vs geometric direction?
Tags: condensed-matter, solid-state-physics, fourier-transform, crystals, electronic-band-theory

Question:
I’m trying to clarify a point about reciprocal lattice vectors in non-orthogonal unit cells.
For a non-orthogonal lattice, the reciprocal lattice vectors $\mathbf{b}_1$, $\mathbf{b}_2$, $\mathbf{b}_3$ are defined as usual:
$$
\mathbf{b}_1 = 2\pi \frac{\mathbf{a}_2 \times \mathbf{a}_3}{\mathbf{a}_1 \cdot (\mathbf{a}_2 \times \mathbf{a}_3)},\quad
\mathbf{b}_2 = 2\pi \frac{\mathbf{a}_3 \times \mathbf{a}_1}{\mathbf{a}_1 \cdot (\mathbf{a}_2 \times \mathbf{a}_3)},\quad
\mathbf{b}_3 = 2\pi \frac{\mathbf{a}_1 \times \mathbf{a}_2}{\mathbf{a}_1 \cdot (\mathbf{a}_2 \times \mathbf{a}_3)}.
$$
In this case, $\mathbf{b}_1$ is generally not parallel to $\mathbf{a}_1$. My question is about the physical meaning when studying electronic transport properties (e.g., effective mass, mobility) along $\mathbf{b}_1$ in momentum space:

Do these properties correspond to the real-space $\mathbf{a}_1$ direction (i.e., along the lattice vector defining the periodicity)? Because of the Bloch theorem, $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_1$ are dual in the sense of Fourier transform.

Or to the geometric direction of b₁ in real space (i.e., perpendicular to the $\mathbf{a}_2$–$\mathbf{a}_3$ plane, the literal direction of the reciprocal vector)?

Or there is even no corresponding real space direction at all.

In other words, when we compute properties along $\mathbf{k}$ = $\mathbf{b}_1$ in the Brillouin zone, which real-space direction does this really correspond to?
I’m looking for derivations in solid-state physics or electronic structure theory that clarify this distinction.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: What is the motivation for the definition of $\omega$-sets?
Tags: category-theory, soft-question, computational-mathematics, topos-theory, constructive-mathematics

Question:
At the CatDat project, we're currently looking into adding the effective topos to the database. As the definition just of objects and morphisms of that category gets fairly complex already, we thought as a first step we could take a look at simpler subcategory of $\omega$-sets, $\omega{-}\mathbf{Set}$ (otherwise known as the category of assemblies $\mathrm{Asm}(\mathcal{K}_1)$ where $\mathcal{K}_1$ is Kleene's first partial combinatory algebra). In this category, an object (an $\omega$-set) is a pair $(X, R_X)$ where $X$ is a set and $R_X \subseteq \mathbb{N} \times X$ is a "realization" relation such that $(p_2)_*(R_X) = X$, i.e. every element of $X$ is "realized" by some natural number $n$. And then, a morphism $(X, R_X) \to (Y, R_Y)$ is a function $X \to Y$ such that there exists a partial recursive function $\varphi : \mathbb{N} \dashrightarrow \mathbb{N}$ such that whenever $(n, x) \in R_X$, then $\varphi(n)$ is defined and $(\varphi(n), f(x)) \in R_Y$. (Note that this partial recursive function, which I'll call a "realizer transformer compatible with $f$", is not part of the data of the morphism; only the existence of at least one is required.)

Among the interesting properties of this category are that it's a quasitopos but not an elementary topos; it has a natural numbers object but one which is not a countable copower of the terminal object, and in fact no countable copower of the terminal object even exists (and therefore the category is not cocomplete); and similarly the category is not complete.

However, in all of the references on the effective topos that I've been able to find, I haven't been able to find a motivation for why these objects in particular are interesting to study. The only motivation I've seen is that in the end, the effective topos (which can be formed as the ex/reg completion of $\omega{-}\mathbf{Set}$) has internal logic with desirable properties reflecting Brouwer's interpretation of intuitionism. However, we were hoping there might be a simpler motivation of $\omega{-}\mathbf{Set}$ that could be provided without requiring reference to the more complex category of the effective topos.

In particular, the language of "realization relation", i.e. "$n$ realizes $x$" for $(n, x) \in R_X$, suggests that there might be some intuitive interpretation behind that language. However, as I said, none of the references I've found explain any such meaning behind the term "realize".

Here are a couple examples I've come up with of possibly interesting concrete $\omega$-sets:

One is where the underlying set is $\mathbb{R}$. To define a realization relation, we fix an enumeration of the open intervals whose endpoints are rational numbers; and then define $n$ to realize $x$ exactly when $x$ is in the $n$th interval. Then for $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, a compatible realizer transformer would correspond to a sound approximation of $f$ in terms of "interval arithmetic". However, this example has the drawback that it only treats soundness, and says nothing about any tightness of the resulting approximation which you would typically be interested in, and it doesn't even include any "continuity" property that as the input interval shrinks to 0 diameter, you would usually want the output interval to shrink to 0 diameter as well.

Another is where the underlying set is the set of computable reals. One possible realization relation (taking off from the construction of reals as equivalence classes of "almost homomorphisms" $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$) is that the realizers of a computable real $x$ are pairs $\langle p, R \rangle := \binom{p+R+1}{2} + R$ where $p$ is a code for a full recursive function $f : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ and $R$ is a uniform upper bound for $|f(m+n) - f(m) - f(n)|$, such that $\frac{f(n)}{n} \to x$ as $n \to \pm \infty$. Then many of the standard real analytic functions should induce morphisms related to this object. (Such things as the reciprocal and Heaviside step functions would be notable exceptions; for those, you would need to restrict the domain to the nonzero computable reals, and augment realizers with an "effective proof" of the nonzero real being separated from 0, e.g. maybe a triple $\langle p, R, n \rangle$ where $p$ and $R$ are as before and $|f(n)| \ge 2R$.)

(And then, if you're interested in working with the almost homomorphisms themselves and in tracking bounds on $|f(n) - g(n)|$ where $f$ and $g$ are equivalent, then that could provide a motivation for wanting to add effective quotients of a PER where there are also realizers of the equivalences, motivating the construction of the effective topos...)

However, I haven't worked with the definitions enough to know whether either of these examples is in fact anywhere close to the sort of object that's contemplated as a "typical" $\omega$-set which is interesting to work with.

Title: What Paid Triangles Identify about Reserve Uncertainty: Information Boundaries in Loss Reserving

Abstract:
Paid triangles identify some components of reserve uncertainty while others enter through modelling assumptions. We distinguish population identification, recovery by free accident-year-level and two-stage second-moment fits, and precision at practical triangle sizes. In a compound frequency--severity hierarchy, the population law identifies the row dispersion governing non-diversifying reserve variance. With one free level per accident year, its profile likelihood attains its supremum only at homogeneity: the levels absorb realised row heterogeneity on every triangle, in amounts and in counts. Anchoring reopens this channel, but supplies only one observation per accident year. On a $10 \times 10$ triangle the anchored estimate remains uncertain by a factor of several. Within-row allocation dispersion survives conditioning on row totals and hence survives free levels. In the predictive experiments, the treatment of mean-structure estimation error separated the procedures by several times more than the choice among plausible variance laws. A law of the correct form improved coverage only when its dispersion came from a prior instead of the free-level fit. On an outcome-free Schedule~P panel, no amount-only procedure approaches nominal coverage. Strongly one-sided misses reveal a displacement of realised reserves relative to the fitted predictive centres that changing the amount-only variance law cannot repair.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: Solve for integer solutions of $x^3+1=2y^2$
Tags: number-theory, contest-math, elliptic-curves, pell-type-equations

Question:
Solve for integer solutions of $x^3+1=2y^2$. This is a mathematical olympiad problem which I didn't solve in contest, and I'd like to see an elementary solution (explicitly including the method of field extension).

The solutions are probably the trivial ones, plus $(23, \pm 78)$.

I've seen the solutions of $x^3-1=2y^2$ here, but this equation is in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{2}]$, which has non-trivial units, which makes it much harder.

Here is my current thought process (might be overcomplicating things):

$(x+1)(x^2-x+1)=2y^2$

$\gcd(x+1, x^2-x+1) \mid 3$

(1) when $\gcd=1$, $x+1=2u^2, x^2-x+1=v^2$, and the case is trivial.

(2) when $\gcd=3$, $x+1=6u^2, x^2-x+1=3v^2$,

$(2v)^2-3(4u^2-1)^2=1$

Let
$\alpha = 2 + \sqrt{3}, \beta = 2 - \sqrt{3}$, then this is a Pell equation with generating sequence $a_i=\frac{\alpha^t + \beta^t}{2}, b_i=\frac{\alpha^t-\beta^t}{2\sqrt{3}}$.

It is obvious that $a_{i+2}=4a_{i+1}-a_i, b_{i+2}=4b_{i+1}-b_i$.

We can let $4u^2-1=b_t$, then it is easily proved that $t$ is even.

Let $t=2s$, then $4u^2=b_{2s}+1=2a_sb_{s+1}$, hence $a_sb_{s+1}=2u^2$.

$\gcd(a_s, b_{s+1})=\gcd(a_s, a_sb_1+a_1b_s)=\gcd(a_s, a_1) \mid a_1=2$

When $\gcd=1$, there is no solutions by $\mod 4$ on sequences $a_i, b_i$.

Hence $\gcd=2$, and so we can let $a_s=2m^2, b_{s+1}=4n^2$.

So this problem becomes a problem on occurrences of squares in linear recurrent sequences, which I still don't know how to solve.

Draft: Alessandro Giannì

Draft text:
Alessandro Giannì (born 12 August 1989) is an Italian contemporary artist whose work encompasses painting, sculpture and multimedia art. [ref: Alessandro Giannì, Quadriennale di Roma] [ref: La Cina come ponte visivo tra pittura e AI. Intervista all'artista Alessandro Giannì, Artribune]

== Biography and work ==
As a painter, sculptor and multimedia artist, Giannì works across traditional media and digital forms, exploring the relationships between painting, sculpture, artificial intelligence and new technologies. A central concern of his practice is the image as an element in continual transformation, moving between physical and virtual states. His work also examines the relationship between contemporary images and historical iconography, reinterpreted through technological tools and digital processes. [ref: Le visioni in transizione di Alessandro Giannì sono in mostra a Modena, Artribune]

In 2014, he participated in Ñewpressionism, an exhibition introduced by Miltos Manetas at the Istituto Svizzero in Milan. Other participating artists included Sylvie Fleury, Olivier Mosset, Petra Cortright, Amalia Ulman, Luca Pozzi and Jon Rafman. [ref: Ñewpressionism in Milan, 1,11,111. From screen to nature and back again, Istituto Svizzero] During the 73rd Venice International Film Festival in 2016, he worked as art director on EGH, a project by Enrico Ghezzi and Emiliano Montanari. [ref: Alessandro Giannì, Tang Contemporary Art]

In 2019, Giannì began developing a custom artificial-intelligence system named VASARI, intended to emulate aspects of his creative and compositional process by generating digital sketches that he would subsequently develop into oil paintings. [ref: Lo squarcio: luci e ombre nella pittura di Alessandro Giannì, Balloon Project] [ref: Alessandro Giannì “Due to the Image”, Italian Cultural Institute of New York]

He was among the founders of Spaziomensa in 2020, an independent artist-run cultural space in Rome. [ref: Nuovi artist run space: nasce a Roma spaziomensa, Artribune] [ref: Vera: Roma, 8 spazi, 54 studi, Quodlibet]

In 2021, he presented the solo exhibition Due to the Image at Postmasters Gallery in New York City. It included paintings developed with the aid of VASARI and was accompanied by a publication featuring a critical text by Renato Miracco.

He held his first solo exhibition in Asia in 2023, Breaking Darkness, at Tang Contemporary Art in Bangkok. [ref: Alessandro Giannì: Breaking Darkness, Tang Contemporary Art] In 2024, he participated in The Power of Painting at the ENNOVA Art Museum in Langfang, China, exhibiting alongside artists including Marlene Dumas, Anish Kapoor, Bernard Frize, Christopher Le Brun and Jörg Immendorff. [ref: Alessandro Giannì, Tang Contemporary Art]

In 2025, Giannì held his second solo exhibition in Asia, Multiple Unrealities, at Tang Contemporary Art in Hong Kong. [ref: Alessandro Giannì Solo Exhibition: Multiple Unrealities, Tang Contemporary Art] Later that year, he opened a solo exhibition at Galleria Mazzoli in Modena, founded by gallerist Emilio Mazzoli.

During this period, his work increasingly explored painting as a means of seeing and as a kind of "screen" on which images are generated and reworked through processes combining pictorial language, visual memory and digital systems. The perceptual dimension of images and the use of algorithmic tools became particular areas of interest. [ref: Per Alessandro Giannì, la pittura accade quando l'immagine incontra lo sguardo, Exibart]

In 2026, Giannì presented the solo exhibition Eterno Antico at the Aurora Art Museum in Shanghai. [ref: Mostra “Eterno Antico” di Alessandro Giannì all'Aurora Art Museum di Shanghai, Italian Cultural Institute of Shanghai] In the same year, he exhibited Eco dal confine at the Complesso Monumentale del Purgatorio ad Arco in Naples. [ref: ECO DAL CONFINE di Alessandro Giannì, Complesso Monumentale Purgatorio ad Arco]

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: How to prove this inequality involving a fixed prime and any three rational numbers?
Tags: inequality, metric-spaces, prime-numbers, normed-spaces, irrational-numbers

Question:
Let $p$ be a fixed prime, that is, $p \in \{ 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, \ldots \}$.

Any non-zero rational number $x$ can be written as
$$
x = p^k \times \frac{r}{s}, \tag{0}
$$
where $k$ is an integer $r$ is a non-zero integer, and $s$ is a positive integer. Let us define
$$
\lvert x \rvert_p := p^{-k}. \tag{Definition 0}
$$
Let us define $\lvert 0 \rvert_p$ to be $0$.

Now let $a, b, c$ to be any rational numbers such that
$$
\big\lvert a-c \rvert_p = p^{-m} \tag{1}
$$
and
$$
\big\lvert c-b \rvert_p = p^{-n}. \tag{2}
$$

Then how to show that
$$
\big\lvert a-b \big\rvert_p \leq \max \left\{ p^{-m}, p^{-n} \right\}? \tag{3}
$$

My Attempt:

From (1) and (2), we have
$$
a-c = p^m \times \frac{r}{s} \tag{4}
$$
and
$$
c-b = p^n \times \frac{u}{v}, \tag{5}
$$
where $r$ and $u$ are some integers and $s$ and $v$ are some positive integers such that neither $r$ and $u$ nor $s$ and $v$ are divisible by $p$.

Now adding (4) and (5), we get
$$
a-b = p^m \times \frac{r}{s} + p^n \times \frac{u}{v}.
$$

Now there are the following three cases according to whether $m < n$, $m = n$, or $m > n$.

How to proceed from here?

Of course if
$$
\big\lvert a-b \big\rvert_p = p^{-l},
$$
then (3) says that
$$
p^{-l} \leq \max \left\{ p^{-m}, p^{-n} \right\},
$$
which is equivalent to saying that

$$
\text{either } \qquad p^{-l} \leq p^{-m} \qquad \text{or } \qquad p^{-l} \leq p^{-n},
$$
which in turn is equivalent to saying that
$$
\text{either } \qquad p^{l} \geq p^{m} \qquad \text{or } \qquad p^{l} \geq p^{n}.
$$

state.text:
Title: Hilton-Zhao vertex-splitting conjecture for triangle-free graphs

Abstract:
Every graph obtained from a regular Class $1$ graph by a vertex-splitting is overfull and hence is of Class $2$; the central question is whether the resulting graph is edge-chromatic critical. We consider a revised version of the Hilton-Zhao vertex-splitting conjecture for triangle-free base graphs, excluding the known cubic exception that arises from the Wagner graph. Let $G$ be a connected $n$-vertex triangle-free $Δ$-regular Class $1$ graph, and let $G^{*}$ be obtained from $G$ by splitting one vertex into two adjacent vertices. We first show that any non-extreme vertex-splitting produces a $Δ$-critical graph provided $Δ>\frac{n-1}{3}$. Consequently, for non-extreme vertex-splittings, the revised version of the conjecture is valid across its entire conjectured degree range, and indeed even under a slightly weaker degree condition. We next turn to arbitrary vertex-splittings, extreme ones included. It is shown that $G^*$ is $Δ$-critical provided $n \ge 10$ and $Δ>\frac{2n-3}{5}$. In addition, for $n>24$, the non-strict condition $Δ\ge \frac{2n-3}{5}$ is already sufficient. This extends the bipartite range $Δ>\frac{2n}{5}$ to the boundary range that the bipartite argument does not cover. In particular, our arguments give a complete treatment of the case of triangle-free $6$-regular base graphs in the conjectured range. The proofs bring together structural properties of full-deficiency pairs, homomorphism theorems for dense triangle-free graphs, and Hamilton decompositions built via graph detachment.

Title: The Prior-Force Family of Implicit Denoiser Priors and Its Decisions in Linear Inverse Problems

Abstract:
Implicit priors given by Gaussian denoisers successfully regularize a wide range of inverse problems in approaches such as plug-and-play (PnP), regularization by denoising (RED) and score-based methods. Such a prior depends on the noise level, and how it selects among signals consistent with the data remains largely uncharacterized. To put implicit and explicit priors on the same footing, we define the prior-force family $W_t=t^{-1}(D_t^{-1}-I)$ of any Gaussian denoiser $D_t$ at noise variance $t>0$ (inverse in the graph sense), the normalized denoising residual as an operator on clean signals. At a common effective prior weight, the equilibrium equations differ only in their prior terms: PnP uses $W_t$, RED/score-based methods the score force (the normalized residual as an operator on noisy inputs), and maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation the MAP force (the negative log-prior gradient). For the minimum mean-square error (MMSE) denoisers of a prior $π$, we compare the corresponding energies at three levels. Without observation, raising the noise level favors PnP minima that retain more posterior variance. On signals consistent with the data, the leading-order PnP energy for separated modes is the proximal hull of the MAP energy, which lets PnP select signals between modes; modes of equal data fit are ranked by peak height at small noise levels and by mass at large ones. For recovery, $W_t$ at the truth bounds the local bias, and an oracle noise level balances this bias against denoiser error. These results show that the noise level is a parameter of the prior rather than a step size. Experiments with exact priors support these predictions, including the mixture components that PnP selects on unseen data.

Title: Finite-State Time-Inhomogeneous Markov Chains Conditioned to Survive

Abstract:
We study conditioning on long survival for time-inhomogeneous Markov chains on finite state spaces. We assume that a sequence of substochastic transition kernels converges to an irreducible substochastic kernel and that the transition probabilities admit asymptotic expansions up to order $n^{-2}$. Under these assumptions, we construct a positive space-time harmonic function and prove that the limiting path distributions under conditioning on long survival are given by the corresponding Doob h-transform. We also investigate the long-time behavior of the resulting conditioned process. Finally, we apply our general theory to an elephant random walk, a generalized Pólya urn model, time-inhomogeneous Wright--Fisher and Moran models, and noncolliding random walks.

Title: Minor revisions stuck with editor for a long time
Tags: peer-review, editors, publishers, humanities

Question:
I submitted a manuscript to a good Q1 journal (humanities), and the timeline has been the following one:

9 months after submission, the editor sent a single review requesting a minor revision.

3 months after I submitted the revision, the editor sent the revision out for further review. In about a month, 2 reviews were completed.

2 months after the completion of the reviews, another minor revision was requested. Reviewer 1 (from the first round) suggested publication. Reviewer 2 (newly-invited) had very positive things to say with minor comments to address.

I submitted the 2nd revision in a few days and it has now been with the editor for over 3 months. No status change has been made in the submission tracking system, which means the editor has likely not begun evaluating the revision yet. I sent two polite status update requests to an editorial assistant over the last 3 months, but nothing has changed.

Overall, the two minor revisions have been awaiting editor's attention for over 6 months in total.

I understand that editors are busy people, but looking at other papers getting published in the same journal, I haven't seen any one with a timeline between submission and publication being this long - for most papers it's about 50% of that. Is there something I should be doing about this, or just accept it as a realistic standard deviation and wait it out?

Draft: Mary Halsey

Draft text:
Mary Halsey is an American viral video performer known as Missy Elliott's "Funky White Sister" after a July 2018 karaoke performance of Elliott's song "Work It" at Goddard Park in Warwick, Rhode Island, was widely shared online and praised by Elliott. [ref: Watch Missy Elliott perform with "funky white sister" Mary Halsey, NME] [ref: Missy Elliott Praises Rhode Island Woman's Viral Rendition of "Work It", Exclaim!] She subsequently performed "Work It" on The Ellen DeGeneres Show on 13 September 2018, where Elliott surprised her on stage for a duet, performed live on Good Morning Britain, and served as a red-carpet correspondent for Ellen at the American Music Awards in October 2018 and the Grammy Awards in February 2019.

== Early life and background ==
Rhode Island Monthly identified Halsey's hometown as LeRoy, New York. She has sung karaoke since 1989. "Work It" became her regular karaoke song after a 2003 contest; she told Ellen DeGeneres that the positive reaction led her to study the lyrics until it became her go-to song. In 2018 she was working as a recreation assistant at Genesis HealthCare's Coventry Center in Rhode Island.

== Viral breakthrough in 2018 ==
In July 2018, Halsey performed "Work It" at "Karaoke Sunday" in Goddard Park, Warwick, Rhode Island, holding a shofar. Her best friend Pamela Wilsey filmed the performance, and Halsey posted it to Facebook that evening. The nickname "Missy's funky white sister" was Halsey's own self-description in her act, which Elliott adopted and amplified when she shared and praised the video on 8 August 2018.

Exclaim! reported that Elliott was among more than 7 million people who had viewed the performance, and quoted Elliott's post describing Halsey as her "FUNKY WHITE SISTER" and saying she "straight killed 'Work It' sound effects and all."

== Television appearances and coverage ==
On 13 September 2018, Halsey appeared on The Ellen DeGeneres Show. She performed "Work It" carrying the shofar, and Elliott surprised her on stage for a duet. [ref: Missy Elliott surprises viral video star who sang "Work It", The FADER] [ref: Missy Elliott Performs "Work It" on 'Ellen' With Viral Video Star, XXL] She received a signed shirt from Elliott and a "Missy's Funky White Sister" jacket from Ellen DeGeneres.

Halsey also performed live on Good Morning Britain. The programme's official clip is titled "Missy Elliot's Funky White Sister, Mary Halsey, Performs Live | Good Morning Britain". [ref: Missy Elliot's Funky White Sister, Mary Halsey, Performs Live, YouTube (Good Morning Britain)]

Two further national items were coverage of the Ellen moment, not separate studio interviews. TODAY published a PopStart video report, "See Missy Elliott surprise viral video star Mary Halsey on 'Ellen'". [ref: See Missy Elliott surprise viral video star Mary Halsey on 'Ellen', TODAY.com] Billboard News published a video segment, "Missy Elliott Surprises Viral Fan Mary Halsey on 'Ellen'". [ref: Missy Elliott Surprises Viral Fan Mary Halsey on 'Ellen', Billboard]

== Red-carpet correspondent work ==
Ellen DeGeneres sent Halsey as a red-carpet correspondent to the American Music Awards on 9 October 2018, accompanied by producer Andy Zenor, and to the Grammy Awards in February 2019. A contemporary American Music Awards report noted that DeGeneres sent Halsey to the AMAs as her special correspondent. [ref: The 46th Annual American Music Awards, Cal Times] Official Ellen videos document both assignments. [ref: Mary Halsey at the American Music Awards (Ellen), YouTube (The Ellen Show)] [ref: Mary Halsey at the Grammys (Ellen), YouTube (The Ellen Show)] In a second studio appearance on Ellen on 30 January 2019, Halsey performed "Anaconda" and received two Grammy tickets.

== Later work and recognition ==
Rhode Island Monthly named Halsey one of its Top Ten Rhode Islanders of the Year in its December 2018 issue. From 6 February 2019, she hosted "Skyline Karaoke Idol" on Wednesdays at Skyline at Waterplace in Providence. She appeared at Creators Live in Branson, Missouri, on 20 June 2020, and hosts The Magic Mary Podcast.

On 15 September 2026, a collaboration video with Nicki Marie was posted on Instagram by nickimarieinc, with Halsey (mary.halsey_) credited as collaborator. [ref: Nicki Marie collaboration reel with Mary Halsey, Instagram]

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: How to prove $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (1 - \tanh(x^2)) \, dx = (\sqrt{2} - 2)\sqrt{\pi}\,\zeta\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$?
Tags: integration, special-functions, riemann-zeta, hyperbolic-functions

Question:
While experimenting with definite integrals in Wolfram Alpha, I stumbled upon a result that evaluates to an absolutely stunning closed form:

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \Big( 1 - \tanh(x^2) \Big) \, dx = (\sqrt{2} - 2)\sqrt{\pi}\,\zeta\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) $$

I am completely blown away by this. We start with a relatively simple-looking integrand involving a hyperbolic tangent, and somehow the exact evaluation yields the Riemann Zeta function evaluated exactly on the critical line ($s = 1/2$).

My partial work:

I wanted to prove this by hand, so I started by rewriting the hyperbolic tangent using its exponential definition: $1 - \tanh(y) = 1 - \frac{e^y - e^{-y}}{e^y + e^{-y}} = \frac{2}{e^{2y} + 1}$.

Applying this to my integral, I got:

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{2}{e^{2x^2} + 1} \, dx $$

Since the integrand is an even function, I integrated from $0$ to $\infty$ and multiplied by $2$:

$$ 4 \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{e^{2x^2} + 1} \, dx $$

Next, I used the substitution $t = 2x^2$, which means $x = \sqrt{\frac{t}{2}}$ and $dx = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} t^{-1/2} dt$. Substituting this in, the integral simplifies nicely to:

$$ \frac{4}{2\sqrt{2}} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{t^{-1/2}}{e^t + 1} \, dt = \sqrt{2} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}(e^t + 1)} \, dt $$

Where I am stuck:

This is where I hit a wall. I can see that the $\sqrt{t}$ in the denominator is likely where the $\sqrt{\pi}$ and the $1/2$ argument for the Zeta function come from, but I don't know how to formally bridge the gap between this simplified integral and the Riemann Zeta function.

Could someone explain the missing steps? What identity or technique is used to turn $\int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{t^{-1/2}}{e^t + 1} \, dt$ into $\zeta(1/2)$?

Any insights into this beautiful connection would be highly appreciated!

Title: On the construction of the Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure
Tags: measure-theory, lebesgue-measure

Question:
While studying the construction of the Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure associated with a non-decreasing and right continuous function $F:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ I am having trouble in understanding something. The author of the notes I'm using starts with the family $\mathcal{E}=\{(a,b]:\; a,b\in \mathbb{R}\}$ of left semi-open bounded intervals and then he considers the outer measure induced by the map $\nu:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow [0,\infty]$ given by $\nu((a,b])=F(b)-F(a)$, and then restricts it to the Borel $\sigma$-algebra in $\mathbb{R}$; so far, so good. But when proving uniqueness, we need the initial measure to be defined on a family that is (at least) an algebra; to save this, the author notes that the family $\mathcal{F}$ of finite disjoint unions of left semi-open intervals, finite or not, in an algebra containing $\mathcal{E}$, and that every measure on the former is determined by its values on the elements of the latter. It is then claimed that $\mathcal{F}$ is even the smallest algebra containing $\mathcal{E}$, and this is what I don't unidestand.

Why is it the smallest? I can see clearly that every algebra containing $\mathcal{E}$ must certainly contain all finite disjoint unions of intervals of the form $(a,b]$, and surely all unions of these and sets of the form $(-\infty, a]\cup (b,\infty)$, these being the complements of our intervals $(a,b]$. But why must it contain the individual pieces $(-\infty,a]$ or $(b, \infty)$? As far as I can check, these cannot be obtained has finite unions of bounded intervals.

One solution that came to my mind was to consider instead the family $\mathcal{E}=\{(a,b],\; -\infty\leq a<b<\infty\}\cup \{\emptyset\}$, and define $\nu$ as $\nu(a,b]=F(b)-F(a)$ if $a\in \mathbb{R}$ and $\nu(-\infty, b]=F(b)-\lim_{x\rightarrow -\infty} F(x)$. Then the family $\mathcal{F}$ decribed above is indeed the smallest algebra containing $\mathcal{E}$, but as the construction of this measure is everywhere stated in terms of bounded intervals, I wondered if I am missing something.

Thank you all in advance.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: Example of ring where $n\cdot a\neq na$
Tags: abstract-algebra, ring-theory

Question:
In Gallian's Contemporary Abstract Algebra he gives the following sidenote when defining rings that had me scratching my head for why such a note would be necessary.

Recall that if $a$ is an element from a group under the operation of addition and $n$ is a positive integer, $na$ means $a+a+\ldots+a$, where there are $n$ summands. When dealing with rings, this notation can cause confusion, since we also use juxtaposition for the ring multiplication. When there is the potential for confusion, we will use $n\cdot a$ to mean $a+a+\ldots+a$ ($n$ summands).

I cannot think of an example where such confusion would happen, and as far as I can tell, Gallian never brings up an example where he needs to appeal to this convention for distinguishing $na$ and $n\cdot a$. If we consider an example like a matrix ring, $nA=\underbrace{A+\ldots+A}_{n-\text{times}}$, and $nA$ here does not denote ring multiplication. However, no ambiguity arises in whether we mean ring multiplication or repeated summation since $n$ is clearly not an element of the ring (and thus not a candidate for ring multiplication).

Can anyone think of an example that has "the potential for confusion?"

"Marcia,

I'm not trying to start a fight, but the naturopath you're seeing is selling you snake oil. She takes a 'bioenergetic photograph' of your fingertips, sees a dim patch on the ring finger, and tells you your liver is failing? That is Kirlian photography with a new label.

The glow in those pictures depends on how sweaty your fingers are, how hard you press on the film, and the room humidity. Controlled studies where the same patient was imaged twice an hour apart got completely different 'diagnoses.' None of them have ever predicted a disease that later showed up on a blood panel.

If you're actually worried about your liver, ask your GP for an ALT/AST test and a hepatitis screen. It's cheap and it means something. Please don't skip your regular checkups because a glowing fingertip said you were fine.

-- Dan"

Abstract:
For $1\leq p\leq n/2$, we derive sharp eigenvalue estimates for the Hodge Laplacian on differential $p$-forms under the curvature condition introduced by Petersen and Wink, and study their equality cases. state.text:
Title: Leveraging Recourse and Size Bounds for OnlineKnapsack with Removable Items

Abstract:
In the online unweighted knapsack problem, items arrive sequentially and must be accepted or rejected immediately for a bounded-capacity knapsack, aiming to maximize the total size of accepted items. When decisions are irrevocable, no algorithm achieves a non-trivial competitive ratio. An essential relaxation that circumvents this impossibility is to allow previously accepted items to be removed from the knapsack (a.k.a. removal). In this work, we investigate possible further improvements on the competitive ratio with removal by bringing together two other previously proposed model extensions: knowledge of an upper bound on the item sizes (a.k.a. bound awareness) and ability to reinsert previously rejected items(a.k.a.recourse). Our contributions are twofold. First, we establish close upper and lower bounds on the competitive ratio under bound awareness, removal and recourse. We show that significant improvements on the best known competitive ratio are possible when the upper bound on the item sizes is not too restrictive and only few uses of recourse are available. Second, we introduce the notion of adaptive online algorithms which do not require to know any upper bound on the item sizes but still achieve performance guarantees comparable to the ones obtained under the bound awareness model.

Title: Relative homological algebra of filter modules

Abstract:
Over an arbitrary ordered set we consider the class of filter modules, i.e. indicator modules of filters in the ordered set. We show that the induced exact structure of filter modules, the so-called filter exact structure, which has filter modules as relative projective modules, admits an explicit projectivization by the distributive lattice of filters. This allows the reduction of the projective-homological properties of the induced exact structure to the standard homological algebra of $k{\operatorname{Fil}(Q)}$, the incidence algebra of $k$-representations on the lattice of filters. In the case of finite join-semilattices, we leverage the combinatorial structure of the distributive lattice of filters to determine the standard global dimension of $k{\operatorname{Fil}(Q)}$. By virtue of projectivization we provide lower and upper bounds for the global dimension of the filter exact structure. Moreover, we call an ordered set filter-tiny if its relative injective modules one-to-one-correspond to the standard injective modules. We exploit relative derived functors to show that filter-tiny ordered sets do not admit relative injective prehulls if the relative global dimension is larger than 1. It is open to which classes of ordered sets $Q$ the filter-tininess condition applies, and what the relative injective modules are in the case of non-filter-tiny ordered sets.

Title: Complexity of finding color-avoiding connected components

Abstract:
Two vertices of a (not necessarily properly) arc-colored digraph are called arc-$\ell$-color-avoiding strongly $k$-arc-connected if, after the removal of the arcs of any at most $\ell$ colors, they remain strongly $k$-arc-connected. The arc-$\ell$-color-avoiding strongly $k$-arc-connected components are maximal sets of vertices such that any two of those vertices belonging to the set are arc-$\ell$-color-avoiding strongly $k$-arc-connected in the graph. We investigate the problems of finding the arc-$\ell$-color-avoiding strongly $k$-arc-connected components and the maximal arc-$\ell$-color-avoiding strongly $k$-arc-connected subgraphs of an arc-colored digraph. We also consider possible generalizations to $k$-vertex-connectivity and to vertex-colored digraphs. We show that despite the seemingly minor differences in definitions, the complexity of these problems varies significantly: some can be solved in polynomial time, while others are NP-hard. It also turns out that in some cases the problem is NP-hard when multiple colors can be assigned to each vertex, but the problem becomes polynomial-time solvable when each vertex is single-colored.

Title: First and second order firing statistics of large neuronal networks with community structure

Abstract:
We study a discrete-time stochastic model for the spiking activity of a network of $n$ interacting neurons partitioned into $k$ communities. The interaction network is a random directed weighted graph generated by a Stochastic Block Model with $k+1$ edge types ($k$ intra-community, $1$ inter-community). Each edge is present independently with a probability that depends only on its type. When present, an edge carries a type-dependent deterministic weight scaled by $n^{-1}$, which is excitatory or inhibitory depending on an independent random sign. Given the interaction network, the spiking process is a stationary Markov chain. Our results describe how the network's community structure manifests itself in the first- and second-order statistics of this chain, as $n \to \infty$ with $k$ fixed. Representing these statistics as explicit functions of the random interaction network, we prove that, with high probability: (i) the vectors of mean firing activity and firing variances are approximated in supremum norm by deterministic vectors that are constant within each community, with an error of order $\sqrt{\log(n)/n}$; (ii) the off-diagonal part of the $0$-lagged firing covariance matrix is approximated in max norm, with an error of order $\sqrt{\log(n)/n^3}$, by a deterministic community-block matrix (constant on each block defined by a pair of communities), with block values determined by the unique solution to a $k \times k$ Stein matrix equation; (iii) in contrast, the $t$-lagged covariance matrix, for every lag $t \ge 1$, is approximated in max norm, again with an error of order $\sqrt{\log(n)/n^3}$, by a random matrix built from two components: a random matrix capturing the interaction network and a deterministic community-block matrix. Finally, we discuss conditions on the model parameters under which these limiting statistics enable the identifiability of the community structure.

Site: Stats Stack Exchange
Title: How should I compare a 4-point ordinal scale between two independent groups?
Tags: t-test, categorical-data, nonparametric, ordinal-data

Question:
I am working with several variables measured on a discrete scale from 1 to 4, where higher values indicate better outcomes. The scale is structured as follows:

1 = Low level
2 = Intermediate-low
3 = Intermediate-high
4 = High level

So although the values are numeric, the variable is essentially ordinal with only four categories.

I want to compare these variables between two independent groups (e.g., males vs females).

My main doubts are:

Would it be appropriate to use a t-test treating the variable as continuous?
Or should I instead use a non-parametric test such as Mann–Whitney U?
Alternatively, would it be more appropriate to analyze the data as categorical (e.g., chi-square test)?

I am particularly unsure because:

The scale is numeric but has very few categories (1–4)
The distance between categories may not be truly equal

What would be the most appropriate approach in this situation, and how would you justify it?

Answer A:
Your variables are definitively ordinal. Therefore a t-test is absolutely not appropriate (and not because your variables are not continuous -t-tests work on discrete variables- but because they are not interval or ratio scale).

So the most basic would indeed be a non-parametric Mann Whitney U test (MWUt). But in fact not a MWUt, but a Brunner-Munzel test (BMt), because the MWUt suffers from the Behrens-Fisher problem (even when the sample sizes are balanced!), and the BMt corrects for this. Think of the BMt as being to the MWUt what the Welch t-test is to the standard t-test. In fact many authors recommend always using the BMt instead of the MWUt, whether the variances and/or sample sizes are "close" or not (e.g. here).

I would also not use a $\chi^2$ test, as this treats the variables as categorical, and loses a lot of information (e.g. that 4 is more than 3 - we do not know how much more, but "more" it is).

You may be tempted to agregate levels 1 and 2 (low), and 3 and 4 (high), and then use tests for categorical variables ($\chi^2$, Clopper-Pearson, etc.), but that should not help with power (again, information is lost).

You could also use an ordinal logistic regression, but this would be preferrable only if you have more than 1 predictor. As stated, you seem to have only 1 predictor (sex).

Last, you mention "several variables". That implies several BMts, which therefore will require some Multiple Comparison Correction (MCC).

Answer B:
If I just had to model the categories and wanted a model that can predict probability of being in each category, then I'd go with an ordinal logistic regression (and you can introduce interactions etc. to avoid the assumption of the odds going from one category to the next always being the same).

If you want to compare things, one can argue that it makes the most sense to determine how important people feel being in each state is (ideally you'd even have everyone having similar opinions), i.e. determine a utility function. There's a nice recent podcast episode that discusses this and the criticisms thereof, which seemed to center to on the subjectivity and that not everyone would rate the different states the same. On the other hand, they point out that other models (linear regression, ordinal logistic regression) have their own implicit utility functions.

Of course, in practice, it is unclear that a non-randomized comparison of male vs. female (or smoker vs. non-smoker, or unversity degree vs. not) makes sense for answering a meaningful quesiton. I assume your example is more a placeholder, but the answer above without anything else added really only works for a randomized trial. For anything else, you need to figure out what else needs to be done to actually adress a practically relevant question (e.g. matching on relevant characteristics, propensity score methods...).

Title: Treatment of an heir’s enforceable claim (opeisbare vordering) under Dutch inheritance law
Tags: civil-law, tax-law, inheritance, netherlands, succession

Question:
Under Dutch civil law, how is a valid and documented debt owed by the deceased to one of the heirs treated when calculating the estate and the forced share (legitieme portie)?

Consider the following hypothetical situation:

During the deceased’s lifetime, one of the heirs performed work and
issued invoices for those services.

These invoices constitute a legitimate, enforceable claim (opeisbare
vordering) under Dutch civil law.

At the moment of death, the claim is still outstanding.

The heir is therefore both a creditor of the estate and an heir.

I am trying to understand how Dutch inheritance law treats this dual position.

Questions:

Is the outstanding claim treated as a normal debt of the estate,
meaning it must be paid before calculating the net estate?

When calculating the forced share (legitieme portie) of another
heir, is the net estate reduced by the full amount of this debt?

If the debt exceeds the available assets, does the forced share
become zero because the net estate is zero or negative?

Does the creditor‑heir receive payment up to the available assets,
and is any remaining unpaid portion of the claim extinguished?

Is the creditor‑heir required to pay inheritance tax over the amount
received as repayment of the debt?

If another heir accepts the inheritance (either purely or
beneficiair), do they ever become personally liable for the debt, or
is liability always limited to the estate assets?

I am looking for a technical explanation of how Dutch civil law handles this situation, specifically regarding:

treatment of debts owed to heirs

calculation of the forced share

priority of creditors

and tax consequences for the creditor‑heir

state.text:
Title: Physically Constrained Kinematic Calibration for High-Precision Robotic Needle Guidance

Abstract:
Percutaneous needle insertion is a common practice in minimally invasive procedures whose clinical success depends on accurate needle placement. However, achieving the necessary precision is a challenge for manual operators. Robotic assistance can improve targeting accuracy and reduce operator dependence, but residual millimeter-scale errors persist because nominal kinematic models do not fully represent the physical manipulator. This paper presents a robust bound-constrained kinematic calibration method designed to improve positional accuracy for a 6-Degree-of-Freedom (6-DoF) robotic needle-guidance manipulator. The approach uses physically plausible parameter ranges to regularize a compact 19-parameter geometric identification model. By treating these bounds as active optimization constraints rather than mere numerical safeguards, the framework effectively mitigates parameter coupling and overfitting, ensuring highly stable parameter identification. In simulation, the proposed method reduced end-effector Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) from 3.422 mm to 0.690 mm (a 79.8% improvement). In benchtop hardware experiments, the calibrated model achieved sub-millimeter validation accuracy, including 0.865 mm RMSE in experimental trajectory validation and 0.610 mm RMSE in a coordinate-lattice verification task. These results demonstrate that physically constrained kinematic calibration can enhance robotic needle-targeting accuracy, establishing a high-precision foundation for future clinical applications.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: What is the minimum area swept underground by a circular arc?
Tags: geometry, optimization, plane-geometry

Question:
Consider a rigid circular arc of radius $r$ and central angle $\theta$, moving in the plane.

Let the $x$-axis represent the ground. Thus the upper half-plane $y>0$ is above the ground and the lower half-plane $y<0$ is underground.

Initially, the arc lies entirely in the upper half-plane. For example, its center can be placed at $(0,r)$, with one endpoint touching the ground.

We are allowed to move and rotate the arc arbitrarily, using any continuous planar rigid motion. The final position must have the entire arc in the lower half-plane.

Define the underground swept area to be the area of the union of all points that are occupied by the arc at some time while those points lie in $y<0$.

Let $A(r,\theta)$ denote the infimum of the underground swept area over all possible motions.

Question: What is $A(r,\theta)$?

Here $\theta$ is the central angle of the arc, with

$$
0<\theta\leq 2\pi.
$$

Some special cases are easy:

If $\theta\leq\pi$ (a semicircular arc or shorter), the swept area can be made $0$: place the center on the ground and rotate the arc by $180^\circ$.

If $\theta=2\pi$, the object is a complete circle. Rotation does not change the circle, and the minimum underground swept area is

$$
2r^2+\frac{\pi r^2}{2}.
$$

The interesting case is therefore

$$
\pi<\theta<2\pi,
$$

where the arc is longer than a semicircle but shorter than a full circle.

Is there a known formula or lower bound for $A(r,\theta)$? Is this problem related to any known swept-area or Kakeya-type problems?

Site: Law Stack Exchange
Title: Would explicitly acknowledging that I chose not to read the Terms and Conditions make them more enforceable?
Tags: contract-law, terms-of-service

Question:
Would explicitly acknowledging that I chose not to read the Terms and Conditions make them more enforceable?

Suppose I run an online service and, before allowing a user to register, I display the following two mutually exclusive options:

○ I have read and agree to the Terms and Conditions.

○ I acknowledge that I have been informed that Terms and Conditions exist, that I have been given access to them, but I choose not to read them.

The user must select one of these options before continuing.

The Terms and Conditions are available through a clearly visible link next to the options, and the user can access them before making their choice.

My question is:

Would the second option make the Terms and Conditions more legally enforceable than a normal "I agree" checkbox?

For example, if the user later claims:

"I didn't know about that clause because I never read the Terms and Conditions."

could the company respond:

"You explicitly confirmed that you knew the Terms and Conditions existed, that you had access to them, and that you deliberately chose not to read them."

Would that make a difference in court?

I am particularly interested in the distinction between:

Consent to the Terms: "I have read and agree to them."

Acknowledgement without reading: "I know they exist and had an opportunity to read them, but deliberately chose not to."

Why I am asking

This question came to mind after the recent Disney wrongful-death lawsuit involving the death of a customer following an allergic reaction at a restaurant at Disney Springs.

Disney initially argued that the plaintiff's claims should be sent to arbitration based, among other things, on an arbitration clause contained in the Disney+ Terms of Service that the plaintiff had previously accepted.

The argument attracted attention because the dispute was unrelated to Disney+, and the plaintiff's use of Disney+ had occurred years before the incident at the restaurant. Disney ultimately withdrew its motion to compel arbitration, so I understand that the court did not ultimately decide the enforceability of that argument on the merits.

This made me wonder about a more general issue: how much does a user's actual awareness of the existence and availability of contractual terms matter?

If a company could show that the user had explicitly acknowledged:

"I know these Terms and Conditions exist, I have been given access to them, and I am choosing not to read them"

would that provide stronger evidence that the user had a reasonable opportunity to become aware of the contractual terms?

Or would the legal effect essentially be the same as simply clicking "I agree"?

[ref: Nantes Université, "Salah EL MONCEF BIN KHALIFA," faculty profile, updated 12 May 2026.] [ref: Jean-Yves Pellegrin, review of Atopian Limits, Transatlantica (2004), DOI 10.4000/transatlantica.707.] [ref: Stephen Watt, "Memory, Trauma, and the Diasporic Subject," Los Angeles Review of Books, 4 April 2015.] [ref: Stephen Watt, "An Enormous, Enigmatic Signifier: Salah el Moncef's Benghazi," Michigan Quarterly Review, January 2023.] [ref: Stephen Watt, "The Art of World-Building: Salah el Moncef's The Woman from Warsaw," Michigan Quarterly Review, 20 February 2026.] [ref: Salah El Moncef, official author site (used only for routine biographical and publication data).]

At Nantes Université, Moncef is a Maître de Conférences in English studies and creative writing, with research interests in contemporary American literature and culture, diasporic literatures, migration and transnational identities. He is the General Issue Editor of Angelaki: Journal of the Theoretical Humanities and an editor of the associated Routledge series Angelaki: New Work in the Theoretical Humanities. Several Angelaki general issues have also used his paintings as cover and interior art. [ref: Nantes Université, institutional profile/CV: maître de conférences in English studies and creative writing; research on diasporic literatures, migration, and transnational identities.] [ref: Taylor & Francis, Angelaki: Journal of the Theoretical Humanities, "About this journal" (editorial team).] [ref: Routledge, Angelaki: New Work in the Theoretical Humanities, series page.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Editorial Introduction: General Issue I 2024." Angelaki 29.5 (2024), artwork list and acknowledgements.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Editorial Introduction: General Issue II 2025." Angelaki 30.6 (2025), artwork list and acknowledgements.]

== Education and academic career ==
A contributor biography published in the academic collection The Matrix in Theory records that Moncef received a Presidential Prize for Distinction in the Humanities in 1987 and was a Fulbright fellow at Indiana University Bloomington from 1988 to 1993. Indiana University lists him among its English PhD alumni, while a University of Colorado contributor profile likewise identifies him as a former Fulbright doctoral fellow there. [ref: University of Colorado Boulder, Genders archive, "Salah El Moncef" contributor profile.] [ref: Myriam Diocaretz and Stefan Herbrechter, eds., The Matrix in Theory (Rodopi, 2006), contributor note for Salah el Moncef bin Khalifa.] [ref: Indiana University Bloomington, Department of English, PhD alumni publications pages.]

Moncef later joined Nantes Université. The university's public profile lists him as a Maître de Conférences in the Department of English and identifies contemporary American literature and culture as his teaching and research field. A more detailed institutional profile describes his work as extending to creative writing, diasporic literature, migration and transnational identities.

== Scholarship and editorial work ==
Moncef's scholarship brings literary and cultural theory to modernist and postmodern American writing. His articles of the 1990s examined Ezra Pound in boundary 2, John Updike's Rabbit at Rest in Arizona Quarterly, Paul Auster's Moon Palace in Angelaki and Thomas Harris's Hannibal Lecter novels in Genders. This line of research was developed in Atopian Limits: Questions of Self, Complexity, and Contingency in Postmodern American Narrative (2002). [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Gold, Representation, and the Reversible Dynamic of Symptomatic Return in Ezra Pound." boundary 2 22.1 (1995): 117–142.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Sounding the Black Box: Linear Reproduction and Chance Bifurcations in Rabbit at Rest." Arizona Quarterly 51.4 (1995): 69–108.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Lecter Knows Worst: Justice, Marginal Value, and the Law in the Series of Thomas Harris's Silence of the Lambs." Genders, 5 July 1999.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Figures in (De)composition: The Genesis of the Paradoxical Self in Paul Auster's Moon Palace." Angelaki 4.3 (1999): 75–91.]

Reviewing Atopian Limits in Transatlantica, Jean-Yves Pellegrin described it as a wide-ranging study of postmodern American narrative organized around systems, limits, ethics and complexity, discussing writers including Paul Auster, Ken Kesey, John Updike, Thomas Harris, Gore Vidal and Kathy Acker. Moncef subsequently co-edited Présence et représentation (2005) with Jacques Gilbert and Borderline Identities in Chicano Culture (2006) with Michele Bottalico. In Aztlán, Antonio C. Márquez reviewed the latter as a collection on border identity and discussed Moncef's concluding contribution, "The Hybrid Self at the Crossroads." [ref: Antonio C. Márquez, review of Borderline Identities in Chicano Culture, Aztlán 32.2 (2007): 213–216.] [ref: WorldCat, bibliographic record for Présence et représentation, Jacques Gilbert and Salah El Moncef (Peter Lang, 2005).]

Title: Letting AI Formulate the Research Question: Autonomous Research Agents

Abstract:
Systems such as The AI Scientist have shown that AI agents can carry out and write up research, but in those demonstrations humans chose the research area and selected the outputs to show. We study letting the AI formulate the research question itself, and we report every run. Our system gives an off-the-shelf coding agent an instruction document and two skills: one for formulating the question, in which the agent diverges from recent technologies into problems of other fields, screens its candidates for known failure modes and obtains a critique from a different model; and one for peer review, in which a reviewer from another model family reruns the study from its records before the agent revises the paper. Over 13 development runs, changes to the one or two sentences that set the research area coincided with large shifts in what the candidate questions and the chosen papers were about, which led us to the area of a new technology applied to a societal problem. We froze the system after a pilot run and report five consecutive runs: the pilot, counted by a disclosed amendment to the pre-registration, and four pre-registered runs. All five runs went from question formulation to a revised, re-computable paper, with local computation on a laptop and no research input from humans, and external AI reviewers reading only the papers judged them at or near workshop level. We release the system, the five papers and the records needed to reproduce them.

state.text:
Title: Early warning of critical transitions: Distinguishing supercritical and subcritical bifurcations from noisy observations

Abstract:
Early-warning methods can indicate that a system is approaching a loss of stability, but they do not usually reveal whether the approaching bifurcation is supercritical or subcritical. We investigate whether this distinction can be made from noisy pre-transition observations. For this investigation, we extend a regression-based stability method by including the leading cubic nonlinear term, whose sign is used to predict the bifurcation type. We test the method on a stochastic pitchfork model and a spatial stochastic Swift-Hohenberg equation. In both models, classification improves with longer observation horizons, closer proximity to the bifurcation, stronger noise, and larger nonlinear effects. However, these conditions are also linked to a higher risk of noise-induced tipping in the subcritical case. The useful early-warning window is therefore determined by a balance between obtaining enough information to identify the bifurcation type and doing so before noise-induced tipping becomes too likely. In spatially extended systems, we find that observing the full spatial field allows classification over shorter observation horizons, and performance improves when a broader range of spatial modes contributes to the observed dynamics. Altogether, we identify the conditions under which the method can reliably distinguish between supercritical and subcritical bifurcations.

state.text:
Title: Model of the instrumental polarization induced by a rotating HWP with anti-reflective sub-wavelength structures for CMB polarimetry

Abstract:
Future CMB polarization experiments require precise control of instrumental systematics in the search for primordial $B$-mode polarization. A rotating half-wave plate (HWP) provides effective polarization modulation, but its non-ideal electromagnetic response can generate HWP-synchronous instrumental polarization. In this work, we characterize the response of a multi-layer sapphire HWP with anti-reflective sub-wavelength structures (SWS) using rigorous coupled-wave analysis. For three asymmetric SWS models, we find no substantial differences in the transmittance, polarization efficiency, or instrumental-polarization response that can be attributed to the type of SWS asymmetry. The fourth-harmonic instrumental polarization relevant to CMB polarization reconstruction is typically of order $10^{-4}$ in the CMB bands, which is expected to be mitigated. We further evaluate an actually fabricated SWS geometry, whose asymmetry enhances the retardance, and compare its response with that of an idealized model having the same type of asymmetry. Comparison of the realistic SWS with the idealized model shows that higher transmittance tends to be associated with lower instrumental polarization. These results suggest that improving the total transmission, including the effect of the fabricated SWS profile, may be more important for reducing HWP-induced instrumental polarization than tuning the SWS asymmetry itself.

Title: Derived products and top-degree inverse limits

Abstract:
We compute top derived products and inverse limits on products of affine lines with doubled origin over $B[s]$, for any nonzero commutative ring $B$. For every $B$-module $M$, the two top obstruction modules fit into an explicit exact sequence and contain $M^{\mathbb N}/M^{(\mathbb N)}$as a natural $B$-module direct summand.This gives exact product dimensions, sharp vanishing bounds for inverse sequences, and faithfulness in the coefficient module. For a Grothendieck category of finite product dimension, we also obtain degree shifts under adjoining commuting locally nilpotent endomorphisms and prove that this construction preserves top-degree vanishing for epimorphic inverse sequences. A fixed Gabriel--Popescu presentation then describes the general top obstruction through actual Ext sequences and separates two module-theoretic terms.

state.text:
Title: RecHash: Segmented Hash-Entangled Chains for Stateful Sequential Authentication

Abstract:
RecHash is a stateful sequential authentication construction based on paired hash-chain openings and an authenticated record history. It develops the decreasing position relation of the 2019 hash-entangled construction, whose exact integer normalization yields a two-coordinate constant-sum antichain. Direct proportional reuse is constrained by integer capacity and multiplicative contraction. The main construction instead assigns each record to a predetermined chain segment, with complementary positions encoding each digest block. All digests fit every scheduled slot, independently of preceding messages. For an $\ell$-bit digest distributed over $k$ equal-length chain pairs, balanced allocation gives $\lfloor L/(2^{\lceil\ell/k\rceil}+1)\rfloor$ slots. A 256-bit digest, 32 pairs, and length 65535 provide 254 application records followed by a renewal certificate, with 2048 bytes of openings per record for 256-bit chain outputs. We give a complete segmented state transition, a worked trace, exact allocation and resource results, and a renewal-free security-composition theorem conditional on authenticated history and an adaptive one-step guarantee. The analysis relates the construction to constant-sum encodings and standardized hash-based signatures; a concrete post-quantum reduction and security across renewal remain open.

Title: On the NP-Hardness of Rank-Metric Minimum Distance and Syndrome Decoding, at Every Rate

Abstract:
In this work, we investigate the hardness of computing minimum distance, as well as the hardness of syndrome decoding, for rank-metric codes. It is known (Gaborit and Zémor, IEEE TIT 2016) that for $\mathbb{F}_{q^m}$-linear rank-metric codes of length $N$, minimum distance when $m=O(N)$ and syndrome decoding when $m=O(N^2)$ are NP-hard under randomized reductions. We obtain a derandomization of these results and a bit more. We show that for any fixed small $\varepsilon>0$, for $\mathbb{F}_{q^m}$-linear rank-metric codes of length $N$ with $m=O(N^{1+\varepsilon})$, the problems of minimum distance, nearest codeword, and syndrome decoding are NP-hard under deterministic reductions. Further, we can prescribe the rate; that is, if we restrict to codes having any fixed rational rate $R\in(0,1)$, then the NP-hardness for all three problems persists. Our main technical contribution is simple, and possibly of independent interest. The reduction of Gaborit and Zémor (IEEE TIT 2016) relies on a distance-preserving embedding of a Hamming-metric code into a rank-metric code, obtained by multiplying its coordinates by a uniformly random vector. We show that we can choose an explicit vector from a slightly larger extension field.

Title: Full-Potential Korringa Kohn Rostoker Study of Structural and Mechanical Properties in SiGeSn Alloys

Abstract:
Accurate first-principles descriptions of open, covalently bonded crystal structures remain challenging within conventional Korringa--Kohn--Rostoker (KKR) approaches owing to the spherical approximations commonly employed for the effective crystal potential. Here, we systematically assess the recently developed full-potential KKR (KKR-FP) implementation in the open-source MuST package and demonstrate its applicability to diamond-structured group-IV semiconductors and SiGeSn alloys. Benchmark calculations for diamond-structured Si reveal substantial limitations of the conventional muffin-tin and atomic sphere approximations, whereas KKR-FP accurately reproduces the experimental equilibrium lattice parameter and bulk modulus, yielding 5.433 and 94.9 GPa. The full-potential treatment also recovers the semiconducting character of Si. Further calculations for elemental Ge and Sn establish the applicability of the approach across group-IV materials. Extending this framework to SiGeSn alloys, we investigate their composition-dependent equilibrium lattice parameters, bulk moduli, and mixing enthalpies. The calculated lattice parameters exhibit positive deviations from Vegard's law, while the bulk modulus decreases substantially with changes in alloy composition. Moreover, positive mixing enthalpies of 180.92 and 346.32 meV/atom are obtained for Si0.5Ge0.375Sn0.125 and Si0.375Ge0.25Sn0.375, respectively, indicating an energetic penalty for homogeneous alloy formation relative to the selected elemental reference states. These findings highlight the importance of nonspherical potential contributions in accurately describing open-structured semiconductors and establish KKR-FP within MuST as a promising framework for investigating the structural properties and mixing energetics of compositionally complex group-IV alloys
