Site: Server Fault
Title: dnsmasq not seeing DHCPDISCOVER
Tags: dhcp, dhcp-server, dnsmasq

Question:
With tcpdump I see incoming DHCPDISCOVER packets from my test client on eth1 but it seems like the dnsmasq DHCP server cannot see them, like they are not being forwarded to the local process. Tried disabling firewall but it makes no difference (it is not blocking broadcast).

Looking for suggestions on what I may have missed and how to troubleshoot this further.

From dnsmasq config:

interface=eth1
dhcp-range=eth1,[ip],[ip],1h
dhcp-authoritative
log-dhcp

Client CLI:

# ifup eth1
udhcpc: started, v1.36.1
udhcpc: broadcasting discover
udhcpc: broadcasting discover
udhcpc: broadcasting discover
udhcpc: no lease, forking to background

Server log:

Oct 20 08:41:04.000 <name> dnsmasq[9845]: started, version 2.90 DNS disabled
Oct 20 08:41:04.000 <name> dnsmasq-dhcp[9845]: DHCP, IP range [ip] -- [ip], lease time 1h
Oct 20 08:41:04.000 <name> dnsmasq-dhcp[9845]: DHCP, sockets bound exclusively to interface eth1

Not seeing any discovers in the above log.

Server tcpdump example of incoming discover on eth1:

09:43:23.956215 IP (tos 0x0, ttl 64, id 0, offset 0, flags [none], proto UDP (17), length 328)
    0.0.0.0.68 > 255.255.255.255.67: BOOTP/DHCP, Request from [ip], length 300, xid 0xf3d4e323, secs 1920, Flags [none]
      Client-Ethernet-Address [ip]
      Vendor-rfc1048 Extensions
        Magic Cookie 0x63825363
        DHCP-Message (53), length 1: Discover
        MSZ (57), length 2: 576
        Parameter-Request (55), length 7:
          Subnet-Mask (1), Default-Gateway (3), Domain-Name-Server (6), Hostname (12)
          Domain-Name (15), BR (28), NTP (42)
        Vendor-Class (60), length 12: "udhcp 1.36.1"
        Client-ID (61), length 7: ether [ip]

Answer A:
This on buildbox or where it's ifup you run? You can use netstat -nau for listen dhcpd port 68 or iptables -L for fierwall rules to show if there it closed by fierwall. Also it can be broken where ps aux | grep dhcp or lsof -l -P | grep dhcp

Answer B:
The most common reason for exactly this symptom is that dnsmasq has no usable address on the interface itself.

Broadcast packets reach tcpdump at layer 2 no matter what, but dnsmasq can only serve DHCP on an interface that has a static IPv4 address assigned in the same subnet. If eth1 on the server has no address at all (or only a link-local or wrong-subnet address), dnsmasq will silently ignore the discovers, even with log-dhcp enabled and the firewall off.

Check with:

ip addr show eth1

If there is no address in [ip]/24 on eth1, give the server a fixed one in that subnet but outside the pool, for example [ip]/24. Then restart dnsmasq after the address is up -- dnsmasq binds its sockets at startup, so starting it before the address exists produces exactly the behavior you are seeing.

A couple of other things worth ruling out:

Confirm this dnsmasq instance is the process actually holding UDP port 67 (ss -ulnp sport :67). A second DHCP server on the box -- even another copy of dnsmasq or one started by a network manager -- can steal the socket while this one still logs startup normally.
[truncated]

Answer C:
[user] made a great answer which could well be the solution in this scenario even if it wasn't in my specific case.

The problem turned out to be in the proxmox environment the server and client was running on. The server had the wrong vmbr set on its network device for eth1. I'm not sure how I could get any traffic at all from the client over it but for some time I was seeing broadcast traffic including the DHCPDISCOVER messages with tcpdump. Possibly some kind of vmbr leakage as it stopped after a restart (which gave me the clue to look at proxmox). It is still odd that this did not produce any log from dnsmasq if the traffic really reached the server. I did not manage to reproduce it but after setting the correct vmbr everything worked as expected right away.

Title: DIFUZZI: A Differential Fuzzing Tool for Code Functional Similarity Assessment

Abstract:
A range of software engineering tasks, such as optimization and refactoring, seek to preserve the behavior of software components and require methods to assess functional similarity. Research has explored formal approaches to prove functional equivalence and used machine learning methods to approximate it, but the former does not scale and does not quantify the extent of similarity and the latter struggles when subtle semantic differences are present. Differential fuzzing offers a scalable approach for differencing programs semantically, but applying it often requires substantial manual effort to construct input generators that are well-suited to a target pair of programs. To address this challenge, we introduce DIFUZZI, which incorporates an LLM-based generator synthesis step that is iteratively validated and repaired. By automating this step, DIFUZZI paves the way for broader applicability of differential fuzzing. We release DIFUZZI at https://github.com/Dristi123/difuzzi_tool, with a demonstration video at https://youtu.be/FlHNOHuo9WE

Draft: Zoopunk

Draft text:
----

Zoopunk is an upcoming action role-playing video game developed and published by the Chinese studio TiGames. The game is a prequel to F.I.S.T.: Forged In Shadow Torch (2021), and changes the earlier game's side-scrolling Metroidvania format into a three-dimensional, third-person action role-playing game.

==Gameplay==
The game is played from a third-person perspective and combines melee and ranged combat with exploration. TiGames has described its areas as wider and more vertically layered than those in F.I.S.T., but not as a seamless open world. [ref: Zoopunk and the revival of wildness beyond wasteland aesthetics, IGN China] Three playable characters were announced: Rayton, an agile rabbit who specializes in close-range attacks; Braton, a rhinoceros who fights with heavy attacks and a large flame sword; and Trixie, a chipmunk who relies on acrobatics and hit-and-run tactics. Each character has a distinct combat role. [ref: Zoopunk shown in a spectacular new trailer, Gamereactor] [ref: ZOOPUNK Gamescom 2026 trailer screenshots, Gematsu]

== Premise ==
The story is set decades before F.I.S.T.: Forged In Shadow Torch, during the origins of Torch City. The discovery of Fire Seed energy accelerates technological development but also awakens mechanical debris, which becomes a self-aware mechanical empire. [ref: ZOOPUNK confirmed for PS5, Xbox Series, and PC; reveal trailer, Gematsu] [ref: Enter the Dieselpunk Chaos of Torch City in ZOOPUNK Coming to Xbox and PC, TheXboxHub] Rayton, Braton, and Trixie travel through territories controlled by competing animal factions as the First Torch War begins, with the characters shown pursuing an object called the Spark. [ref: Xbox Partner Preview November 2025 Everything Announced From Our Amazing Partners, Xbox Wire] [ref: 動物たちによるド派手なアクション『Zoopunk（ズーパンク）』の発売が決定。発売時期は明かされず【Xbox Partner Preview】, Dengeki Online]

== Development and release ==
TiGames began informal discussions about the project in early 2023 and began prototype development in 2024. Studio chief executive Tao Zhang said that the development team had grown from about 20 people to approximately 50, while retaining members of the earlier game's action-design team and composer Caisheng Bo. Chinese concept artist Su Jian was invited to contribute to the visual design. The game is being made with Unreal Engine 5, replacing the predecessor's use of Unreal Engine 4. TiGames cited the newer engine's handling of fur, feathers, lighting, and larger environments as reasons for the change. The term animal punk was used by the developers to describe the combination of anthropomorphic characters, industrial machinery, ruins, and resistance to technological domination.

The January 2025 Nvidia technology demonstration was the first public announcement of the game, which was then described as a project in the same setting as F.I.S.T. [ref: TiGames announces ZOOPUNK for console PC, Gematsu] In an interview published during CES 2025, Zhang called Zoopunk a provisional title and described it as a conventional PC and console game rather than an AI-focused experiment. [ref: Interview with TiGames CEO Tao Zhang on expanding the Animal Punk universe, TapTap] However, following the November 2025 gameplay reveal, the game's visual assets and an in-game tool allowing players to use generative AI for creating content sparked online discussion. TiGames publicly clarified that the core game is entirely human-made. [ref: Zoopunk Says The Game Is All Human Made But Lets Players Use Gen AI To Make Stuff, Kotaku] [ref: Rabbit action game Zoopunk was made by humans not AI says Chinese dev TiGames, Eurogamer]

TiGames formally revealed the game with a gameplay trailer during the Xbox Partner Preview on November 20, 2025. [ref: Every big announcement from the Xbox Partner Preview, Polygon] A second trailer premiered during Gamescom Opening Night Live on August 25, 2026, followed by an extended five-minute gameplay presentation. [ref: Animal Punk action RPG Zoopunk is coming to PC and consoles, RPG Site] [ref: All the Xbox and PC game announcements at Gamescom 2026 Opening Night Live, Windows Central] The game is set to be released for Windows, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X and Series S in 2027.

== Reception ==
Writing after the 2025 reveal, Alberto Zaragoza Lerma of MeriStation characterized the move from a Metroidvania to a three-dimensional action role-playing game as a substantial change from F.I.S.T.. [ref: A standout Chinese game makes the leap to 3D action in its prequel, MeriStation] Michael Hoglund of Windows Central praised the game's "grizzled combat and wondrous colors" but noted that certain visual elements felt off. [ref: ZOOPUNK showcases grizzled combat and wondrous colors but something feels off, Windows Central]

At Gamescom 2026, GamesRadar+ compared the presentation's premise and large-machine combat to other third-person action games, but commented that the density of the trailer made the action difficult to follow. [ref: Gamescom Opening Night Live 2026 Everything announced, GamesRadar+] Fabiano Uslenghi of GameStar called it his action game "surprise" of the event. [ref: Zoopunk was my action surprise of Opening Night Live, GameStar]

Title: Optimal detuning and gate time for strongly driven single-qubit gates beyond the rotating-wave approximation

Abstract:
Single-qubit quantum gates are implemented as the time-controlled unitary evolution of a two-level system under harmonic driving. The rotating-wave approximation (RWA) provides closed-form gate parameters for weak coupling. Larger amplitudes, desirable to speed up the dynamics, make the RWA-designed gates inaccurate because of the neglected counter-rotating term, which also shifts the resonance (Bloch-Siegert shift). Here we study theoretically the infidelity of gates beyond the RWA, using the effective Magnus-Taylor Hamiltonian through second order in the inverse of the driving frequency. By detuning the driving frequency by an amplitude-dependent shift of Bloch-Siegert type and rescaling the operation time, the RWA gate conditions are recovered with corrected parameters. Numerical solutions of the Schrodinger equation show that these corrections lower the gate infidelity by several orders of magnitude, extending the range of usable amplitudes

Title: Model Collapse Is Avoidable Even as Real Data Vanishes: A Sharp Criterion for Iterative Gaussian Estimation

Abstract:
Large generative models are commonly trained on data collected from the open web, which may contain data produced by previous generations of the same model. Previous work has shown that recursively training on model-generated data can progressively degrade model performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse. Yet, generative models continue to improve dramatically over time. Existing theory suggests that this is enabled by the availability of new real data at each iteration, kept separate from generated data. However, exact separation is not realistic, and uncurated data is still commonly used. We bridge this gap by considering a more realistic setup in which real and generated data are not handled differently during training. Specifically, we present a comprehensive theoretical study of iterative estimation of the mean and covariance of a multivariate Gaussian distribution. At each iteration, samples are drawn from a mixture of the real data distribution and the estimated distribution from the previous iteration, but are used indistinguishably. We provide a single equivalent condition for consistency of the mean and covariance estimators in Euclidean norms, and convergence to zero of the expected squared 2-Wasserstein distance between the estimated and true distributions. Using this result, we show that consistency holds, i.e., model collapse is avoided, for any fixed real data fraction above zero, and even for a fraction that vanishes across iterations, provided it does not vanish too quickly. However, more real data (or data curation) remains important at practical finite times: the convergence rate of the mean estimator deteriorates as the real data fraction approaches zero. We support our results with an empirical investigation of the theoretical setup, and with experiments on iterative training of a diffusion model on CIFAR-10 that correlate with our theory.

Title: Sheaves on quoric manifolds

Abstract:
Quoric manifolds are quaternionic analogues of quasitoric manifolds introduced by Hopkinson. Given a quoric manifold over a simple polytope, we study the stratification induced by the faces of the polytope. We then show that the equivariant derived category of constructible sheaves with respect to the face stratification is equivalent to the derived category of constructible DG-modules over a DG-algebra defined on the orbit space. Finally, we prove that the associated DG-algebra is formal.

Title: Projected Brion's theorem

Abstract:
We present an analogue of Brion's theorem for the projected integer-point transform. Brion's theorem writes the integer-point transform of a rational polyhedron $P$ as the sum of the rational functions associated to its vertex cones. The pushforward $π_*$ along a lattice projection $π$ turns the transform of $P$ into the generating function of the numbers of lattice points in the fibres of $π$. We group the vertices of $P$ into contracted classes, generated by the edges whose direction $π$ kills, and show that the sum of the rational functions associated to the vertex cones in a contracted class can be pushed forward along $π$, yielding a rational function decomposition of the projected integer-point transform. For a lattice polytope, the classes correspond to the connected components of the fixed locus of the associated toric variety under the action of a subtorus, and our formula resembles the localization formula for this subtorus. We use this decomposition to provide an explicit formula for the projected integer-point transform of a linear family of polytopes. We illustrate this result with families of Gelfand--Zetlin and string polytopes.

Draft: Bahamas Airways

Draft text:
----

Bahamas Airways was an airline based out of Nassau that operated from 1936 to 1970. It was a part of the BOAC group of companies and was one of the first airlines based out of the Bahamas. The company had a large impact during an important period in the development of tourism in the country. It was sold to the John Swire & Sons in 1968 but went out of business 2 years later.

== History ==

=== Establishment ===
Bahamas Airways was founded in 1936 [ref: Bahamas Air Holdings Ltd., Encyclopedia.com] by Charles Collar. [ref: Origins of Bahamian Aviation, The Nassau Institute] Collar was an American who had served in the US Naval Reserve and flown with Pan Am.

The airline took over the routes of Inter-Island Charter Services which had gone out of business after just three years. Millionaire Harry Oakes, one of Collar's customers, invested in the airline, allowing it to buy a Douglas Dolphin.

=== Operations (1941–1970) ===
In 1941, Collar returned to the US and sold the airline to Pan Am. In 1944, American Airways also took an interest in the fledgling airline. [ref: Index to vol. XLVI: July to December 1944, Flight and Aircraft Engineer] In 1947, the airline started flying to a cluster of islands nicknamed the French Leave islands.

In January 1949, the airline was acquired by H. G. Christie's British South American Airways. [ref: B.S.A.A. Acquire Bahamas Line, Gloucestershire Echo] [ref: ] In March 1956, the airline started flying to Grand Turk in the Turks and Caicos Islands via San Salvador, Mayaguana and Great Inagua. [ref: Bahamas Airways '59, Bluegrass Airlines]

In the 1950s, the government subsidised the airline. [ref: Air, Colonial Office Report on the Bahamas for the Years 1952 and 1953] [ref: Air, Colonial Office Report for the Bahamas for the Years 1954 and 1955] [ref: Air, Colonial Office Report for the Bahamas for the years 1956 and 1957]

In April 1959, the new Skyways (Bahamas) purchased a stake in the airline.

Bahamas Airways tried to break into the market flying to Florida, however, it didn't have a lot of success. It acquired bigger airplanes but American passengers still didn't fly with them and opted instead to fly with Pan Am and Mackey Airlines. In addition, the airline had to pay nearly double the cost of maintenance as other carriers. [ref: Flight 24 May 1962 (Britten-Norman Hovercraft Cutaway, Aurora, Bahamas Airways)] In 1958, the airline was also affected by the General Strike. [ref: B. O. A. C. 1957–58, Flight and Aircraft Engineer]

Several other airlines like Pan Am and British Eagle would propose replacements for Bahamas Airways around the same time as the crisis at Bahamas Airways.

However, the airline remained competitive in the domestic market with flights often being overbooked. [ref: ]

Parent company BOAC looked for a buyer for the airline. [ref: Bahamas Airways Pt2: Swire’s Flamingo -, Yesterday's Airlines] In 1961, questions were asked in the House of Commons when Bahamas Airways was sold by BOAC to Eric Rylands and David Brown and then bought back by BOAC in 1960. [ref: Air Commerce... Clearing the Bahamas Air, Flight (magazine)] MPs wanted to know the amount of money that exchanged hands.

The Bahamian government refused to take and interest and, in 1969, BOAC approached John Swire & Sons, which owned Cathay Pacific and had purchased Hong Kong Airways during the 1950s.

=== Collapse ===
In 1968, John Swire & Sons took an 80% stake in the airline, [ref: ] [ref: ] and set about rebranding the airline. [ref: New Image, Twin Falls Times News] The new flamingo motif and flight attendant uniforms, reminiscent of the Royal Bahamas Police Force, attracted attention. The airline ordered a couple of BAC 1-11s to allow it to carry more passengers and fly further. However, it was still bested by competitors flying Boeing 727. A long range BAC 1-11-500 was created by BAC especially for the airline. The airline took on 35 more flight attendants and, in July 1970, the airline announced that it was planning jet services to the Cayman Islands. [ref: Bahamas Airways to Introduce Jet Service, The Caymanian] In total, John Swire spent $30 million dollars. [ref: ]

On 9 October 1970, Bahamas Airways abruptly ceased operations, [ref: Airline going into liquidation, Shropspire Star] $35 million in debt.

The company cited the impact of a US recession on tourism; it had also failed to convince the Bahamian Government to invest in the airline. [ref: Bahamas Airways Ends Operation, Citing Recession, The New York Times] However, the Minister for Transport countered that the government had been been prepared to take a 51% interest in the carrier but the company insisted on a non-negotiable term that was unacceptable to the government and an immediate injection of cash. [ref: ] When the airline went out of business, 600 employees lost their jobs, including 80 pilots.

The airline was eventually wound up in 1973. The same year, the national carrier Bahamasair was born taking over the routes of Flamingo Airlines and Out Island Airways.

== Fleet ==
The airline would utilize a number of airlines during its lifetime:

* a Loening Air Yacht was the first aircraft in the Bahamas Airways fleet
* Douglas Dolphin in the 1930s and 1940s.
* six Vickers Viscounts. All of them removed from the fleet by the end of 1968.
* four Hawker Siddely HS 748; none of them the fleet by 1970 when the airline ceased operations.
* single Canadian Vickers Catalina was removed from the fleet in 1956.

Title: How to politely ask to continue research article solo (pure math)
Tags: research-process, mathematics

Question:
I started a research project in pure math with a coauthor while we were overlapped during my first postdoc and his graduate program. We then moved on to other institutions but have ended up at the same institution again, as second postdocs for both of us.

In the first three or so months of collaboration, we proved several results but not enough for a full paper. After the initial bout of results, which I feel like were primarily my input, he seemed to withdraw from the collaboration, e.g. repeatedly rescheduling meetings or only engaging in the material during the meeting instead of thinking about the problems leading up to the meeting. I set the project aside, but since we're at the same institution again, I figured we could pick it back up. However, throughout the last academic year, I have asked him several times about meeting, and he keeps putting me off, but assuring me we'd find time to work on it again.

I want to finish the project, but because of his repeated delaying, we have yet to meet seriously about it even once since the initial discussions, so I feel like it would be best if I continued it on my own. I also have a sensitive career reason to pursue the topic solo.

Does anyone have any advice for politely broaching the subject of continuing the project on my own? I plan to invite him to look over the file and remove anything that he feels is mainly his contribution, and assure him that I am interested in collaborating with him in general even if I want to pursue this one alone, but I wanted to seek advice on any other way to approach the discussion.

Answer A:
Dr A, there is the possibility that Dr B himself has some ideas on this very project and may steal the thunder of your planned paper if you delay engaging with him much longer.

That aside, you are the senior researcher here. You have a life and a career to crack ahead with. This other guy can't seriously expect you to allow him sit on the combine indefinitely while he shows no urgency in harvesting your common fields.

Show more determination to engage on this matter.

If Dr B is evasive, I see little wrong in seeking support from your Dean of Research in getting a meeting to resolve this. A breakdown in relations with someone evasive is no significant loss anyway.

Good luck with your plans.

Answer B:
The comments @[user]'s are good, but to more directly address your question of how to approach this, here's my suggestion, assuming that you still want to proceed:

Go talk to your collaborator in person.  Explain that you understand if he's busy focusing on other projects now, and you'd like to continue collaborating with him. But you would also like to complete this project by [insert timeline.] (Hopefully you have a compelling reason for this that you can communicate to him also.)

Then you can propose a couple of ideas, and see what he thinks or if he has other suggestions, and then negotiate about this.

You focus on the project now and he can contribute whatever he feels time to.  Then you can write a joint paper as planned and you're not booting him from the project.  (Warning: there is still the possibility that he could delay things inevitably, say wanting to review the paper before submission etc but being very slow about it.  Some collaborators are like this, and if you do co-author the work you will need his final approval before posting/submitting.  This is something you need you need to assess based on your interaction/knowledge of him.)

Answer C:
This is a common problem: collaborators with different levels of urgency/interest in a given joint project. A few things to think about:

In my experience of writing joint math papers, it's pretty common for one person to take the lead and do most of the work after a certain point. This isn't the ideal way to collaborate, but it's what a lot of people do. It tends to even out over the long run, especially if you write multiple papers with the same people. (And if it doesn't even out, you should find different collaborators.)

The norms around authorship in math are pretty generous. Some might even say too generous. People who semi-bail out of a project halfway through are usually included in the author list, as long as they did a nontrivial amount of work for the project at some point.

If  your collaborator has already done enough to warrant authorship, then there is probably no ethical way to remove him at this stage, unless he volunteers to remove himself.

Wiki: English Wikipedia
Draft: Kutcho deposit

Draft text:
The Kutcho deposit (also Kutcho Creek deposit) is a copper–zinc volcanogenic massive sulphide (VMS) deposit in the Cassiar Mountains of northern British Columbia, Canada, about from Dease Lake. [ref: MINFILE No. 104I 060: Kutcho, Main, Sumac, Kutcho Creek, Esso West, MINFILE Mineral Inventory] Discovered in the early 1970s, it has been the subject of exploration and mine proposals by a succession of companies, and of geological research because its host rocks record a primitive Permo-Triassic island arc unlike other VMS settings in the Canadian Cordillera.

==Geology==
The deposit lies within the Kutcho Assemblage (formerly Kutcho Formation), a latest Permian to Early Triassic volcano-sedimentary sequence within the fault-bounded King Salmon allochthon. [ref: Geological setting, U–Pb geochronology, and radiogenic isotopic characteristics of the Permo-Triassic Kutcho Assemblage, north-central British Columbia, Canadian Journal of Earth Sciences] The assemblage comprises basaltic to basaltic andesite flows and tuffs and rhyodacitic to rhyolitic flows, mass flows and pyroclastic flows, intruded by gabbro, diorite, trondhjemite and quartz–plagioclase porphyry. The ore is hosted by rhyolite mass flows near the top of the assemblage; rhyolites from the hanging wall and footwall have U–Pb ages of about 242 million years, and a nearby porphyry intrusion is dated at 244 ± 6 million years. Lead and neodymium isotope signatures indicate formation in an intra-oceanic island arc, probably on oceanic crust, and are inconsistent with the adjacent Stikine or Quesnel terranes. The stratigraphic, lithogeochemical and tectonic setting of the deposit was described by Barrett, Thompson and Sherlock in 1996. [ref: Stratigraphic, lithogeochemical and tectonic setting of the Kutcho Creek massive sulfide deposit, northern British Columbia, Exploration and Mining Geology]

Mineralization occurs in three stratabound, lenticular lenses — Main (Kutcho), Sumac and Esso (Esso West) — along about of a single stratigraphic horizon. The lenses strike about 280° and dip north at 40 to 45°. Sulphides include pyrite, sphalerite, chalcopyrite and bornite, with minor chalcocite and traces of tennantite and galena; the lenses have copper-rich cores and zinc-rich margins. They are surrounded by an alteration halo depleted in sodium and enriched in potassium that extends about 300 metres into the footwall.

Childe and colleagues (1998) interpreted Kutcho as a distinct type of Cordilleran VMS deposit formed in a primitive intra-oceanic arc, and noted similarities with the Sitlika assemblage and the Venables Valley–Red Hill area, which they considered prospective for similar deposits. [ref: Primitive Permo-Triassic volcanism in the Canadian Cordillera: tectonic and metallogenic implications, Economic Geology]

==History==
Sumac Mines Ltd. (controlled by Sumitomo Metal Mining) and Esso Minerals of Canada staked the deposit in 1972 and 1973 respectively, and carried out more than 50,000 metres of drilling and a bulk-sampling crosscut. Esso sold its interest to Homestake Mining (Canada) in 1989; Teck-Cominco held an option from 1992. Western Keltic Mines acquired the property from Barrick Gold and Sumitomo in 2004 and was purchased in 2008 by Sherwood Copper, which merged with Capstone Mining later that year. In June 2017 Desert Star Resources agreed to acquire the project from Capstone, and renamed itself Kutcho Copper Corp. in December 2017.

===Resource and reserve estimates===
All figures below are as reported by the companies and compiled by MINFILE:
* 1986 (published estimate, CIM Special Volume 37): Kutcho lens 17 million tonnes at 1.62% Cu and 2.32% Zn; Sumac about 10 million tonnes at 1.0% Cu and 1.2% Zn.
* 2017 (Desert Star Resources pre-feasibility study): probable reserves of 10.4 million tonnes at 2.01% Cu, 3.19% Zn, 0.37 g/t gold and 34.61 g/t silver.
* March 2019 (Kutcho Copper Corp.): measured and indicated resources (Main, Esso and Sumac combined) of 17.26 million tonnes at 1.85% Cu and 2.72% Zn, plus 10.7 million tonnes inferred.

===Environmental assessment===
A proposal for a 2,500-tonne-per-day underground mine in the Andrea Creek watershed, a tributary of Kutcho Creek, was assessed federally; in 2011 the assessment was downgraded from a comprehensive study to a screening after a redesign, and it was terminated on 20 June 2016. [ref: Kutcho Copper Zinc Silver Gold Mine Project, Dease Lake (Registry 36352), Canadian Impact Assessment Registry] A revised proposal for an underground copper–zinc mine of about 3,500 tonnes of ore per day with a mine life of up to 14 years entered British Columbia's environmental assessment process under the 2018 Environmental Assessment Act in December 2019. [ref: Kutcho, EAO Project Information Centre (EPIC)]

Title: Mean curvature bounds for CMC foliations of manifolds with sectional curvature bounded below

Abstract:
Let $M^{n+1}$ be a complete Riemannian manifold with $\sec_M\ge-K_0$, $K_0\ge0$, and let $\mathfrak{F}$ be a codimension one foliation of $M$ by hypersurfaces of constant mean curvature, the constant depending on the leaf. We prove that the mean curvature of every leaf satisfies $|H|\le(n+1)\sqrt{K_0}$. In particular, the mean curvature of the leaves of a CMC foliation of a complete manifold with $|\sec_M|\le1$ is bounded by $n+1$, which answers positively a conjecture of Meeks III, Pérez, and Ros.

state.text:
Title: Tangential center problem for planar Hamiltonian differential equations

Abstract:
Consider a planar Hamiltonian differential equation with a nondegenerate center at the origin. The Tangential Center Problem asks for a characterization of polynomial perturbations for which the center persists at first order. This problem plays a fundamental role in the study of the center-focus problem. We propose an effective algorithmic approach to the Tangential Center Problem for planar polynomial Hamiltonian differential equations. Using this approach, we obtain a complete solution of the quadratic Tangential Center Problem. We further apply it to a non-generic family of cubic Hamiltonian differential equations containing the planar Hamiltonian Lotka--Volterra equation. For a general cubic polynomial perturbation, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the vanishing of the corresponding first Poincaré--Pontryagin--Melnikov function and characterize all tangential centers.

----

Solace Health is a healthtech platform that matches patients with healthcare advocates who help them navigate the U.S. healthcare system. Established in 2022, the privately held company is based in Redwood City, California.
== History ==
Jeremy Gurewitz and Sara Sargent co-founded Solace Health in 2022 after Gurewitz watched his mother struggle to navigate the healthcare system while she battled pancreatic cancer. His mother had difficulty even though she was a radiologist with an understanding of the medical system [ref: Solace Health expands care navigation services to commercially insured patients, Fierce Healthcare] who led a women's imaging center in Long Island, New York. [ref: Medicare Coverage Fuels Solace’s $60 Million Series B, Wall Street Journal]

Patients initially paid for Solace services out-of-pocket. This changed in 2024 when Medicare started covering patient advocacy services for chronic and complicated health conditions. [ref: VCs Give Solace Health $1 Billion Valuation for Patient Advocacy Tech, Bloomberg] Gurewitz told the Wall Street Journal that investor interest increased once patient advocacy was covered by Medicare. In April 2025, Solace announced a $60 million Series B, which was twice the amount they intended to raise. In February 2026, Business Insider reported that the need for help navigating the U.S. medical system had propelled the company to a $1 billion valuation.

In 2026, Solace announced additional insurance coverage from major health plans, including United Healthcare and Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield. Fierce Healthcare quoted Gurewitz that this expanded coverage extended the opportunity for patient advocacy to millions of Americans. The company also partnered with Disabled American Veterans (DAV) [ref: DAV announces new partnership with Solace Health supporting veterans’ care, DAV] and the American Legion [ref: Solace Health, American Legion announce partnership to help veterans navigate healthcare system, American Legion] to help U.S. military veterans navigate healthcare. They announced a partnership with Walmart’s Better Care Services in September 2026. [ref: Solace Health Expands Access to Healthcare Advocacy Through Walmart’s Better Care Services Platform, Businesswire]

== Advocacy services ==
Solace advocates include registered nurses and other healthcare professionals who, according to a 2026 press release have 16 years of experience on average. When Medicare reimburses advocates, Solace receives a share in exchange for use of its platform. In early 2026, Solace had more than 2,000 participating advocates providing services to more than 20,000 patients each month.

Advocate services include helping clients understand medical bills and treatment plans, as well as finding physicians, scheduling appointments, and coordinating care across multiple providers. Advocates can also go to appointments with patients, either virtually or in person. Gurewitz told MedCity News in 2026 that Solace advocates specialize in doing the work for patients, rather than simply providing advice on what patients should do.

Patients interact with advocates through text and phone calls as well as video calls embedded in the Solace platform. [ref: Solace Health Reaches Unicorn Status by Taking the ‘Homework’ Out of Care Navigation, MedCityNews] Solace's proprietary electronic health records system assembles a patient's health history. The platform also handles Medicare billing. Gurewitz informed Founder Brew in a 2026 interview that while the Solace platform incorporates AI to help advocates do their jobs, many aspects of the U.S. healthcare system cannot be completed by AI and still require human interaction.

state.text:
Title: String-averaging bargaining in solidarity cooperative games

Abstract:
We consider the situation that the grand set of all players, in a cooperative game in characteristic function form with a nonempty core, consists of recognizable subsets of players. The underlying assumption is that the players of each subset have something in common between themselves which is not shared by the players of other subsets. For example, the members of these subsets are distinguishable by their nationalities or by their geographic locations or by some other market-related economic or social property. In addition to the agreement of all players to play the game to reach a point in the core, the members of each subset want to steer the iterative orbit of the bargaining process to a point in the core that will reflect the strength of their solidarity within their subset. This is why we call such subsets solidarity sets. The solidarity means that players of a solidarity set are willing to participate in coalitions that include only members of their solidarity set and are not willing to participate in coalitions of other solidarity sets. The question is how can such a game be played? Is there an iterative bargaining scheme that will generate a sequence of payoffs that converges to a point in the core which reflects the solidarity of the members of the solidarity sets? We propose bargaining schemes that allow the members of each solidarity set to perform, independently from other solidarity sets and, therefore, simultaneously in time, a full but finite sweep of intercoalitional collaboration. Then the end-points of all these sweeps are combined into a single payoff vector via a convex combination wherein the coefficients of the convex combination may reflect some a priori knowledge about the relative strengths of the different solidarity sets. These bargaining schemes are applied to a new type of cooperative game that we call solidarity cooperative game (SCG).

Site: Academia Stack Exchange
Title: My thesis was published without my approval
Tags: publications, research-process, thesis, masters, psychology

Question:
I conducted my MSc research entirely on my own and I wrote and analysed everything from start to finish. I told my supervisor that I wanted to publish, so they got in touch with a journal. However, because I had already graduated, all journal emails were sent to my university email address, which had been deactivated. As a result, I never saw those emails.
When my supervisor forwarded reviewer emails to me, I still couldn’t access the documents because I no longer had an active account. When I told them I couldn’t access the files and asked them to send me the documents so I could make edits, I was told, “It’s fine, we’ll handle it.”
In the end, my thesis was published as a journal article without my approval. The dataset and analyses were handled incorrectly, and the published results are wrong and substantially different from my original findings.
On top of that, in the “Writing – original draft” section, it doesn’t list only my name; it also includes my supervisor’s name and a colleague my supervisor added. I feel deeply disappointed, because I was eager to share the most striking results of my work. I wanted the paper published mainly so I could share a link when talking about it.

I genuinely don’t know what to do right now, and I’m not even sure what is considered right or wrong in this situation. I’m also considering applying for a PhD, and I need my supervisor as a referee, so I’m afraid of damaging the relationship. But I honestly don’t understand why they took my original work, changed it, and published it in the way they wanted, as if it were theirs.

When I pointed out that the participant number was wrong, my supervisor apologised and agreed that I was right — but at that point it no longer felt like my work.
What should I do now? Also, for PhD applications, if I say that my thesis project was entirely mine and that I led the full research process, the paper lists “Conceptualization, Formal analysis, Writing – original draft” as shared among multiple authors.

Wiki: English Wikipedia
Draft: Joseph B. Rasmussen

Draft text:
Joseph B. Rasmussen is a Canadian aquatic ecologist. He is Professor Emeritus of Biological Sciences at the University of Lethbridge, where he held a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Aquatic Ecosystems and directed the Water Institute for Sustainable Environments. He developed stable-isotope methods now widely used to quantify food web structure and trophic position, and applied tracer-kinetic models to the study of contaminant biomagnification and in situ fish bioenergetics. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada in 2016.

Rasmussen was appointed in 2010 to a federal advisory panel reviewing environmental monitoring of the Athabasca oil sands, one of six scientists named by then-environment minister Jim Prentice. In 2024, University of Lethbridge researchers named a newly described species of parasite, Myxobolus rasmusseni, after him in recognition of his career in aquatic biology.

== Early life and education ==
Rasmussen studied zoology at the University of Alberta in the 1960s and 1970s, completing an honours BSc and an MSc in limnology, and went on to a PhD in aquatic ecology at the University of Calgary in 1983.

== Career ==
Rasmussen joined the Department of Biology at McGill University in 1984 as an NSERC postdoctoral fellow, and was later promoted to full professor. During his time at McGill, he worked on lake zoobenthos, stable-isotope food web ecology, and contaminant biomagnification, and in 1998 was among the faculty who established the McGill School of Environment.

He moved to the University of Lethbridge in 2003 to take up a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Aquatic Ecosystems, renewed in 2010, and to direct the Water Institute for Sustainable Environments. He later chaired the Department of Biological Sciences before retiring in 2019 as Professor Emeritus.

Later in his career, Rasmussen's group turned toward the conservation of native salmonids in western Canada, studying how introduced brook trout affect bull trout (Salvelinus confluentus) populations and how rainbow trout introductions affect the genetics of native westslope cutthroat trout (Oncorhynchus clarkii lewisi), and tracing selenium from coal mining through mountain stream food webs. This work fed into his appointment to the federal oil sands review panel and to provincial panels on environmental monitoring and selenium impacts on Athabasca rainbow trout.

== Research ==
In the 1980s, whether persistent contaminants biomagnify up aquatic food webs was disputed; some chemists argued, from equilibrium partitioning, that it was thermodynamically implausible. Rasmussen and collaborators built kinetic models accounting for uptake, elimination, and bioenergetics to show that biomagnification is expected for contaminants that are readily assimilated but slowly eliminated, and that much lake-to-lake variation in fish PCB and mercury levels can be explained by food web structure.

His group adapted nitrogen stable-isotope (δ¹⁵N) methods, until then used mainly in marine geochemistry, to freshwater food webs, showing that δ¹⁵N signatures track trophic position more efficiently than traditional stomach-content analysis while also predicting mercury bioaccumulation; they also showed that comparing trophic position across different food webs requires correcting for variation in baseline isotope signatures. Combining isotope measurements with long-term lake data, the group traced how species introductions, such as smallmouth bass, reshaped the trophic position of native lake trout, and his student Anthony Ricciardi produced widely cited estimates of extinction rates among North American freshwater fauna. Rasmussen's group also extended radiotracer bioenergetics techniques to estimate feeding rates and metabolic costs of wild fish populations in the field.

== Awards and honours ==
* Fellow, Royal Society of Canada (Academy of Science, Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences division), 2016.
* Ingrid Speaker Award for Outstanding Research Achievement, University of Lethbridge, 2012.
* Frank H. Rigler Memorial Award, Society of Canadian Limnologists, 2010.
* Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Aquatic Ecosystems, 2003 (renewed 2010).

In 2024, a newly discovered myxozoan parasite infecting fathead minnows in southern Alberta was named Myxobolus rasmusseni in his honour by researchers Molly Tilley and Cameron Goater. Goater, a longtime colleague, described Rasmussen as one of the most decorated aquatic biologists in the country.

Title: Waveform Bandwidth and Frequency Diversity in FDA-MIMO Range-Angle Estimation: A CRLB Perspective

Abstract:
Frequency-diverse array multiple-input multiple-output (FDA-MIMO) radar introduces range-dependent phase diversity through element-dependent carrier-frequency offsets, in addition to the delay information carried by transmitted waveforms. This paper develops a bandwidth-aware Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) framework to characterize how these two mechanisms jointly affect range-angle estimation. Starting from a Nyquist-rate sampled observation model that retains waveform delays and FDA frequency offsets, we derive an equivalent Fisher information matrix (EFIM) after eliminating an unknown quasi-static complex scattering coefficient as a nuisance parameter. We derive closed-form CRLB approximations that reveal the interplay between waveform root-mean-square (RMS) bandwidth and FDA frequency diversity. A three-factor decomposition of the squared normalized cross-information further characterizes range-angle coupling. Results show that when increased independently, both waveform RMS bandwidth and FDA frequency diversity reduce the range CRLB, but FDA frequency diversity increases the angle CRLB at fixed nonzero waveform bandwidth, whereas waveform RMS bandwidth reduces it. Additionally, under a fixed aggregate spectral budget, the range CRLB exhibits an interior maximum, whereas the angle CRLB increases monotonically with the FDA spectral-allocation fraction. Numerical results corroborate the closed-form approximations and the predicted trends.

Nicholas Bakalar is an American author and editor. [ref: Bakalar, Nicholas, Encyclopedia.com]

== Early life and career ==

Nicholas Bakalar was an editor at Doubleday, HarperCollins, and other publishing houses from 1976 to 1991, acquiring both fiction and a wide range of nonfiction books. His column, called “Vital Signs” and later “In Brief,” appeared weekly. [ref: Mr Nicholas J Bakalar, Healthed]

== Journalism ==

Bakalar wrote more than 2,200 articles for The New York Times between 2004 and 2023, covering health, medicine, science, sports, and other subjects. [ref: Below the Fold: A New York Times X-Ray Dashboard, Below the Fold]

His writing has also appeared in Discover, National Geographic News, and Wildlife Conservation.

== Books ==

*Green Diamonds: The Pleasures and Profits of Investing in Minor League Baseball (1993, Kensington; ISBN 9780821744864).
*The Wisdom of John Paul II: The Pope on Life’s Most Vital Questions, with Rick Balkin (1995, HarperCollins; ISBN 9781456609894).
*Coping With Social Anxiety, with Eric Hollander, M.D. (1995, Henry Holt; ISBN 9781429997034).
*The Baseball Fan’s Companion: How to Watch the Game Like an Expert (1996, Macmillan; ISBN 9780756756673).
*AIDS and People with Severe Mental Illness, with Francine Cournos, M.D. (2007, Yale University Press; ISBN 9780300067576).
*Republicanisms (1996, John Wiley; ISBN 9780471164562).
*American Satire: An Anthology of Writings from Colonial Times to the Present (1997, Penguin; ISBN 9780452277984).
*Wiping Out Head Lice (1997, Penguin; ISBN 9780451191670).
*Understanding Teenage Depression, with Maureen Empfield, M.D. (2001, Henry Holt; ISBN 9781466850095).
*Hepatitis A to G, with Alan Berkman, M.D. (2000, Warner; ISBN 9780759584228).
*Where the Germs Are: A Scientific Safari (2003, John Wiley; ISBN 9780470252444).

*The Medicine Cabinet of Curiosities (1996, Henry Holt; ISBN 9781429964548).

== Personal life ==

Nicholas Bakalar lives in New York City and Juneau, Alaska. He is married to Francine Cournos, M.D.

Title: From pq-webs to magnetic quivers and back II: distributional indices and 5d theories breaking bad

Abstract:
This is the second of two companion papers in which we study five-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ theories engineered by $(p,q)$ five-brane webs and their associated three-dimensional magnetic quivers. Leveraging the exact parameter dictionary between the $N+\mathrm{SU}(N)_0^{k-1}+N$ theories and their magnetic quivers at infinite coupling, proposed in the first paper, we investigate nilpotent moment-map VEV deformations and their three-dimensional counterparts. We show that, when the Higgsing is excessive, the five-dimensional superconformal index becomes distributional, mirroring a characteristic feature of bad and broken theories in three dimensions. We also develop a five-brane web interpretation of these results, identifying the Hanany-Witten moves associated with the Higgsing cascade and relating inequivalent frames to distinct tessellations of the generalised toric diagram.

== Life and activities ==

Baradaran attended school in Tehran and graduated from the University of Tehran with a degree in sociology. She later continued her studies at the University of Hanover in Germany. She was imprisoned in Evin Prison during the mass executions of Iranian political prisoners in the summer of 1988.

== Arrests and imprisonment ==

Baradaran was first arrested in June 1978 and released in December that year. Following the Iranian Revolution of 1979, she was arrested again in October 1981, alongside her brother and sister-in-law. Her brother was executed 40 days later. Baradaran remained imprisoned for nine years and was released in October 1990. Nick Thompson is an Australian professional triathlete from Perth, Western Australia, who races long and middle distance. He won IRONMAN Cairns in 2026, his first full distance win. He finished seventh at the 2025 IRONMAN World Championship in Nice and fourth in the 2025 IRONMAN Pro Series. He won 70.3 Sunshine Coast in 2023 and 70.3 Tasmania in 2024. He finished third at IRONMAN Western Australia in 2023. He placed ninth in the elite men's criterium at the Australian Road Nationals Criterium in January 2026.

== Early life ==
Thompson is from Perth, Western Australia. He ran a 15:07 for 5000m on the track in Perth in December 2020. He finished second in the open category at IRONMAN 70.3 Western Australia in Busselton in May 2021.

== Professional career ==
=== 2023 ===
Since turning professional in 2023, in his first season Thompson was 7th at 70.3 Luxembourg and 9th at IRONMAN Switzerland. 23rd at the 70.3 World Championship in Lahti, Finland, 27 August. Won 70.3 Sunshine Coast, 10 September, in a time of 3:40:02, by more than a minute, first professional win. Later in the year he went on and placed 2nd at 70.3 Melbourne, 12 November. In his final race for 2023, Thompson placed 3rd at IRONMAN Western Australia, Busselton, 3 December, in a time of 7:48:22, his first full-distance podium. In the same race, winner Daniel Bækkegård set the fastest IRONMAN time recorded in Australia. The result gave Thompson his qualification for the IRONMAN World Championships in Kona in 2024.

=== 2024 ===
In Thompson's second year as a professional triathlete he went on to win 70.3 Tasmania in Hobart in February, in wet conditions, achieving a time of 3:54:10, finishing ahead of Mitch Kibby, Cameron Wurf, in a field which included Javier Gómez and Braden Currie.This was Thompson's fourth consecutive podium at an Oceania 70.3.

Thompson later went on to compete at IRONMAN Texas coming 14th, 9th at IRONMAN Cairns, and a DNF at IRONMAN Frankfurt.

In October, Thompson competed at the IRONMAN World Championships for the first time, coming 21st, where he was near the front after the swim and bike before fading on the run.

Thompson then went on to finish the year with a 15th at 70.3 Western Australia and the 70.3 World Championships Taupō.

=== 2025 ===
Thompson achieved 7th at IRONMAN Texas, 26 April in a time of 7:39:42 and was second at IRONMAN Cairns on 15 June and qualifying himself for the men's World Championship in Nice.

Thompson finished 3rd at 70.3 Zell am See-Kaprun in Austria, 31 August in a time of 3:48:30, with the fastest bike split in the professional field.Heading into IRONMAN World Championships in Nice where he was sitting 13th in the Pro Series standings.

Thompson finished seventh at the IRONMAN World Championship, 14 September, in a time of 8:10:32.

A 16th place at the 70.3 World Championship in Marbella, Spain in November resulted in him finishing in 4th in the final 20205 IRONMAN Pro Series standings, on 18,415 points, behind Kristian Blummenfelt, Casper Stornes, and Kristian Høgenhaug.

=== 2026 ===
Thompson finished 18th at IRONMAN Texas in April, followed by claiming the title at IRONMAN Cairns on 14 June, in a time of 7:49:48, as his first full-distance win, and finishing more than seven minutes clear of Ben Hill, and Jumpei Furuya in third.

Thompson took the lead inside the first 20km of the bike and led to the finish.

Thompson placed 11th at the IRONMAN 70.3 World Championship in Nice on 12 September, in a time of 3:56:04, in a race won by Hayden Wilde. He then went on to place 11th at the IRONMAN World Championship in Kona on 10 October, 8:01:12, where Vincent Luis won; Thompson had the 3rd-fastest bike split of those that finished in the field (4:12:36).

== References ==

Title: Rosemary: Efficient and Adaptable In-Storage Acceleration for Fully Homomorphic Encryption

Abstract:
Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables computation on encrypted data and is promising for privacy-preserving computing. However, FHE deployment remains constrained due to massive computational, memory, and data-movement overheads. Existing acceleration strategies often overlook the storage I/O bottleneck caused by the enormous size of FHE data in large-scale applications, as most prior works focus on small benchmarks that fit in main memory. Our studies show that state-of-the-art FHE systems spend 71\% to 85\% of their execution time moving data between storage and compute units rather than performing useful computation. To address the I/O bottleneck, we present Rosemary, a heterogeneous FHE acceleration system that incorporates a novel in-storage processing (ISP) architecture with compiler-level and algorithmic optimizations. Our key innovations include 1) an adaptable hardware-aware FHE engine inside a NAND flash-based solid-state drive (SSD) for efficient and cost-effective in-storage FHE processing, 2) a Throughput-Data-Aware Program Allocator (TDAP) that partitions FHE workloads into heterogeneous programs, and 3) a Compiler-Level Ciphertext-Aware Optimizer (CLCAO) that exploits ISP-friendly FHE kernels for low-cost ISP execution. Across a diverse set of FHE workloads, including encrypted deep learning inference and cloud database queries, Rosemary achieves geometric-mean speedups of $185.7\times$ over state-of-the-art CPU/GPU implementations and $3.7\times$ over prior FHE accelerators, while improving energy efficiency by up to $3.9\times$ and Energy-Delay-Area-Product (EDAP) by up to $16.5\times$.

Question:
Imagine you place two identical 1m^2 metal plates on the ground in direct sunlight, A and B.

Everything about them is equal, in terms of heat loss to the ground and to the air, the metal they are made from, colour etc.

Above B, you place a 1m^2 fresnel lens, such that it "collects" exactly the 1m^2 patch of sunlight that the plate would have by absorbed itself - in other words, both set ups A and B receive only 1m^2 of sunlight.

After let's say exactly 1 hour, which plate is hotter?

My intuition wants to say that B with the fresnel lens is hotter, because let's say A in 1 hour, reaches 60C. B with the fresnel lens, has a hot patch in the centre of let's say 5cm^2 at 800C or more, and during the hour, that heat conducts throughout the plate. Surely a concentrated 800C+ for an entire hour gets that plate absolutely cooking? At least, more than 60C.

However, my first principles reasoning says that 1m^2 of sunlight for 1 hour, let's say it's giving you 3000w on this particular day. Both systems, A and B, are only receiving 3000w of energy, therefore, there can only be the same overall increase of temperature, and that 800C hotspot, when it has conducted across the full plate, must only average to the same 60C as plate A.

So, which plate is hotter and why?

Is there something to do with efficiency of transformation of light in to heat? Do light waves when concentrated multiply, rather than simply sum their amplitude? What's going on in this scenario?

Title: Reference-based multiple imputation for longitudinal bounded discrete outcomes

Abstract:
Reference-based multiple imputation has been developed for binary and ordinal responses. We develop a parsimonious formulation for longitudinal bounded scores and counts that preserves their finite integer support and gives partial and complete reference borrowing an explicit distributional interpretation. Discrete Kumaraswamy margins provide closed-form cumulative distribution and quantile functions, simplifying fitting and imputation under a Gaussian copula. Borrowing is defined through a regression model indexed by a smooth median anchor, allowing continuation under the assigned treatment, partial borrowing, or jump to reference after a specified trigger. With shapes shared across arms, complete borrowing replaces the active marginal distribution with the reference distribution at the same visit and covariate values, while conditional imputations remain informed by retained outcomes. Bayesian estimation uses latent variable augmentation, and all sensitivity rules share one fitted posterior. Completed datasets are analyzed using a beta-binomial random intercept model, with treatment comparisons expressed as standardized mean score differences. Simulations assess parameter recovery and imputation followed by analysis. An application to depression scores illustrates attenuation of the treatment benefit at the final visit as borrowing increases, with confidence intervals including zero under all rules.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: Inhomogeneous Besov spaces and Sobolev spaces: missing some details
Tags: fourier-analysis, sobolev-spaces, besov-space

Question:
Sometimes ago I wrote this question on the link between Sobolev inhomogeneous spaces $H^s(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and Besov inhomogeneous spaces $B_{2,2}^s$. At the time I believed the answer given to me satisfactory, however looking back at it and trying to carry out the details I realized I'm not sure I understand the matter yet. Since the question is a bit old I thought it would be better to open a second post.

What I understood: We need to bound the Besov norm, which in this case will be
\begin{equation*}
\Vert u \Vert_{B_{2,2}^s}^2 = \sum _{j \geq -1} 2^{2js}\Vert\Delta_ju\Vert_{L^2}^2
\end{equation*}
Observe that even when $u$ is a tempered distribution, the Paley blocks are smooth functions. We can start by bounding the Paley-Littlewood scaled blocks $2^{js} \Vert \Delta_j u \Vert_2 \lesssim \Vert \nabla^s\Delta_ju\Vert_2 = \Vert \rho_j(\xi) \cdot |\xi|^s \cdot \hat{u}(\xi)\Vert_2$, for $j \geq 0$, since with these $j$ the Fourier transform of $\Delta_ju$ is supported in an annulus $2^j \mathcal{A}$ (with $\mathcal{A}$ a fixed annulus) and we can use the Bernstein inequality (which should hold for any $s \in \mathbb{R}$, not just natural $s$). Raising to the power of $2$ we get a bound exactly for the term appearing in the Besov norm. Summing these new found quantities, we get:

\begin{equation*}
\sum_{j \geq 0} \Vert \rho_j(\xi) \cdot |\xi|^s \cdot \hat{u}(\xi)\Vert_2^2 = \sum_{j \geq 0} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |\rho_j(\xi)|^2\cdot |\xi|^{2s} \cdot \hat{u}(\xi)^2\,d\xi = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} (\sum_{j \geq 0} \rho_j^2(\xi))\cdot |\xi|^{2s} \cdot \hat{u}(\xi)^2 \,d\xi.
\end{equation*}

In the homogeneous case, I believe this is it. One can do this at all frequencies and sum over all $j \in \mathbb{Z}$. Here the lower frequencies are all gathered in a ball and the dyadic partition stops at $j = -1$. Now of course I need to add the frequencies in the $j = -1$ component of the Besov norm: here the scaling factor will be $2^{js} = 2^{-s}$ and we cannot use Bernstein inequalities, since for those you need the Fourier transform to be supported in an annulus while the Fourier transform of $\Delta_{-1}u$ is supported in a ball. One has that $2^{-s}\Vert \Delta_{-1}u\Vert_2 = 2^{-s}\Vert \rho_{-1}(\xi)\hat{u}(\xi)\Vert_2$. I don't know how one could bound this term. Depending on the sign of $s$, the scaling factor can be bounded by $1$ (when s is positive) or cannot be touched at all (when $s$ is negative). Moreover, I still cannot see how the term $(1 + |\xi|^2)^s$ pops up when summing everything together.

Title: Critical fluctuations in the edge--triangle exponential random graph models

Abstract:
We prove quantitative limit theorems for the edge density $Q$ in the dense edge--triangle exponential random graph model at criticality and under parameter perturbations of order $n^{-1}$. At the fixed critical parameters $(α_c,h_c),$ the centered fluctuations satisfy $n^{2/3}(Q-\mathbb{E} Q)\Rightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,σ_0^2)$, with explicit variance $σ_0^2>0$. This disproves the quartic fluctuation conjecture of Bianchi, Collet and Magnanini (2024). Gaussian limits also hold $(α_c+ λ/n,h_c + γ/n)$, except when the coefficients satisfy $-\frac{11}{16}+\frac{2}{9}(γ+\frac49λ)=0$. Under this linearity condition, the limiting laws of $\sqrt n(Q-2/3)$ have densities proportional to $\exp\{-81z^4/64+9θz^2/8\}$, where $θ=-57/16+8λ/27$. We obtain a sharp $n^{-1/3}$ rate in $1$-Wasserstein distance for the Gaussian limits and an $O(n^{-1/2})$ bound for the quartic limits. The proofs combine Stein's method for exchangeable pairs with conditional row estimates and a local Dobrushin contraction.

Title: Conditional Neural SDEs for Financial Time-Series Generation

Abstract:
Conditional generation of time-series paths is a central problem in probabilistic modeling, where the goal is to simulate future trajectories that are both realistic and responsive to external context. It has direct applications in finance and economics. Neural stochastic differential equations provide a natural framework for this task by combining continuous-time stochastic dynamics with learnable drift and diffusion functions. However, directly modeling the target state can be unstable in conditional settings, especially when the target and conditioning variables have strong level dependence, limited training data, or different dimensions.We propose a residualanchor Neural SDE architecture that decomposes the target into a learned conditional anchor and a stochastic residual. The anchor captures the context-dependent baseline, while the Neural SDE (Stochastic Differential Equation) models the residual dynamics around this baseline. This separation reduces the burden on the stochastic dynamics and generalizes spread-based representations to more general conditioning settings.We evaluate the approach on real-world financial time series, including conditional interest-rate scenarios and a comparison with a time-series foundation model. The results show that the proposed model can generate plausible conditional paths, maintain competitive point accuracy, and provide calibrated uncertainty estimates.

Title: Sharp Bounds on Torsional Rigidity of Metric Graphs with Signed Delta-Vertex Strengths

Abstract:
We study torsional rigidity on finite compact connected metric graphs with real \(δ\)-vertex strengths in the regime of strictly positive torsion. For a fixed total length \(L>0\), let \(I_+\) be the sum of the positive strengths and \(I_-\) the sum of the magnitudes of the negative strengths, with \(I_+>I_-\). We determine the sharp infimum and the exact threshold for a finite universal supremum. The supremum is finite precisely when \(I_-<I_+/(1+LI_+)\). In this regime, an interval with strengths \(I_+\) and \(-I_-\) at opposite endpoints attains the sharp Saint--Venant bound. At and beyond the threshold, torsional rigidity is unbounded even among three-vertex paths with the same data and strictly positive torsion. The sharp infimum is \(L^2/(I_+-I_-)\) throughout the range \(I_+>I_-\ge0\). It is not attained by any finite graph and is approached by graphs with two vertices joined by increasingly many parallel edges of equal length, preserving both strength totals separately. A vertex-matrix formulation and explicit path examples clarify the relation between strength placement, spectral positivity, and solvability.

Rachel Ann Pepper is a Judge at the Land and Environment Court of New South Wales, Australia. She was appointed to the Court in 2009. [ref: Judicial officers and decision makers, Land and Environment Court of New South Wales]

== Early life and education ==
Rachel Pepper was born in Canada and immigrated to Australia in the early 1980s. She graduated from the Australian National University with a Bachelor of Arts, majoring in French, in 1992 and a Bachelor of Laws with First Class Honours in 1994. [ref: Judicial speeches and papers, Land and Environment Court of New South Wales]

== Legal career ==
Pepper practised as a solicitor with Allen Allen & Hemsley in 1995. In 1996, she served as associate to Justice Michael McHugh in the High Court of Australia. [ref: ANU]

She was called to the New South Wales Bar in 1997, reading with John Marshall and Justin Gleeson. She practised as a barrister at 7 Wentworth Chambers and 12 Wentworth Selborne Chambers until her appointment to the Court in 2009. [ref: LEC Swearing in ceremony]

Between January 2017 and April 2018, Pepper served as Chair of the Scientific Inquiry into Hydraulic Fracturing of Onshore Unconventional Gas Reservoirs and Associated Activities in the Northern Territory. [ref: Home, Northern Territory Government]

In 2021, she was made a fellow of the Australian Academy of Law. [ref: Rachel Pepper, Australian Academy of Law]

== Professional activities ==
Pepper serves on the editorial board of the Australian Journal of Administrative Law and is the Environment Section Editor of the Australian Law Journal. [ref: Environmental Law, The Australian Law Journal]

From 2009 to 2018, she was a Co-Consulting Editor of the Australian Environment Review published by LexisNexis. [ref: Co-consulting Editors, Australian Environment Review]

She has served on the committee of the Australian Institute of Administrative Law and was its President. [ref: National Executive, Australian Institute of Administrative Law] She is also a member of the Ngara Yura Committee of the Judicial Commission of NSW [ref: Ngara Yura Committee members, Judicial Commission of New South Wales] and a judicial member of Football Australia. [ref: Constitution, Football Australia]

Pepper served as Secretary of the Australian Association of Constitutional Law from 2013 to 2017 and as Vice President from 2017 to 2018. [ref: UNSW]

She was elected to the NSW Bar Council in 2000 and served until her appointment to the bench in 2009, including as Secretary from 2005 to 2009. [ref: ANU alumnae trailblazers in law: an intimate discussion, Australian National University]

From 2019 to 2023, Pepper was a board member of Twenty10. She also served as Vice President of ACON from 2001 to 2003. [ref: ACON Annual Report 2001/2002]

Pepper has authored and edited books, journal articles, book chapters and other publications in the fields of environment, administrative, constitutional, criminal and discrimination law [ref: Thomson Reuters]. She has also participated in the teaching and training of judges from overseas in environmental law and environmental dispute resolution through programs supported by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Asian Development Bank. [ref: 2022 IUCN Academy of Environmental Law Colloquium]

Pepper is an Adjunct Professor at the University of Sydney Law School [ref: University of Sydney Law School].

She has been a judicial fellow and visiting scholar at the Australian National University College of Law [ref: ANU Law School] and Melbourne University Law School [ref: Melbourne University Law School]. She has also taught law courses at the University of New South Wales, the University of Technology Sydney and the University of Sydney. [ref: University of Sydney Law School]

Title: On edge-ordered Ramsey numbers of hypergraphs

Abstract:
For an integer $h\geq2$, an edge-ordered $h$-uniform hypergraph $H^<$ is an $h$-uniform hypergraph with a linear ordering of its hyperedges. For an integer $q \geq 1$, the edge-ordered Ramsey number $R_{\mathrm{edge}}(H^<;q)$ of $H^<$ is the smallest positive integer $N$ such that there exists an edge-ordered $h$-uniform hypergraph $G^<$ on $N$ vertices such that, for every $q$-coloring of the hyperedges of $G^<$, there is a monochromatic copy of $H^<$ in $G^<$ preserving the hyperedge order. In this note, we show that, for every edge-ordered $h$-uniform hypergraph $F^<$ on $n$ vertices with $m\geq1$ hyperedges, $R_{\mathrm{edge}}(F^<;q) \leq R_h(F;q)^{Cm^2}$ where $F$ is the underlying unordered hypergraph, $R_h(F;q)$ is its standard $q$-color Ramsey number, and $C=C(h,q)>0$ is a constant. For fixed $h\geq3$ and $q\geq2$, this shows that prescribing the hyperedge order does not require an increase in the tower height of the classical upper bound. It also settles a problem posed by Fox and Li (2020), and for $h=2$ gives the bound $2^{O(n^4\log n)}$, improving their bounds for every fixed $q \geq 3$.

Site: Stats Stack Exchange
Title: Funnel analysis models
Tags: logistic, classification, markov-process

Question:
What sort of modeling tools are appropriate for "funnel analysis"? The broader idea being a linear chain of states, each with their own probability of advancement. While, the concept of a funnel is somewhat unique to business/marketing, the idea of state transitions reminds me of markov chains, which is a pretty broad mathematics field itself.

My general thought is to divide the funnel into a series of states for example:

Inactive

View item

Add item to cart

Purchase item

We might define the funnel states on a weekly or monthly cadence with mutually exclusive binary variables:

only viewed one or more items, $v_{i, t}$

viewed one or more items, adding one or more to cart, $c_{i, t}$

viewed 1+ items, added 1+ items to cart, purchased 1+ item, $b_{i, t}$

(inactive becomes the intercept, zeroes for all binary variables).

If we introduce some new treatment that is supposed to foster funnel progress, we might condition on the state in the previous interval: $[v_{i, t-1}, c_{i, t-1}, b_{i, t-1}]$ for customer $i$ as well as the treatment exposure, $d_i$.

Then use a multi-class logistic regression to predict the subsequent state: $[v_{i, t}, c_{i, t}, b_{i, t}]$

Because of the time-path dependency issue, may need to borrow inspiration from dynamic models, eg marginal structural model, dynamic double machine learning, etc. Which includes conditioning on the previous state (already discussed) and time-path propensity. How many states are preserved in memory is a choice. Full history is impractical for several reasons and a single look-back state, while correct by Markov Chain literature is likely incorrect under the causal lens. But k=2 or k=3 previous states seems plausible enough.

Title: Nondegeneracy of low-energy nodal solutions to the Yamabe equation

Abstract:
We study the linearized Yamabe equation in $\R^n$, or equivalently on $\s^n$, at a low-energy sign-changing solution with two nodal domains. We consider odd dimensions $n=2k-1$ and a solution invariant under $Γ=O(k)\times O(k)$. Its regular level sets are isoparametric hypersurfaces, which foliate the sphere away from the two focal submanifolds. This symmetry reduces the equation for the solution to a singular ODE. In the balanced case, we choose a single-node profile that is odd under reflection across the midpoint. We prove nondegeneracy in the $Γ$-invariant subspace for every $k\ge2$, and in the full space $H^1(\s^n)$ for sufficiently large $k$: every kernel element is generated by a conformal invariance of the equation. The proof uses separation of variables, Wronskian identities and comparison functions adapted to the singular equations for the angular modes.

Title: Who Called? V33DA: A Physically Verified Multimodal Benchmark for Vocal Attribution in Zebra Finch Groups

Abstract:
Deciding which member of an animal group produced a vocalization and where that vocalization was produced are central to studying social communication but are rarely evaluated with physically verified ground truth. Existing resources either localize sounds without identifying the caller, or recognize individuals from isolated vocalizations without reliance on the 3D candidate geometry. We close this gap with V33DA, a dataset-centered multimodal benchmark for spatial vocal attribution in social zebra finches: it comprises 33,625 verified events coupling 5-channel audio with three camera views, calibrated 3D pose for every visible candidate, and per-bird radio telemetry across 10 individuals and three experiments. Caller identity is verified from an on-body accelerometer-derived vibration signal; this channel is withheld from benchmark models and used only by an on-body reference ceiling. Given a detected vocalization and the visible candidate birds, the task is to select the caller. We evaluate it under three regimes: session-disjoint testing on familiar birds from held-out recording dates, held-out-experiment transfer to a new cohort, and leave-one-individual-out evaluation on a bird whose vocalizations are held out from training. Reference methods expose a consistent gap between in-domain accuracy and transfer to unseen individuals: methods that can exploit familiar vocal identity perform well on known callers but degrade sharply on unseen ones, whereas candidate-aware methods preserving explicit spatial reasoning transfer substantially better. The on-body reference stays near-perfect across regimes, confirming the internal consistency of the accelerometer-verified labels. We release V33DA with fixed protocols and code for the evaluated methods, and V33DA++, an unevaluated companion set of verified overlapping-call events and +/-2 s context windows.

Title: Rigidity of Kähler-Finsler Metrics with Constant Radial Curvature

Abstract:
In this paper, we prove that a smooth strongly pseudoconvex Kähler--Finsler metric $F$ satisfying the constant radial curvature condition \[ Ω(χ,\barχ)χ=cF^2χ, c\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}, \] is induced by a Hermitian Kähler metric of holomorphic sectional curvature $2c$. Under the Abate--Patrizio curvature symmetry \[ \langleΩ(\cdot,\barχ)χ,χ\rangle =\langleΩ(χ,\barχ)\cdot,χ\rangle, \] this result gives Hermitian rigidity for nonzero constant holomorphic sectional curvature and the classification of complete simply connected metrics of negative curvature. As an application, we show that the Kobayashi metric of a bounded strongly convex domain with smooth boundary is Kähler--Finsler if and only if the domain is biholomorphic to the unit ball. We also prove that the universal cover of a bounded strongly pseudoconvex domain $D $ with smooth boundary is biholomorphic to the unit ball if and only if its Kobayashi metric is a smooth strongly pseudoconvex Kähler--Finsler metric. Furthermore, we give two explicit examples to illustrate the distinction between the weakly Kähler--Finsler and Kähler--Finsler conditions.

Site: Academia Stack Exchange
Title: Attending undergraduate institution for PhD due to severe disability
Tags: phd, health, humanities

Question:
I have applied for PhD programs in the humanities and have a promising offer from my home university. Of course, I have heard attending the same university that I have completed my undergraduate degree at for a PhD is not advised.

However, I have a severe physical disability where I require significant care and live at home where the home is fully adapted. The university is close by and this is why I was wondering whether this specific circumstance of doing the PhD at my undergraduate institution would have any effect on how I would be perceived in academia? My goal is to remain in academia.

Answer A:
Some things are more important than other things. Some things are more possible than other things. While it is true that attending a different institution for doctoral study is an advantage, it is, IMO, mostly because you get a different perspective from different people.

However, it might also be true that the doctoral faculty at your "home" institution don't teach a lot of undergraduates and so, you may not have seen all that they can offer in a doctoral program.

There are also more important things than where you get your degree. How you do and what you accomplish and how you are perceived are much more important.

I'd also guess that success is more likely if your life is as comfortable as you can make it under your circumstances.  You will struggle with your health and you will struggle with your studies. Lessening the one can ease the other.

Answer B:
You say:

Of course, I have heard attending the same university that I have completed my undergraduate degree at for a PhD is not advised.

Where have you heard this? I haven't, and I don't think there is any such general principle.

Of course it may be that you have the opportunity to do a PhD at a different institution which happens to be a better place for your intended direction of study. But any advantages that institution may have over your home institution are not because it is different, but inherent advantages that would apply even if you were already there.

In my experience (admittedly, not in the humanities) many strong people do a PhD at their home institution. There is nothing wrong with this, and many people can find it difficult to move, or simply prefer not to, for a wide variety of reasons. Indeed, if someone moved institutions for PhD then, unless it was an obvious upgrade, I would suspect they simply didn't get an offer from their home institution.

Title: Search for long-lived heavy neutral leptons in signatures with one prompt muon and a secondary vertex formed by two non-prompt muons in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 and 13.6 TeV

Abstract:
A search for heavy neutral leptons (HNLs) in the decay of W bosons is performed in final states with three muons, with one originating promptly from the primary interaction vertex and the other two stemming from a common secondary vertex. The analyzed proton-proton collision data correspond to an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$ recorded at a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV in 2016$-$2018, and of 34.6 fb$^{-1}$ recorded at 13.6 TeV in 2022. The analysis strategy is optimized for large HNL decay lengths by requiring highly non-prompt muons forming a secondary vertex far from the beam line, and hence reconstructed only in the muon system of the CMS experiment at the CERN LHC. This enhances the analysis reach in the high HNL lifetime region, corresponding to low HNL masses (2$-$4 GeV) and small mixing parameters with the standard model neutrinos (10$^{-6}$$-$10$^{-5}$), where prompt and tracker-based non-prompt analyses have limited acceptance. No excess over the background prediction is found. Under the Majorana HNL hypothesis, exclusion limits at 95\% confidence level are set on the HNL mixing parameter as functions of the HNL mass in the range of 1$-$5 GeV.
