Wiki: English Wikipedia
Draft: Jim Dai

Draft text:
Jiangang "Jim" Dai (戴建岗) is an operations researcher and applied probabilist known for work on stochastic processing networks, queueing theory, and fluid and diffusion approximations. He is the Leon C. Welch Professor of Engineering in the School of Operations Research and Information Engineering at Cornell University. [ref: Jim Dai, Cornell Duffield Engineering] Dai received the 2024 John von Neumann Theory Prize for contributions to stochastic systems theory [ref: Jim Dai, INFORMS] and the 2018 ACM SIGMETRICS Achievement Award for his analysis of queueing networks. [ref: Dr. Jim Dai 2018 ACM SIGMETRICS Achievement Award, ACM SIGMETRICS]

== Education and career ==

Dai earned bachelor's and master's degrees in mathematics from Nanjing University and a doctorate in mathematics from Stanford University in 1990. [ref: DAI, Jiangang Jim, School of Data Science] He joined the faculty of the Georgia Institute of Technology in 1990 and remained there until moving to Cornell in 2012. At Georgia Tech, he held the Chandler Family Chair in Industrial and Systems Engineering. At Cornell he became the Leon C. Welch Professor of Engineering.

Dai has also held appointments at Tsinghua University, the National University of Singapore, Aarhus University, Stanford, and the University of Wisconsin–Madison. At the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, he has served as dean and later honorary dean of the School of Data Science. He was editor-in-chief of the journal Mathematics of Operations Research from 2013 to 2018.

== Research ==

Dai's research concerns mathematical models for allocating resources in processing networks, including communication and computer systems, manufacturing systems, data centers, call centers, hospitals, and transportation services. His work develops fluid and diffusion approximations for analyzing the stability and control of such networks.

In a 1995 paper, "On Positive Harris Recurrence of Multiclass Queueing Networks: A Unified Approach via Fluid Limit Models", Dai established a general connection between the stability of deterministic fluid models and positive recurrence of stochastic processing-network models. INFORMS described the result as a foundation for later work on stochastic-network stability. His later research has addressed heavy-traffic diffusion approximations, reflected Brownian motion, max-weight scheduling, and quantitative approximation bounds based on Stein's method.

With J. Michael Harrison, Dai wrote the monograph Processing Networks: Fluid Models and Stability, published by Cambridge University Press in 2020. [ref: Processing Networks: Fluid Models and Stability, Cambridge University Press]

== Awards and honors ==

INFORMS awarded Dai the 2024 John von Neumann Theory Prize for "fundamental and sustained contributions" to stochastic systems theory, particularly stochastic-network stability and heavy-traffic diffusion approximations. The prize recognizes a body of fundamental, sustained theoretical work in operations research and the management sciences. [ref: John von Neumann Theory Prize, INFORMS]

The ACM SIGMETRICS Achievement Award recognized Dai's contributions to fluid and diffusion analysis of queueing networks and their applications to computer, communication, and processing systems. He is an elected fellow of the Institute of Mathematical Statistics and of INFORMS. His earlier honors include the 1998 Erlang Prize and the 1997 and 2017 Best Publication Awards from the INFORMS Applied Probability Society.

Title: Largest ratio of odd vs even numbers in a Collatz sequence
Tags: collatz-conjecture

Question:
Let $r(n)$ be the ratio of odd numbers vs even numbers occurring in a Collatz sequence starting from $n$. It is known that the largest possible value for $r(n)$ is $\ln(2)/\ln(3) \approx 0.63093$. For $n \leq 10^{11}$, I have found that the starting number $n=63,728,127$ has the largest $r(n) \approx 0.60304$, as it visits 357 odd numbers and 592 even numbers. It seems that there is still some room left to reach the upper bound. Is there a starting number $n$ with a larger value of $r(n)$?

Title: Multi-Timescale Deliverability of Shared Hybrid Storage for AI Data Center Campuses

Abstract:
Artificial intelligence data center (AIDC) campuses contain sustained power variations and subsecond power fluctuations, requiring both sufficient stored energy and fast response. A shared hybrid energy storage system (HESS) can mitigate aggregate AIDC power deviations, but interval-based schedules cannot capture the delay between commanded and delivered power at the campus point of common coupling (PCC). To this end, this paper proposes a multi-timescale scheduling model for mitigating AIDC power fluctuations with the shared HESS. First, it models electrical pooling at the campus bus and constrains the shared HESS to a single PCC injection. Second, a two-layer model passes five-minute scheduled power, energy state, and reserve capacity to a causal fast response model that distinguishes commanded power from delivered power. Case studies using the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) GenAI Power Profiles Dataset show reductions in both PCC and fast integral absolute error (IAE), while retaining most of the improvement available under ideal response.

Hurricane Trudy is an active hurricane west of Mexico. It is the twenty-first named storm, twelfth hurricane, and tenth major hurricane of the 2026 Pacific hurricane season.

==Meteorological history ==

On October 6, at 06:00 UTC, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) stated a tropical wave entered the East Pacific south of Guatemala, and started monitoring it for development in the next 7 days. [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/xgtwo/gtwo_archive.php?basin=epac&fdays=7¤t_issuance=202610060600] On October 12, the NHC noted the disturbance gained a surface low and stated it had a very high chance of development. [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep21/ep212026.public.001.shtml]Six hours later, the depression intensified into a tropical storm and was given the name Trudy. [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep21/ep212026.public.002.shtml] By October 14, Trudy had been upgraded to Category 1, and rapidly strengthened to Category 3 the next day, with it expected to further strengthen into a Category 4. [ref: Hurricane Trudy approaches Mexico’s coast: What you need to know about its path, El Cronista]

However, the eye started to decay and it was no longer visible around 18:35 UTC. At the same time The Hurricane Hunters flew into the storm, and noticed that Trudy rapidly weakened below major hurricane strength. [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep21/ep212026.update.10161833.shtml] [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep21/ep212026.public.014.shtml]

== Preparations ==
On October 15, The National Hurricane Center issued Tropical Storm Watches for southern Mexico. [ref: Hurricane Trudy strengthens; warnings issued along Pacific Coast, nj] The next day they were upgraded into Hurricane Warnings, with tropical storm watches and warnings being issued for additional areas around the coast. Title: Stable and efficient covariance estimation for sample L-moments using Hájek projections

Abstract:
L-moments are useful summary statistics and are widely used in statistical analysis. The joint covariance matrix of sample L-moments not only describes their sampling uncertainty but is also needed for covariance-weighted distances and related statistical procedures. An exact unbiased covariance estimator is already available. However, in our previous applications, this estimator sometimes produced singular or indefinite covariance matrices. Such matrices cause problems when matrix inversion is required. The present paper addresses this difficulty. We examine standard positive-definite corrections and two covariance estimators based on leave-one-out sample L-moments: the delete-one jackknife estimator and an estimator based on the Hájek projection. Both are positive semidefinite by construction. Simulation results show that the projection estimator generally has smaller estimation error and better numerical stability than the exact unbiased estimator. The jackknife estimator overestimates the variances of higher-order sample L-moments and has larger estimation error than the projection estimator. We also develop fast rank-prefix algorithms for the three covariance estimators considered. These algorithms substantially reduce computation time.

Title: Evidence for an effective gauge field in flakes of superconducting 4Hb-TaS2

Abstract:
Understanding the normal state of unconventional superconductors is central to uncovering the origin of superconductivity itself. Unconventional superconductivity often emerges from correlated electronic states characterized by intertwined symmetry-breaking orders. A striking example is 4Hb-TaS2, whose superconducting state exhibits a remarkable range of phenomena, including an unusual magnetic memory effect. Previous experiments showed that magnetic memory can be encoded above Tc and later revealed through spontaneous vortices below Tc, suggesting time-reversal symmetry breaking. However, since memory and vorticity are intertwined, this prevents establishing whether the effect results from trapped flux, weak conventional magnetism, or a true hidden electronic order. Here, we show that magnetic memory persists in the vortex-free Meissner regime of exfoliated 4Hb-TaS2 flakes, where it appears as a stable remanent modification of the superconducting screening response. Our results rule out explanations based on trapped vortices. Furthermore, the spatial profile of the flux generated by trained samples at zero field is inconsistent with conventional weak magnetism, suggesting a hidden electronic phase that imprints an effective flux on the superconducting condensate.

state.text:
Title: Moments of characteristic polynomials at random matrix Gram points

Abstract:
We evaluate the characteristic polynomial of a random unitary matrix at the points on the unit circle where the polynomial takes real values. In analogy to the Riemann zeta function we call these the ``random matrix Gram points''. On the random matrix side we answer in the affirmative a question of Richard Hall, who expected that zeta on the Gram points should be larger than typical. We prove that for any fixed positive $k$, the $2k$th moment of the characteristic polynomial averaged over the random matrix Gram points is larger than the $2k$th moment of the characteristic polynomial averaged over the whole unit circle. For large $N$ the leading-order asymptotic term is the same size, but all lower-order terms are larger. In an appendix we show how to adapt the heuristic recipe of Conrey--Farmer--Keating--Rubinstein--Snaith to conjecture moments of zeta at Gram points, and show by example that the second and fourth moments calculated by following the recipe agree with previously proven results.

Draft text:
The Haggis Wildlife Foundation is a Scotland-based folklore, publishing and digital storytelling initiative whose work centres on the wild haggis, an animal associated with Scottish humour and folklore. The Foundation produces documentary-style films, illustrated species guides, fictional field reports, online publications and interactive community projects. Its stated purpose is to document, reinterpret and share the cultural legend for contemporary audiences, rather than to operate as a conventional wildlife conservation charity. [ref: About the Haggis Wildlife Foundation, Haggis Wildlife Foundation] [ref: Our Work, Haggis Wildlife Foundation]

Its activities span a main website, an online catalogue of films and books, an interactive sightings register, social-media and mailing-list communities, a related research-style publishing network, and a retail website. Although much of its work adopts the conventions of zoology, conservation and historical archives, those conventions are employed in a fictional and folkloric setting. [ref: Haggis Wildlife Foundation, Haggis Wildlife Foundation] [ref: About the Haggis Wildlife Foundation, Haggis Wildlife Foundation Official Shop]

== Purpose and organisational identity ==
The Foundations work is the preservation and continuation of a Scottish storytelling tradition. It uses encounters with wild haggis to encourage participation in folklore through watching, reading, sharing stories and submitting sightings. Its online About Us statement distinguishes this activity from conventional wildlife conservation and characterises the work as cultural storytelling and community-building.

The main website presents the Foundation as an archive of wild haggis lore. It organises material into areas such as species guides, videos, news, books, the Grand Survey and a map of reported sightings. The stated motto is To document and preserve, also rendered there as describendum et conservandum. Its Our Work statement identifies storytelling, documentary production and online discussion as its principal methods and places particular emphasis on the social communities formed around humorous folklore.

== Historical narrative ==
The Foundation's website contains an extensive fictionalised foundation history. Its Our Story page attributes an establishment date of 1892 to Sir Archibald MacTavish, described as the 7th Earl of Glenfinnan. It introduces a purported early team comprising photographer Neil McKinnon, zoologist Edwin McTaggart, and Highland guides Duncan and Harris MacLeod, and situates the fictional expeditionary programme around the Heatherlie estate and the Highlands. [ref: Our Story, Haggis Wildlife Foundation]

The narrative describes late nineteenth-century photographic expeditions, the use of glass-plate equipment, purported discoveries of haggis burrows and archival photographs. These episodes are elements of the Foundation's constructed history and are not independently established events in the organisation's actual legal or operational history. No independently corroborated nineteenth-century incorporation or continuous operating history is asserted here.

The historical framework extends beyond the Foundation's own website. Publications attributed to its fictional archives include photographs and purported field records dated to the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Their historical dates describe the setting of the stories, not independently verified dates of the Foundation's real-world activities. [ref: Wildes Haggis, German-language Wikipedia]

== Activities and projects ==

=== Films and digital documentaries ===
Documentary-style video is one of the Foundation's principal forms of publication. Its website hosts a film catalogue covering imagined wild haggis species, habitats, seasonal migrations and encounters. Listed titles include White Tash Haggis Animal, The Round Woodland Haggis, Wild Forest Haggis, Subspecies of Wild Scottish Sea Haggis, The Great Return: Scotland's Wild Haggis Awaken, Winter Subspecies of Wild Haggis Animals, The Great Migration of Wild Scottish Haggis Animals and A Spotters Guide to Wild Scottish Haggis Animals. [ref: Videos, Haggis Wildlife Foundation]

The films use natural-history presentation techniques to describe impossible or invented animals as though they were subjects of wildlife photography. A September 2024 community-contributed article on Daily Kos discussed the Foundation's YouTube videos, including What Is Scotland's Wild Haggis Animal?, The Ancient Art of Scottish Wild Haggis Shearing and The Truth Behind Commercial Haggis Farming. The author described the documentaries as humorous fiction and commented on their computer-generated imagery and narrated presentation. [ref: Kitchen Table Kibitzing 9/3/2024: The Haggis Wildlife Foundation, Daily Kos]

=== Species guides ===
The Foundation publishes introductory descriptions of invented wild haggis varieties, including the Common Garden Haggis and the Stirling White Tash. Its website combines species names and illustrations with instructions framed as spotting advice, while linking to longer guides and films.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: Computationally efficient algorithm for multivector inverses.
Tags: clifford-algebras, geometric-algebras

Question:
I am currently writing a code library for geometric algebra, just as a side project, as a way of better understanding both programming an geometric algebra. I now face the hurdle of finding the inverse of multivectors. Currently I am just working with multivectors with signature $(d,0)$. For $d\le5$, the paper https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amc.2017.05.027 provides some algorithms for this, however for $d>5$, everything I can find seems to point to converting multivectors to matrices and inverting those. However, it seems that the matrix representation of a multivector is $2^{d}\times2^{d}$. Given that matrix inversion is $M^{-1}\in\mathcal{O}\left(n^{\log_{2}(7)}\right)$, it directly implies that $v^{-1}\in\mathcal{O}\left(7^{n}\right)$, which is ludicrously slow for something as used as calculating inverses.

I am wondering if there is some other algorithm for finding multivector inverses that works better for computers, I find it hard to believe that $\mathcal{O}\left(7^{n}\right)$ is the best possible method. I know the aforementioned paper lists a few isomorphisms, however as far as I can tell they either relate clifford algebras different signatures, or relate clifford algebras to matrix algebras, neither of which seems to be particularly helpful for algorithms that computers can calculate sufficiently quickly.

Title: Stability of the $L^p$ Poisson-Neumann problem under small perturbations of the coefficients and the domain

Abstract:
In this article, we obtain three stability results for the Poisson-Neumann problem: (1) the stability of the $L^p$ Poisson-Neumann problem under small Carleson perturbations of the coefficients, (2) the preservation of the $L^p$ Poisson-Neumann problem when transitioning from the Laplacian to operators in a special form with oscillations satisfying a small Carleson condition (''small special DKP operators''), and (3) the stability of the $L^p$ Poisson-Neumann problem under small bi-Lipschitz transformations of domains. In contrast to the Neumann problem, the Poisson-Neumann problem is notably more self-contained, as results pertaining to it do not require assumptions regarding the $L^{p'}$ Dirichlet problem, making it a more suitable object for a perturbation theory. As intermediate steps, we establish estimates on the square functional for solutions to the Poisson problem and their gradients on chord arc domains, which are of independent interest for specialists.

Title: Hydrodynamic regimes of the edge-tone in a simplified recorder mouthpiece

Abstract:
The acoustic mechanism of flue instruments originates in the interaction of an air jet with a sharp edge, the labium. Previous studies have examined isolated edge-tones or full instruments in which acoustic resonance obscures the underlying hydrodynamics, and a systematic understanding of how geometric parameters govern jet stability is lacking. We present a large-scale parametric study of the jet-labium interaction in a simplified recorder mouthpiece without a resonator, using more than 200 two-dimensional direct numerical simulations with an immersed boundary method. We vary the mouth distance, the labium angle, the vertical offset of the labium, and the Reynolds number (Re), and characterize the dynamics through spectra of the transverse force on the labium. The baseline configuration oscillates as a predominantly periodic Stage I edge-tone with Strouhal number St ~ 0.07, nearly constant for Re >= 330 and for all labium angles at the baseline mouth distance, so the frequency is set by the geometry rather than by viscosity. The mouth distance has the strongest influence: it is the only parameter that introduces a second oscillation stage, and the Stage I frequency is inversely proportional to it. The second stage is weakly present at five and six windway heights, established from six and a half, and dominant from eight, where it strongly modulates the amplitude. The vertical offset mainly affects the strength of the oscillation, and the labium angle does not change the instability mechanism. A baseline configuration is identified for future aeroacoustic coupling studies.

Site: Physics Stack Exchange
Title: Does a reciprocity theorem hold for Ampère's law when exchanging the current loop and the integration path?
Tags: electromagnetism, magnetic-fields, vector-fields

Question:
Consider a physical closed loop, C₁, carrying a steady current I. This current generates a magnetic field $\vec{B}_{1}$ in space. According to Ampère's circuital law, if we choose a second imaginary closed path, C₂, the line integral of $\vec{B}_{1}$ along C₂ satisfies:
$$\oint _{C_{2}}\vec{B}_{1}\cdot d\vec{l}_{2}=\mu _{0}I_{\text{enclosed by }C_{2}}$$
Now, suppose we exchange the roles of the two loops. We remove the current from C₁ and pass the exact same current I through a physical wire along the path C₂. This new configuration produces a magnetic field $\vec{B}_{2}$. We then evaluate the closed line integral along the original path C₁:
$$\oint _{C_{1}}\vec{B}_{2}\cdot d\vec{l}_{1}=\mu _{0}I_{\text{enclosed by }C_{1}}$$
Is it universally true that these two integrals will always yield the exact same value?
$$\oint _{C_{2}}\vec{B}_{1}\cdot d\vec{l}_{2}=\oint _{C_{1}}\vec{B}_{2}\cdot d\vec{l}_{1}$$

My Intuition

This seems closely related to the reciprocity theorem for mutual inductance (M₁₂ = M₂₁), where the flux linkage geometry remains symmetric regardless of which loop acts as the source. Topologically, if C₁ links through C₂, then C₂ must link through C₁, meaning the enclosed current term should evaluate to either ± I or 0 identically in both cases.
However, I want to ensure I am not overlooking any subtle edge cases—such as non-trivial spatial topologies, specific geometric boundaries, or limiting cases—where this equivalence might break down. Is there a formal vector calculus proof or a Stokes' theorem identity that explicitly establishes this reciprocity?
Let me know if you would like me to adjust any specific phrasing or help you draft the title box separately!

Answer A:
So long as the Biot-Savart Law holds, this does hold true. If the field $\vec{B}_1$ is produced by a current $I$ along the loop $C_1$ then we have
$$
\vec{B}_1(\vec{r}_2) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi} \oint_{C_1} \frac{\vec{\mathscr{r}}_{21} \times d\vec{r}
_1}{\mathscr{r}_{21}^3}
$$
where $\vec{\mathscr{r}}_{21} = \vec{r}_2 - \vec{r}_1$.  Denote the path integral of $\vec{B}$ along loop 2 due to the current in loop 1 as $Q_{21}$.  This will then be
$$
Q_{21} = \oint_{C_2} \vec{B}_1 \cdot d \vec{r}_2 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi}  \oint_{C_2} \oint_{C_1} \frac{(\vec{\mathscr{r}}_{21} \times d\vec{r}
_1) \cdot d\vec{r}_2}{\mathscr{r}_{21}^3}.
$$
But using the triple product rule we have
$$
(\vec{\mathscr{r}}_{21} \times d\vec{r}
_1) \cdot d\vec{r}_2 = (\vec{\mathscr{r}}_{12} \times d\vec{r}
_2) \cdot d\vec{r}_1
$$
which would be the numerator of the integrand if we calculated the corresponding path integral $Q_{12}$.

So when does the Biot-Savart Law hold?  It can be shown (see, for example, Griffiths §5.3.2) that the field predicted by the Biot-Savart Law in $\mathbb{R}^3$ will satisfy $\vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{B} = 0$ and $\vec{\nabla} \times \vec{B} = \mu_0 \vec{J}$ so long as a certain integral involving the current vanishes:
$$
\iiint \vec{J}(\vec{r}') \cdot \vec{\nabla}_\vec{r} \left( \frac{\vec{r} - \vec{r}'}{|\vec{r} - \vec{r}'|^3} \right) d^3\vec{r}' = 0,
$$
where the integral is over the support of $\vec{J}$.
In particular, it is not hard to show (see Griffiths) that this integral will vanish if two conditions hold:

The current distribution satisfies $\vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{J} = 0$ everywhere (i.e. the currents are steady)

$\vec{J}$ is compactly supported (which allows us to argue that a certain surface integral vanishes)
[truncated]

Answer B:
However, in a transformer, the two current-carrying loops are not interlinked as they are in your example.

To understand why $M_{12}=M_{21}$, it's better to analyze three linked loops rather than just two. The current loop, the magnetic field-line loop, and the other current loop. A field line contributes to $M$ only if it intersects both current loops. Your identity holds for each of these imaginary field lines, so it also holds for the entire flux.

Title: On the Stability Analysis of Infinite-Dimensional Port-Hamiltonian Systems Within the Variational Framework

Abstract:
This paper addresses the stability analysis of a class of linear infinite-dimensional port-Hamiltonian systems formulated within the variational framework. We derive verifiable conditions for the equivalence of the Hamiltonian-induced energy norm and the natural state-space norm, as well as for the generation of a contraction semigroup by the associated system operator. The semigroup generation result is obtained by establishing dissipativity and verifying the required range condition. The proposed conditions simplify the functional-analytic stability analysis of this class of systems in a manner similar to established results for the Stokes-Dirac setting.

Site: Stats Stack Exchange
Title: Unified uncertainty for aggregate class prevalence under misclassification, sampling noise, and domain shift
Tags: machine-learning, classification, confusion-matrix

Question:
I estimate country-level class shares from per-instance predictions produced by a classifier trained on a labeled dataset. The pipeline is:

Train a classifier on labeled data.

Apply it to an unlabeled set of domains in each country.

Aggregate predictions to get naive classify-and-count (CC) shares.

Correct for systematic misclassification using adjusted Classify-and-Count (ACC) (i.e. invert the confusion matrix estimated on a labeled holdout; cf. Forman, 2008).

Construct confidence intervals via a two-layer bootstrap:

resample domains within country (sampling variability),

resample the labeled holdout (uncertainty in the confusion matrix).

This yields confidence intervals for the corrected share vector

This setup captures two sources of uncertainty:
(A) Misclassification bias + its estimation uncertainty (through the confusion matrix),
(B) Sampling variability from having a finite number of instances per country,

However, I worry about a third thing (which might be a bigger issue)

(C) Parameter drift / domain shift: the conditional distribution P(Y∣X) (or equivalently the confusion matrix) may differ between training/holdout data and deployment countries.

I am looking for a unified framework that can represent all three sources jointly:

sampling noise in observed units

uncertainty in misclassification correction

instability of the classifier across domains (domain shift / transportability failure)

I should mention, that my training data covers multiple countries, so I have some avenue for estimating the impact of domain shift on instance-level predictions.

More formally (let me know if this is correct?):

$$
\pi_c \quad \text{: true class prevalence in country } c
$$

$$
\hat{\pi}^{\mathrm{CC}}_c \quad \text{: naive classify-and-count estimate}
$$

$$
C \quad \text{: confusion matrix estimated on labeled data}
$$

ACC estimator:$$\hat{\pi}^{\mathrm{ACC}}_c = C^{-1} \hat{\pi}^{\mathrm{CC}}_c$$Current inference approximates:$$\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\hat{\pi}^{\mathrm{ACC}}_c \mid C\right) + \mathrm{Var}(C)$$But ignores:$$C_c \neq C \quad \text{(domain-specific confusion matrix)}$$

So far, my research on this topic has beem mostly based on this text:

Forman, G. (2008). Quantifying counts and costs via classification. Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery, 17, 164–206. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10618-008-0097-y

Title: Lipschitz volume rigidity for non-collapsed $\rm RCD$ spaces with boundary

Abstract:
We study Lipschitz-volume rigidity for non-collapsed ${\rm RCD}(K,N)$ spaces, possibly with boundary. We prove that a measure-preserving $1$-Lipschitz map between such spaces restricts to an isometry from the interior of the domain onto its image, where the latter is equipped with the intrinsic length distance. We then characterize when this interior rigidity extends to an isometric bijection between the whole spaces, in terms of the behavior of the map on the boundaries. Along the way, we establish a rigidity result of independent interest in a more general class of rectifiable metric spaces.

Title: How many mutations does it take to evolve a new function?

Abstract:
Biochemical and genetic networks in cells evolve to produce new functions. Evolution is guided by the genotype to phenotype map which describes how mutations at the molecular scale lead to changes in network function at the cellular scale. The number of genotypes is astronomically large which makes these maps very high dimensional. In this context, the simple question: How many mutations does it take to evolve a new function?, is usually hard to answer. Here we consider this question in the context of a simple Boolean-network model of a genotype-phenotype map. The nodes and edges of the Boolean network represent the genotype while the Boolean function the network computes is the phenotype. The network evolves by rewiring of its edges, while keeping the number of nodes fixed. We compute the number of mutations needed to achieve a new Boolean function as a function of the number of nodes in the network. We show that the number of mutations scales with the number of nodes of the network as a power-law with an exponent determined by local geometrical features of the genotype-phenotype map. Our theoretical study emphasizes the role of the genotype-phenotype map in determining the time to evolve a new function.

Title: The Miyaoka-Yau inequality and the delta invariant for Fano varieties II -soliton case-

Abstract:
Inspired by recent work of Inoue and Hallam-Lahdili, we prove an equivariant Miyaoka-Yau inequality with a correction term for smooth Fano manifolds admitting Kähler-Ricci solitons. It recovers the usual Miyaoka-Yau inequality in the Kähler-Einstein case. Our proof uses weighted equivariant Bogomolov-Gieseker and Langer inequalities for torsion-free sheaves, together with a weighted slope estimate for the canonical extension sheaf. We also construct toric examples showing that the existence of a soliton implies neither weighted semistability of the canonical extension sheaf nor nonnegativity of the equivariant Miyaoka-Yau number.

Wiki: English Wikipedia
Draft: John O'Leary

Draft text:
John O’Leary is an American business executive who is the President and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Daimler Truck North America (DTNA). He assumed the role on April 1, 2021, succeeding Roger Nielsen. [ref: John O’Leary to Succeed Roger Nielsen as CEO of DTNA, Transport Topics] He is also a member of the Board of Management of Daimler Truck Holding AG, representing the North American region. [ref: Daimler Truck extends John O’Leary’s term on management board, FreightWaves]

O’Leary has been cited in national and business media in connection with U.S. manufacturing trends, tariffs, and the transition to electric vehicles. In coverage by The New York Times, he commented on the impact of tariffs on domestic steel pricing, noting that U.S. producers had “more headroom” to raise prices. [ref: U.S. Steel Producers Raise Prices After Tariffs Stymie Imports, The New York Times] He has also been quoted in The Wall Street Journal regarding infrastructure limitations affecting the adoption of electric heavy-duty trucks. [ref: Sales of Electric Heavy-Duty Trucks Are Hitting a Regulatory Wall, The Wall Street Journal]

O’Leary previously served as Chief Transformation Officer and Head of Mercedes-Benz Trucks in Germany from 2020 to 2021, and earlier was Chief Financial Officer of DTNA from 2012 to 2020. [ref: Daimler Trucks NA Names New CEO, School Bus Fleet] In 2024, he joined the board of directors of Portland General Electric. [ref: John O'Leary will join Portland General Electric board of directors, effective January 1, 2024, Portland General Electric] That same year, he co-chaired Oregon’s Clean Tech Manufacturing Task Force alongside Governor Tina Kotek and U.S. Senator Ron Wyden. [ref: Governor Kotek Releases Clean Tech Manufacturing Task Force Recommendations, Office of the Governor of Oregon]

== Career ==

O’Leary began his career in the commercial vehicle industry in 1989 at Paccar. He joined Freightliner (now DTNA) in 2000, where he held several leadership roles, including Internal Audit Director. He later served as President and CEO of Thomas Built Buses from 2002 to 2010, followed by Senior Vice President for DTNA’s aftermarket business from 2010 to 2012.

In 2012, O’Leary was appointed Chief Financial Officer of DTNA, a position he held until 2020. [ref: Daimler Truck extends John O’Leary’s term on management board, FreightWaves] In September 2020, he relocated to Germany to serve as Chief Transformation Officer and interim head of Mercedes-Benz Trucks.

Following the retirement of DTNA CEO Roger Nielsen, O’Leary was named President and CEO effective April 1, 2021. [ref: John O’Leary to Succeed Roger Nielsen as CEO of DTNA, Transport Topics] After the spin-off and public listing of Daimler Truck Holding AG on December 10, 2021, he joined the company’s Board of Management, representing North America. [ref: Daimler Truck launched on stock exchange as an independent company, Daimler Truck]

During his tenure, O’Leary has been cited in industry and business publications in connection with market transitions in the North American Class 8 truck sector, including supply chain disruptions, tariffs, and shifts in demand. [ref: DTNA’s O’Leary Reflects on Time of Transition for Company, Class 8 Market, Transport Topics] He has also been referenced in reporting on DTNA’s investments in electric truck development and engineering in the United States, including projects in Portland, Oregon, [ref: Daimler goes big on electrics in Portland, Portland Business Journal] as well as broader industry trends such as partnerships and acquisitions among truck manufacturers. [ref: Truck makers pursue acquisitions and joint ventures, Axios] Additional reporting has noted the company’s strategic focus on expanding its vocational truck segment in response to changing market conditions. [ref: As on-highway sales slump, DTNA sees opportunity for Western Star, FleetOwner]

In October 2023, the Daimler Truck Supervisory Board extended his management board term through March 2026. [ref: Daimler Truck extends John O’Leary’s term on management board, FreightWaves]

O’Leary’s tenure as president was marked by a focus on modernizing production and expanding technological capabilities. In August 2026, DTNA announced plans to build a new truck manufacturing facility in the United States. [ref: Daimler Truck plans to build a new truck production facility in the USA, FinanzNachrichten] [ref: Daimler Truck expands US business with new plant, Reuters] [ref: Daimler Truck Eyes New USA Plant, North American Orders Surge, Bloomberg] Following the announcement, O’Leary commented, “We want to have the best, most modern plants out there, because we know that will give us a best-cost position.” The expansion followed the company’s plans to upgrade technology across its manufacturing operations. O’Leary added that the new facility would “strengthen our ability to deliver industry-leading products while supporting long-term growth in the United States.” [ref: Daimler Truck North America Plans to Build New U.S. Manufacturing Facility, Daimler Truck]

Wiki: English Wikipedia
Draft: Abuqatrania

Draft text:
Abuqatrania is an extinct genus of parapithecid primates known from the Paleogene of North Africa. It was established in 2001 by Elwyn L. Simons, Erik R. Seiffert, Prithijit S. Chatrath and Yousry Attia for the type species Abuqatrania basiodontos, based on fossils from the late Eocene of the Fayum Depression in Egypt. [ref: Earliest record of a parapithecid anthropoid from the Jebel Qatrani Formation, northern Egypt, Folia Primatologica]

Its taxonomic status has been debated, as some authors have treated it as a synonym of the related genus Qatrania. [ref: A Companion to Paleoanthropology, Wiley-Blackwell] In 2024, isolated teeth from the earliest Oligocene of southern Morocco were tentatively referred to Abuqatrania cf. basiodontos.

== Discovery and occurrence ==

The original fossils of Abuqatrania basiodontos came from Quarry L-41 in the Jebel Qatrani Formation of the Fayum Depression, northern Egypt. The species was described as a late Eocene anthropoid and provided evidence for the presence of Parapithecidae in the oldest productive vertebrate-bearing deposits of the formation.

A second, tentative occurrence was reported in 2024 from the Samlat Formation in the Dakhla region of southern Morocco, near the northern border of Mauritania. The material comes from locality DAK C2, in the uppermost part of the formation along the Atlantic margin of the Rio de Oro, east of the Dakhla peninsula. The fossil-bearing deposits date to the earliest Oligocene, approximately 33.5 million years ago. The specimens were recovered from estuarine sediments using wet-screening techniques. [ref: A new primate community from the earliest Oligocene of the Atlantic margin of Northwest Africa: Systematic, paleobiogeographic, and paleoenvironmental implications, Journal of Human Evolution]

== Description ==

The original description characterized Abuqatrania basiodontos as a parapithecid with no clear autapomorphies, or derived characteristics exclusive to the species. Its most parsimonious phylogenetic interpretation placed it as the sister taxon of a clade containing Qatrania, Parapithecus and Apidium.

Body mass estimates for specimens tentatively assigned to Abuqatrania cf. basiodontos range from approximately 371 to 561 grams. These estimates were calculated from the dimensions of an isolated first lower molar and an isolated third lower molar from the earliest Oligocene of Morocco. This mass range is similar to that of New World Monkeys of the genus Callithrix. [ref: Quantitative assessment of grasping strength in platyrrhine monkeys, American Journal of Biological Anthropology]

The Moroccan material referred to Abuqatrania cf. basiodontos consists of isolated teeth rather than an associated skeleton. The published specimen records include a lower canine, lower molars, an upper molar identified as either the first or second molar, a lower incisor tentatively identified as either the first or second incisor, two lower second premolars and an upper third molar. Some of the teeth are worn, corroded or broken. [ref: 3D models related to the publication: A new primate community from the earliest Oligocene of the Atlantic margin of Northwest Africa: Systematic, paleobiogeographic and paleoenvironmental implications, MorphoMuseuM]

== Taxonomic history ==

Simons and colleagues established Abuqatrania as a distinct genus in 2001. They interpreted A. basiodontos as closely related to other early parapithecids, particularly a clade containing Qatrania, Parapithecus and Apidium.

In their review of Paleogene anthropoids, Seiffert and colleagues (2010) recognized Abuqatrania separately from Qatrania. They also discussed the possibility that Abuqatrania basiodontos was close to the ancestry of other parapithecids, noting that its fossils were approximately one million years older than those of Qatrania wingi. [ref: Cenozoic Mammals of Africa, University of California Press]

The distinction between Abuqatrania and Qatrania was not accepted by all authors. In 2013, K. Christopher Beard treated Abuqatrania as a synonym of Qatrania, using the combination Qatrania basiodontos for the species. Under this classification, the species belongs to the same genus as Qatrania wingi and Qatrania fleaglei.

The name has continued to be used in subsequent scientific literature. Marivaux and colleagues (2024), for example, tentatively assigned the Moroccan material to Abuqatrania cf. basiodontos.

== Paleobiogeography ==

The Moroccan locality DAK C2 preserves a diverse primate community from the Eocene–Oligocene transition. Marivaux and colleagues identified at least eight primate species, including anthropoids assigned to Oligopithecidae, Propliopithecidae, Parapithecidae and Afrotarsiidae, as well as several strepsirrhine groups.

Comparisons between the primates and rodents from Dakhla and those from the Jebel Qatrani Formation in Egypt led the authors to propose that an east–west environmental connection existed across North Africa during the latest Eocene and earliest Oligocene. They also suggested that tropical habitats along the northwestern margin of Africa may have acted as refuges during the cooling associated with the Eocene–Oligocene transition. These interpretations concern the broader fossil assemblage and its environment, rather than Abuqatrania alone.

== See also ==

* Qatrania
* Parapithecidae

== References ==

Title: Global existence and uniqueness of Lions' weak solutions for the 2D inhomogeneous Navier-Stokes equations in bounded domains

Abstract:
The global well-posedness for Lions' weak solutions to the inhomogeneous incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in two-dimensional bounded domains is concerned. When the initial density $0\leq ρ_0\in L^\infty(\Om)$ (allowing for vacuum) and initial velocity $u_0\in L^2_σ(Ω)$, the global existence, regularity, and exponential decay-in-time rates of weak solutions are established via a priori estimates, which rely crucially on the duality of BMO and Hardy space for the pressure term, and the classical Sobolev extension theorem. In particular, for the non-vacuous case where $0< ρ_0\in L^\infty(\Om)$ is bounded away from zero, we further prove the uniqueness of weak solutions in the sense of approximation by strong solutions, based on the key estimate \(t^{1/2}\nabla u\in L^2(0,T;L^\infty(Ω))\), which essentially follows from a delicate localized point-wise bound for \(\nabla u\) near the boundary. The latter bound is derived by the Green functions estimate for the nonhomogeneous Dirichlet Stokes problem, and the uniform \(C^1\) boundary estimate on the remaining homogeneous Stokes problem, through a Stokes decomposition on suitably constructed local \(C^2\) domains.

Title: Dynamic Persuasion: Managing Reputation under Censored Feedback

Abstract:
We study a long-run sender who repeatedly communicates about a state to a sequence of myopic receivers and whose credibility is a public score updated from past interactions. Receivers face a lemon loss and an opportunity loss, and their behavior depends on these only through a single index, the tolerance. Because the score records only detected misrepresentations, it rests above the sender's true honesty rate; we characterize this credibility premium in closed form. In a fluid limit in which the score adjusts slowly, no policy earns more than operating at a single credibility level, and the sender's gain from managing credibility equals the value of the premium: against receivers who correct for imperfect detection, that gain vanishes. At a fixed adjustment speed, every policy is bounded by the fluid value plus a term linear in the speed. We then study three policy classes, linear, (s,S), and threshold, obtain the optimal parameters of the linear and threshold classes in closed form, show how receiver losses shape them, and show that, under an approximation, the optimal (s,S) band collapses to a threshold. Simulations of the dynamics agree with the closed forms and indicate where the single-level conclusion stops: bands pay when switching modes is costly, and cycles pay when demand is seasonal.

Title: L-PASSO: Adaptive Log-penalized Variable Selector, with Sparse Selection and Robustness to the Pilot Estimator

Abstract:
We study L-PASSO, a penalized least-squares regression method based on the logarithmic penalty $λ\sum_j\log(1+|β_j|/τ)$, and its two-stage adaptive form, in which the scales $τ_j$ come from a pilot estimator. Although this concave penalty has been proposed previously, its variable-selection properties and sparsity relative to other popular penalties have not been fully characterized. We derive the exact orthogonal-design solution, and show that the single-stage estimator selects the true model under a weighted irrepresentable condition that holds for every design once $τ$ is small. We further establish that, under matched tuning, the two-stage estimator possesses the oracle property and has half the asymptotic bias of the adaptive LASSO. Our main theoretical contribution concerns the robustness of the two-stage procedure to the pilot estimator. We show that two-stage L-PASSO remains selection consistent even when the weights associated with relevant variables are as small as $\exp\{-o(1/ζ_n)\}$, whereas the adaptive LASSO fails to retain relevant variables whose pilot weights are sufficiently small relative to its tuning parameter $ζ_n$. We establish that both thresholds are sharp. In high-dimensional settings, we prove support recovery for a local minimizer without imposing any lower-bound condition on the weights of relevant variables, and provide conditions under which this local minimizer is also the unique global minimizer. We additionally establish the selection consistency of a BIC-based tuning-parameter selection procedure. Finally, simulations comparing L-PASSO with the LASSO, SCAD, MCP, SELO, uniLasso, and the adaptive LASSO show that L-PASSO most frequently recovers the true support. Two real-data examples further illustrate the method.

Title: Tracy-Widom law for sample covariance matrices under quadratic form concentration

Abstract:
We study sample covariance matrices formed from vectors $q_i = Σ^{1/2}u_i \in \mathbb{R}^M$, $1 \leq i \leq N$, where $u_1, \ldots, u_N$ are independent, centered, isotropic random vectors whose coordinates may not be independent. We assume that the random vectors $q_i$ satisfy a concentration bound for their quadratic forms $q_i^T A q_i$. Under this assumption and a regular right edge condition on $Σ$, we establish edge universality and obtain the Tracy-Widom law for the largest eigenvalue of the sample covariance matrix after appropriate centering and scaling. In particular, for log-concave ensembles, our result removes the unconditionality assumption imposed in existing edge universality results~\cite{BX}, resolving the question that originally motivated our work. The concentration assumption also allows us to extend the result beyond the log-concave class.

Title: On a class of meromorphic functions with three singular values

Abstract:
We give a parametrization of the class of real meromorphic functions in the plane for which the preimage of $\{0,1,\infty\}$ is contained in the real line, and all singular values belong to $\{0,1,\infty\}$. As corollaries, we obtain a new parabolic type criterion and prove that all such functions are limits of rational functions of the same class.

Title: Detection of HNCOH+ in the interstellar medium

Abstract:
Only five out of the $\sim$350 molecules detected in the interstellar medium (ISM) carry the isocyanate functional group (NCO), the essential substructure of peptide bonds in proteins. Among them are isocyanic acid (HNCO) and its most stable N-protonated isomer H$_2$NCO$^+$. Previous studies have predicted that the O-protonated isomer HNCOH$^+$ should be present in the ISM; yet this species has remained elusive. We search for the metastable HNCOH$^+$ towards the Galactic Center molecular cloud G+0.693-0.027, where H$_2$NCO$^+$ has already been detected. We use an ultra-deep broadband spectral survey carried out towards G+0.693-0.027 with the Yebes 40-m, IRAM 30-m and APEX telescopes covering nearly 150 GHz of bandwidth between 31 and 275 GHz. We report the first detection of HNCOH$^+$ in the ISM with a column density of $N$ = (9.9 $\pm$ 0.5)$\times$10$^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$, which corresponds to a molecular abundance relative to H$_2$ of (7.3$^{+1.3} _{-1.0}$)$\times$10$^{-11}$. With the measured H$_2$NCO$^+$ column density of $N$ = (2.6 $\pm$ 0.3) $\times 10^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$, this yields a HNCOH$^+$/H$_2$NCO$^+$ ratio of 3.8$^{+0.5} _{-0.4}$. This result is consistent with recent kinetic calculations that favour the formation of HNCOH$^+$ over H$_2$NCO$^+$. The detection of HNCOH$^+$ in the ISM broadens the inventory of molecules known to contain the isocyanate functional group and reinforces recent works showing that isomer abundances in the ISM do not necessarily correlate with thermodynamic stability.

Question:
I am trying to solve a problem from the german math olympiad. This problem deals with a coloring algorithm that is defined as follows:

First off, we are given two integers $0\lt m\lt n$ that are colored red and all the other numbers are colored white, then on each step execute the following rules:

It is checked, whether there are any red numbers left. If there is at most one red number, the process terminates.

Let k be the smallest red number on the current step, it is then colored black.

Then we look at the numbers $m+k$ and $n+k$. Every red number among these two is changed to black, every white number among them is changed to red, and every black number remains black.

We are asked to prove that

a) The process terminates after finitely many steps with exactly one red number $r$, no matter the choice of $m$ and $n$

b) For all $m,n$ the last number $r\le 2^n-1$

I know that I have to provide my own progress, but I sadly couldn't do much. I established that it suffices to consider coprime $m$ and $n$ since otherwise we could "divide the whole algorithm" by the $\gcd(m,n)$ and it doesn't change whether it terminates or not.

I also came up with a family of polynomials that simulates the behavior of the colored numbers.
$$P_i(x)=\sum_{j-red}x^j$$
where $j$ runs through all red numbers on the $i$-th step. These polynomials can be defined differently, namely:
$$P_{i+1}(x)=(1+x^m+x^n)(x^{k_0}+x^{k_1}+\dots +x^{k_i})-1 \mod 2$$

where $k_i$ is the minimal red number on the $i$-th step and the coefficients of this polynomial are then taken modulo $2$. If we don't take the coefficients $\mod 2$, $x$ to the red power will have the coefficient $1$ and $x$ to the black power will have a coefficient exactly $2$

This idea seemed pretty promising at first but I couldn't get much out of it.

I tried a bunch of smaller cases and it seemed that on each step    (the biggest red number)-(smallest red number)$\le n$. However this pattern breaks on the third step with $m=2$ and $n=3$ where the biggest red number is $9$ and the smallest one is $5$.

At this point I have thought on this problem for a week and have no idea how to proceed further. I would really appreciate any sort of help.

Site: Physics Stack Exchange
Title: How did Michelson achieve interference fringes with an unpolarized and incoherent light
Tags: optics, interferometry

Question:
In the original Michelson and Michelson-Morley experiments there is no mention of using a polarizer. How did Michelson achieve interference fringes with an unpolarized and incoherent light. Was the polarization obtained via reflection from flat mirrors sufficient to get visible interference?

Answer A:
Well first of all let us make the diagram clear. The diagram of the experiment consists of a source, a lens a half silvered mirror M, a compensator plate,mirror M1 all in a single line and mirror M2 perpendicular to M and has a telescope perpendicular(below) mirror M

Now let the light come from the source. The lens collimates the rays from the source, without which the rays would diverge here and there.

When the light reaches M,let us divide it into two beams A and B. B is reflected from the mirror M's silver part and goes towards M2.A is transmitted through mirror M,passes through the compensator plate and goes towards M1.

Now beam A comes back from M1 and when it again reaches M,it is reflected downwards. Similarly after being reflected from M2, it is transmitted from the mirror M. Now both A and B travel towards the telescope where we observe the interference.

My point for writing the whole experiment was to give you the feel. You might have noticed that A and B are actually from the same source,from the beam falling on mirror M. They are coherent sources because they have been derived from the same source.

Now talking about polarization,yes in the beginning it is unpolarized. But after coming in contact with mirror M, the beams A and B both undergo the similar amount of reflection and transmission. In reality an unpolarized light is a collection of many states. Thus due to the arrangement,the S-polarized part of beam A and B and P polarised part of beam A and B are similar and it gives rise to overlapping polarization fragments sufficient for interferenc.The magic of this experiment indeed lies in the arrangement which creates such situations of sufficient overlap of reflection and transmission which makes them have compatible polarization states. The beams don't have to be fully polarised at all. But the arrangement can create a sufficient overlap of polarization states for them to interfere

Answer B:
What you may have in mind, making you come up with this particular question:

It is the case that if you split a beam of light, and one beam is polarized in one plane, and the other polarized in a perpendicular plane, then when those beams are put to a screen there will not be a visible interference pattern.

But being polarized at all is not a necessity.

Not being polarized is not a factor.

General remarks about the setup of the Michelson-Morley experiment

The Michelson-Morley experiment used white light as light source.

It's not the case that the temporal coherency of a laser source is an absolute necessity to be able to elicit interference effect. The advantage of having a laser source is that it makes other aspects of the setup less demanding.

Here is an example of interference effect that occurs with daylight:

Soap film bubbles tend to have colorization effect.
The soap film doesn't have a uniform thickness. Different areas of the soap film have different thickness. When the thickness is an integer multiple of the wavelength of the light that is interacting with the soap film then there is opportunity for destructive interference. Different areas have different thickness, and in different areas different colors from the spectrum are suppressed relative to other colors.

Another example is the phenomenon referred to as Newton's rings

Newton's rings are more vivid when monochromatic light is used; when using wide spectrum light there are colorization effects, but the point is that in a Newton's rings setup the conditions for interference effect to be visible are met.

The first double-slit-experiment-with-light was set up with daylight, entering the room through a small opening.

In a double slit setup with white light: in order to obtain an interference pattern the source that illuminates the double slit must be a point source.

Let the two slits be named slit A and slit B.

When the light source that illuminates the slits is a point source then:
The light that has traveled from source through slit A, arriving at a particular spot on the projection screen, and the light that has traveled from source through slit B, arriving at that same particular spot, those two paths are in a definite phase relation to each other.

It's the phase relation that counts; being in a definite phase relation is sufficient for an interference pattern to be elicited.

Daylight has extremely short temporal coherence.

Title: Sizes of cross-intersecting families

Abstract:
The size of cross-intersecting families ${\cal F}_1, \dots, {\cal F}_d$ is usually measured by the sum or the product of the sizes $|{\cal F}_i|$. These two natural size functions have different extremal structures, and different techniques have been developed for them. We introduce the cross-degree of a size function and show that the potential extremal structures of maximum cross-intersecting families are the same for all size functions of finite cross-degree, including the sum and the product. Our main tool is a strengthened form of the generating family method of Ahlswede--Khachatrian, based on standard generating families and on local modifications of cross-intersecting families, which we call mutations. It treats two completely different types of extremal structures in a unified way and, unlike the original method, needs shifting in only one step.

Question:
I am trying to evaluate the following indefinite integral:

$$I = \int \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{(x^4+1)^{1/4}}$$

I have tried several substitutions, including trigonometric substitutions and algebraic rearrangements, but I have not been able to reduce it to an elementary form.

I tried the substitution $x=\sqrt{\tan\theta}$.

Since $x^2=\tan\theta$, differentiating both sides gives:

$$\newcommand{\d}{\mathrm{d}}
2x\,\d x=\sec^2\theta\,\d\theta$$

or

$$\d x=\frac{\sec^2\theta}{2\sqrt{\tan\theta}}\, \d\theta$$

Also,

$$x^4+1=\tan^2\theta+1=\sec^2\theta$$

Therefore,

$$(x^4+1)^{1/4}=(\sec^2\theta)^{1/4}=\sqrt{\sec\theta}$$

Substituting these into the integral:

$$I=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{\sec^{3/2}\theta}{\sqrt{\tan\theta}}\, \d\theta$$

Simplifying:

$$\frac{\sec^{3/2}\theta}{\sqrt{\tan\theta}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\sin\theta}\cos\theta}$$

Hence,

$$I=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{\d\theta}{\sqrt{\sin\theta}\cos\theta}$$

However, I am unable to simplify this further.

Does this integral have an elementary antiderivative? If not, how can it be expressed in terms of special functions such as elliptic integrals or hypergeometric functions?

[truncated]

Answer B:
There seems to be a basic misconception.  RAM is memory.  Non-volatile storage can be also be used as memory.  You can use non-volatile memory/storage instead of RAM.  You can use any algorithm you want, and store everything in non-volatile memory/storage instead of in RAM.  Basically, RAM is a big array, where you can read or write to address A (i.e., index A in the array), and non-volatile memory/storage is also a big array, and you can also read or write to address A.  So any time that an algorithm talks about storing or reading in memory, it can use non-volatile storage instead of RAM.  That makes solving your problem trivial.  Just do any base conversion algorithm, and store everything (all intermediate results) in non-volatile memory/storage.

In real computers, non-volatile storage is often a lot slower than RAM, depending on the specific technology, so if you're motivated by a real-world problem, this approach might be slow, but it will work.

Site: Chemistry Stack Exchange
Title: Boiling point of two miscible solvents
Tags: organic-chemistry, boiling-point, distillation, refractive-index

Question:
When isobutanol and ethanol are volumetrically even, why is it that during distillation, some isobutanol comes over with ethanol?

Was doing simple distillation and tested their refractive index every 10mL, where there was a gradual change present. The temperature change was also gradual, when I assumed there would be a pause at ethanols boiling point, where all extra heat added would remove only ethanol before the solution would raise any higher.

I assumed that some isobutanol was in the distillate, but is that a false assumption?

Answer A:
What you are seeing is expected behavior. The ethanol-isobutanol (more commonly/properly called 2-methyl-propan-1-ol or perhaps 2-methyl-1-propanol) is close to an ideal solution at 1 atm (i.e., it obeys Raoult's Law to good approximation). Its phase diagram at 101.33 kPa is below, with experimental data (circles) from Duran et al., Fluid Phase Equil. 338: 128–134 (2013).

I don't know what the mole fraction is for your "volumetrically even" mixture (btw, what do you mean? Do you mean you took, say, 50 mL of ethanol and 50 mL of isobutyl alcohol and dumped both into a container, or did you take, say, 50 mL of isobutyl alcohol and fill the container to 100 mL? Those will technically give you slightly different total volumes, and slightly different mole fractions, though since the solution is nearly ideal, they'll be close). However, let's say for simplicity that you started with an equimolar mixture of the two, so $x_1 = 0.5$. That means $y_1$ (fraction in the distillate at equilibrium) will be about 0.89, which is pretty far from 1 of course.

As you keep distilling, the fraction of ethanol in the liquid goes down more and more (because it was 89% of the distillate at first), so the temperature of the liquid will follow the bubble line (the lower of the two enveloping lines in the diagram). Eventually, the entire mixture will have boiled away, and the last drop of liquid would be 11–12% ethanol (interpolating from the $x_1$ corresponding to $y_1 = 0.5$), and the temperature would be about 388 K (again interpolating).

Answer B:
At the temperatures involved ethanol and isobutanol have reasonable vapor pressures. For a homogeneous mix of similar compounds the solution approximates an ideal solution and the vapor pressure of the solution is expressed by Raoult's Law [Look it up!]. The vapor pressure of the solution is a function of the mole fractions and the pure vapor pressures so the vapor of a equal mix will contain both. In this case the higher VP will be in excess. As the distillation proceeds the more volatile component is removed and the BP approaches the higher boiling component. Your data probably shows this so analyse it carefully, report back in the comments with your findings.

This precludes any chemical reaction happening among the materials in the flask.

Answer C:
Distillation is not guaranteed to separate all compounds.

First, temperature is an aggregate property, with a distribution of energies. Consider that water, with a boiling point of 100°C, evaporates (well sublimes) even below freezing, 0°C, because some molecules have sufficient energy to leave the solid.

Second, some substances form an azeotrope, where as the more volatile substance is lost, the concentration of the less volatile in the vessel, increases, thereby increasing, by the law of mass action, the probability of it evaporating in greater quantity. A common example is distilling ethanol from water, where separation stops at ~95.6 wt% ethanol and ~4.4 wt% water. An azeotrope cannot be separated by distillation alone, though it can be separated by adding another substance which can trap one of the components.

Though isobutanol and ethanol themselves do not form an inseparable azeotrope, they both, separately or combined, form an azeotrope with water... and unless great care has been taken to start with anhydrous reagents, and to exclude all water vapor, you can be certain that some water has been absorbed.

Summary

You might be doing nothing wrong. Product at the beginning and at the end of the distillation are purest, but expect a bit of mixture in the middle of the process.

On the other hand, any moisture in the system will decrease separation of the two alcohols.

Site: Physics Stack Exchange
Title: My axiomatization attempt of Newtonian spacetime
Tags: general-relativity, newtonian-gravity, differential-geometry, geodesics

Question:
I was recently re-watching Friedric Schuller's axiomatization of Newtonian 4-spacetime $M$ with a position dependent force density, in which he lists the the following axioms:

(i) there exists a time function $t \colon M \to \mathbb R$ with $\left(\mathrm dt\right)_p \neq 0$ for all $p \in M$,

(ii) there is a torsion free-connection $\nabla$ with $\nabla_X \mathrm dt = 0$ for all vector fields $X$,

(iii) Newton's second law on a test particle with mass $m$ is then

$$\nabla_{\dot \gamma} \dot \gamma = f/m, \quad \left(\mathrm dt\right)_p(f) = 0.$$

For reasons Schuller do not really mention, (i) implies that spacetime foilates

$$M \cong \bigsqcup_{\tau \in \mathbb R} \left\{ p \in M : t(p) = \tau \right\},$$

and (ii) implies that "time flows uniformly into the future".

My formalization attempt is a bit different. I find it weird to introduce absolute time, when time should only be affine (no objective $t = 0$). I also want to start with lengths of curves, instead of postulating what autoparallellness means, because I want:

$$\Delta \tau = \int_\gamma \sqrt{ \pm g(\dot \gamma, \dot \gamma)}.$$

So instead I am imaging a unit vector field $g(X, X) = 1$. Having $g(X, \dot \gamma) = 1$ means traversing with unit speed into the future. So I postulate the existence of a unit "time flowing" vector field $X$.

Bilinearity of $g$ leads me to guess the requirement that

$$g \not \equiv 0, \quad g(Y, Y) = g(Y, X)^2 \text{ for all vector fields } Y.$$

This seems to imply that $g(Y, Z) = \omega(Y)\omega(Z) = g(X, Y)g(X, Z)$, because for any two arbitrary vector fields $Y$ and $Z$ we can write:

$$g(Y + Z, Y + Z) = g(Y, Y) + 2g(Y, Z) + g(Z, Z).$$

Call $\omega(Y) := g(X, Y)$. This is a (linear) 1-form. The linearity will be important in a moment.

Thus we have

$$\omega(Y + Z)^2 = \omega(Y)^2 + 2g(Y, Z) + \omega(Z)^2,$$

and now linearity $\omega(Y + Z) = \omega(Y) + \omega(Z)$ implies $\omega(Y + Z)^2 = (\omega(Y) + \omega(Z))^2$. Expanding gives:

$$\omega(Y)^2 + 2\omega(Y)\omega(Z) + \omega(Z)^2 = \omega(Y)^2 + 2g(Y, Z) + \omega(Z)^2.$$

Cancelling the squared terms on each side yields

$$g(Y, Z) = \omega(Y)\omega(Z).$$

This implies $g = \omega \otimes \omega$ or, in a chart, $g_{ij} = \omega_i \omega_j$.

Geometrically, $g$ only measures the projection of a vector along the line spanned by $X$. This is exactly the property I want to have.  My only problem is that this approach currently does not seem to incorporate any force.

Since my $g$ is degenerate, there is of course no unique induced Levi-Civita connection. Is the remaining freedom enough to encode any arbitrary position dependent force field in a torsion-free connection $\nabla$?

There is also a problem with foilation. How do I avoid the time vector field $X$ from preventing a foilation in time?

Title: Characterizing $\pT$-differential Radial-Flow Fluctuations in Au+Au Collisions at FAIR with a Multi-Phase Transport Model

Abstract:
We report the first predictions of the transverse-momentum ($\pT$)-differential radial-flow fluctuation observable, $\vzpT$, in Au+Au collisions at the top SIS100 energy, $\snn=4.9$~GeV, which will be available at the FAIR accelerator complex. Radial flow and its fluctuations are studied for different centrality intervals and reference-$\pT$ selections to investigate the properties and robustness of the calculated long-range correlation. $\vzpT$ displays a characteristic evolution from negative values at low $\pT$ to positive values at higher $\pT$. The integrated $v_0$, obtained with different reference-$\pT$ intervals, follows a common trend, with an approximately inverse-square-root dependence on the inclusive charged-particle multiplicity ($\nch$). The $\vzpT$ signal changes little when the pseudorapidity gap is varied between 0.2 and 0.8, or when the edges of the reference-$\pT$ interval are varied, in the bulk region. For identified particles, the pion and proton $\vzpT$ are ordered at low $\pT$, qualitatively similar to the mass ordering seen at higher energies. However, unlike at higher collision energies, $\vzpT$ does not exhibit constituent-quark number scaling, so the results do not support an interpretation in terms of partonic collectivity. The results are also in partial contradiction with the behavior of hadronic elliptic flow in these low-energy collisions. These results provide constraints on the evolution of radial correlations toward lower collision energies and motivate comparisons with complementary observables to clarify their connection to collective dynamics.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: Binomial identity but with squares on the binomial coefficients: $\sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i}^2 x^i y^{n-i}$
Tags: combinatorics, analysis, binomial-coefficients

Question:
We know the binomial identity

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} x^i y^{n-i} = ( x + y )^n.$$

But if I have squares on the binomial coefficients,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i}^2 x^i y^{n-i},$$

does that admit any interesting representation?

Answer A:
Your question is essentially same to find interesting representation of $$\sum_0^n\binom{n}{r}^2x^r.$$

Legendre polynomial $P_n(z)$ has representation $$P_n(z)=\sum_0^n\binom{n}{r}^2\left(\frac{z-1}{2}\right)^r\left(\frac{z+1}{2}\right)^{n-r}.$$

If we use substitution $z=\frac{1+x}{1-x}$, then $\frac{z-1}{2}=\frac{x}{1-x}$ and $\frac{z+1}{2}=\frac{1}{1-x}$ so
\begin{align}
P_n\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right) &= \sum_0^n\binom nr^2\left(\frac{x}{1-x}\right)^{r}\left(\frac{1}{1-x}\right)^{n-r} \\
&= (1-x)^{-n}\sum_0^n\binom nr^2x^r.
\end{align}

Therefore, $$\sum_0^n\binom nr^2x^r=(1-x)^nP_n\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right).$$

$$P_n(z)=\sum_0^n\binom{n}{r}^2\left(\frac{z-1}{2}\right)^r\left(\frac{z+1}{2}\right)^{n-r}$$
can be obtain almost immediately when we use Liebniz rule $(fg)^{(n)}=\sum_0^n\binom nrf^{(r)}g^{(n-r)}$ for Rodrigues' formula $$P_n(x)=\frac{1}{2^nn!}\frac{d^n}{dx^n}\left((x-1)^n(x+1)^n\right).$$

Answer B:
Here is a complement to [user]'s answer, in the case where you would like an integral representation too. It can be constructed with the help of Egorychev's method, which provides a contour integral representation on the complex plane for the binomial coefficient, namely
$$
\binom{n}{k} = \oint_C \frac{\mathrm{d}z}{2\pi i} \frac{(1+z)^n}{z^{k+1}},
$$
hence
$$
\begin{align}
(x-y)^n P_n\left(\frac{x+y}{x-y}\right)
   &= \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}^2 x^ky^{n-k} \\
   &= \oint_C \frac{\mathrm{d}z}{2\pi i} \frac{(1+z)^n}{z} \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} \left(\frac{x}{z}\right)^ky^{n-k} \\
   &= \oint_C \frac{(\frac{x}{z} + x + y + yz)^n}{2\pi iz} \,\mathrm{d}z
\end{align}
$$
thanks to the binomial theorem.

Title: Influences of $N_2$ flow rate on the superconducting properties and dimensionality of epitaxial TiN thin films

Abstract:
TiN thin films have received great attention in the field of superconducting quantum computing due to their low loss characteristics derived from stable chemical and thermal properties, as well as excellent electrical conductivity. In this study, TiN thin films with a thickness of 35 nm were epitaxially grown on MgO substrates using the DC reactive magnetron sputtering technique. The crystal structure, film thickness, and surface morphology of the thin films were characterized. The films exhibit a very flat surface with a root mean square roughness of only a few tenths of a nanometer. The influences of nitrogen ($N_2$) flow rate on the surface morphology, superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$), residual resistivity ratio (RRR), normal-state resistivity ($ρ_n$), upper critical field, and superconducting dimensionality were investigated systematically. The experimental results show that the TiN film deposited with a $N_2$ flow rate of 1.5 sccm exhibits optimal performance, including the highest $T_c$ (4.93 K), the largest RRR, the lowest $ρ_n$, and the lowest slope of the out-of-film upper critical field near Tc. Moreover, it is found that the background vacuum inside the growth chamber has a significant impact on the superconducting properties of TiN films, and the degradation of vacuum degree can lead to the decrease of $T_c$. The upper critical field reveals a significant anisotropic feature. Importantly, the in-film upper critical field data demonstrates that the optimization of sample quality leads to deviation from two-dimensional superconducting behavior, which provides a new perspective on the influencing factors of superconducting dimensionality beyond the thickness of films. The present results provide useful references for a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between growth parameters and the superconducting properties of thin films.

Draft text:
----

The settlement of Los Castillejos, located in the municipality of Sanchorreja in the province of Ávila in Spain, was a hill fort or oppidum (also known as a castro) where people lived between the late Chalcolithic or Early Bronze Age and the fifth century BC. Although some archaeological excavations have taken place, the ruins are hardly visible here. [ref: Guía. Castro de Los Castillejos. Sanchorreja, Ávila]

The oppidum of “Los Castillejos” is one of the most important archaeological sites in the province of Ávila. The stratigraphic sediments have a depth of 2.0 meters. The range of the sediments can be traced from the late Chalcolithic or early Bronze Age until the fifth century BC, when the settlement was gradually abandoned by its inhabitants without any signs of cultural Romanization. [ref: Vetones: historia y arqueología de un pueblo prerromano, UAM Ediciones]

These people are considered as the predecessor of what would become later the Vettones, who founded new relevant settlements in the province of Avila like La Mesa de Miranda, Las Cogotas, Ulaca or El Raso.

The first archaeological excavations took place in the decade of 1930 by Joaquín María de Navascués, Emilio Camps Cazorla, and Juan Cabré. But the first findings were not published until 20 years later by Juan Maluquer [ref: El Castro de los Castillejos en Sanchorreja. Estudio de las excavaciones realizadas por D. Juan Cabré, D. Joaquín María de Navascués, y D. Emilio Camps, de 1931 a 1935]. An additional archaeological excavation took place later in the years 1981, 1982 and 1985 by F. J. González-Tablas Sastre.

The archaeological findings include many different types of ceramics, personal items made of bronze (buttons, needles, brooches, belt buckles), and utensils made of iron (axes, knives).

Some metal recipients found in the settlement, the ceramic techniques and types used, as well as one of the belt buckles with the representation of a griffin, are typical samples of western cultures like the Phoenicians, which had colonies around the Mediterranean area of the Iberian Peninsula at that time. Therefore, those items found at Los Castillejos are a confirmation that there was some type of exchange between the people who lived here and the coastal inhabitants of the Peninsula.

== References ==

GONZÁLEZ-TABLAS SASTRE, F.J. y DOMÍNGUEZ CALVO, A.; Los Castillejos de Sanchorreja. Campañas de 1981, 1982 y 1985. Acta Salmanticensia 117. Salamanca. 2002.

Draft text:
China Everbright Bank (Europe) S.A. is a credit institution incorporated in Luxembourg. It serves as the European subsidiary of China Everbright Bank (中国光大银行), a Chinese joint-stock commercial bank founded in August 1992, headquartered in Beijing, and listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange (SSE: 601818) and the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (SEHK: 6818).

When China Everbright Bank set up its Luxembourg operation in 2017, it did so through two separate legal structures: the subsidiary covered in this article, and a directly operated branch, the China Everbright Bank Luxembourg Branch. At the time, this made China Everbright the seventh Chinese bank with a presence in the Grand Duchy. Academic research on Chinese banks' European expansion has noted that Luxembourg's early diplomatic ties with China, dating to 1972, and its role as a financial gateway have made it a recurring choice for Chinese lenders structuring their EU market entry.

== History ==
China Everbright Bank obtained a banking licence from the European Central Bank and clearance from Luxembourg's financial regulator, the CSSF, to open the subsidiary in 2017. Press coverage at the time framed the move partly as a way of securing a foothold in the EU single market ahead of Brexit, and partly as part of the bank's wider push to support trade tied to China's Belt and Road Initiative.

The bank marked the opening with a launch event in Luxembourg on 8 September 2017, held alongside the "Forum for Belt and Road Initiative and Investment of Chinese Enterprises in Europe". Those attending included Luxembourg's then prime minister Xavier Bettel, finance minister Pierre Gramegna, CSSF director general Claude Marx, China's ambassador to Luxembourg Huang Changqing, and China Everbright Group and Bank chairman Tang Shuangning.

Research on the sector has characterised such moves by Chinese state-linked banks as part of a broader, legally-structured pattern of foreign direct investment into the European Union, in which a Luxembourg subsidiary combined with a parallel branch is a common structural choice.

== Operations ==
The subsidiary is built around corporate banking rather than retail services. Its business centres on deposits and loans for corporate clients, multi-currency accounts (it handles euros, US dollars and renminbi), trade finance instruments such as letters of credit and guarantees, and international settlement and money-market activity. In practice, its client base consists mainly of European firms doing business in China, Chinese companies investing into the EU, and other banks needing a correspondent relationship in Luxembourg.

== Regulation ==
As a Luxembourg-licensed credit institution, the bank is supervised jointly by the European Central Bank under the Single Supervisory Mechanism and, at national level, by the CSSF, the country's financial regulator. The entity is listed in the CSSF's public register of authorised credit institutions and in the European Central Bank's official list of supervised entities. The licence also gives it EU passporting rights, so it can offer services across the wider European Economic Area without separate authorisation in each country. Deposits are covered up to €100,000 per depositor under Luxembourg's deposit guarantee scheme, the *Fonds de garantie des dépôts Luxembourg*.

Its identifying codes are: BIC/SWIFT EVERLULX; LEI 22210018MLEVW7CTGU78; Luxembourg trade and companies register (RCS) number B213668; and ECB monetary financial institution code LUB00401. The company's registration and corporate filings can be consulted through the official Luxembourg Business Registers portal.

== Financial position ==
As of 2025, the bank reported total assets of around €105 million and net profit of roughly €2 million, with a small workforce of six employees. Its registered office is at 10, Avenue Émile Reuter, in Luxembourg City.
