Alberto Fassi (born 30 July 1975 in Bergamo) is an Italian entrepreneur and the founder and chief executive officer of Legami S.p.A. Società benefit, a company active in the stationery and lifestyle sectors.

== Biography and career ==

After graduating from Bocconi University with a degree in Business Economics, Fassi spent an exchange period at ESSEC Business School in Paris. Following an internship at the Italian embassy in Ankara and an experience as a financial consultant for KPMG, he embarked on a Master's degree in creativity and innovation at the Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore in Milan. [ref: "[https://kpmg.com/it/it/insights/2025/11/alumnus-kpmg-anno-2025-alberto-fassi.html 'Alumnus KPMG dell'Anno': a Alberto Fassi il riconoscimento per il 2025]", KPMG, November 2025.]

During the Master's programme, Fassi developed a book strap in a variety of colours, each associated with a feeling. The product became the basis for Legami, which he founded in Bergamo in 2003. The company was initially based in his parents' garage. [ref: Elisa Britzelmeier, "[https://www.sueddeutsche.de/wirtschaft/legami-hype-tierstifte-erfolg-bergamo-li.3351222 Legami: Der Stifte-Hype in deutschen Schulen und die Erfolgsgeschichte aus Italien]", Süddeutsche Zeitung, 29 December 2025.]

Between 2005 and 2014, Fassi oversaw Legami's expansion in the Italian market and its subsequent growth abroad, including the opening of new concept stores and the acquisition of key accounts in Italy and internationally. [ref: Rachele Anconetani, Federico Colantoni and Federico Pippo, "[https://iris.unibocconi.it/handle/11565/4045577 We are young, we are curious, we are dreamers: the Legami growth path]", Bocconi University, 2020.]

In 2023, Fassi opened Legami's share capital to the Flexible Capital Fund, managed by DeA Capital Alternative Funds, which acquired a 42% stake while he retained control of the company. [ref: Sara Bennewitz, "[https://www.repubblica.it/economia/2023/06/30/news/dea_capital_investe_sulla_cartoleria_e_le_penne_di_legami-406227496/ DeA Capital investe sulla cartoleria e le penne di Legami]", la Repubblica, 30 June 2023.] In 2025, De Agostini Group acquired the fund's entire stake, becoming the company's second-largest shareholder. [ref: Giovanna Mancini, "[https://en.ilsole24ore.com/art/de-agostini-takes-over-42percent-links-and-strengthens-growth-path-AHBEbSzD De Agostini takes over 42% of Legami and strengthens growth path]", Il Sole 24 Ore, 27 November 2025.]
Fassi remained at the helm of Legami as chief executive officer and continued to be directly involved in product development.

== Sustainability projects ==

Fassi promoted the development of Legami's sustainability strategy. In 2023, Legami became a Società Benefit, committing to allocate 5% of its annual profits to environmental and social sustainability projects. [ref: Giulia Cimpanelli, "[https://www.repubblica.it/dossier/economia/imprese-sostenibili/2026/01/30/news/legami_quando_la_sostenibilita_e_nel_dna_dell_impresa-425128036/ Legami, quando la sostenibilità è nel Dna dell'impresa]", la Repubblica, 30 January 2026.]

Fassi also oversaw the development of Dreamland, a protected natural area in Bergamo created to support biodiversity. [ref: "[https://www.compromisorse.com/rse/2026/06/04/dreamland-el-parque-natural-protegido-de-legami-cumple-tres-anos/ Dreamland, el parque natural protegido de Legami, cumple tres años]", Compromiso RSE, 4 June 2026.] Established in 2023 on approximately three hectares, the project subsequently expanded to more than 30 hectares. [ref: "[https://www.ansa.it/sito/notizie/economia/2026/05/27/legami-fa-crescere-dreamland-oltre-30-ettari-di-parco-natura-protetta-a-bergamo_1a471b99-9149-4d9a-bae0-5d59bdca90d9.html Legami fa crescere Dreamland, oltre 30 ettari di parco natura protetta a Bergamo]", ANSA, 27 May 2026.]

== Writing ==

In 2026, Fassi published his debut novel, We Are Dreamers - La battaglia delle fragole, an adventure novel for young readers released by Magazzini Salani. [ref: "[https://www.huffingtonpost.it/life/2026/05/23/news/un_mondo_senza_sbavature_quattro_ragazzi_pieni_di_difetti_il_romanzo_desordio_del_fondatore_di_legami-21978902/ Un mondo senza sbavature, quattro ragazzi pieni di difetti: il romanzo d'esordio del fondatore di Legami]", HuffPost Italia, 23 May 2026.] The novel debuted in the weekly top ten of children's books published by la Repubblica. [ref: Ilaria Zaffino, "[https://www.repubblica.it/robinson/2026/05/24/news/libri_per_ragazzi_un_romanzo_che_celebra_i_legami-425364157/ Libri per ragazzi, un romanzo che celebra i Legami]", la Repubblica, 24 May 2026.]

== Recognition ==

In 2025, Fassi received the Alumnus KPMG dell'Anno award from KPMG.

Title: New bounds for online coloring three-colorable graphs

Abstract:
We prove new lower and upper bounds for online coloring of three-colorable graphs, improving classical bounds of Vishwanathan [FOCS'1990] that have stood for more than three decades. For the lower bound against deterministic algorithms, we improve Vishwanathan's $Ω(\log^2n)$ to \(\exp\!\bigl(Ω((\log n)^{1/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3})\bigr)\). For the upper bound of randomized algorithms, we give a randomized algorithm that achieves $O(\sqrt{n})$ improving Vishwanathan's $O(\sqrt{n \log n})$. Technically, for the lower bound construction, we introduce the language of $t$-fold coloring for simpler description of recursive construction, and the notion of post-degree for future control, and use the flexibility of two-sided colors of bipartite graph, constructed using the independent set amplification method of Vishwanathan, as building blocks to ensure three-colorability. The randomized algorithm integrates, in a new way, some of the ideas in offline coloring of Wigderson and Blum with ideas of Vishwanathan in the online setting, such as the degree control from Wigderson, the offline-monochromatic class from Blum, and the anchor-sampling from Vishwanathan and the CBIP algorithm by Lov{á}sz, Saks and Trotter.

Title: Fully Dynamic All-Pairs Min Cuts on Planar Graphs via Planar Pattern Emulators

Abstract:
We study the fully-dynamic all-pairs minimum cut problem on planar graphs. Given an $n$-vertex undirected planar graph $G=(V,E)$ undergoing edge insertions and deletions, the goal is to efficiently process these updates while supporting $s$-$t$ minimum cut queries for any pair of vertices $s$ and $t$. We give a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate dynamic algorithm that supports edge updates and minimum cut queries in $n^{o(1)}$ time, for any $1/\text{poly}(\log n) < \varepsilon < 1$. For general graphs, previous results either are limited to partially dynamic settings or achieve only logarithmic-factor approximations. The main conceptual and technical contribution is to show that a suitable adaptation of the planar emulator of Chang, Krauthgamer, and Tan~[STOC'22] satisfies the stronger pattern emulator introduced by Chen and Tan~[ICALP'25]. This leads almost immediately to a nearly linear-time construction of pattern emulators, which, when combined with the recent fully dynamic $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate all-pairs shortest paths algorithm of Filtser, Goranci, Patel, and Probst Gutenberg~[FOCS'24], yields our result.

Site: Physics Stack Exchange
Title: Validation of approach for fluid problem from SS Krotov's aptitude problems (1.113)
Tags: fluid-dynamics

Question:
I was doing problem 1.113 from S.S. Krotov's physics book. I got the correct answer, but my method was very different. I wanted to verify the correctness of this method.

Question:
A jet plane with a cabin of length $l = 50 \text{ m}$ accelerates horizontally at $a = 1 \text{ m/s}^2$. The air density is $\rho = 1.2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ g/cm}^3$. Find the difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the rear and middle of the cabin.

Textbook Solution:
The air layer of thickness $\Delta x$ at a distance $x$ from the front of the cabin experiences the force of pressure
$$[p(x + \Delta x) - p(x)]S,$$
where $S$ is the cross-sectional area of the cabin. Since air is at rest relative to the cabin, the equation of motion for the mass of air under consideration has the form
$$\rho S \Delta x a = [p(x + \Delta x) - p(x)]S.$$
Making $\Delta x$ tend to zero, we obtain $\frac{dp}{dx} = \rho a$,
whence $p(x) = p_1 + \rho a x$.
Since the mean pressure in the cabin remains unchanged and equal to the atmospheric pressure $p_0$, the constant $p_1$ can be found from the condition
$$p_0 = p_1 + \frac{\rho a l}{2},$$
where $l$ is the length of the cabin. Thus, in the middle of the cabin, the pressure is equal to the atmospheric pressure, while in the front and rear parts of the cabin, the pressure is lower and higher than the atmospheric pressure by
$$\Delta p = \frac{\rho a l}{2} \approx 0.03 \text{ Pa} \text{ respectively.}$$

My Method:
I assumed that since air is also a fluid, it will act like a liquid in the cabin.
I used the well-known result that the tilt angle is given by $\tan\theta = \frac{a}{g}$.

Using the pressure a depth $d$ formula,
$$\Delta p = \rho \cdot g \cdot \left(\frac{al}{2g}\right)$$
$$\Delta p = \frac{\rho a l}{2}$$

Is this method correct? Which one is objectively better?

Title: An infinite family of conservation laws for perfect compressible fluids

Abstract:
We prove the existence of an infinite family of conservation laws and, more generally, balance laws, satisfied by plane-symmetric flows of perfect compressible fluids, allowing all components of the velocity vector to be possibly non-vanishing. We cover general pressure laws satisfying solely hyperbolicity and asymptotic conditions. We exhibit an almost quadratic formulation of the Euler equations, which we refer to as the J-formulation, and introduce a reduced Euler system based on an effective mass-energy density and an effective pressure law which account for transverse velocities. We establish the existence of a fundamental kernel which we use to generate all spacetime (quasi-)currents, also called mathematical entropy pairs. We derive explicit formulas for their density and flux components, together with the source-terms of the corresponding balance laws. Furthermore, we establish regularity and asymptotic estimates covering the whole range of physical variables, including vacuum. We prove that the kernel is positive on the interior of its support provided the pressure law satisfies a genuine nonlinearity condition, and we also investigate the future-convexity of the spacetime currents. Throughout, the fluid momentum parallel to the orbits of plane-symmetry is kept arbitrary. In turn, this family of spacetime quasi-currents provides a key ingredient in our companion study of torus-symmetric Einstein-Euler flows with weak regularity.

Site: Physics Stack Exchange
Title: What is the motivation for the definition of fugacity given here?
Tags: thermodynamics, chemical-potential

Question:
I am currently reading the thermodynamics section of the second edition of Separation Process Principles by J. D. Seader and Ernest J. Henley, and on p. 31 they write:

Chemical potential cannot be expressed as an absolute quantity, and the numerical values of chemical potential are difficult to relate to more easily understood physical quantities.
Furthermore, the chemical potential approaches an infinite
negative value as pressure approaches zero. For these reasons, the chemical potential is not favored for phase equilibria calculations. Instead, fugacity, invented by G. N. Lewis
in 1901, is employed as a surrogate.

The partial fugacity of species i in a mixture is like a pseudo-pressure, defined in terms of the chemical potential by

$$\displaystyle \tilde{f}_i=C\exp\left(\frac{\mu_i}{RT}\right) \tag{2.8}$$

where $C$ is a temperature-dependent constant.

This entire definition seems very taken-out-of-nowhere. In fact, it doesn't even really look like a definition but instead something derived. Is this really the definition and if so, what is the motivation for giving it this form?

Title: Renegotiable Options Fail to Prevent Hold-Up Between Two Profit-Maximizing Frontier LLM Agents

Abstract:
Do contract terms that protect investment between people also protect it between profit-maximizing language-model agents? In the hold-up problem, a seller can adapt a unit to one buyer at a cost before the price is set. Once that cost is sunk, the buyer can offer almost nothing and the seller will still accept, so a seller who foresees this does not adapt. One remedy is an option: the buyer may buy at a fixed price. In theory the option stops working if the buyer can let it lapse and offer its own price instead. Yet in a laboratory experiment by Hoppe and Schmitz, this renegotiable option raised human investment from 41.5% of pairs without a contract to 67.2%. We had Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, each told to maximize its side's profit, play a one-shot game with the same strategic structure under their four contract regimes and a reference-price control. The agents did what game theory predicts: under the renegotiable option no seller adapted, and under the option that rules out this renegotiation every seller did. In a second experiment in which sellers no longer stated their expected revenue before deciding, removing the profit instruction left investment unchanged under no contract and both options. When we changed the numbers so that the buyer would exercise the option even without adaptation, adapting only added cost, and no seller adapted: the agents did not simply adapt whenever an option was offered or whenever its price covered the cost. Under our protocol, a contract term that raised investment between people did not protect it between agents.

state.text:
Title: Ghosts in the nanomachine: dynamical slowing-down in the phase-space of nanomechanical strings

Abstract:
The linear behavior of micro- and nanomechanical devices has been the topic of intense study over the past years. Their nonlinear behavior, on the other hand, continues to provide new and interesting dynamics. This work leverages a cavity opto-mechanical system whose very high sensitivity and low dissipation rate allows to capture the dynamics of fast transients that occur when strongly-driven nonlinear resonators relax to their equilibrium state. We experimentally study the ringdown dynamics of a nanomechanical Duffing resonator in both the time domain and in phase space. The resonator exhibits very different ringdown dynamics depending on whether it is subject to one or two tone driving. In the former case the ringdown follows a regular exponential decay, whereas the latter case shows exotic dynamics such as libration, slowing-down while scattering in phase-space, and ghost slowing-down. We demonstrate that this distinct difference can be attributed to the structure of the phase space itself. Surprisingly, we find that the energy in the resonator changes non-monotonously and that long delay between turning off the drive and the decay of the motion amplitude results in dynamical meta-states.

Title: Riccati Equations and the Third Problem of Halmos

Abstract:
Rencently, Fang, Hou, Jiang, and Zhang reduced Halmos's third problem to invertible operators with conjugate bi-geometric form. An operator has such a form if, with respect to an orthogonal decomposition, it admits a representation $$ T = \begin{pmatrix} A & C \\ 0 & B \end{pmatrix}, \quad A^*, B \in B_1(O_δ),$$ where $O_δ=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<δ\}$ for some $δ>0$, and $B_1(O_δ)$ denotes the rank-one Cowen--Douglas class. We restrict our attention to the case $B=A^*$ with strictly positive coupling $C$, and settle Halmos's third problem for this class of operators. More precisely,we prove that every such operator $T$ is invertible and that $T^{-1}$ has a nontrivial closed invariant subspace. This result contributes to the study of Halmos's third problem within the conjugate bi-geometric framework.The proof combines monotone solutions of operator Riccati equations with strong operator convergence to construct invariant subspaces for associated Hamiltonian operator matrices.

Title: On $κ$-covering minima

Abstract:
We introduce $κ$-covering minima by requiring the permutation simplices of one independent lattice frame to fit into translates of a common dilate of a convex body. We prove a lower bound for their normalized product, with coefficient $(n+1)/2^n$ for centrally symmetric bodies and an explicit dependence on Minkowski asymmetry in general. On Euclidean balls, the supremum over full-rank lattices of the ratio of the resulting fitting radius to the covering radius has order $\sqrt n$. We also establish basic comparisons with classical lattice minima and bounds under products, projections, Minkowski addition, and free direct sums. We extend the definition by allowing projected periodic lattice triangulations. These extended minima agree with the classical covering minima on ellipsoids.

state.text:
Title: What is Work For? Labor, Politics, and Meaning in the Age of AI

Abstract:
This paper investigates the role of work in providing meaning, purpose, community, and other non-monetary benefits. Using an original cross-national survey of 8,234 working-age adults across the UK, US, Denmark, and India, I study the factors that motivate people in their work, with an eye toward the future AI economic transformation. I find that 81% of respondents report being satisfied with their job, and a majority across all four countries are strongly motivated by the non-monetary components of their employment. Using an original "Work Values" Index, I show that one third of working respondents are motivated intrinsically by their job--valuing their role for its own sake. Nearly one quarter are driven by social and community-related aspects of their employment, 17% by social status, and just over one quarter by the transactional financial benefits of their job. Although a majority of people would leave their role if offered their current salary as a guaranteed income, one fifth of workers would stay even if offered up to 120% of their salary. Intrinsically motivated workers were disproportionately likely to refuse a basic income at any substitution level. Groups attached to their job for non-monetary reasons were also more likely to pursue volunteering or work-like activities if they received guaranteed income substitution but could no longer perform their role. Crucially, these non-monetary work motivations are evenly distributed across the income distribution and between white- and blue-collar workers. I argue that these findings have implications for managing the AI transition, understanding attitudes to AI, and making sense of policy preferences. Guaranteeing a basic income may indeed be necessary for managing any future AI labor shock, yet it could ultimately fail to compensate workers for any loss of the non-monetary benefits they derive from work.

Abstract:

We show that in these models maximum likelihood estimates of the variance of true impacts can be sensitive to a small number of extreme observations. We propose a bounded influence maximum likelihood estimator (BIMLE) that downweights such observations in proportion to their inconsistency with the model, reducing sensitivity while retaining the full sample in estimation. Absent extreme observations, BIMLE coincides with the standard MLE. In an application to A/B tests run at Amazon, BIMLE reduces instability in the estimated prior variance by over 50 percent while downweighting less than 0.1 percent of observations.

Title: Inflation of p-values of likelihood-ratio tests in longitudinal data analysis, Part 2
Tags: mixed-model, likelihood-ratio, permutation-test, false-positive-rate

Question:
This post is a follow‑up to my earlier question:
Inflation of p-values of likelihood-ratio tests in longitudinal data analysis.
We assume a parallel group design of two randomized groups where
longitudinal data is captured. The scientific question is whether the
groups differ in their time trends. The null hypothesis assumes
identical time trends; the alternative allows group‑specific trends.

To test this, we fit two nested linear mixed‑effects models with random
intercepts. Of notice we don’t infer on the variance components:

r1 <- lmer(y ~ TIME*trt + (1|id), data=d, REML=FALSE)
r0 <- lmer(y ~ TIME + (1|id), data=d, REML=FALSE)

and run:

anova(r1, r0)

The output is a LR-test and I am demonstrating in my first post, that
the error rate is inflated. Since the example was on 11 repeated
measures with a correlation of 0.8 between visits, the question arose,
at how many repeats and what correlation between visits, the LR-test
become unreliable?

The answer is summarized in the figure below. The figure contains 4
panels corresponding to correlations 0, 0.1, 0.5, and 0.8. The false
positive rate is displayed over a series of models ordered by increasing
numbers of measurement occasions. The false positive rate (bold lines)
is depicted together with the Monte-Carlo-error of the permutation test
(dotted lines). The figure was produced with R=2000 the code needs
approx. 100 minutes to run. With the help of the Monte-Carlo-error one
can see at what number of repeats the false positive rate begins to
exceed 0.05.

False positive rate over models with increasing repeated measures (R=2000 permutations).

Observations:

We start with the simplest case: one repeated measure. The
appropriate test is the t-test, which correctly controls the false
positives rate on a 0.05 level!

With two repeated measures, the standard approach is ANCOVA,
treating the first measurement as baseline. anova() uses as a
default a F-test for comparing the two ANCOVA models. The false
positives rate is controlled at a 0.05 level!

Then next in the series indicated by LR2, is a likelihood-ratio test
on two repeated measures. The LR-test begins to inflate the false
positive rate, and inflation increases substantially with number of
repeated measurements and with higher correlations. This analysis
can be performed with or without adjusting for baseline; these two
cases are displayed in different colors in the figure. One can see
that correcting for baseline does not matter with respect to
inflated false positives.

Questions

Is this inflation of the LR-test expected in linear mixed‑effects
models with repeated measures?

If so, what are the theoretical reasons?

Are there recommended alternatives to the LR-test that control Type
I error more reliably for this type of design?

Is there any consensus in the statistical community on whether the
standard LR-test should be avoided for time‑trend comparisons in
longitudinal mixed models?

I would greatly appreciate insights from others who have studied this
issue or are aware of relevant references.

Below the code I used for producing the critical figure.

library(mvtnorm)
library(data.table)
library(lme4)

Two functions:

genData() produces a data set of repeated measures in
a ‘wide’ format, where the length of the vector m0 determines the number
of repeats. The correlation structure is compound symmetry of a given
correlation between visits.

mc() is a function for calculating the
Monte-Carlo-error.

set.seed(61)
genData=function(n=30,
         m0=c(8, 10, 12, 13, 13, 13, 12, 10,  8,  6,  4),
         m1=c(6,  6,  6,  7,  8,  9, 10, 10, 10, 10,  9),
          s=c(2,  2,  2,  2,  2,  2,  2,  2,  2,  2,  2),
         cor1=0.8){
  ntime <- length(m0)
  time <- 1:ntime
  COR <- matrix(data=rep(cor1, ntime*ntime), nrow=ntime)
  diag(COR) <- 1
  COV <- COR * outer(s,s)
  Y0 <- rmvnorm(n=n, mean=m0, sigma=COV)
  Y1 <- rmvnorm(n=n, mean=m1, sigma=COV)
  w <- round(rbind(Y0,Y1),2)
  w <- as.data.table(w)
  w$id <- 1:(2*n)
  w[id <= n, trt:=0]
  w[id > n, trt:=1]
  setnames(w, c(paste0("V",1:11)), c(paste0("y",0:10)))
  w
}

mc=function(x){
  b=binom.test(x=sum(x), n=length(x)) # Now with Monte-Carlo error
  c(b$estimate, b$conf.int)
}

R is the number of permutations used to generate a null-distribution,
cori is a vector of correlation coefficients.

R=200 # 10 min with my laptop
cori=c(0,0.1,0.5,0.8)

Below the simulation. There are four loops, three are nested. The first
goes through cori. Within the first loop is the second loop and is the
permutations. Within the second loop is the third loop, going through
models modeling data sets with increasing repeats and correcting for
baseline. The forth loop is on the same level as the third loop and is
going through models modeling data sets with increasing repeats and not
correcting for baseline. At the end the false positive rates are
collected in a list.

fp1=fp2=list()
system.time(
  for (j in 1:4){
    w=genData(cor=cori[j])
    STA=STA0=matrix(rep(9, R*11), ncol=11)

    for (i in 1:R){
      wx <- w
      wx$trt <- sample(w$trt) # permute

      l <- melt(wx, id.vars=c("id","trt","y0")) # switch back to long-format
      l$time <- as.numeric(l$variable)-1
      l$variable <- NULL
      l[, TIME:=factor(time)]
      l[, TRT:=factor(trt)]
      setnames(l, "value", "y")

Title: Post-SQLFix: Property-Guided Repair of LLM-Generated SQL with Runtime Verification

Abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) for Text-to-SQL frequently generate queries with syntax errors, invalid identifier references, or violations of SQL scoping and typing rules. Repairing these errors is a program correctness problem, yet existing approaches rely on Execution Feedback (EF), whose symptom-level, dialect-specific error messages force the LLM to speculate on root causes. We identify an Arbitration Paradox in this paradigm: the system relies on unverified models both to propose repairs and to make the final judgment on whether those repairs satisfy the required properties. We resolve this paradox by reformulating Text-to-SQL repair as property-guided program repair. Our framework, Post-SQLFix, canonicalizes SQL into a dialect-aware Canonical Query Structure (CQS) and validates it through a hierarchical static analyzer with three stratified property layers (Syntactic, Context-Free Structural, Context-Sensitive Semantic). The analyzer produces precise, schema-aware violation diagnostics to guide the LLM's repair proposals. A Verify-Before-Apply Temporal Monitor then accepts only repairs that reduce the violation count, do not reintroduce resolved violations, and satisfy the operator contracts. These runtime invariants are bounded by the declared rule family and operator contracts, while a finite retry budget ensures halting. On three established benchmarks (BIRD, Spider, Mini-Dev) spanning over 3,000 evaluation instances, three SQL dialects (SQLite, MySQL, PostgreSQL), and six model configurations, Post-SQLFix resolves 77.8% of the execution errors that EF leaves unrepaired, while requiring less than half as many repair iterations and 30% fewer tokens. Crucially, accepted transitions under the monitor introduce no statically detectable structural regressions in our evaluation, translating checked repair fidelity into absolute accuracy improvements of up to +11.6 percentage points.

Title: The Welfare Limits of Market Segmentation with Captive Consumers

Abstract:
In a duopoly with captive and contested consumers, I characterize every pair of consumer and producer surplus that can arise under some market composition and some public segmentation, and construct a market that produces each pair. The set is lens-shaped. At any level of industry profit, consumers do worst when captive and contested consumers are perfectly separated and best in an unsegmented market in which the two firms have equally many captives. A market with unequal captive bases and some contested consumers cannot reach this upper frontier under any segmentation. Between Bertrand competition and monopoly, the frontier itself lies strictly below what consumers would get if everyone paid a single deterministic price yielding the same profit. Firms must randomize, and with downward-sloping demand the resulting price dispersion lowers consumer surplus.

Title: The fundamental solution of a family of anisotropic fourth-order parabolic equations: small-time asymptotics and related Gaussian estimates

Abstract:
We study the fundamental solutions of a class of uniformly elliptic fourth-order parabolic equations in two dimensions, whose principal symbols are not necessarily strongly convex. For constant-coefficient operators, we derive precise small-time asymptotic formulas along certain special directions. These formulas are obtained by the method of steepest descent and reveal the dependence of the asymptotic behavior on the coefficients of the symbol. We subsequently consider operators with bounded measurable coefficients, subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions, and establish Gaussian bounds for their fundamental solutions by means of Davies' exponential perturbation method. The exponential constant in these bounds is shown to be sharp, as a consequence of the constant-coefficient asymptotics.

Title: Locality, Probability and the Relevance of History

Abstract:
Relativistic theory and experiments teach us that causal influences are constrained by the speed of light. Deterministic theories incorporate this lesson in $\textit{functional}$ terms: whether an event occurs or not is functionally determined by events that occur in its immediate causal past. In this paper we suggest a natural generalization of this constraint that applies to probabilistic theories: the $\textit{probability}$ that an event occurs is to be functionally determined by the $\textit{probability}$ of the event-occurrences in its immediate causal past. This constraint differs from Bell's criterion of local causality and turns out to imply it only under an additional assumption that requires history to be, in a sense, $\textit{ir}$relevant. Bell-inequality-violating quantum phenomena are thus arguably $\textit{not}$ in tension with relativity, locality, "statistical independence", nor with a supposed "realism". What they instead show is that history is, in a sense, $\textit{relevant}$.

Title: Scaling Limits as Extensions of Continuous Bundles of C*-algebras

Abstract:
We analyze scaling limits in algebraic quantum field theory using continuous bundles of C*-algebras. Different conditions of continuity on such bundles encode different strengths of approximation of the theory by its scaling limit. As a proof of concept, we consider the small-distance scaling limit of the theory of a massive free scalar field, which corresponds to a massless free scalar field. We provide a number of examples of local algebras of observables for which the corresponding bundle of C*-algebras representing the scaling limit is merely lower semicontinuous. Further, we construct an algebra of nonlocal observables for which the corresponding bundle of C*-algebras representing the scaling limit is uniformly continuous.

I can only comment on thermal recalibration in general. Some new
drives perform it in order to increase overall integrity of data
writes. Basically, the firmware instructs the actuator to perform
a test to see if the data tracks are within a certain physical
tolerance, since when the media heats up or cools down, *some*
track drift is inevitable, and the drive has to monitor it. This
becomes especially critical at very high recording densities, and
so was used primarily on very large-capacity mechanisms, but it
seems to be finding its way into more smaller drives as a way of
boosting the drive's long-term reliability and MTBF ratings.

I first became aware of thermal recalibration when it was pointed
out that the technique conflicts with prolonged write times when
digitizing, say, audio or video to hard disk. Some manufacturers
explicitly state that drives with thermal recalibration are NOT
to be used for applications that have prolonged disk writes.

state.text:
Title: Sink polynomials of line graphs and weighted matching polynomials

Abstract:
Chromatic quasisymmetric functions and unicellular LLT polynomials give symmetric-function interpretations of graph orientations counted by sinks. For natural unit interval graphs, we prove that the acyclic sink polynomial is real-rooted for every nonnegative ascent weight. Equivalently, the elementary coefficients of the chromatic quasisymmetric function, grouped by partition length, form a real-rooted polynomial. The Carlsson--Mellit relation expresses this polynomial as a plethystic specialization of the corresponding LLT polynomial, and the Hessenberg correspondence gives an interpretation in cohomology. More generally, the acyclic sink polynomial is real-rooted for chordal claw-free graphs, and the all-orientations sink polynomial is real-rooted for every claw-free graph. We also study a real-rooted polynomial counting joint minima in local edge orders. It agrees with the acyclic sink polynomial of the line graph exactly for forests. An exact formula for unicyclic roots gives a line-graph counterexample to acyclic sink real-rootedness.

Site: Law Stack Exchange
Title: A political campaign texted me after I sent them a STOP message, does this violate the Telephone Consumer Protection Act?
Tags: united-states, communications-law, texting

Question:
Eight days ago I received a fundraising message via SMS. It included the Telephone Consumer Protection Act's "reply STOP to opt out" disclaimer. I replied "STOP" and received an acknowledgment. Today I received another fundraising SMS message from the same political campaign. Is this a violation of the TCPA?

It seemed clear-cut to me, so I looked up how to report violations, and instead of that I found articles from 2025 which seemed to suggest that the Roberts Court has eviscerated TCPA (which I confess is not surprising in the least).

So I guess I don't know what the law is, or whether this is a violation of it.

Answer A:
Apparently different courts are divided as to whether TCPA even covers text messages as if they were unsolicited phone calls.

With the Supreme Court's 2024 ending of Chevron deference the FCC's guidance no longer determines this.  Congress has amended the TCPA on other points but not to resolve this issue.

So perhaps nobody knows what the law is or whether this is a violation of it.

Answer B:
No

The Act does not apply to tax-exempt non-profit organisations like political campaigns. Express your displeasure at the ballot box.

Answer C:
Political calls are not exempt from the TCPA.

The possibility of political campaigns facing TCPA lawsuits is not purely hypothetical. President Donald Trump has seen both of his presidential campaigns sued for text messages that allegedly violated the TCPA. Recently, his re-election had to shut down its entire texting operation due to anti-spam measures employed by telephone carriers. It is not a partisan issue, either, as the 2020 primary campaign for Bernie Sanders also faces a TCPA lawsuit. And the risks extend beyond the scope of massive, national campaigns as a state legislator in Georgia has been sued for TCPA violations allegedly committed in service of her congressional campaign.

The FCC says, specifically about political campaigns:

for calls and texts that require consent, the caller must honor the called party's request to revoke consent. The called party can revoke consent at any time and in any reasonable manner, such as replying "stop" to a text or asking not to be called again on a voice call.

Avenues for redress include:

filing an informal complaint with the FCC

bringing a private action, either individually or as a class action, under 47 USC § 227(b)(3) (e.g. Buller et al. v. Bernie 2020 Inc., D. Minn. Case No. 0:20-cv-01368, Class Action Complaint)

Site: Law Stack Exchange
Title: Equal treatment of equals vs. budget constraints
Tags: untagged

Question:
The question is applicable in any jurisdiction in which the constitution enshrines the value of equality, or more specifically, "equal treatment of equals". Specifically, the government must give equal treatment to people with equal relevant conditions. For example, a government hospital must give the same quality of treatment, and at the same price, to all patients with the same medical and financial conditions.

QUESTION 1: Suppose that, in such a jurisdiction, Alice comes to a government facility for a treatment. The treatment costs money, but the clerk makes a mistake and does not charge Alice. Alice gets the treatment for free and walks away and it is not possible to charge her. The next day, 1000 people with the exact same conditions as Alice come and ask to get the same treatment for free, based on the principle of "equal treatment of equals". How would courts react to such a claim?

QUESTION 2: Suppose the clerk did not a mistake, but on purpose decided to give Alice the treatment for free, e.g. because he likes her or has some personal connection to her. Probably, the clerk should be punished for acting against the relevant regulations. But how would this affect the claim of the 1000 people with equal conditions to Alice - do they have a valid claim to get the same treatment for free?

QUESTION 3: What if the mistake was not made by the clerk but by the government itself: the minister in charge of this facility decided that the treatment should be free, but did not take into account the large number of people who would require this treatment. When they see that too many people want the same treatment for free, they say "wait, we cannot afford so many free treatments. From now on we will charge $1000 per treatment." Do these 1000 people (who came to the facility before the change in fee) have a claim to get the treatment for free?

In all three cases, the main problem is that the government does not have the budget to give the treatment for free to 1000 people. There is a dilemma between the principle of equality, and the reality of the budget. How would courts resolve this dilemma?

Site: Physics Stack Exchange
Title: Tension in a vibrating string
Tags: forces, waves, acoustics, string, continuum-mechanics

Question:
My book Advance Acoustics by D.P. Roychaudhury has a part where it derives the velocity of transverse waves along a string. The amplitude of displacement is supposed to be small, and its mentioned:

As the string is perfectly flexible, the tension $T$ will be the same throughout and act tangentially at every point on AB (an element taken on the string).

My question: Assuming we want to discover the nature of vibrations on a string, we must start off with assumptions which have nothing to do with the movement of the string when its vibrating, as thats what we are trying to figure out. So keeping that in mind, how do we conclude that tension across the entire string will be constant and not like changing at different points?

Answer A:
Actually tension in a string is
$$T = T_x \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}$$

Which can be calculated easily
$$\vec{T} = \vec{T}_x + \vec{T}_y$$
$$T = \sqrt{T_x^2 + T_y^2}$$

Tension in $x$-direction is constant and
$$T_y = T_x \tan \theta$$
$$= T_x \frac{dy}{dx}$$

So,
$$T = \sqrt{T_x^2 \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2 + T_x^2}$$
$$T = T_x \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}$$

Now if amplitude is small and wave length is large then slope of wave is very small thus $\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2$ is negligible
$$T \approx T_x$$
which is constant at all points.

Answer B:
If the tension varies from point to point, there will be longitudinal acceleration of the string parallel to itself. We are interested, however, in small-amplitude transverse motions, where the longitudinal motion can be neglected.

For large amplitude motions, the string's length increases. The string is stretched so it's tension increases. In this case  there may be  a variation of the tension along the string, but this is a harder problem.

Site: Stats Stack Exchange
Title: Using contr.sum for Type III ANOVA but contr.treatment for reporting regression coefficients in R – is this reasonable?
Tags: r, anova, contrasts, lm

Question:
I am analyzing a 2×2 factorial design in R with two categorical predictors (Bewirtschaftung and Bodenstoerung) and a continuous response variable (Infiltration).

For hypothesis testing I want to use a Type III ANOVA, which requires sum contrasts. Therefore I fit the model like this:

options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))

fit_Inf <- lm(Infiltration ~ Bewirtschaftung * Bodenstoerung,data = df_1)
Anova(fit_Inf, type = 3)

However, for the appendix of my thesis my supervisor wants me to report the regression coefficients from summary(lm), and these are easier to interpret with treatment contrasts.

So I refit the same model with treatment contrasts:

"Someone asked how bad a big solar particle event would be for a crew in transit to Mars. Here's a rough estimate from a class exercise.

Take the August 1972 event as a worst case: an integrated proton fluence above 30 MeV of about 5E9 protons/cm^2. Behind 1 g/cm^2 of aluminum (a thin capsule wall), the skin dose comes out to roughly 10-20 Sv. Behind 20 g/cm^2, say inside a water-walled 'storm shelter', it drops to well under 1 Sv. NASA's career limits are in the low single Sieverts, so an unshielded crew could get a lifetime's allowance in a day.

The practical question is mission design. Do you carry a dedicated shelter mass, put the crew quarters behind the propellant tanks, or rely on early warning from a solar monitor parked at L1? Also, flare activity follows the 11-year cycle, so launching near solar minimum trades lower flare risk for higher galactic cosmic ray flux. Does anyone know what the Mars Direct proposal assumed for shielding mass?"

Last 2 statements describe very similar situation but the order of words in each sentence is so different and the example so narrow that I had trouble figuring out what these really mean:

If the primary member template is explicitly (fully) specialized for a given (implicit) specialization of the enclosing class template, the partial specializations of the member template are ignored for this specialization of the enclosing class template.

If a partial specialization of the member template is explicitly specialized for a given (implicit) specialization of the enclosing class template, the primary member template and its other partial specializations are still considered for this specialization of the enclosing class template.

Eventually I managed to figure out the example only showcases the first statement and that the difference between these 2 situations is this:

struct A<short>::B {}; - full spec of member B template for implicitly-instantiated A template (replaces all B for A<short>)

struct A<short>::B<T&> {}; - partial spec of member B template for implicitly-instantiated A template (adds another spec to A<short>, merging it with specs from primary A template)

To confirm I reason correctly, I wrote some sample code to have a more comprehensive example. I did not expect to encounter 3 different outputs from 4 different compilers. And I don't think you can reach UB on templates alone.

https://godbolt.org/z/8z7vde1PE

The code from godbolt link (in case not available):

template <typename T>
struct A
{
    template <typename U> // member template (primary)

    template <typename U> // member template (partial specialization)

// adds B<void*> specialization to A<long>

// adds B<U&> specialization to A<long>

Site: Academia Stack Exchange
Title: Visibility of papers in pure math
Tags: publications, mathematics

Question:
I would like to know what the best journals are to choose in terms of visibility for mathematicians:

Do I understand it right that the most crucial aspect is indexing in ZB and MathSciNet, because that is where other mathematicians will look for your work?

And that indexing in Scopus and WoS does not matter at all? For example, Mathematics Magazine is not indexed in WoS (while some journals not indexed in ZB and MathSciNet are indexed there), but nobody seems to care about this fact.

And finally, is it correct that an arXiv publication is inferior to a paper in a journal indexed in ZB and MathSciNet, but superior to a publication in journals not listed in ZB and MathSciNet (even if they are listed in Scopus and WoS)? Again, I mean in terms of the visibility of a paper for mathematicians.

Answer A:
I would like to know what the best journals are to choose in terms of
visibility for mathematicians:

Today, a mathematician's result is first seen by the rest of the mathematical community when the mathematician publishes it on arXiv. So journals play no role in terms of making a result "visible." They can play a role regarding the reputation of the result and/or the mathematician, but that's another story.

Answer B:
Well, if a "mathematics" journal is not indexed in MathSciNet and ZBmath, then that is a major red flag. But there is a huge range of reputation among journals that are indexed, so merely being indexed doesn't mean very much. Of course, there are good journals that are not indexed merely because they're not mathematics journals (even broadly interpreted), and mathematicians do sometimes publish in them.

FWIW I have no idea whether the journals I publish in, referee for, or even am an editor for, are indexed in Scopus and WoS, and I don't care.

There is no such thing as "arXiv publication". You can put stuff on arXiv (and they will let you, as long as they can tell it's supposed to be a math paper), but there is no peer review and anything that's only on there could be wrong, irrelevant, or both. No-one working in math research would count it as a publication.

(You still should put your work on arXiv, as it has benefits in terms of early availability and open access. But you do this before publication in a proper (i.e. peer-reviewed) venue, not instead of.)

Title: Statistical Inference under Performativity: From Policy Feedback to Self-Evolving Systems

Abstract:
Performativity arises when prediction-informed decisions change the data-generating process, creating feedback between deployment and learning. This phenomenon occurs in policy-making and in self-evolving AI systems that shape their own future training data. Statistical inference is challenging because estimation errors in earlier predictors affect subsequent data distributions and propagate into later updates. We develop an end-to-end framework for statistical inference under performativity. For repeated risk minimization and repeated gradient descent, we establish central limit theorems at fixed deployment rounds and derive covariance recursions that capture both current-round sampling variation and uncertainty inherited from earlier deployments. We develop consistent covariance estimators using policy perturbations and score matching. These results can yield asymptotically valid confidence regions for population iterates and the performative stable point. We further extend prediction-powered inference to this dynamic setting, combining labeled observations with predictions on additional unlabeled data to improve statistical efficiency. We evaluate our framework in synthetic, semi-synthetic educational, and self-evolving large language model routing settings. Our experiments demonstrate that ignoring propagated uncertainty can lead to substantial undercoverage even after repeated retraining. Together, these results provide statistical tools for learning systems that help determine the distributions from which they learn. Our work establish a complete statistical inference under performativity, introducing new challenges and inference settings that we believe will provide substantial value to policy-making, statistics, and machine learning.

Hungered is a 2026 debut novel by Amanda Rizkalla, published by Henry Holt and Co. on May 19, 2026. Oprah Winfrey selected it for Oprah’s Book Club in October 2026, the club’s 125th pick. The novel follows a twelve-year-old girl named Sofia as she navigates homelessness and family instability after her mother leaves her father. [ref: Hungered By Amanda Rizkalla] [ref: ]

== Plot ==
Sofia is twelve when her mother wakes her and her younger brother at night, packs them into the car, and drives away from Sofia’s father called “baba” in the book. What follows is a stretch of parking lots, school mornings, fast food, and the effort to seem ordinary while the family is unhoused. Sofia narrates in short, diary-like sections. She remembers the girl now living in her old bedroom, a girl with a “belly bulging out of her shirt,” and tries to make sense of adults whose choices she can only partly see. The book stays close to Sofia’s view. Readers learn about her mother’s fear, her father’s absence, and the casual cruelty of teachers and classmates mostly through what Sofia notices, overhears, and misreads. [ref: Hungered, Literary Hub]

== Themes ==
Hungered addresses themes of poverty, housing insecurity, and class consciousness through the lens of a child's perspective. Kirkus Reviews noted that the novel encapsulates "the heaviness of class, race, and adolescence," and praised Rizkalla's ability to render "the gut-wrenching powerlessness Sofia often feels as she treads through a world rife with inequality". The novel also examines family bonds, memory, and the search for home in its various forms. Reviewers have described it as "a pointed social commentary" that captures the contradictions of Sofia's world through "spare, elegant prose". [ref: Oprah Wants You to Read The Book of Menopause, Oprah Daily]

== Reception ==
Kirkus Reviews called it "a heart-wrenching and powerful debut" and "a well-written and haunting look into a childhood marked by instability". Library Journal wrote that Rizkalla's "powerful debut captures the heartbreak of a family in crisis and the quiet resilience of a young girl who can't make sense of the world but still dares to dream". Writing for Shelf Awareness, Debra Ginsberg described the book as "thoughtful and wise" and "a powerful and resonant read".

Following its selection for Oprah's Book Club, The Independent reported that Winfrey praised the novel as "riveting" and said it "compassionately tackles the difficult subject of families who live outside the margins, living unhoused, and makes us see not only their struggles, but their hopes, dreams, and the perseverance it takes to face another day". [ref: Oprah Winfrey taps a 'riveting' debut novel for her book club, The Independent] USA Today noted that the pick was Winfrey's 125th selection, chosen during the 30th anniversary celebrations of her book club. [ref: Oprah's book club pick is a 'riveting' coming-of-age from a new voice. What is it?, USA TODAY]

== Author background ==
Amanda Rizkalla is a Los Angeles native who lives in the Bay Area. She was an undergraduate at Stanford University and received a Master of Fine Arts in creative writing from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, where she was a Kemper Knapp Fellow. She is a recent Steinbeck Fellow and Wisconsin Institute for Creative Writing Fellow, and has been a writer-in-residence at Ragdale, Hedgebrook, Djerassi, and other arts organizations. Hungered is her first novel. [ref: Oprah Winfrey taps a 'riveting' debut novel for her book club] Rizkalla learned of her Oprah's Book Club selection after receiving a surprise call from Winfrey, and said in a statement that she was "so stunned I could hardly believe it was real". [ref: Oprah's book club pick is a 'riveting' coming-of-age from a new voice. What is it?, USA TODAY] [ref: ]

state.text:
Title: Satisficing Regret Minimization in Bandits with Knapsacks

Abstract:
We study satisficing regret minimization in bandits with knapsacks (BwK), where a learner sequentially selects randomized policies, i.e., distributions over arms, to obtain mean rewards above a satisficing threshold as frequently as possible while respecting finite resource budgets. The performance is measured by satisficing regret, the cumulative deficits of the selected policies' mean rewards below this threshold. Resource constraints introduce two difficulties: an algorithm can incur linear satisficing regret even with small standard regret as deficits to the threshold cannot be compensated, and random consumption can cause early resource depletion even when policies are feasible in expectation. To address these challenges, we propose SELECTwK, a general algorithmic template that uses a BwK learning oracle algorithm with sub-linear expected (standard) regret upper bound to search for and test candidate satisficing policies (i.e., policies whose mean rewards exceed satisficing threshold and whose expected resource consumption is feasible over the time horizon). Our regret analysis, supported by an LP-duality argument, establishes that SELECTwK attains constant expected satisficing regret when a satisficing policy exists. We further introduce a stronger regret condition that bounds the expected sum of positive reward deficits to the optimal one at each time step, under which SELECTwK achieves a sharper constant bound together with a sub-linear bound in the time horizon. As a complement, SELECTwK still preserves the oracle's sub-linear expected standard regret bound if the satisficing threshold is unattainable. Finally, we establish the oracle conditions and corresponding satisficing regret bound for existing finite-armed BwK and dynamic pricing algorithms, and conduct numerical experiments on dynamic pricing with limited inventory to demonstrate the empirical performance of SELECTwK.

Draft text:
Schiavello Group is a privately owned Australian company engaged in commercial furniture design and manufacturing, interior construction and fit-out, property development and workplace technology. It was founded in Melbourne in 1966 by Italian-born furniture maker Tony Schiavello with his younger brother Joe, initially as a partitioning and joinery business. The group is headquartered in Tullamarine, employs around 1,100 people and reported revenue of approximately A$700 million in 2025. It has been described as one of Australia's oldest manufacturers of high-end furniture and is ranked among the country's top 100 private companies.

== History ==

=== Founding and early years (1966–1979) ===
Tony Schiavello, a furniture maker by trade, migrated to Australia from Calabria, southern Italy, in the 1950s. In 1966 he secured a labour-only subcontract to install toilet partitions at 15 William Street, Melbourne, and registered the partnership TT&G with his brother Joe Schiavello and friend Tony Cipollone. Schiavello Bros Pty Ltd was established two years later.

The company's early product was MK1, a series of demountable partitions, and its first large-scale partition project was completed for Victoria Insurance in 1968. Growth led to new factory premises in Airport West from 1970. In 1971 the company produced more than 8,000 voting booths for the Australian Electoral Office ahead of the 1972 Australian federal election. The office furniture operation was established in 1978 with the Series 35 and Series 45 foldable desk collections.

=== Office furniture and expansion (1980s–1990s) ===
In 1982 Schiavello designed its first ergonomic, height-adjustable desks to meet Federal Government requirements for computer desks; the resulting Primatic desk, launched in 1983, was among the first ergonomic desks with a fully user-adjustable main worktop. The company's first workstation system, Interstat, was exhibited at the Orgatec furniture fair in Cologne in 1986, its first international trade show. Interstate offices opened in New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory in the late 1980s, with Queensland, Western Australia and South Australia following by 1993.

In 1990 Tony Schiavello won the National Australia Bank Ethnic Business Award, broadcast live on SBS. In 1992 the company won a contract to supply more than 20,000 workstations to the World Bank headquarters in Washington, D.C., which the company describes as the start of its significant international presence. The following year it completed one of its largest interior construction projects as head contractor for Clayton Utz in Sydney, and launched the Sesto desking system with a worktop height-adjustment design.

In 1995 the Newtech height-adjustable workstation received an award for excellence in design and manufacture of systems furniture at the Australian Furniture Fair, and Schiavello developed the "Hot Desk" concept, described as Australia's first mobile workplace, in collaboration with RMIT's federally funded EcoReDesign programme. Schiavello carried out interior construction and joinery for the opening of Crown Melbourne in 1997, beginning a long-term relationship that included hotel refurbishments in 2007. The company also obtained ISO 14001 environmental management accreditation in the late 1990s.

=== Diversification (2000s) ===
Schiavello established bathroomware company Omvivo and, in 2003, Italian architect Mario Bellini commissioned the company to manufacture the NGV bench for the reopening of the National Gallery of Victoria. In 2005 Victorian Premier Steve Bracks opened the group's purpose-built 70,000 square metre headquarters and factory in Tullamarine, which consolidated the group's divisions on one site. The project was recognised with the 2005 Victorian Master Builder of the Year award. Tony Schiavello was inducted into the Victorian Manufacturing Hall of Fame in 2008.

The group entered property development in 2007 with The Artist, a multi-residential building in Fitzroy developed in joint venture with PDG and completed in 2011. In the same year it took a shareholding in Melbourne hospitality operator Atlantic Group, founded by Hatem Saleh, in which Schiavello (Vic) Pty Ltd became a joint shareholder and Tony Schiavello a director. The group's venues and contracts expanded from Central Pier in Docklands to The Atlantic restaurant at Crown Melbourne, opened in 2011, catering at the Melbourne Cup Carnival from 2011 and the Australian Grand Prix from 2013, Gardens House in the Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria and the Port Melbourne Yacht Club. By 2019 Atlantic Group was Central Pier's anchor tenant; the pier was closed by Development Victoria that year on safety grounds, and Atlantic Group led tenants in a A$100 million Federal Court claim against the agency. Peter Schiavello, Tony's eldest son, who had run the furniture operation since 1982 and served as Deputy Managing Director from 1992, was appointed Managing Director of the group in 2009.

=== Recent history (2010–present) ===
In 2010 the company released Climate, a workstation system designed around the concept of "malleability", in which electronics, shelving and panels are housed in a channel independent of the work table so that layouts can be reconfigured without rebuilding. Schiavello was appointed head contractor for the Sydney Commonwealth Parliament Offices in the early 2010s.

[ref: Academy selects 17 new members, Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]

== Early life and education ==
Gërxhani began her academic studies in Tirana, Albania, where she completed an M.A. at the Faculty of Economics, University of Tirana. She moved to the Netherlands, where she earned an M.Phil. and a Ph.D. in Economics through the Tinbergen Institute and the University of Amsterdam, completing her doctorate in 2002 with her thesis "The informal sector in transition: Tax evasion in an institutional vacuum".

== Career ==
Gërxhani began her academic career at the University of Amsterdam, holding successive positions as postdoctoral researcher, assistant professor, and associate professor. She subsequently held a full professorship in the Department of Political and Social Sciences at the European University Institute in Florence, Italy, from 2015 to 2022. She joined VU Amsterdam as Professor of Behavioral Socio-Economics in January 2023. From 2023 to 2025 she served as Head of the Department of Ethics, Governance and Society and from 2026, as Associate Dean of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion at the School of Business and Economics. [ref: Klarita Gërxhani, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam] She is also a research fellow at the Tinbergen Institute. [ref: New Research Fellow: Klarita Gërxhani, Tinbergen Institute]

Gërxhani has supervised fourteen doctoral students to completion, with one ongoing, and has mentored seven postdoctoral researchers.
== Research ==
Gërxhani's research lies at the intersection of behavioral economics and economic sociology, combining laboratory experiments, field experiments, vignette studies, and traditional surveys. Her work spans several interconnected themes.

Her early research examined the informal economy and tax evasion in post-communist countries, particularly Albania. Using surveys and experiments, she showed how a clash between formal institutions and rules on the one hand and informal institutions on the other drives informal economic activity, with tax evasion varying systematically by income source, gender, and institutional context.

A related strand of her work investigates how formal and informal institutions shape individual behavior and how social norms evolve and change over time. In the more than two decades since the start of her career, she has also studied norm compliance, institutional change, and the relationship between social values and collective decision-making.

Her most prominent recent work examines how competitive settings generate gender inequality. Her experiments demonstrate that men and women perform equally well when there is no competition, but that status-ranking competition against peers improves men's outcomes while worsening women's. This effect is observed even when men and women do not differ in ability; it is driven by gendered expectations. [ref: Academy selects 17 new members, Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences] This research was the subject of a feature interview in Het Financieele Dagblad, referenced on the newspaper's front page. [ref: Hoogleraar Gërxhani: 'Meritocratie is een fabel, weten we nu', Het Financieele Dagblad]

She has also studied employer behavior extensively, including how firms recruit workers, how social networks and contacts influence hiring decisions, and how gender and intersectional biases shape the evaluation of job candidates. This work combines laboratory experiments with field and vignette studies to isolate the mechanisms behind labor market discrimination.

An earlier strand of her research explored the role of social capital in post-communist societies, examining how trust and informal networks differ between Eastern and Western Europe and how they relate to economic participation, welfare attitudes, and political behavior.

Gërxhani's work has been covered by De Telegraaf, NPO Radio 1, [ref: Bar weinig vrouwen zijn hoogleraar economie, NPO Radio 1] ABC News Albania, [ref: Interview with Klarita Gërxhani, ABC News Albania] and A2 Business CNN Albania, [ref: Interview with Klarita Gërxhani, A2 Business CNN Albania] and she has been invited by corporations including KPMG and Heineken to discuss the application of her research to workplace inclusion. She has delivered keynote lectures at institutions including the MIT Summer School, the German Institute for Employment Research (IAB), the Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research (ZEW), and the European University Institute.

Title: Wearable Biosensors for Early Detection and Continuous Monitoring of Postpartum Depression: A Human-Centered Approach

Abstract:
Postpartum depression (PPD) is the leading cause of maternal mortality in the United States. However, there are significant gaps in PPD screening, detection, and treatment. A main challenge stems from limitations in existing methods for early PPD diagnosis and subsequent monitoring and intervention. Mobile technology that incorporates interactive interfaces and continuous wearable biosensors holds major potential to augment clinical decision-making and enhance PPD care. A number of compelling research directions exist in effectively developing such systems, including user experience design, sensing accuracy during perinatal stages, clinical integration and interoperability, acceptance and adoption, and privacy and ethics. By focusing on wearable devices that center women and their experiences, this paper discusses such challenges and opportunities at the intersections of HCI, inclusive physiological computing, and women's health.

Title: Automated CR-39 pit detection for energy and angular characterization of laser-driven ion beams

Abstract:
Accurate characterization of ion beams from sub-MeV to multi-MeV energies is essential for diagnostics in laser-driven ion acceleration and fusion research. CR-39 detectors are widely used to measure absolute ion yields, while ion energy and incidence angle can be inferred from etched-pit geometries. In this study, we present an automated CR-39 pit detection method that enables reliable extraction of pit geometries from two-dimensional optical micrographs, with improved discrimination of overlapping pits under high-flux conditions. This capability enables reliable analysis in high-density regimes where conventional methods are limited by significant track overlap. By integrating the detected pit shapes with a pit-formation model based on Monte Carlo simulations of restricted energy loss, energy and angular characterization of laser-driven proton beams is achieved with enhanced precision and computational efficiency. The proposed framework provides a robust and scalable approach for automated CR-39 analysis and is applicable to a broad range of ion-beam diagnostics and spectroscopy.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: $f(\frac{\sqrt {13} - 1}{2}),f(1),f(2)$ are all primes implies irreducible polynomial?
Tags: elementary-number-theory, prime-numbers, irreducible-polynomials

Question:
Define integer polynomials $f(x)$ of prime degree $d$ with coefficients in $[0,1,2]$ and every one of $[0,1,2]$ occurs at least once.

Consider $f(\frac{\sqrt {13} - 1}{2}),f(1),f(2)$ all giving distinct primes.

Is it true that $f(x)$ is then irreducible ?

Notice every natural number can be uniquely written in base $3$ with coefficients in $[0,1,2]$ and every natural number can also be uniquely written in base $Q = \frac{\sqrt {13} - 1}{2}$ with coefficients in $[0,1,2]$ since $Q^2 + Q = 3 $ , $3$ is prime, $13 = 4*3 + 1$ is prime and thus $Q$ generates a UFD.

If you are thinking about Bunyakovsky or its reverse, you are right. That is the inspiration combined with ring theory.

credit to my mentor for similar ideas and making me realise $Q$ can work as a 'ternary' base.

Consider

Cohn's irreducibility criterion: If $b>1$ and $0\le a_i<b$ are all integers and $\sum_0^n a_ib^i$ is prime, then $\sum_0^n a_ix^i\in\mathbb Z[x]$ is irreducible polynomial.

Taking base $b=3$ directly says that if $f(3)$ is prime then the polynomial is irreducible.

This does not answer the question however.

Filtering has not yet had its foundation-model moment: state estimation is still dominated either by online Bayesian filtering algorithms that require known dy- namics as inputs, or by learning-based neural filters trained from scratch for a single system or parametric family. The core challenge is structural heterogene- ity: dynamical systems differ in their governing dynamics, physical scales, and noise levels, precluding a shared representation space for a reusable filter. To bridge this gap, we introduce FilterFM, the first pretrained model for Bayesian filtering that estimates latent states across heterogeneous dynamical systems with a single checkpoint. FilterFM employs a hierarchical two-level observation se- quence encoder and a prior-to-posterior state-reconstruction module that together handle varying observation and state dimensions across heterogeneous systems, while modeling state uncertainty via quantile prediction. Trained on a mixture of heterogeneous filtering tasks, FilterFM exhibits superior in-domain performance, delivering significant gains in estimation accuracy, runtime efficiency, and noise robustness compared to existing baselines. Beyond in-domain performance, it marks the first model to successfully enable zero-shot filtering on unseen dynamics, bridging the generalization gap in state estimation. Furthermore, we uncover clear scaling behaviors in foundation-model-based Bayesian filtering, which combined with comprehensive component ablation studies, validate the structural optimality of our design and broaden the generalization scope for this research field.

Title: Spectra of stochastic matrices with a Toeplitz interior

Abstract:
For stochastic matrices of order $n$, the Karpelevič region is the set of all possible eigenvalues. We study matrices whose first and last $m$ rows are arbitrary probability vectors, while the remaining middle rows come from one probability vector by successive cyclic shifts to the right, moving the last entry to the first position each time. As $m$ increases, their eigenvalue regions expand from the polygon spanned by the $n$th roots of unity. For $n\ge3$, they first equal the full Karpelevič region at $m=\lceil(n-1)/4\rceil$. Reproducing all $n$ eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, of every stochastic matrix of the same order requires $m=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. Thus, in even order $n\ge4$, retaining two consecutive rows with the Toeplitz pattern can exclude eigenvalue lists even when every possible eigenvalue occurs individually. The boundary of the Karpelevič region consists of arcs joining roots of unity. We determine the least $m$ for which every point of each arc occurs as an eigenvalue in our family. For arcs whose nonreal points first become possible eigenvalues at order $n\ge4$, and for $m\ge1$ below this minimum, no point on the arc other than its endpoints occurs in the family. At the minimum, every point on the arc becomes attainable. At the smallest order $n\ge4$ at which a nonreal point on a boundary arc away from its endpoints can occur as an eigenvalue, that point determines the characteristic polynomial of every stochastic matrix of order $n$ having it as an eigenvalue. Further results describe the smaller regions and the angles at which their boundaries approach roots of unity.

Title: Timbre: Reliability-aware harmonic consensus for label-free multimodal test-time rexinforcement learning

Abstract:
Label-free test-time reinforcement learning adapts vision--language models using rewards derived from their own predictions. However, misinterpreted visual evidence and sensitivity to textual formulation can produce a consistent but incorrect consensus that majority voting reinforces. Cross-view aggregation can expose such errors, but image and text transformations may themselves degrade task-relevant evidence to different extents. We introduce \method, a reliability-aware harmonic consensus framework for multimodal test-time reinforcement learning. \method constructs a $2\times2$ grid combining original and perturbed images with direct-solving and reframing modes, selects pseudo-labels through weighted harmonic aggregation, and adapts modality-level weights using batch-averaged, temporally smoothed shifts in pseudo-label confidence as a heuristic reliability signal. We formulate consensus as a weighted $χ^2$-barycenter problem whose unique minimizer is the normalized weighted harmonic aggregate, without requiring correct-answer invariance. An exact support--dispersion decomposition characterizes when harmonic aggregation preserves or corrects arithmetic rankings, while a sensitivity analysis establishes how modality reweighting changes pairwise ranking margins, informing interpretation of the heuristic updates. Across six benchmarks and three Qwen3-VL model scales, \method outperforms TTRV in 16 of 18 benchmark--model settings on adaptation instances and 17 of 18 settings on held-out instances under matched estimation and optimization rollout counts. These results demonstrate improved target-task adaptation and transfer to unseen instances without further updates.

Title: HotPOT: Operator Transformer with Heterogeneous Physics Experts for Large-Scale PDE Pre-training

Abstract:
Large-scale PDE pre-training trains a single model on the data from multiple partial differential equations (PDEs). However, adding heterogeneous PDEs with different governing equations, physical variables, and variable interactions does not always improve predictive performance across tasks. Existing PDE mixture-of-experts models mitigate cross-task interference through learned routing, but typically use homogeneous expert architectures, making it difficult to directly reflect differences in state evolution across equations. We introduce HotPOT, an operator transformer with heterogeneous physics experts for large-scale PDE pre-training. HotPOT uses a shared encoder to capture information common across PDEs, while each PDE family uses a neural-numerical expert that pairs a learnable predictor with a fixed numerical update containing no trainable parameters. Each predictor outputs the quantities required by its paired numerical update, which then computes the next state. This design allows different PDEs to share a common encoder while retaining their own learnable predictors and numerical updates. Experiments across five PDE families and six settings show that HotPOT outperforms MoE-POT in all 24 matched-scale comparisons before and after fine-tuning, reducing rollout error by 50.7% on average. Notably, the 17M model also surpasses substantially larger MoE-POT models, and the performance gains extend to zero-shot prediction under unseen physical conditions. Code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/HotPOT-code.

Title: Optical clock network tracks tidal variations of the gravity potential

Abstract:
Gravity affects the passage of time, as described by General Relativity. On Earth, the rate of a clock as seen by a fixed observer changes by about one part in $10^{16}$ per metre in height. Chronometric levelling exploits this effect to directly measure differences in gravity potential by comparing distant clocks. It has been proposed as a complementary approach to established geodetic techniques for linking height reference systems and monitoring the terrestrial gravity potential. Experimental demonstrations have to date focused primarily on static potential differences. Yet, the potentials of the Moon, the Sun and other celestial bodies as well as the Earth's response to their tidal forcing change clock rates by several $10^{-17}$, providing a predictable test signal to demonstrate optical clock networks resolving small variations in relativistic time dilation. Here, we report chronometric observations of time-varying gravity potential differences using a network of optical clocks and phase-stabilized fibre links in Europe. Two distinct geographical configurations, with baselines of about 800 km each, result in different combinations of diurnal and semidiurnal tidal components. One comparison uses a transportable optical clock as a remote sensor. The measured rate shifts track the tidal variations, resolving the predicted signal within 1 d of measurement and agreeing with model predictions. These results extend experimental chronometric levelling from static to dynamic potential differences and highlight the need to account for the time dependence of relativistic time dilation in frequency metrology. They also open the prospect for quantum clock networks with improved stability and availability to move beyond known tides and monitor other gravity potential variations, such as those arising from surface deformation and mass redistribution in geologically or volcanically active regions.

Title: An HDG-type discretization of 1D embedded blood flow in complex networks with Riemann-coupled junctions

Abstract:
We present a hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin (HDG) method for one-dimensional blood flow in arterial networks with Windkessel boundary conditions. The scheme uses a Harten--Lax--van Leer (HLL) numerical flux and implicit time integration. After spatial discretization, the complete network---including cell states, hybrid traces, junction conditions, and dynamic $\mathrm{RCR}$ terminal pressures---is written as a residual index-one differential--algebraic equation (DAE) and integrated with variable-step, variable-order backward differentiation formulas. The implicit formulation removes the CFL stability restriction of explicit schemes and allows variable-order, variable-step solvers. The resulting single global residual and Jacobian for the network and its terminal dynamics also provide a natural interface for monolithic coupling with external nonlinear models. We establish local solvability and a semi-discrete energy balance, and show numerically optimal convergence rates for both solution variables in the $L^2$ norm and the broken $H^1$ seminorm. The solver is validated against established benchmarks, including an aortic bifurcation and a $37$-artery network, and is further applied to a cerebral arterial network. Mass conservation is observed in a synthetically generated anatomical liver network of $8\,\mathrm{k}$ vessels, and strong-scaling studies are performed on synthetic networks of $50\,\mathrm{k}$ and $100\,\mathrm{k}$ vessels.

Title: Sequince: a modular sequential Monte Carlo toolkit

Abstract:
Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods approximate sequences of probability distributions using populations of weighted samples and are widely applicable, including in Bayesian inference and particle filtering. We present sequince, a modular Python toolkit for constructing SMC algorithms from reusable and extensible components. The toolkit provides modular steps for weighting, resampling, mutation, transformation, and control operations that are composed to implement different algorithms. It also includes prebuilt samplers for tempered SMC, persistent sampling and nested sampling via SMC. Its core components follow the Python Array API standard, supporting NumPy, JAX, PyTorch, and CuPy, enabling analyses on CPUs or GPUs. Random-number control and checkpointing support reproducible scientific workflows. This paper describes sequince v0.1.0 and its design as reusable infrastructure for methodological research and application of SMC methods.

Title: Under US copyright and trademark law, what legal protections apply to independently recreated historical website interfaces?

Question:
I'm interested in the legal distinction between reproducing a historical website's visual appearance and copying its copyrighted materials.

For example, suppose an independent developer creates a non-commercial, open-source project that recreates the appearance and basic interactions of an older version of the Google Search homepage.

The project has the following characteristics:

All HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are independently written.

The purpose is historical preservation and nostalgia, rather than commercial competition.

The project is publicly available on GitHub and may include a demonstration website.

A prominent disclaimer states that the project is unofficial and is not affiliated with or endorsed by Google.

The recreated interface may use historical Google logos, icons, or other recognizable visual elements.

Under United States law, I would like to understand:

To what extent are historical website layouts, visual arrangements, and interface designs protected by copyright, as opposed to their underlying ideas and functional elements?

How does copyright law distinguish independently recreating an interface from directly copying the original website's source code or graphical assets?
