Site: Academia Stack Exchange
Title: No response from journal editorial office after multiple follow-ups—what is standard practice?
Tags: publications, peer-review, journals, editors

Question:
I am seeking advice on typical editorial practices regarding communication with academic journal editorial offices.

I have contacted a journal editorial office regarding questions about the peer-review and editorial process of a published article. My initial inquiry was sent several months ago, followed by a reminder and a second follow-up email. I have not received any response to date.

My question is not about the specific article itself, but about general expectations in academic publishing:

What is the usual expected response time for editorial offices in such cases?

Is it common for journals to not respond to inquiries about peer-review processes from readers or researchers?

At what point is it considered appropriate to escalate the matter, and what are typical escalation channels (e.g., Editor-in-Chief, publisher, ethics committee)?

Are there any recognized guidelines (e.g., COPE or others) regarding responsiveness to such inquiries?

I would appreciate insights from those familiar with academic publishing norms.

Answer A:
I used to work full-time in academic publishing.

What is the usual expected response time for editorial offices in such cases?

If you reach the publisher, expected action time (i.e., time from when your message is received till some kind of action is taken) is a few days. At least, I would be displeased if a subordinate didn't do something for a few days, unless they are overloaded and/or on holiday. The action might not be a response to you, however.

Is it common for journals to not respond to inquiries about peer-review processes from readers or researchers?

This depends somewhat on how the journal is structured and/or how motivated the editor is. They might answer you themselves, or they might forward your query to the editorial board member responsible (who is much less likely to answer quickly). It is not normal to ignore it, unless they are making a decision immediately (e.g. if they are rejecting your manuscript then it's kind of pointless for them to answer your question).

At what point is it considered appropriate to escalate the matter, and what are typical escalation channels (e.g., Editor-in-Chief, publisher, ethics committee)?

If there is an editor-in-chief you could ask them. Otherwise if there is a publisher-level email you could also ask them (although they are likely to forward your query to the journal-level email). Ethics committee is not going to get involved in this, it is not an ethical issue.

Are there any recognized guidelines (e.g., COPE or others) regarding responsiveness to such inquiries?

No, or if there are, they are likely to be internal policies of the publisher and hence not publicly available.

See also: Journal Editor does not respond about status of paper ~1 year

Answer B:
I'm an associate editor at a journal. There is essentially no expectation that editorial offices will respond to the kind of inquiry you're describing. Questions about "how journals work" are usually better directed to your advisor or postdoc mentor. They can give you field-specific norms and practical advice.

Editors have very limited time and they prioritize it for handling submissions: finding referees, making decisions, dealing with revisions, etc. General questions from readers about peer review processes, especially for already published papers, are typically very low priority. Some questions in that vein (e.g., "who was the referee?") cannot be answered at all. It is not unusual for those emails to go unanswered, although I myself would prefer to at least send a response saying that I won't answer.

So to your specific questions:

What is the usual expected response time for editorial offices in such cases?

It is not typical to receive a response at all.

Is it common for journals to not respond to inquiries about peer-review processes from readers or researchers?

Yes, that is common and expected. It's not their job.

At what point is it considered appropriate to escalate the matter, and what are typical escalation channels (e.g., Editor-in-Chief, publisher, ethics committee)?

I would argue that it's never appropriate because you are barking up the wrong tree. You will just waste the time of more people.

Are there any recognized guidelines (e.g., COPE or others) regarding responsiveness to such inquiries?

Not that I'm aware of. Any such guidelines would only kick in if you are raising a concrete issue (e.g., suspected misconduct, undisclosed conflicts of interest, or a formal complaint). In those cases, contacting the editor-in-chief or publisher can make sense.

Title: {DEMAND}: {A}n organic glass scintillator array for direct measurements of $(α,n)$ and $(p,n)$ reactions in inverse kinematics

Abstract:
We have developed an array of up to 20 organic glass scintillator detectors, each consisting of a $3~\mathrm{cm}\times3~\mathrm{cm}\times3~\mathrm{cm}$ scintillator cube coupled to a photomultiplier tube. Sensitive to neutrons from a few hundred keV to several tens of MeV, the array was designed for use with recoil separators in inverse-kinematics measurements of astrophysical $(α,n)$ and $(p,n)$ reactions. It provides a prompt start signal for identifying recoil-neutron coincidences from the recoil time of flight. We characterize eight detectors used in an inverse-kinematics measurement of $^{22}\mathrm{Ne}(α,n)^{25}\mathrm{Mg}$, using source and in-beam data. From the widths of $γ$-ray Compton-edge peaks at 311, 341, 477, and 1062 keVee, we find an energy resolution described by $\mathrm{FWHM}(E)/E=\sqrt{A^2/E+B^2/E^2+C^2}$, with $A=0.00(7)$, $B=0.0618(54)$, and $C=0.135(5)$. The time-difference spectrum of nearest-neighbor $γ$-$γ$ coincidences from a $^{22}\mathrm{Na}$ source (250--600 keVee) gives a FWHM coincidence timing resolution of $910(40)$ ps, corresponding to a single-detector resolution of $640(30)$ ps. Mixed neutron-$γ$ fields from the in-beam reaction and a $^{241}\mathrm{AmBe}$ source show pulse-shape discrimination with an $n$-$γ$ figure of merit $>1$ down to about 100 keVee. Below 100 keVee, the total neutron yield can still be extracted using two-Gaussian fits to energy-gated pulse-shape discrimination spectra. Monte Carlo simulations of the present $^{22}\mathrm{Ne}(α,n)^{25}\mathrm{Mg}$ measurement give a neutron singles detection efficiency of $1.56(45)%$, with uncertainty dominated by systematic effects in the simulation inputs.

Title: Numerical schemes for 1D capacitively coupled plasma fluid simulation

Abstract:
Capacitively coupled plasmas (CCP) are widely used in semiconductor manufacturing, where fluid models provide an efficient approach to the simulation of the low-temperature discharge. The model considered in this work couples the electron and the ion continuity equations, the electron energy equation and the Poisson's equation for the electric potential. We investigate the numerical schemes for the simulation of the 1D-CCP. In particular, a semi-implicit Scharfetter-Gummel (SG) scheme is adopted for the Poisson's equation, while the remaining equations are solved using the implicit SG schemes. The proposed strategy can be naturally extended to the 2D cases. Several alternative schemes are also discussed and tested. Numerical experiments compare these methods in terms of the admissible time step $Δt$, total simulation time, accuracy against a reference solution and robustness of the scheme. We propose a numerical scheme for the 1D-CCP and, to the best of our knowledge, provide the first detailed numerical analysis of such a scheme for CCP.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: Estimation of Riemann integral over subinterval
Tags: real-analysis, calculus, analysis

Question:
Problem

Suppose a real-valued function $f$ be Riemann integrable over an interval of length $L$ and its integral is $I$. For what positive number $r$ can we guarantee that there must exists a subinterval of length $r$ whthin this interval such that the integral of $f$ over this subinterval is $Ir/L$ ?

Some trivial answer is $\{L/n:n\in\mathbb{N}^+\}$ since we can apply the pigeonhole principle and Riemann integral is always continuous to deduce the feasibility. But how about the remain part $(0,L]-\{L/n:n\in\mathbb{N}^+\}$ ? I can not find a general counterexample to claim that all the number in this set are not feasible.

Answer A:
Here is a simple visual demonstration that you've found all of them.

Let's suppose that $L = nr + x$ with $0 < x < r$. The idea is to place Dirac deltas at $n+1$ spots. The total integral of the function is now $n+1$. The average is now $\frac{n+1}{n + x/r} > 1$. However an interval of length $r$ can contain at most one Dirac Delta. And therefore $1$ is an upper bound for the integral over a length of $1$.

Of course with a Riemann integral, we can't really use Dirac deltas. But we can place narrow thin bumps of width $a$ and height $\frac{1}{a}$. If $a$ is small relative to $x$, then we can get the effect of a Dirac Delta. (We just need it to be small enough that no interval of length $r$ intersects two bumps.)

For the case where $r$ divides evenly, you have stated the right reasoning. Just in confusing terms. Here is how I'd state that.

The overall integral is the sum of $n$ piecewise integrals. And therefore the average integral is the average of $n$ numbers. If none of those numbers exactly match the average, then at least one is smaller, and at least one is larger. Then if we slide an interval of that length between those two spots, we get a continuous function on the start of that interval. At one point it is below our desired value, at another it is above. By the intermediate value theorem, we somewhere hit the average.

Answer B:
The lengths you found are the only ones. This is Lévy’s universal chord theorem for

$$ G(x)=\int_0^xf(y)dy-\dfrac{I}{L}x.$$

Title: Using domain walls to benchmark fast quantum anneals

Abstract:
We consider the distribution of domain walls arising in ground states of frustrated 1-dimensional Ising spin chains with anti-parallel boundary spins. For ideal chains, a sine-squared particle-in-a-box distribution of domain walls is expected in the quantum setting, and a uniform distribution expected classically. However, for chains with random imperfections, prior work [Chancellor et al., npj Quantum Inf. 8, 73, 2022] found that the distribution in a physical implementation corresponded to neither. Instead, the domain wall distribution forms a U-shaped profile arising from a classical model with random fields, where the combination of averaging over these fields and thermal averaging produces the characteristic U-shape. With D-Wave's newer fast anneal feature, we access anneal times shorter than the coherence time and observe the expected coherent quantum behavior in the form of a sine-squared distribution. For the shortest available anneal time, the dynamics have not yet reached the sine-squared shape and instead display a different U-shape in the middle of the chains. This motivates using the extent of the domain wall distribution tail in this regime as a platform independent metric that provides a signature of both coherence time and noise levels.

Title: A multiprobe $Λ$CDM consistency analysis with gravitational-wave standard sirens

Abstract:
Multi-messenger cosmology offers an independent path to stress-test the $Λ$CDM model as gravitational wave (GW) catalogs grow in size. We present the first multiprobe assessment of $Λ$CDM tensions incorporating GW standard sirens: LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration (LVK) fifth Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog (GWTC-5.0) standard sirens are combined with Dark Energy Survey (DES) Year 6 weak lensing and galaxy clustering (3$\times$2pt), baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), and type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia), together with Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) BAO, and confronted with primary cosmic microwave background (CMB) measurements from Planck, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT), and the South Pole Telescope (SPT). All probes are analyzed under homogeneous priors and combined via normalizing flows, and we quantify the $S_8$ discrepancy and $H_0$ tension with respect to CMB. Adding standard sirens to the 3$\times$2pt analysis improves the constraints in the $Ω_m$-$S_8$ plane by $\sim$30%, while constraining $H_0$ to 6.2%. We present cosmological constraints from the low-redshift probes including standard sirens, yielding $S_8 = 0.793 \pm 0.010$, $Ω_m = 0.308^{+0.007}_{-0.006}$, and $H_0 = 69.4^{+4.1}_{-4.4}$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$. At current GW sensitivity, however, both the $S_8$ discrepancy and the $H_0$ tension remain essentially unchanged. Our analysis nonetheless delivers the first assessment of $Λ$CDM tensions computed with standard sirens included among the probes, and establishes them as a mature cosmological probe -- ready to be combined on equal footing with established datasets in forthcoming surveys such as the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), Euclid, and Roman.

Title: On convex envelopes of bilinear terms over polygonal domains

Abstract:
We develop an algorithm for computing the convex envelope of the bilinear function $f(x,y)=xy$ over possibly nonconvex polygonal domains. Building on existing methods for convex polytopes, our approach uses the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions and an analysis of the contact points between affine underestimators and the graph of $f$. Nonconvex domains admit additional contact configurations that prevent several simplifications available in the convex case. We resolve these configurations explicitly and show that the envelope admits a finite polyhedral subdivision with affine, quadratic, or rational expressions on its cells. For orthogonal polygons, whose edges are horizontal or vertical, we establish substantial reductions in the generator sets needed to compute the envelope. We also present methods for constructing such domains as relaxations of two-dimensional projections of nonlinear optimization problems. An illustrative example quantifies the loss in relaxation strength caused by convexifying the domain before computing the envelope. Computational experiments on MINLPLib instances show that cuts derived from orthogonal polygons strengthen root relaxations and reduce branch-and-bound nodes in aggregate.

Title: Evaluating Generalization and Long-Term Stability of Smartwatch-Based Cuffless Blood Pressure Monitoring

Abstract:
Smartwatch-based cuffless blood pressure (BP) monitoring is a promising low-burden solution for long-term cardiovascular management, but practical deployment remains constrained by model complexity, uncertain cross-dataset generalization, and insufficient evidence on long-term tracking stability. This study presents an efficient Signal-Context Gated Fusion Network (SCGBPNet) for cuffless BP estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) signals. SCGBPNet integrates signal-level representations through self-attention and further incorporates subject-specific contextual information via a compact gated fusion module. On Aurora-BP, SCGBPNet achieved SBP/DBP mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 7.08/4.90 mmHg, compared with 6.44/4.89 mmHg under within-dataset validation on the private smartwatch dataset, indicating a modest within-dataset discrepancy. Cross-dataset transfer from Aurora-BP to the smartwatch dataset increased the MAEs to 8.98/6.47 mmHg, demonstrating substantial cross-dataset degradation. For long-term stability, the proposed method showed low week-to-week performance variation and a low daily decay rate, indicating good stability over a follow-up period of more than one month. Nevertheless, estimation accuracy deteriorated when BP deviated substantially from an individual's baseline. These findings indicate that favorable aggregate MAE alone should not be interpreted as evidence of deployment-ready performance. More systematic and stratified evaluation across dataset settings, BP ranges, and baseline-deviation levels is needed to assess the practical reliability of smartwatch-based cuffless BP monitoring.

He leads a ministry called Awaken Ministry, under the motto "Awakening Young Hearts", which aims to host worship nights and other events for young people across Australia.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: Why is the notion of strongly differentiable so little known?
Tags: derivatives

Question:
If $U$ is an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$ and $f \colon U \to \mathbb R^m$ is a function, then we say $f$ is strongly differentiable at $a \in U$ if there is a linear map $T$ such that
$$
f(x)-f(y) = T(x-y) + \epsilon(x,y)\|x-y\|,
$$
where $\epsilon(x,y) \to 0$ as $x,y \to a$ or equivalently,
$$
\frac{\|f(x)-f(y)-T(x-y)\|}{\|x-y\|} \to 0 \text{ as } x,y \to a.
$$
If it exists, we say $T=df_a$ is the strong derivative of $f$ at $a$. There are lots of reasons to like this definition:

If $f$ is strongly differentiable at $a$ then it is Lipschitz continuous at $a$.

With the obvious definitions, the existence of strong partial derivatives implies the existence of the total strong derivative (and conversely)

if $f$ is strongly differentiable at $a$ and $df_a$ is invertible then $f$ is locally invertible, i.e. the inverse function theorem holds for $f$ at $a$.

In the 1-variable case the definition asks that
$$
\lim_{x,y \to a} \frac{f(x)-f(y)}{x-y} \to df_a,
$$
that is, the slopes of chords near $a$ converge to $df_a$, which seems a very natural way of defining what the tangent line should be -- arguably more natural than only considering the slopes of cords with $a$ as one end-point.

Despite the above, the definition seems to be much less well-known that the standard (Frechet) definition. Of course, strong differentiability is implied by continuous differentiability, and in most circumstances one is happy to work with $\mathcal C^1$ functions instead of simply differentiable functions, but this is often precisely because the $\mathcal C^1$ condition ensures things like properties 1 to 3 above hold.

Given both the good properties it enjoys (1 to 3 above say) and the fact (4.) that it seems at least as natural if not more natural than the standard definition, is there a reason why it is comparatively unknown?

== Skura Style ==
Skura Style is an American company that sells kitchen cleaning products. Founded in 2017 by Linda Sawyer and Alison Matz, the company initially focused on kitchen sponges and later expanded its product range to include scouring pads, microfiber cloths, and kitchen towels. [ref: Two Rockland Natives Rethink The Kitchen Sponge, Daily Voice]

=== History ===
Skura Style was founded by Linda Sawyer, a former advertising executive, and Alison Matz, a media and publishing executive. The company launched in October 2017 with a kitchen sponge as its first product. Sawyer's previous career included serving as CEO and Chairman of the advertising agency Deutsch, while Matz spent the majority of her career as a media executive, serving as Publisher at Condé Nast and Meredith. Independent trade publication Digiday covered the founders' transition from advertising and publishing to consumer products in January 2018. [ref: Life After Advertising: From Deutsch CEO to cleaning supplies startup founder, Digiday]

In May 2022, actress Eva Mendes acquired an ownership stake in the company and became a co-owner and brand ambassador. Her involvement included collaboration on product design and marketing. The partnership subsequently expanded to include a collection of kitchen cleaning products associated with Mendes. [ref: Eva Mendes comes clean, Forbes Australia]

=== Products ===
The company's product range includes kitchen sponges, scouring pads, microfiber cleaning cloths, Swedish dishcloths, and cotton kitchen towels.

Its Skrubby Sponge incorporates a printed pattern that fades with use, providing a visual indication of when the sponge may need replacing. The product is also treated with an antimicrobial agent, according to descriptions of the product published by the company and media outlets.

Other products include Very Skrubby, a double-sided scouring pad; Wipe Envy, a microfiber cleaning cloth; and Towel Ta-Da, a cotton kitchen towel. The company has also released products in collaboration with Eva Mendes. [ref: Allow Eva Mendes to Explain Why She’s Bubbly Over Sponges These Days, Architectural Digest]

Title: BYOD: Build Your Own DLM - Efficient Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Language Model Conversion

Abstract:
Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion language models (DLMs) permit parallel token updates, flexible generation, and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. We present Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), a generalizable LoRA-only recipe for parameter-efficient AR-to-DLM conversion. Without architecture-specific tuning, BYOD induces diffusion generation in Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B; to our knowledge, this is the first reported AR-to-DLM conversion of a Mistral model. The adapters comprise 4.1-5.8% of final parameters while every base-model parameter remains frozen; each 25,000-iteration conversion needs at most 102.4M tokens, processed in 3.1-4.0 hours on one Google Colab GPU. All four models generate from fully masked sequences, use bidirectional context in a controlled attention test, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge. BYOD-Gemma is the strongest BYOD conversion on our nine-task evaluation, reaching 50.6% average accuracy compared with 51.9% for LLaDA 8B Instruct in the same harness. Open-generation quality at low network function evaluation (NFE) budgets remains the principal limitation: BYOD perplexity is 8.3-11.1 versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.2-3.0 for the AR parents when generating 128 tokens in 64 steps. To enable further experimentation and inspection, we provide a standalone training and evaluation implementation and interactive demos for all four conversions. BYOD thus provides a practical route for extending diffusion generation to other existing model families while identifying the gap that efficient conversion must next close.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: Can trigonometry for obtuse angles be rigorously derived using purely synthetic geometry
Tags: geometry, trigonometry, euclidean-geometry, synthetic-geometry

Question:
In classical synthetic geometry (e.g., Euclidean geometry without coordinates), trigonometric ratios like $\sin \theta$ and $\cos \theta$ are naturally defined for acute angles ($0^\circ < \theta < 90^\circ$) using right-angled triangles and similar triangles.

However, when extending trigonometry to obtuse angles ($90^\circ \le \theta < 180^\circ$), standard modern curricula almost universally switch to analytic geometry, defining these functions via the unit circle on a Cartesian coordinate plane.

I am interested in whether it is possible to rigorously extend and prove trigonometric identities for obtuse angles within a purely synthetic framework, without introducing a coordinate system, analytic extensions, or vector algebra.

Clearly, some results for obtuse angles have synthetic equivalents. For instance, Euclid's Elements (Book II, Proposition 12)  proves a geometric equivalent of the Law of Cosines for obtuse-angled triangles:

In obtuse-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the obtuse angle is greater than the squares on the sides containing the obtuse angle by twice the rectangle contained by one of the sides about the obtuse angle, namely that on which the perpendicular falls, and the straight line cut off outside by the perpendicular towards the obtuse angle.

While this bypasses the need for a negative cosine by dealing with lengths and extensions, it raises a few questions regarding a unified synthetic trigonometry:

How can we synthetically define $\cos \theta$ or $\sin \theta$ for an obtuse angle $\theta$ in a way that naturally yields properties like $\cos(180^\circ - \theta) = -\cos \theta$ without relying on Cartesian signs? Is it inevitable to introduce directed segments into the synthetic axioms?

Has any historical or modern literature successfully built a complete system of trigonometry (including the addition formulas) for angles up to $180^\circ$ (or beyond) using strictly synthetic methods?

I would appreciate any insights, proofs, or references to literature addressing this axiomatic approach to trigonometry.

Title: A polynomial method over formal power series

Abstract:
We give new upper bounds on families of integer vectors with prescribed coordinate multiplicities and a forbidden scalar product. Our method uses coefficient functions over formal power series and recovers the Frankl--Wilson bound for binary vectors. For vectors in $\{-1,0,1\}^n$, we obtain an exponential improvement over the ordinary polynomial count in a wide range; in certain regimes, we determine the lower limit of the exponential base. We use the new bounds to make progress on several questions in combinatorial geometry. In particular, we improve the base of the exponent in Borsuk's partition problem: we construct finite subsets of $\mathbb R^N$ requiring at least $(1.37+o(1))^{\sqrt N}$ parts of smaller diameter for all sufficiently large $N$, and obtain a base of $1.3839$ along a subsequence of dimensions.

state.text:
Title: On Statistical-Computational Gaps in Graph Combinatorial Testing Problems

Abstract:
We study high-dimensional graph combinatorial hypothesis testing problems in which a signal is supported on the edge set of an unknown subgraph drawn from a class invariant under vertex relabeling. For Gaussian observations, we characterize sharp statistical and computational thresholds (at polynomial order) for the signal magnitude required for strong detection across various combinatorial graph alternatives. Our analysis is based on bounding the second moments of the full and low-degree likelihood ratios in terms of the overlap of two independent latent structures and comparing the resulting lower bounds with scan, average, and coordinatewise maximum tests. Under an appropriate low-degree conjecture for computational hardness, we obtain planted-clique thresholds matching those known for Gaussian submatrix detection and identify new statistical-computational gaps for multiple planted cliques and hypercliques, thick cycles and thick paths. We also establish a novel transfer principle across natural exponential family observation models: matching the one-coordinate chi-square divergence preserves full likelihood-ratio second moments exactly and makes low-degree second moments equivalent up to constant factors under a degree condition. Under local regularity, we obtain corresponding testing upper bounds in terms of an effective signal strength. When these upper and lower bounds match, they yield universal threshold scales in the local alternative regime. As a consequence, statistical-computational gaps for planted-clique detection in Erdős--Rényi settings can be deduced from the Gaussian model.

Title: The trace distribution of $r$-primitive $k$-normal elements of finite fields

Abstract:
Let \(q=p^e\) be a prime power and \(n\geq1\). Let \(L=\F_{q^n}\) and \(K=\F_q\). We study the trace distribution of \(r\)-primitive \(k\)-normal elements of \(L\) over \(K\). We first derive exact formulas for the number of \(k\)-normal elements of \(L\) with a prescribed trace in \(K\). For \(r\mid q^n-1\), \(0\leq k\le n-1\), and \(a\in K\), let \(\mathcal{N}_{r,k}(a)\) denote the number of \(r\)-primitive \(k\)-normal elements of \(L\) with trace \(a\). We establish a sufficient condition for \(\mathcal{N}_{r,k}\) to be constant on \(K^\times\). We also identify a subgroup \(H_r\) of \(K^\times\) and prove that \(\mathcal{N}_{r,k}\) is constant on each coset of \(H_r\). Finally, we obtain a necessary and sufficient character-sum condition for \(\mathcal{N}_{r,k}\) to be constant on \(K^\times\).

Site: Travel Stack Exchange
Title: Moving during Schengen visa application—which address to state?
Tags: visas, schengen-visas, finland

Question:
I am a Turkish citizen living in the US on an F-1 visa, and I want to get a Finland Schengen visa to attend a conference on May 18th. I am planning to use the VFS in Chicago.

The problem is, due to an emergency, I have to move from address A to address B on March 23rd (which is when my current lease at address A ends, but the new lease at address B starts on March 15th). The questions are: If I can get a VFS appointment on March 18th, should I list address A as my address in my application? If so, would asking VFS to send my passport back to address B look sketchy? Or should I try to get an appointment before March 15 so address A is (I guess officially) still my address?

I wanted to apply before I moved to address B because my bank statements etc. will have address A on them, but does that really matter? Or should I just apply a later date in April or something after all of this is settled, but then the May 18 deadline might be tight.

Answer A:
You can use whatever address you want in VFS. It is purely to receive the passport and it won't be verified.

For mine, I used my co-working space address, which is not mentioned anywhere and it was delivered correctly, no questions asked.

Answer B:
You're overthinking this. If VFS will physically mail your passport back to you, use the address where you can receive it, namely address B.

If you're worried about the address mismatch between bank statements etc, you can add a note to state that until March 23rd you were resident at address A.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: How to find values of $n$ in double counting problem?
Tags: combinatorics

Question:
Problem:

We have $n$ students in a given school, and we know the following statements:

(a) Every student has either $10$ or $11$ friends;

(b) Choosing two students at random, they have exactly $5$ friends in common.

Find all values of $n$ that satisfy these conditions.

I thought of the following for my solution, but I am unsure about the constraints for $n$.

Let $d_{i}$ be the number of friends each student has (either 10 or 11). From the problem statement, we can see that the total number of pairs of n with 5 common friends will equal the sum of the pairs of $d_{i}$. In mathematical terms:

$$5\binom{n}{2}=\sum _{i=1}^{n} \binom{d_{i}}{2}$$

Let $x$ be the quantity of students who have 10 friends and $y$ be those who have 11 friends, where $n=x+y$. It holds that:

$$5{n \choose 2}=\sum _{i=1}^{n}{d_{i} \choose 2}={10 \choose 2}x+{11 \choose 2}y$$

From this equality, we get:

$$n^{2}-19n-4y=0$$

How do I find the values of $n$ from the equation given above? I only found values of the form $n=6p+21$ or $n=6p+15$ for any positive integer $p$ when I tried to look at the discriminant $\Delta=361+16y$ in the solution. However, this approach does not seem correct to me.

Title: A five-species counterexample to the Hofbauer--Kon--Saito conjecture on qualitative permanence

Abstract:
Hofbauer, Kon and Saito showed that a Lotka-Volterra interaction matrix $A$ with negative diagonal can be qualitatively permanent only if (C1) every cycle of length $\ge 2$ of $A$ is nonpositive and (C2) every negative cycle contains exactly one negative entry. They conjectured that these conditions are also sufficient, and proved this for $n\le 3$. We give a $5\times 5$ integer matrix with seven nonzero off-diagonal entries that satisfies (C1) and (C2) but is not qualitatively permanent. For an explicit integer growth vector, in which one species is an obligate consumer as the definition allows, the system has an interior equilibrium, and an asymptotically stable heteroclinic cycle on the boundary of the orthant attracts an open set of interior orbits. Adding non-interacting species gives counterexamples for every $n\ge 5$. The interactions form a one-way feedback loop together with a predator of two prey. The verification is elementary except for one heteroclinic connection, which lies in a face that is not Volterra-Lyapunov stable. For it we prove a connection lemma based on invasion graphs, which reduces the question to a smaller, stable face. The failure is robust. It persists under small perturbations, including weak additional interactions, so every sign pattern that satisfies (C1) and (C2) and contains ours is a counterexample, and it occurs for an open cone of growth vectors. For $n\ge 6$ there are also counterexamples in which every species grows when alone. Finally, we announce that the conjecture holds for $n=4$ and that, for $n=5$, four minimal sign patterns characterise its failure.

Title: Wav2Aug: A Drop-In Speech Augmentation Policy

Abstract:
SpecAugment is the dominant speech augmentation policy, but researchers have studied it primarily for automatic speech recognition (ASR), and it operates on spectrograms, limiting its applicability to other speech tasks and waveform models. We propose Wav2Aug, a drop-in waveform augmentation policy that randomly samples two augmentations from a calibrated pool of waveform transformations. We calibrate the augmentation hyperparameters once and reuse them across tasks and architectures, eliminating task-specific tuning. Experiments on ten speech benchmarks show that Wav2Aug achieves ASR performance comparable to SpecAugment while improving over it on average across non-ASR tasks, yielding an average relative error reduction of 12.8% over the strongest compatible SpecAugment baseline. We further show that multi-view training provides additional gains, with two augmented views offering the best tradeoff between performance and computational cost.

state.text:
Title: Thermal Stability and Structural Relaxation Kinetics of Commercially Pure Titanium

Abstract:
This work explores the structural relaxation of cryorolled commercially pure titanium subjected to subsequent annealing.Nanostructured specimens with an average grain size of ~50 nm were produced by plastic deformation via cryogenic rolling at 100 K to a true strain of 1.20, followed by annealing at 425 K, 525 K, 725 K, and 945 K. Microstructural evolution was examined using electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction. Cryogenic rolling was found to induce pronounced grain fragmentation, with coherent scattering regions (CSRs) of 30-50 nm dominating the substructure. X-ray diffraction analysis revealed that annealing drives crystallite growth: a slight increase at 525 K, accelerated coarsening at 725 K, and complete recrystallization at 945 K. The kinetics of grain growth follow the classical Lifshitz-Slyozov-Wagner model, with a growth exponent of ~4, reflecting the role of triple junctions and defect-controlled boundary diffusion. The activation energy, estimated at ~97 kJ/mol, corresponds to typical values for grain boundary diffusion in α-Ti, confirming that cryogenic deformation produces a highly non-equilibrium microstructure whose relaxation is strongly temperature dependent.

Site: Physics Stack Exchange
Title: Does light reach geometrically inaccessible cavities without path measurement (analogy to the double-slit experiment)?
Tags: quantum-mechanics, interference, geometric-optics, diffraction, wave-particle-duality

Question:
I have a conceptual question that mixes geometrical optics and quantum behavior of light, and I would like to understand whether my reasoning is valid.

Consider a structure similar to a “Penrose room”: a nearly oval cavity with multiple small side pockets (“cavities”) arranged along the walls. Due to the geometry, rays from a light source placed on one side can only reach the pockets on that same side; the pockets on the opposite side are geometrically inaccessible (no direct ray paths).

Now, consider the quantum nature of light. In the double-slit experiment, a particle (electron or photon) behaves like a wave when no which-path measurement is performed, and interference arises from the superposition of multiple paths.

This leads to my question:

If the interior surfaces of the pockets are coated with a photosensitive material (e.g., photographic emulsion), and the rest of the structure is reflective, and no intermediate measurement is performed (i.e., only final detection by the photosensitive material), would light “reach” all pockets in some wave-like sense?
In other words, can the absence of intermediate observation allow light to populate regions that are classically inaccessible, or are such regions strictly determined by boundary conditions (e.g., solutions of Maxwell's equations), regardless of measurement?

I would appreciate clarification on whether this situation is fundamentally different from the double-slit experiment, or if I am incorrectly extending the concept of superposition to regions with no available paths.

Link to an interactive demonstration of the Penrose Room in Wolfram website: The Penrose Unilluminable Room

Title: Meromorphic order from Taylor coefficients, least singular values of Hankel matrices and rational approximants

Abstract:
We introduce a natural notion of generalized order for entire and meromorphic functions and express it in terms of their Taylor coefficients. More precisely, one formula uses the least singular values of Hankel matrices of the coefficients, and the other uses their determinants. These formulas generalize the classical coefficient formula for the order of entire functions and its extensions by Edrei and Sheremeta. The proof combines a theorem of Pommerenke with a bound for the Nevanlinna characteristic that results from a convergence theorem for rational approximants introduced by Prokhorov. We also characterize the largest class of growth scales for which the associated generalized order is well-behaved.

Site: Law Stack Exchange
Title: What point is Thomas trying to make in his dissent in Trump v. Barbara?
Tags: us-supreme-court, citizenship, fourteenth-amendment, official-immunity

Question:
From the slip opinion in Trump v. Barbara, page 61, dissent of Clarence Thomas:

The Court understands this category to exempt all children of “representatives of foreign sovereigns,” endeavoring to capture a longstanding principle that such children were
not entitled to citizenship. Ante, at 15. Although the Court gestures toward diplomatic immunity as a basis for this exception, diplomatic immunity extends to “only a narrow set”
of “diplomatic official[s],” not to all foreign representatives.  Brief for Sen. Ted Cruz et al. as Amici Curiae 28–29. Most foreign officials receive a partial immunity, such as immunity for their official acts. See Dept. of State, Diplomatic and Consular Immunity (July 2019), www.state.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/2018-DipConImm_v5_Web.pdf (archived at perma.cc/LK63-C3YL). But, partial immunity cannot render a person not “subject to the jurisdiction” of the United States for Fourteenth Amendment purposes.  After all, a variety of clearly American government officials—such as judges, prosecutors, and police officers—have similar partial official immunity.

What is the point?  I get the impression that Thomas thinks he is calling attention to an inconsistency in the applicability of diplomatic immunity to the jurisdiction requirement of the 14th amendment's citizenship clause.  By longstanding practice, however, the US has indeed recognized that partial immunity does not "render a person not “subject to the jurisdiction” of the United States for Fourteenth Amendment purposes"; US-born children of people who enjoy such immunity are US citizens.

(The cited amicus brief of Cruz et al. is somewhat incorrect in its reasoning, but at least it explains the reasoning explicitly.  One point it makes is that "there is no diplomatic official who is fully immune from all forms of civil liability, i.e., being
haled [sic] into the jurisdiction of a court. See id., App’x C (for example, all types of diplomatic officials can be issued traffic citations)."  It omits, however, that this doesn't reflect a lack of immunity: on the contrary, the source document describes how traffic citations should be sent to the Department of State so they can form the basis to request a waiver of immunity.  It also attacks the "invading soldiers" exception with an example that does not include the "hostile occupation" condition.)

Since Thomas leaves the reasoning implicit, it is more difficult to understand what his point might be.

Was Thomas unaware of, or glossing over, the fact that US born children of foreign representatives with official acts immunity are granted citizenship?  Or is there a line of reasoning that supports his position even taking that fact into account?

Title: Robustness of Median-based Splitting Rules for Causal Trees

Abstract:
Causal forests (Athey and Imbens, 2016) are a widely used method for the estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects. Standard implementations use mean-based splitting criteria, which perform well when the outcome distribution is well-behaved and free of contamination, such as outliers or heavy tails. However, real-world data are rarely clean. Outcome perturbations can affect the tree structure selected by mean-based splitting rules and lead to unreliable treatment effect estimates. In this study, we systematically examine the robustness of causal forests to irregularities in the outcome distribution. Building on the median-based splitting criteria introduced by Maßmann and Gliszczyńska-Schroeder (2026), we empirically investigate three median-based splitting criteria: Median Absolute Deviation (MAD), Least Median of Squares (LMS), and Median Squared Deviation (MSD). We conduct Monte Carlo experiments and apply the methods to empirical benchmark datasets from the causal inference literature to compare the performance of the median-based approaches with standard causal forests. We additionally examine pointwise confidence interval coverage using the Bootstrap of Little Bags and the infinitesimal jackknife. The results indicate that median-based splitting criteria can reduce sensitivity to outcome irregularities in specific scenarios, particularly in the presence of extreme heavy-tailed noise and nonlinear treatment effect heterogeneity. However, these benefits are scenario-dependent and do not consistently lead to more accurate conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: Do degenerate pivots in the network simplex method for optimal transport as presented in Peyré's book break the algorithm?
Tags: linear-programming, optimal-transport

Question:
In Peyré & Cuturi's Computational Optimal Transport (§3.5), the network simplex loop is: given a candidate transport plan $\mathbf{P}$ and its associated graph $G(\mathbf{P})$, compute complementary dual variables $(\mathbf{f}, \mathbf{g})$, find a violating pair $(i,j')$ of the dual constraint, and add the edge $\{i,j'\}$ to $G$. Two cases follow:

If this creates no cycle, $\mathbf{P}$ is unchanged, but $(\mathbf{f}, \mathbf{g})$ are recomputed on the enlarged graph.

If it creates a cycle, flow is rerouted along the cycle by an amount $\theta$ equal to the smallest flow among the negatively-oriented edges in the cycle, and that edge is dropped from the tree.
\end{itemize}

My question: suppose the first case occurs repeatedly, each new edge fails to close a cycle, so $\mathbf{P}$ stays fixed while $G$ keeps growing (this happens when $\mathbf{P}$ is degenerate, i.e. $G(\mathbf{P})$ is a forest rather than a spanning tree). Eventually some added edge does close a cycle. But if that cycle contains one of the previously-added zero-flow edges among its negatively-oriented edges, then $\theta = \min(\text{flow}) = 0$, so the pivot moves zero flow: $\mathbf{P}$ doesn't change even though a genuine cycle was found.

Peyré doesn't discuss this possibility at all. So I'm just confused, does this not happen in practice? And if it does happen, since the $\mathbf{P}$ transport plan isn't changed at all, isn't the algorithm essentially stuck?

Site: Physics Stack Exchange
Title: Understanding of Induced $E$ field when $B$ is Changing with Time
Tags: electromagnetism, maxwell-equations, electromagnetic-induction

Question:
Somewhat basic question here.  I'm trying to understand the $\bf E$ field created in conducting material when a steady state $\bf B$ field from a nearby electromagnet suddenly drops to zero. I think this is what Griffiths calls a "pure Faraday field."  I know that

$$ \nabla \times \mathbf{E} = - \frac{ \partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} $$

But isn't it also true that $\bf E$ is defined as

$$ \mathbf{E} = - \nabla V $$

where V is the potential (voltage) distribution in the conducting material?

The first equation says that $\bf E$ is not curl-free and therefore not conservative.  But the second equation implies that it is, and I know that relative voltages between two points on the material should be path-independent.

What am I missing here?

Answer A:
But isn't it also true that $\bf E$ is defined as

$$ \mathbf{E} = - \nabla V $$

No, this is not true. $\mathbf E$ can be defined by $$\mathbf E = -\nabla V -\frac{\partial \mathbf A}{\partial t}$$ where $V$ is the electric potential (usually written $\phi$) and $\mathbf A$ is the magnetic vector potential defined by $\mathbf B = \nabla \times \mathbf A$.

So $$\mathbf E = -\nabla V -\frac{\partial \mathbf A}{\partial t}$$$$\nabla \times \mathbf E = -\nabla \times \frac{\partial \mathbf A}{\partial t}$$$$\nabla \times \mathbf E = -\frac{\partial( \nabla \times \mathbf A)}{\partial t}$$$$\nabla \times \mathbf E = -\frac{\partial \mathbf B}{\partial t}$$

Answer B:
The electric field within a conductor can be arbitrary. Only sometimes, in a special case can it be represented as a potential gradient.

For instance, if you pass a magnet through a stationary conducting loop, an electric field exists within the conductor, and there is a proportional current, yet you will not be able to assign potential values at different points along this wire in a self-consistent manner.

You can break down any field into a sum of potential and vortex components

$\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{E_1} + \mathbf{E_2} = -\nabla\cdot\mathcal{G}(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}) + \nabla\times\mathcal{G}(\nabla\times\mathbf{E})$

but this split is just a convention and exists only in your head — while the field itself remains whole.

state.text:
Title: RadioTraj3D: Height-Aware Adaptive Sampling for 3D Radio-Map Reconstruction from Ultra-Sparse Trajectories

Abstract:
Aerial networks require radio propagation information at unvisited positions and heights to plan routes, select links, and allocate wireless resources. A three-dimensional radio map (3D RM) represents propagation conditions over the service area, enabling these decisions before flight. However, constructing such a map from autonomous aerial vehicle (AAV) measurements is challenging, since radio measurements are available only along the trajectory, whereas the target covers the 3D service volume. Existing methods use fixed AAV trajectories that ignore how building distributions and heights affect electromagnetic propagation, missing the heights most informative for RM reconstruction. To address these issues, we propose RadioTraj3D, which uses building-height information to coordinate measurement selection and layer-wise reconstruction. Building-height variations reveal propagation-sensitive layers that guide height-adaptive sampling. We therefore propose G-METS to select geometry-sensitive heights and allocate an exact budget across edge, corridor, and open regions before channel acquisition. A dual-view reconstructor then integrates local three-dimensional boundaries with full-height context through one bounded coefficient per layer. Simulated outdoor and indoor maps demonstrate state-of-the-art reconstruction across environments and vertical grids. On real-world AAV measurements from the LACN dataset, RadioTraj3D improves peak signal-to-noise ratio by 0.84 dB and reduces normalized mean squared error by 17.5% over Completion AE.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: Asymptotic density of the set of gapless positive integers.
Tags: number-theory, prime-numbers

Question:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. I define $n$ to have the property of being gapless if, for any prime numbers $p$ and $p'$ that divide $n$, every prime number $p''$ in between $p$ and $p'$ also divides $n$. For example, $30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5$ is a gapless positive integer, but neither $10 = 2 \times 5$ nor $14 = 2 \times 7$ is a gapless positive integer. Of course, every prime number and every power of a prime number is gapless.

My question is, what is the asymptotic density of the set of gapless positive integers within the set of positive integers? Does it even have an asymptotic density? I conjecture that the asymptotic density is $0$.

Answer A:
Let G be the set of gapeless integers
$$G(N)=\#\{n\leq N:n\in G\}$$
Then, the natural density:
$$d(G)=lim_{N\rightarrow \infty}=\frac{G(N)}{N}$$
By your definition, im assuming that "every prime number p'' between p and p'" also means that, if I were to take 77=11*7 would be a gapless number, because there is no prime between 7 and 11.
Then basically, if we order the prime numbers:
$$p_1<p_2<...<p_k$$
We can redefine a gapless number as any consecutive block in this sequence.
Then, fix any number $K\in\mathbb{N}$
We can divide the gapless numbers in three cases:
$$\\$$
If the smallest prime is greater than K.(e.g. we choose K=6, then, any number that has 2,3,5 as a prime is out).
So, the integer is not divisible by any prime $q\leq K$, by the Chinese Remainder Theorem(CRT), the exact proportion of integers not divisible by any prime up to K is given by:
$$
\prod_{q \le K} \left(1 - \frac{1}{q}\right)
$$
This product can be approximated for large K(Merten's third theorem):
$$
\prod_{q \le K} \left(1 - \frac{1}{q}\right) \sim \frac{e^{-\gamma}}{\ln K}
$$
But notice that it is being divided by a logarithm of K, which diverges when K tends to infinity, therefore that proportion diverges to zero when $K\rightarrow \infty$
Then, the gapless numbers in this case can be made arbitrarily small by making K larger.
$$\\$$
Now, if the smallest prime is at most K. Fixing a prime $Q>K$, if the largest prime divisor is less than Q:
Every prime factor of the number is at most Q. There are only finitely many primes that correspond to that, so the number of possible $n\leq N$ is at most:
$$
O_Q((\log N)^{\pi(Q)})=o(N)
$$
Therefore these integers have density zero.
$$\\$$
Now if a prime divisor is at least Q, let $p\leq K$ be the smallest prime divisor. Since n is gapless, it is divisible by every prime between p and Q:
$$
(\prod_{p\leq q\leq Q} q )\mid n
$$
Therefore there are at most $\frac{N}{\prod_{p\leq q\leq Q} q }$ possible multiples up to N. Summing over the possible primes $p\leq K$:
$$
\frac{\#(\text{integers where the prime divisor is }\geq Q \text{ up to N})}{N}\leq \sum_{p\leq K,\text{ }p \text{ prime}}\frac{1}{\prod_{p\leq q\leq Q} q }
$$
Fixing K and letting $Q\rightarrow \infty$, every product on the fraction tends to infinity:
$$
\frac{1}{\prod_{p\leq q\leq Q}}\rightarrow 0
$$
[truncated]

Answer B:
In fact, almost all gapless numbers are primes, so that their counting function is $\sim x/\log x$. Outline of proof:

Let $p$ be the smallest prime factor of a composite gapless integer $n\le x$. Set $k = k(p) = \lfloor (\log x)/\log p$, so that $x^{1/(k+1)} < p \le x^{1/k}$. Then $n$ can have at most $k$ prime factors.

Each gapless composite integer with smallest prime factor $p$ is represented by a binary string of length at most $k-1$: a $0$ means that the next prime factor is equal to the previous one, while a $1$ means that the next prime factor is the prime following the previous one. In particular, there are just under $2^k$ such strings.

Therefore the number of gapless composite numbers up to $x$ whose smallest prime factor lies in $(x^{1/(k+1)},x^{1/k}]$ is at most $2^k \pi(x^{1/k}) \le 2^k x^{1/k}$. In particular, for any $K\ge 2$, the number of gapless composite numbers up to $x$ whose smallest prime factor is at least $x^{1/K}$ is bounded above by $\sum_{k=2}^{K-1} 2^k x^{1/k} \le \sum_{k=2}^{K-1} 2^k x^{1/2} < 2^k x^{1/2}$.

Choose $K = K(x)$ appropriately, perhaps $K=\sqrt{\log x}$. Then the only gapless composite numbers not counted by the above argument have smallest prime factor at most $x^{1/K}$, and thus their largest prime factor is also essentially at most $x^{1/K} \approx e^{\sqrt{\log x}}$. The number of integers with this last property will be small, thanks to standard results on friable (or smooth) integers.

I think that this argument can be refined to show that the $k=2$ term is dominant among composite gapless numbers.

Title: Phonon Fluctuations Enhanced Superconductivity in a Three-Band Cuprate Model

Abstract:
The microscopic origin of high-$T_c$ superconductivity in cuprates remains an outstanding puzzle due to the interplay of intertwined orders. Experimental observations and theoretical studies have suggested crucial roles of phonons, with the $B_{1g}$ oxygen buckling mode emerging as a promising candidate. Here, we investigate the microscopic influence of this phonon in a three-band cuprate model. We find that the $B_{1g}$ phonon plays opposite roles in superconductivity depending on whether it lies in the adiabatic or antiadiabatic regime at a given temperature. Thermally populated adiabatic phonons suppress $d$-wave pairing through the loss of quasiparticle coherence, whereas antiadiabatic phonons simultaneously enhance coherence and the attractive $d$-wave pairing vertex, strengthening superconductivity across multiple diagnostics. This enhancement also exhibits pronounced electron-hole asymmetry arising from the different orbital characters of doped carriers. Our results therefore establish a microscopic mechanism through which $B_{1g}$ phonons can cooperate with electronic correlations to substantially enhance $d$-wave superconducting pairing in cuprates.

Title: Optimal Decay Exponents for Fractional Burgers Rarefaction Waves

Abstract:
We establish decay estimates toward rarefaction waves for the one-dimensional fractional Burgers equation when the order of dissipation lies between one and two. The initial data are bounded, and their perturbation from the Riemann step belongs to the critical weak-Lorentz space determined by scaling; the perturbation need not be small or integrable. We obtain optimal algebraic decay exponents, improving the known decay rates, and extending convergence to every Lebesgue space above the critical exponent, including the supremum norm. We prove optimality by constructing a single solution with Riemann step initial data whose lower decay estimates have exactly the same algebraic exponents as our upper estimates. These lower bounds establish that neither the algebraic decay exponents nor the range of convergence can be improved under the stated assumptions. The upper estimates contain a logarithmic factor whose necessity remains open. The proof combines convex truncation estimates, fractional interpolation, and a one-sided slope estimate for the supremum norm.

Draft text:
The Interior Design Society of Kenya (IDSK) is a professional association representing interior designers, spatial planners, design studios, material suppliers, and allied manufacturers in Kenya. [ref: About Us – Interior Design Society of Kenya (IDSK), Interior Design Society of Kenya] Headquartered in Nairobi, the society advocates for formal industry regulation, professional accreditation, ethical practice, and sustainable interior architecture across residential, commercial, and public sectors in Kenya. [ref: IDSk Supports New Bill With Amendments and Demands Legal Recognition, Jicho News]

== History and Governance ==
The organization was established to serve as a unified voice for practitioners in Kenya's built-environment sector, where interior design had historically operated without a dedicated statutory framework.

IDSK is governed by an executive board led by President Cecilia Nakhungu Mbati. [ref: Architects' alliance opposes bill on regulation of built environment professions, Kenya News Agency] The society engages with national educational bodies, TVET institutions, and universities to ensure academic curricula align with evolving professional standards, spatial safety regulations, accessibility requirements, and building codes. [ref: IDSK Industry Integration Programme, Interior Design Society of Kenya]

== Key Objectives and Programs ==
The society's core mandate includes regulating professional practice, protecting consumers from unqualified operators, and facilitating professional development. Its main initiatives include:

* Industry Integration Programme (IIP): A structured transition and mentorship framework designed to connect interior design graduates and emerging professionals with practical studio experience, site mentorship, and industry network opportunities.
* Workforce Placement Programme: A professional pathway program matching qualified interior designers with employment opportunities across corporate fit-out firms, architectural practices, and design agencies.
* Circular Design and Sustainability: Advocacy initiatives promoting eco-friendly spatial planning, energy efficiency, acoustic design, indoor air quality, biophilic elements, and the sourcing of local timber, stone, and sustainable materials.
* Interior Design Summit: An annual flagship convention uniting design professionals, policy leaders, suppliers, and real estate developers. The 2026 summit took place at the Sarit Expo Centre in Nairobi under the theme "Building the Interior Design Economy." [ref: Interior Design Summit 2026: Building the Interior Design Economy, Interior Design Society of Kenya]

== Legislative Advocacy ==
In 2026, IDSK actively participated in legislative discussions before the National Assembly Committee on Housing, Urban Planning and Public Works regarding the Architectural and Quantity Surveying Practitioners Bill, 2026 (National Assembly Bill No. 47 of 2026), which sought to replace the colonial-era Architects and Quantity Surveyors Act (Cap. 525). [ref: Parliament Seeks Stakeholders’ Views on Bill to Regulate Architects and Quantity Surveyors, KTN News Kenya]

During parliamentary stakeholder submissions, IDSK President Cecilia Mbati expressed general support for statutory regulation while submitting clause-by-clause amendments aimed at safeguarding the independence of interior design practitioners:

1. Title and Scope Expansion: Requesting that the legislation be renamed the Built Environment Practitioners Act to explicitly encompass interior designers, landscape architects, and construction project managers.
2. Regulatory Council Representation: Advocating for dedicated statutory representation for interior designers on the proposed joint regulatory board under Clause 71D.
3. Transitional Grandfathering Provisions: Demanding clear grandfathering mechanisms under Part X (Clause 58) to register existing interior design professionals with over five years of verified experience who had operated legally prior to statutory enactment.
4. Stamping Authority for Fit-Out Documentation: Requesting statutory recognition under Clause 46(1) for technical documents, spatial planning layouts, material specifications, and interior fit-out drawings stamped by registered interior designers.

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: Does convergence of the Flint-Hills series imply convergence of the Cookson-Hills series?
Tags: sequences-and-series, trigonometry, convergence-divergence, pi, open-problem

Question:
The Wolfram MathWorld page on the Cookson Hills series states:

It is not known if this series converges since $\sec^2 n$ can have sporadic large values.

The series is

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sec^2 n}{n^3}.
$$

While reading OpenAI, The irrationality exponent of $\pi$ is 2, I noticed Corollary $1.2$ asserts that the classical Flint-Hills series converges:

$$
F:=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^3\sin^2 n}<\infty.
$$

Does convergence of the Flint-Hills series imply convergence
of the Cookson-Hills series? Specifically,

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^3\sin^2 n}<\infty
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sec^2 n}{n^3}<\infty
$$

Answer A:
A simple identity for $\cos$:
$$\cos(n) = \frac{\sin(2n)}{2 \sin(n)}$$
$$\sec(n) = \frac{2 \sin(n)}{\sin(2n)}$$

$$C=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sec^2 n}{n^3}$$
Substitute for $\sec(n)$
$$=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{2 \sin(n)}{\sin(2n)}\right)^2 \frac{1}{n^3}$$
$$=4\times\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sin^2(n)}{\sin^2(2n)} \frac{1}{n^3}$$
Change of variable $m=2n$.
$$=4\times\sum_{m=2, 4, 6, \dots}^{\infty}\frac{\sin^2(m/2)}{\sin^2(m)} \frac{1}{(\frac{m}{2})^3}.$$
$$=32\times\sum_{m=2, 4, 6, \dots}^{\infty}\frac{\sin^2(m/2)}{\sin^2(m)} \frac{1}{m^3}$$
$$C=32\times\sum_{m=2, 4, 6, \dots}^{\infty}\frac{\sin^2(m/2)}{m^3 \sin^2 m}$$

Here is the sum of the Flint-Hills Series:
$$F=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^3\sin^2 n}$$

Compare, term-by-term.

All terms of both series are non-negative.

The odd terms of $C$, after change-of-variable, are $0$.

For even terms, the numerator of $C$ is strictly less than the numerator of $F$.

Every term in $C$ is less than every term in $F$, However $C$ has a constant coefficient of 32.

Ergo, if $F$ convergent, then $C$ must also be convergent.

Answer B:
Assume the Flint-Hills series conclusion of Corollary $1.2$ of the cited OpenAI manuscript:

$$
F:=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^3\sin^2 n}<\infty.
$$

Claim

The Cookson-Hills series converges:

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sec^2 n}{n^3}<\infty.
$$

Proof

Using

$$
\sin(2n)=2\sin n\cos n,\quad
\sin^2(2n)=4\sin^2 n\cos^2 n,
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sec^2 n
&\le\frac{1}{\sin^2 n}+\sec^2 n
\quad\left(\frac{1}{\sin^2 n}>0\right)\\
&=\frac{1}{\sin^2 n}+\frac{1}{\cos^2 n}\\
&=\frac{\cos^2 n}{\sin^2 n\cos^2 n}
 +\frac{\sin^2 n}{\sin^2 n\cos^2 n}\\
&=\frac{\cos^2 n+\sin^2 n}{\sin^2 n\cos^2 n}\\
&=\frac{1}{\sin^2 n\cos^2 n}\\
&=\frac{4}{4\sin^2 n\cos^2 n}\\
&=\frac{4}{\sin^2(2n)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The partial sums satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{\sec^2 n}{n^3}
&\le\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{4}{n^3\sin^2(2n)}\\
&=4\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1}{n^3\sin^2(2n)}\\
&=4\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{8}{(2n)^3\sin^2(2n)}
\quad\left(\frac{1}{n^3}=\frac{8}{(2n)^3}\right)\\
&=4\cdot8\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1}{(2n)^3\sin^2(2n)}\\
&=32\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1}{(2n)^3\sin^2(2n)}\\
&=32\sum_{\substack{1\le m\le2N\\2\mid m}}
\frac{1}{m^3\sin^2 m}\quad(m=2n)\\
&\le32\sum_{m=1}^{2N}\frac{1}{m^3\sin^2 m}\\
&\le32\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{m^3\sin^2 m}\\
&=32F<\infty.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the partial sums are increasing and bounded above by $32F$,

$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\sec^2 n}{n^3}
&=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{\sec^2 n}{n^3}\le32F<\infty.
\end{aligned}
}
$$

Answer C:
Suppose

$$
\sum^{\infty}_{n=1}\frac{1}{n^{3}\sin^{2}n}<\infty .
$$
We prove below that
$$
\sum^{\infty}_{n=1}\frac{1}{n^{3}\cos^{2}n}<\infty .
$$
It suffices to verify that the sum of these two series converges:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum^{\infty}_{n=1}\left(\frac{1}{n^{3}\sin^{2}n}+\frac{1}{n^{3}\cos^{2}n}\right)
&=\sum^{\infty}_{n=1}\frac{1}{n^{3}\sin^{2}n\cos^{2}n}\\
&=\sum^{\infty}_{n=1}\frac{4}{n^{3}\sin^{2}(2n)}\\
&=32\sum^{\infty}_{n=1}\frac{1}{(2n)^{3}\sin^{2}(2n)}\\
&\le 32\sum^{\infty}_{n=1}\frac{1}{n^{3}\sin^{2}n}<\infty .
\end{aligned}
$$

Title: Stable Electroweak Strings and Nambu Monopoles Nested at Inert-Higgs Interfaces

Abstract:
Electroweak $Z$ strings are generally unstable, and their Nambu-monopole endpoints lack topological protection in the bulk. Using degenerate inert and inert-like Higgs vacua as a solvable reference, we show that their interface supports both defects. The analytic interface carries a normalizable $SU(2)$ relative-orientation field. Its effective theory supports locally stable unit-flux $Z$ strings in a one-vacuum phase and fractional $Z$ strings in a two-vacuum phase. The fractional string carries an $S^2$ orientation field; a Nambu monopole is a second kink between symmetry-related, equal-tension $Z$ strings. We identify phases in which Nambu monopoles are confined or deconfined within the interface: in the confined phase, their $Z$ flux is concentrated into fractional strings, whereas in the deconfined phase, the monopole becomes a vortex within the interface and its $Z$ flux spreads radially through the interface. The electromagnetic magnetic field extends outside the interface in both phases. We determine analytic string profiles, effective-theory stability regions, and the unchanged electromagnetic magnetic charge across this confinement transition.

Jean-Yves Parisot (born 1964) is a French business executive and the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Symrise, a German publicly listed manufacturer of fragrances, flavors, and ingredients for food, nutrition, and cosmetics headquartered in Holzminden, Germany. Parisot studied veterinary medicine at the École nationale vétérinaire de Lyon [ref: Jean-Yves Parisot appointed CEO of Symrise, Symrise], where he earned a Doctorate in Veterinary Medicine (DVM). He later obtained a Master of Business Administration (MBA) from HEC Paris. [ref: Jean-Yves Parisot appointed CEO of Symrise, Symrise]

== Career ==
Parisot began his career in leadership roles at several international companies, including Pfizer, Rhône-Poulenc/Rhodia, Danisco, and Air Liquide. [ref: Jean-Yves Parisot – Executive Profile, Bloomberg]

In 2009, he joined the Diana Group, a company specializing in natural ingredients that was later integrated into Symrise. He initially led the Food Division before becoming head of the Diana Division. [ref: Jean-Yves Parisot appointed Symrise CEO, Nutraceutical Business Review]

In 2016, Parisot became a member of the Executive Board of Symrise AG. [ref: Symrise board member Jean-Yves Parisot named IOFI president, Perfumer & Flavorist]

He was appointed Chief Executive Officer of the company in April 2024, with a contract running until September 2028. [ref: Jean-Yves Parisot CEO Analysis, Paragon Intel]

As part of the company's "One Symrise" strategy, Symrise has pursued greater global integration of its business activities. [ref: Unleashing the full beauty of one Symrise, Dairy Industries International]

The company has also expanded initiatives in sustainability, digital transformation, and artificial intelligence, including the establishment of an AI hub in Barcelona. [ref: Exclusive Interview with Symrise CEO Dr Jean-Yves Parisot, The Beauty Influencers]

Symrise has set sustainability targets including achieving net-zero emissions by 2045 and aligning with several United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. [ref: Symrise Corporate Report 2024, Symrise]

== Other roles ==
Parisot has served on several corporate boards. [ref: Jean-Yves Parisot – Executive Profile, Bloomberg]

* Chairman of the Board, Probi AB (Lund, Sweden)
* Chairman of the Board, VetAgro Sup (Lyon, France)
* Board member, Swedencare AB (Malmö, Sweden)

From 2023 to 2025, he also served as President of the International Organization of the Flavor Industry (IOFI). [ref: Symrise board member Jean-Yves Parisot named IOFI president, Perfumer & Flavorist]

Wiki: English Wikipedia
Draft: Ouled Djellal ( sheep )

Draft text:
The Ouled Djellal (also known as the Algerian Arab or Western Thin-tailed) is a breed of domestic sheep native to the steppe and high plains of Algeria. It is the most dominant, widespread, and economically important sheep breed in the country, accounting for approximately 63% to 65% of the national flock with an estimated population of over 11 to 12 million head. It is primarily kept for meat production and wool, and is highly favored for its exceptional adaptability to arid and semi-arid pastoral systems.

== History ==
The breed takes its name from the town of Ouled Djellal, located southwest of Biskra, which represents its historical cradle. Historical hypotheses suggest that the thin-tailed, fine-wooled ancestors of the breed may have been originally introduced to North Africa from Italy by the Romans during the fifth century.

Due to its high commercial profitability and productivity, the breed expanded dramatically over the late 20th and early 21st centuries. Driven by the mechanization of the steppe and changing transportation infrastructures, its population increased from roughly 10 million in 1989 to over 11–12 million head, overrunning the geographical ranges of smaller native breeds. Today, it has spread far beyond its central-eastern Algerian origin into the western steppes and cross-border regions of western Tunisia.

== Characteristics ==
The Ouled Djellal is a large, long-legged, and slender thin-tailed breed explicitly built for high mobility and long-distance walking across sparse rangelands. It is entirely unicolored white, with white skin, a thin head, a convex or sub-convex facial profile, and long, drooping ears. The fleece is white and consists of a light, refined, carpet-grade wool. Rams generally display strong, spiral horns, whereas the ewes are typically polled (hornless).

At maturity, rams average 81 kg (with some selection strains reaching up to 140 kg) in weight and stand approximately 84 cm tall at the withers. Ewes average 49 kg (ranging up to 75 kg in optimized systems) and stand about 74 cm tall.

The breed is an exceptionally hardy and active forager, showing remarkable tolerance to extreme heat and prolonged nutritional stress in arid environments. Under standard management systems, ewes demonstrate high maternal capacity and produce an average litter size of 1.5 lambs. Lambs display excellent growth potential and rapid fattening profiles, typically starting at a birth weight of 3.5 kg and scaling efficiently to 30 kg by five months of age. Ewes also maintain a substantial dairy performance, lactating for approximately 180 days and yielding around 75 kg of milk.

== Economic Importance ==
The Ouled Djellal serves as the definitive cornerstone of Algerian agropastoralism and food security. It is the absolute reference breed for the national Eid al-Adha holiday market, commanding the highest buyer demand, commercial volume, and investment yields across local livestock corridors. Its meat is highly valued, and the breed produces a heavier, fat-retentive carcass profile compared to smaller regional types.

== Genetic Homogenization Impact ==
The commercial superiority of the Ouled Djellal has driven a widespread trend toward livestock homogenization across the North African steppes. To maximize economic returns, pastoralists throughout western Algeria have systematically introduced heavy Ouled Djellal rams into native western herds. This aggressive crossbreeding practice has resulted in severe genetic dilution and the absorption of smaller indigenous breeds—most notably pushing the native, high-meat-quality Hamra breed to the brink of extinction.

Site: Electronics Stack Exchange
Title: Chip marked TDA1543 only translates last nine bits
Tags: integrated-circuit, fpga, dac, i2s, digital-audio

Question:
I am driving a DAC chip with a Papilio One 250K FPGA board (contains a Spartan 3E 250K chip). I am using the I2S protocol. Both a logic analyzer and a PCM5102 chip (on an Adafruit breakout board) show exactly what I expect. But this chip marked as a Philips TDA1543 ignores the first seven bits I send, but works perfectly with the last nine bits (where the ninth bit is a sign bit).

I got the chip in a 2-pack on Ebay. I then bought a ten-pack from someone else on Ebay or AliExpress. Some of the chips are marked Philips and some are marked NXP. Some leave black residue when I rub them, some do not. But they all behave the same way. Ignore the first seven bits, listen to the last nine.

I've asked Gemini about this a dozen different ways. It usually insists that I have a TDA1543A, which uses the EIAJ protocol. But switching between the protocols doesn't seem to change anything, including the response to higher bits. The PCM5102 responds exactly as anticipated, giving sensible output when the signal is EIAJ and the chip is set to EIAJ, and also when the signal is I2S with the chip set to I2S.

For those less familiar: The I2S protocol has a bit clock, a Word Select line, and a data line. The word clock toggles between left stereo channel and right stereo channel. When the Word Select toggles, the next bit (measured when the bit clock transitions low->high) is the LSB of the last audio sample, and the bit after that is the MSB of the new audio sample. The EIAJ protocol just starts the MSB right after the Word Select toggles.

Both protocols transmit stereo PCM audio of arbitrary length (usually 16, 24, or 32 bit words). Two's complement is used for negative numbers.

The Papilio is putting out 3.3V TTL at a high slew rate. Gemini suggested level shifting to 5V, which I have tried without result.

So do I have strange mystery chips? Or am I missing something basic? I can't seem to find chips with this behavior online.

Each chip has separate left and right channel outputs. I have a variable resistor hooked up to the bias pin, and the signal responds to it.

More info on request. I am open to suggestions of stupid things I have overlooked.

Site: History Stack Exchange
Title: Were the Etruscans the first developers of pasta?
Tags: ancient-history, food

Question:
In multiple articles I found across the web, Etruscans were mentioned as the first creators of pasta, however, there seems to be almost no evidence to support their claims.

Articles such as these:

https://historycooperative.org/who-invented-pasta/

https://edibleorigins.com/edible-stories/origin-of-pasta-part-1/

https://web.archive.org/web/20251116060809/https://www.seacoastonline.com/story/news/local/portsmouth-herald/2008/02/27/the-saucy-history-pasta/52595972007/

The last article is used as a reference in Wikipedia's pasta article.

It's not that any of these articles make unreasonable assumptions, they just don't provide any sources to validate their claims. The first article references one of Archestratus of Gela's works on cuisine as evidence for pasta's existence in the time of the Etruscans. In one of his works of c. 320 BCE, he mentions laganon, a possible precursor to pasta. Archestratus was a major Greek poet on cuisine at the time, so it is not altogether crazy to distrust him. However, that does not provide evidence for the claims that the Etruscans developed pasta.

Two of the articles claim that there is an Etruscan tomb that either has preserved pasta in it or depicts it on the murals inside, but I cannot find any resources of these findings. An image of a tomb in the second article is said to show a mural of grain preparation, but that has nothing to do with pasta, only the process of grain preparation, which could be used to make any type of dough.

Is the aforementioned tomb found in any research, and if it is, does it depict pasta or preserve physical pasta?  Is there any real historical evidence that the Etruscans developed it?

Answer A:
I should have left a comment to [user]'s answer, but this is a bit too long.

First, here is an image of the relief in question from the Tomba dei Rilievi at the Banditaccia necropole near Cerveteri. You can faintly make out some horizontal lines on the framed board; the proportions would indicate there were eleven of them.

Remondino, F., Rizzi, A., Jimenez Fernandez-Palacios, B., Agugiaro, G., Baratti, G., De Amicis, R., 2011: The Etruscan in 3D: from space to underground. Geoinformatics FCE CTU Journal, vol. 6, pp. 283-290 have produced a 3D model of the grave, cf this YouTube video.

The interpretation of the large board as a spianatoia (pastry board) and the tool at the bottom right, ending in a star-like shape as a speronella (pastry wheel) is widespread, but I cannot identify a clear source; most mentions are either sourceless or only lead to works without proper sourcing. Some even claim to see a matterello (rolling pin). Curiously, this interpretation has wormed its way even into articles that present opposite opinions. The Pasta museum at Parma publishes an article on its website about the history of the speronella that unambiguosly states that it is an invention of the late middle ages:

Designed to goad the horse, the spur took the form of a semicircle for centuries, featuring a prick positioned centrally on its outer edge. Attached to the heel of a boot and struck against the horse's flanks, it served to urge the animal to greater effort.

During the Late Middle Ages, the spur underwent a radical transformation: the prick was replaced by a toothed wheel—rotating around a central pin—set within a bifurcated shank; hence the names speronella or rosetta.
[truncated]

Answer B:
According to Bobba (1999), whether or not the Etruscans may have known something like pasta, the mural claim specifically has been debunked.

The “waters” of the pasta invention controversy were somewhat muddied
by one Italian archaeologist who supplemented linguistic evidence with that
of an artifact represented in an Etruscan tomb. The rock-cut supports of the
Tomba dei rilievi at Cervetri are decorated with reliefs of objects of all kinds, some for warfare, others of household equipment. One seemed to be an ancient spuinatora, a board for rolling out pasta, complete with a little bag of extra flour hanging from one handle. Alas, definitive study of the reliefs has now
identified the object as a gaming board precisely like one shown on an Etruscan mirror being used by two competing Greek heroes.This does not
negate Etruscan knowledge of pasta, however, and at least one museum devoted to history of the genre holds that they even rolled flat noodles about
metal needles to fashion macaroni (much as medieval and Renaissance cooks
would anticipate extruded manufacture of spaghetti at a later date).

There are a couple of footnotes on that paragraph if you care to dig further.

The answer to the larger question of when and where pasta developed remains unresolved and complex. In addition to Bobba you may want to look at Pasta and Noodles: A Global History by Shelke (2016).
