Site: Academia Stack Exchange
Title: How to get sponsors for a mathematics conference?
Tags: mathematics, funding, conference

Question:
We are planning a two-day conference in pure mathematics at our university in India. This would be my first time as a organizer. The university, being relatively new, has already provided some financial support; however, this funding is not sufficient to cover all expenses. The programme is intended to be fully academic and scholarly, there will be no registration fee, and participants will be provided with local support (accommodation and meal). We therefore require a modest additional amount (approximately €500). While this may be a small sum internationally, it represents a significant amount in Indian currency.

Since this is a conference in pure mathematics, industrial sponsorship is unlikely. I would therefore like to know whether there are international mathematical organizations that offer financial support for such events. In particular, I have noticed that some mathematics conference posters acknowledge academic journals as sponsors. How does sponsorship by a journal typically work, and what is the appropriate way to approach a journal to request a small amount of financial support?

Thanks for suggestion

Answer A:
As someone who has been the Executive Chair of a few conferences, I usually solicit patrons who might be interested in hiring the students or funding the research further.  In the USA, we often have the research sponsor in the paper under acknowledgements. I'll then reach out to those organizations to see if they'd be willing to be a "patron" of the conference.  Also, I try to have undergraduates come to the conferences, and I've found some university patronage there too.  (Going to a conference sorta accidentally as an undergrad put me into research, so I try to extend the opportunities to others).

Answer B:
The European Mathematical Society has some funding for conferences in the Global South.

https://ems.grantplatform.com/page/aPwOlanL

From the website:

Funding for the organization of training events and conferences in the Global South. This grant can only be used to support participants from the Global South. Typical grants range from €1000 to €2000.

Answer C:
A few suggestions, but they may not work out on short notice.

In the US, textbook publishers in the field often help fund conferences. They need space for displays and time to talk to participants. This works best for large conferences, of course.

Next, look at the announcements of similar conferences in India and elsewhere. They often publish a list of sponsors and you might consider contacting some of them. Those conference committees might be able to help.

Third, look to those companies that hire your graduates. They have an interest in your success and might be able to help.

Good luck.

Answer D:
You have probably already seen ANRF's standing call for support for conferences, as well as the page by the National Board for Higher Mathematics.  As the answer by [user] points out, publishers might also offer support.  I have seen equipment/reagent manufacturers and journal publishers (e.g. Wiley, ACS etc.) support conferences in India in the natural sciences, though admittedly I have not seen such support for a pure mathematics conference.   If your topic is related to theoretical computer science, IARCS might be another place to look for support.

Title: Quantization of Large Models with Weight Outliers and Sparsity

Abstract:
Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory burden of large model deployment by casting the high precision trained weights to fewer bits. While this promotes memory-efficient inference, it also incurs quantization error that impairs model performance. To compensate for quantization error, the present contribution decomposes the original trained weights into a quantized matrix, a low-rank component, and a sparse matrix that accounts for outlier rows in the weights. Due to analytical intractability and the discrete structure of the decomposition, a simulated annealing search is employed to explore candidate decompositions while avoiding poor local minima. Numerical tests demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach across a broad suite of large language models, including Llama 3.2 1B, Llama 3.2 3B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen2.5 7B, evaluated on natural language generation benchmarks using 4-bit NF4 and FP4 quantizers. The novel method can markedly outperform direct quantization while incurring minimal memory overhead.

Title: Generative AI as a Mediator in Creator Collaboration: Challenges, Design Opportunities, and Concerns

Abstract:
As Generative AI (GenAI) expands beyond individual workflows and becomes increasingly integrated intocollaborative creative work, its potential to address the fundamental challenge of building common groundamong creators with diverse expertise remains underexplored. Specifically, we lack empirical understandingof how GenAI can mediate collaboration asymmetries among heterogeneous creators. To address this gap,we conducted a multi-method study with narrative writers (N = 10) and visual designers (N = 10) in thecontext of game development. Our findings demonstrate that GenAI goes beyond individual assistance toserve as a collaborative mediator by aligning creative intent, sustaining shared understanding, and mitigatinginterpersonal friction among creators. At the same time, we highlight concerns that GenAI may reducecommunication among creators, undermine mutual trust, and reshape interpersonal dynamics and collaborativeprocesses. Based on these insights, we identify design opportunities for GenAI tools that nurture collaborativesynergy while preserving the creativity and values of human work.

Title: Numerical analysis of linear finite element methods for the Gross--Pitaevskii eigenvalue problem

Abstract:
In this paper, we analyze the standard and the mass-lumped linear finite element methods for the Gross--Pitaevskii eigenvalue problem. For the standard method, we give a new proof of the uniqueness of the discrete ground state up to sign for sufficiently small mesh sizes, which only requires the $H^1$-convergence of the discrete ground states. For both methods, we establish optimal convergence rates in the $L^p$- and $W^{1,p}$-norms for $1 \le p < \infty$. Under additional regularity assumptions on the potential, we further obtain an optimal convergence rate in the $W^{1,\infty}$-norm and an almost optimal convergence rate, up to a logarithmic factor, in the $L^\infty$-norm. Moreover, we prove that the discrete ground states superconverge to the Ritz projection of the exact ground state in the $W^{1,p}$-seminorm. The analysis is based on a perturbation argument. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical results.

Shubha V. Iyengar also known as Shubha Venkatesha Iyengar is an Indian scientist. She is best known for her contributions to civil aviation, defence and indigenous technology sectors in India. She served at the CSIR-National Aerospace Laboratories for a period of approximately five decades (46 years). [ref: A Bengaluru Aerospace Scientist Built the Made-in-India System That Reads Fog for Pilots, thebetterindia.com] [ref: Who is Dr. Shubha V Iyengar? == Biography ==
She was born in Bengaluru as the youngest in a family of nine children. She faced barriers to continue her higher studies in science, at a time when girls in India had severe societal restrictions to pursue their education and career choices. [ref: This Indian woman scientist’s research was published by NASA and her technology now guides flights across India, The Times of India] However, she was encouraged by her father to pursue her studies in science.

== Career ==

Iyengar was a batch topper in academics during her higher studies by achieving distinction in both her graduation and post-graduation studies at the Bangalore University. She also received gold medals in the field of Physics and obtained first rank in MSc physics examination in 1974. Following her distinction pass, she subsequently received a Government of India merit scholarship. [ref: https://www.news18.com/amp/india/one-has-to-persevere-scientist-behind-indias-indigenous-aircraft-landing-system-shares-her-journey-at-news18-amrit-ratna-ws-l-10156554.html] She joined as a research scientist at the National Aerospace Laboratories in 1974, where she was assigned at Material Science Division and Airport Instrument Division. [ref: Meet Padma Shri Shubha V Iyengar, the scientist behind India’s aviation safety tech, India Today] During her stint with, National Aerospace Laboratories, her job role was emphasised heavily on designing and improving devices that support safer aircraft operations. She also focused mainly in developing gadgets to combat challenging weather and low-visibility conditions, which were central to the aviation industry. She also engaged in creating devices incorporating portable, FPGA-based humidity and temperature sensors.

In 2011, Shubha collaborated with the Indian Meteorological Department and conceptualised a unique model to monitor aviation weather and runway visibility measurement, which was later named as "Drishti". Her innovative model "Drishti" transmissometer has since been approved by the Government of India and has been predominantly used in across various international airports in India as well as by the Indian Air Force. [ref: Meet Dr. Shubha Venkatesh Iyengar, Agni missile scientist, whose tech is now being used by every international airport in India, The Economic Times] Prior to her innovation, the aviation industry had faced the longstanding issue with regards to making arrangements to fly the aircraft safely onto fog-covered runways. [ref: 'She helps planes land through fog': Anand Mahindra calls Indian scientist his motivation. Who is Dr Shubha V Iyengar? - The Economic Times, m.economictimes.com] Shubha pioneered to build a cost-effective, indigeneous homegrown system which could measure runway visibility and weather conditions, as well as to detect possibilities for aeroplanes to land safely even when issues pertaining to poor visibility exist. Prior to the introduction of "Drishti", Indian airports had long practiced the approach of purchasing expensive runway visibility measuring instruments from Finland and Australia. Over the years, Drishti also gained widespread international attention, where prominent organizations such as World Meteorological Organization and the International Civil Aviation Organization had recommended the usage of Drishti. She also actively involved in India's defense system and during an occasion, she served as a chief architect to solve complex technical issue that had prevented the Agni missile from reaching its intended target.

She devised a blueprint to develop indigenous components which could withstand temperatures of 3000K, while operating at optimum speed levels of Mach 5. Eventually the indigenous components developed by Iyengar had been mandatorily used for missile systems and ramjet-scramjet engines. Those components have also been vital in India's satellite launch initiatives which have been carried out over the years. Some of her research papers were also published as official reports by NASA, taking insights from Iyengar's technical knowledge on aviation and space.

In 2015, she was conferred with the "Make in India" award, in recognition of her contributions in indigenous technological development and self-reliance. She retired from National Aerospace Laboratories in 2020 after having served for 46 years. [ref: Eight from Karnataka to be honoured with 2026 Padma awards, The Hindu] Shubha was also conferred with the Padma Shri award, India’s fourth-highest civilian honour, in the category of Science and Engineering in 2026, in recognition of her contributions to aerospace technology. [ref: They started small, but left lasting impact: from Anke Gowda to Shubha Iyengar, meet Karnataka’s Padma Shri winners, The Indian Express] [ref: Eight luminaries from Karnataka win Padma awards, The New Indian Express]

Wiki: English Wikipedia
Draft: Ashendye

Draft text:
----

Ashendye (Amharic: አሸንድዬ) is a religious festival celebrated in Lasta, Lalibela, and Gondar of the Amhara region of Ethiopia. [ref: Bete Amhara: A Journey Through Wollo’s Living Heritage, Landscapes, and Seasonal Festivals, Rex Clarke Adventures] In different localities of Amhara, the festival is also known as Shadey (ሻደይ) or Solel (ሶለል). It explicitly commemorates the Old Testament story of Moses and the reed basket in which he was saved. In contrast, Ashenda in Tigray (ኣሸንዳ) is a secularized civic festival that centers on female social autonomy, gendered freedom, and modern regional political expression. [ref: Tigrayans in North Texas preserve culture, tradition through Ashenda, a day to honor women, www.keranews.org/]

== Historical and Cultural Roots ==

The Amhara highlands of Bete Amhara and Gondar serve as the foundational cradle of the Ashendye festival due to the region's ancient roots in early Jewish tradition. [ref: Falasha anthology, New Haven, Conn.; London: Yale University Press] This deep Hebraic heritage is preserved through the historic use of the Tabot (Ark covenant replica) ceremony. This celebration predates the Aksumite Christian era and goes back before the spread of Christianity.

Girls participating in Ashendye traditionally wear fresh green Cyperus sedge grass, known as Ashenda (Amharic: አሸንዳ), woven and tied around their waist. This grass is prepared as a thick, layered belt or skirt and serves as one of the festival's most recognizable elements.

Within this historical framework, the connection centers on the symbolism of the reed basket. In Amhara tradition, the primary reason young women weave and wear the native green Cyperus sedge grass around their waists is to symbolise the papyrus reed basket that saved the infant Moses on the Nile. According to the Old Testament narrative, Moses's mother placed him in a basket hidden among the reeds of the Nile River to protect him from Pharaoh's decree. The fresh river grass used in the festival acts as a living monument to this biblical event of preservation and divine protection. [ref: Travels to discover the source of the Nile, in the years 1768, 1769, 1770, 1771, 1772, and 1773, Edinburgh, Printed by J. Ruthven, for G. G. J. and J. Robinson, London]

Title: $\Delta ABC$ is inscribed in a circle, AP is its circum-diameter which cuts BC at D. Do we have $\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{\sin 2C}{\sin 2B}$ and why?
Tags: trigonometry, coordinate-systems, plane-geometry

Question:
Let us look at the co-ordinates of the circumcenter:
$$O=\left (\frac {x_A \sin 2A+ x_B \sin 2B+x_C\sin 2C}{\sin 2A+ \sin 2B+\sin 2C},\frac {y_A \sin 2A+ y_B \sin 2B+y_C\sin 2C}{\sin 2A+ \sin 2B+\sin 2C}\right),$$
vis a vis those of incenter (I), centroid(G) and orthocenter(H).

If $\Delta ABC$ is inscribed in a circle, AP is its circum-diameter which cuts BC at D. Do we have $$\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{\sin 2C}{\sin 2B}$$ and what could be a proof? Any help or suggestion is welcome.

Answer A:
This follows fairly immediately from the Inscribed Angle Theorem, which tells us here that $\angle AOB = 2\angle C$ and $\angle AOB = 2\angle B$.

For acute $\angle B$ and $\angle C$ ... Perpendiculars dropped from $B$ and $C$ to $\overline{AP}$ have respective lengths $r\sin 2C$ and $r\sin 2B$, where $r$ is the circumradius; and they determine similar right triangles from which we deduce
$$\frac{|BD|}{|DC|}=\frac{\sin2C}{\sin2B} \tag1$$

For obtuse $\angle B$ or $\angle C$, the essence of the result remains true, with some accommodations.

First (as @[user] noted), we'd need to replace "$\overline{AP}$ [...] cuts $\overline{BC}$ at $D$" with something like "$\overleftrightarrow{OA}$ meets $\overleftrightarrow{BC}$ at $D$".

Also, we need to account for the fact that the sine of twice an obtuse angle is negative. We can do this by simply invoking an absolute value:
$$\frac{|BD|}{|DC|}=\left|\frac{\sin2C}{\sin2B}\right| \tag2$$

Alternatively, we can treat $\overline{BD}$ and $\overline{DC}$ as directed segments (think vectors) with signed lengths, having like (or opposite) signs when they point in the same (or opposite) direction. Under this convention, $(1)$ holds as-is.

Answer B:
Yes, and it's fairly easy. But you must assume that $\angle B$ and $\angle C$ are acute or the geometry does not work. (Try it!)

Draw the figure and note that $\angle DBA=\angle B$ and $\angle BAD$ intercept supplementary arcs. Therefore these angles are complementary, $|\angle BAD|=90°-\angle B$. Similarly $|\angle CAD|=90°-\angle C$.

Then apply the Law of Sines to the two triangles containing $\overline{AD}$ to obtain

$\dfrac{BD}{AD}=\dfrac{\cos\angle C}{\sin\angle B}$

$\dfrac{CD}{AD}=\dfrac{\cos\angle B}{\sin\angle C}$

Divide one equation by the other to eliminate ${AD}$ and plug in $\sin(2\theta)=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ to obtain the claimed result.

This is consistent with the diameter bisecting the hypotenuse in the case of a right triangle. I will let the reader see why.

Answer C:
See the Fig. attached below $\angle PCB=90^\circ-\angle C$ and $\angle A_1$ are made on the same arc BP. Similarly, $\angle PBC=90^\circ-\angle B$ and $\angle A_2$ are made on the same arc PC.
Hence, $$\angle A_2=90^\circ-\angle B, \quad \angle A_1=90^\circ-\angle C\tag{1}.$$ By the sine rule in $\Delta ABD$ and $\Delta ACD$ we have
$$\frac{BD}{AD}=\frac{\sin A_1}{\sin B}=\frac{\cos C}{\sin B} \quad \& \quad \frac{DC}{AD}=\frac{\sin A_2}{\sin C}=\frac{\cos B}{\sin C}\tag{2}$$
giving us $$\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{\sin 2C}{\sin 2B}.$$

Title: TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents

Abstract:
Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. To address this gap, we introduce TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that translates negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement, and evaluates outcomes via an Economic Health Index (EHI). To solve this execution-grounded task, we propose TACTIC (Trade-aware Adaptive Consolidation and Theory-of-mind for International Commerce), an agent that iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes-without updating base LLM weights-by leveraging prior experience, opponent behavior, and past settlement outcomes. Despite using zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI (*100), whereas TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC also exhibits smaller performance degradation than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM. These results indicate that CoT deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation in TradeWar.

Draft text:
----

Good Shepherd Rehabilitation is an independent, not-for-profit rehabilitation network headquartered in Allentown, Pennsylvania.Pediatric, adolescent and adult patients receive treatment at Good Shepherd for stroke; brain injury; spinal cord injury; bone and joint conditions; aches, pains and strains; cardiac and respiratory illnesses; chronic neurological conditions; and developmental disabilities.

Types of treatment include inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation for adults, adolescents and children; physical medicine and rehabilitation physician services; long-term care; long-term acute care; and supported independent living for people with disabilities.In all, Good Shepherd operates 30 facilities throughout eastern Pennsylvania.Good Shepherd is accredited by the Commission on Accreditation of Rehabilitation Facilities (CARF). Good Shepherd Rehabilitation Hospital and Good Shepherd Rehabilitation Hospital Pediatric Unit have a combined six CARF-accredited inpatient rehabilitation programs [ref: ] [ref: Find a Provider - Good Shepherd Rehabilitation Hospital]
Good Shepherd is also accredited by the Joint Commission. [ref: About Us - Find Accredited Organizations - Good Shepherd Rehabilitation Hospital]

== History ==

The Rev. John ("Papa") and Estella ("Mama") Raker founded the Good Shepherd Home in Allentown in February 1908 to care for orphaned children with disabilities. [ref: REV. OR. JOHN H. RAKER; Lutheran Minister Founded Good Shepherd Home, Allentown, Pa., The New York Times]While serving as the director of the Lutheran Orphan Home in Topton, Pennsylvania, the Rev. Raker met a local woman who had a disabled son. The woman said she had no way to provide care for her son. Despite his reservations, the Rev. Raker had to turn the mother and boy away because the home's charter allowed only "healthy children." [ref: History's Headlines: A Good Shepherd for over 100 years, WFMZ.com]In 1907, the Rev. Raker moved to Grace Lutheran mission in South Allentown but insisted that he be allowed to do mission work among children with disabilities as time allowed. His regular pastoral work with the church, however, did not leave much time initially.Then, his wife gave birth to a daughter, Viola, who passed away in infancy. Following the funeral, the Rev. Raker received a letter from another local minister about a child with a disability named Viola Hunt, who he hoped someone could take in.Seeing it as an omen, the Rakers took Viola Hunt in, and she became the first resident of what is now Good Shepherd.

=== Expansion ===
Good Shepherd opened its rehabilitation hospital in Allentown in 1967 and expanded the facility in 1983. [ref: ]In August 1980, Good Shepherd opened Good Shepherd Home - Raker Center on its South Allentown campus, providing a long-term care home for individuals with severe disabilities, such as cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, multiple sclerosis, spina bifida and traumatic brain injuries. Good Shepherd opened a second long-term care home in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania in 2000.

Good Shepherd announced a partnership in 2007 with Penn Medicine, forming Good Shepherd Penn Partners in 2008 to provide rehabilitation and therapy services in the greater Philadelphia area and parts of New Jersey. [ref: Penn, Good Shepherd to form partnership ** Philadelphia's Graduate Hospital will be transformed into a rehabilitation specialty center., The Morning Call] [ref: Good Shepherd Penn Partners Announces Administrative Team, Rehab Management] Good Shepherd Penn Partners changed names to GSPP Rehabilitation in 2024. [ref: ]Good Shepherd opened the region's first pediatric inpatient rehabilitation unit in Bethlehem in 2009. [ref: Samuel Miranda Jr.: Good Shepherd's pediatric unit reaches milestone, The Morning Call]

=== Good Shepherd Today ===
In 2023, Good Shepherd opened a free-standing, 123,000-square-foot, 76-bed inpatient rehabilitation hospital in Center Valley, Pennsylvania. [ref: Good Shepherd Rehabilitation Center opens new hospital in Upper Saucon Twp., WFMZ.com]Good Shepherd also opened the Fleming Center for Robotics in Rehabilitation in 2023.

In June 2026, Good Shepherd announced it would open the first Autism and Neurodevelopmental Wellness Center in the greater Lehigh Valley region in fall 2026. The center will be located on Cetronia Road in Upper Macungie Township. [ref: Good Shepherd Rehabilitation says it will open region's 1st Autism and Neurodevelopmental Wellness Center, WFMZ.com] [ref: ]

== Partnerships ==

Good Shepherd's partnership with the Temple University Hospital Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (PM&R) Residency Program matches candidates in the field of physiatry for a training program at Good Shepherd Rehabilitation Hospital. [ref: Residency Program, Lewis Katz School of Medicine]In 2025, Good Shepherd and Lehigh University established a formal partnership, which included conducting a Community Health Needs Assessment to collect information on the needs of individuals with autism and other neurodivergent conditions in the greater Lehigh Valley [ref: Lehigh University and Good Shepherd Rehabilitation Join Forces to Advance Disability Health Equity, Lehigh University News], which led to the development of Good Shepherd's new Autism and Neurodevelopmental Wellness Center.

Title: Penalized Likelihood Inference in Highly Multivariate Sparse Spectral Graphical Gaussian Processes

Abstract:
We develop a penalized likelihood inference approach for highly multivariate Gaussian stochastic processes. Since zeros in the inverse cross-spectral density encode process-level conditional independence, sparse modeling of this object provides a natural route to scalable inference in the highly multivariate case. We introduce a latent variable representation which, combined with random Fourier features, yields a stochastic approximation expectation--maximization algorithm for penalized maximum likelihood estimation of a sparse inverse cross-spectral density matrix under a graphical LASSO penalty. The augmentation is crucial because sparsity is present in the inverse spectral density of the latent variable, whereas the marginal inverse covariance remains dense in the presence of a spatial nugget. Our frequency domain formulation enables joint penalized likelihood estimation of process-specific spatial covariance parameters and sparse process-level conditional dependence without requiring a pre-specified reference set of locations. The method is demonstrated on both synthetic and the MERRA-2 aerosol reanalysis data sets, yielding benefit over existing alternatives, especially for prediction at unobserved locations under spatial misalignment.

= Benjamin Riley =

Benjamin Riley is an American education writer, policy advocate and former government lawyer. He is the founder of Cognitive Resonance, a self-described "think-and-do tank" that examines generative artificial intelligence through the lens of cognitive science.[1][3] Before that, he founded and for nearly a decade led Deans for Impact, a nonprofit that works to bring findings from the science of learning into teacher preparation programs.[1][6]

Riley is one of the more widely cited skeptics of AI in schools. He argues that large language models imitate the communicative side of human language without doing the thinking that language usually reports, and that heavy student reliance on chatbots can erode the mental effort learning depends on.[11][13] His writing on cognitive science, AI and education has appeared in outlets including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, The Washington Post, Le Monde, The Guardian, Education Week, Education Next, The 74 and NPR.[1]

Contents
# Education and legal career
# Education policy work
# Deans for Impact
# Cognitive Resonance
## Education Hazards of Generative AI
## Language and intelligence
## "Cognitive hot dog"
# Views
# Reception and criticism
# Selected works
# Media appearances
# References

== Education and legal career ==
Riley earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Washington and a Juris Doctor from Yale Law School.[1] His early career included about four years in private legal practice, a short period on Wall Street, and a summer clerkship with the Land Claims Court of South Africa.[5]

He later served as a deputy attorney general in the California Department of Justice. In that post he advised then–Attorney General Jerry Brown on California's first Race to the Top application and related education policy, helped draft legislation connected to the program, and represented the California State Board of Education, including a stint as the board's interim chief counsel. A Northern California legal publication named him one of two "Rising Stars" in education law in 2009.[5]

== Education policy work ==
After leaving state government, Riley became director of policy and advocacy at NewSchools Venture Fund, where he worked from Washington, D.C., on a policy agenda aimed at supporting education entrepreneurs.[5] He also carried out research on the New Zealand education system.[4]

== Deans for Impact ==
Riley founded Deans for Impact in 2015 and served as its executive director. Based in Austin, Texas, the organization brought together leaders of U.S. educator-preparation programs who wanted teacher training to draw more directly on research-backed principles of how students learn.[7][6]

The group's best-known early publication, The Science of Learning (2015), condensed findings from cognitive psychology into six questions every new teacher should be able to answer, each paired with classroom implications. It was produced by the organization's member deans with University of Virginia cognitive scientist Daniel Willingham and former middle-school science teacher Paul Bruno.[8] At its public launch, Riley urged educators to reconsider teaching one concept to mastery before moving on, and pointed to research-dissemination bodies in the United Kingdom as a model.[9] British education writer David Didau praised the document as clearer than comparable summaries.[10]

In April 2022, Deans for Impact announced that Riley would step down later that year, ending almost ten years with the organization. Board chair David Chard credited him with bold and creative leadership.[6]

== Cognitive Resonance ==
Riley has said his move into AI grew out of his own interest in deep learning in the years before ChatGPT, and from the view that AI belongs alongside psychology, neuroscience, linguistics and philosophy as one of the cognitive sciences.[12] He founded Cognitive Resonance to help people understand both human cognition and generative AI, and to replace hype with a clearer picture of how the systems work.[3][16] The venture publishes the Substack newsletter Build Cognitive Resonance, which had passed 3,000 subscribers, and runs a YouTube channel.[2][15]

=== Education Hazards of Generative AI ===
The organization's first publication, Education Hazards of Generative AI, was released on 7 August 2024 and co-written with Paul Bruno of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.[11][14] Aimed at teachers, administrators, parents and policymakers, it gives a plain-language overview of how large language models work and draws out practical consequences for classrooms. The report does not reject classroom AI outright but warns that the hype around it obscures real risks.[14] Riley told Education Week that schools need not adopt the technology simply because it exists.[11]

=== Language and intelligence ===
In late November 2025, The Verge published Riley's essay arguing that the AI boom rests on a basic error: treating fluency in language as if it were intelligence.[17] Drawing on a 2024 Nature paper by Evelina Fedorenko and colleagues, which concluded that language is primarily a tool for communication rather than thought, he argued that human reasoning depends largely on brain systems separate from language. On that view, scaling up language models would yield ever better text generation but not general intelligence or new scientific discoveries.[16][17] The piece drew wide international coverage.

Title: A logarithmic error term for subset sums of zero-sum-free sets

Abstract:
For a positive integer $k$, let $f(k)$ be the minimum number of distinct nonempty subset sums of a zero-sum-free $k$-element set, where the minimum is taken over all finite abelian groups. We prove $f(k)\ge \frac{k^2}{2}-13k\log(k+1)-116k$. Together with the classical upper bound, this gives $f(k)=k^2/2+O(k\log k)$, with the optimal leading coefficient. As a consequence, the Olson constant of every finite abelian group $G$ satisfies $\mathrm{Ol}(G)\le\sqrt{2|G|}+O(\log|G|)$. The argument combines a triangular lower bound for repeated supports, a count using blocks of two and three copies, and a greedy expansion argument. No restriction is imposed on the order of the group or on the stabilizer of the set of subset sums.

Title: On stable twist 2-groups of quasi-Hopf algebras

Abstract:
For any finite-dimensional quasi-Hopf algebra $A$, we define the notion of a stable twist of $A$. We show that stable twists form a strict 2-group $\2ust(A)$, which is equivalent to $\OAut(\C{A})^{\rev}$. Given a group homomorphism $ρ: G \to \ost(A)$, we determine the obstruction in $H^3(G,Z_G(A))$ to lift $ρ$ to a $G$-action on $\C{A}$. We also establish a bijection between such liftings and cocentral cleft extensions of $\k[G]$ by $A$. The main application of $\2ust(A)$ is the computation of $\OAut(\C{A})$, together with an explicit description of the corresponding tensor autoequivalences. We apply this framework to pointed Hopf algebras $A$ that arise as central extensions of Taft algebras by cyclic groups, and we explicitly determine all of their tensor autoequivalences. The equivariantizations of $\C{A}$ by $\ost(A)$ produce a new family of Hopf algebras $\N(n,ξ)$ of dimension $2nm$, where $ξ$ is a scalar of order $m\mid n$ such that neither $\N(n,ξ)$ nor its dual has the Chevalley property. In dimension 24, we prove that $\N(6,-1)$ and its dual are precisely the Hopf algebras $H$ for which neither $H$ nor $H^*$ has the Chevalley property. This completes the classification of nonsemisimple Hopf algebras of dimension 24.

Title: CalibCause: A Quality-Gated, Interpretable and Calibrated Deep Learning Framework for Diabetic Retinopathy Grading

Abstract:
Most deep learning systems for diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading are evaluated on a single data source, with limited evidence of cross-site generalisation, uncertainty calibration, and interpretability. We propose CalibCause, a quality-gated mixture-of-experts framework that combines per-expert visual explanations, label-free image-quality conditioning, knowledge distillation, and calibrated confidence with deferral. We evaluated the framework using 51,310 fundus images from EyePACS, DDR, and APTOS 2019, with IDRiD and DeepDRiD for external testing. Evaluation included pooled testing, leave-one-environment-out experiments, paired bootstrap confidence intervals, and local grade-threshold adaptation. On the pooled test split, the label-free distilled student achieved quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.863 and accuracy of 0.865 with 27.8 million parameters, 52% fewer than its teacher. Across held-out environments, the label-free model achieved mean QWK of 0.741 compared with 0.743 for a plain ConvNeXt-Tiny baseline, while adversarial invariance did not improve cross-site grading accuracy. Refitting grade thresholds using 200 labelled images increased held-out EyePACS QWK from 0.533 to 0.621 for the label-free model. After vector scaling, expected calibration error ranged from 0.025 to 0.036 across CalibCause variants, and deferring the least confident 20% of images increased student accuracy from 0.865 to 0.923 on the remaining images. These findings demonstrate that quality-aware grading, interpretable expert routing, model compression, and calibrated deferral can be integrated without sacrificing cross-site performance relative to a plain baseline, although reliable deployment still requires local validation and adaptation.

Suppose that the finite dimensional marginals of $X_\alpha$ converge to the ones of a process $X := \{X(t) : t\in T\}$ and also suppose that $X_\alpha$ is asymptotically uniformly $\rho$-equicontinous in probability. Prove that there exists a version $\tilde{X}$ of $X$ with trajectories in $\ell^\infty(T)$ such that $X_\alpha \Rightarrow \tilde{X}$ in $\ell^\infty(T)$.

I've done the following: for every $t\in T$ we have that $X_\alpha(t) \Rightarrow X(t)$ and because $\mathbb{R}$ is a polish space we have that $X(t)$ is tight so by a previous result we have that $\{X_\alpha(t)\}$ is asymptotically tight. We saw in class that if $\{X_{\alpha}(t)\}$ is asymptotically tight for every $t\in T$ and additionally $\{X_{\alpha}(t)\}$ is asymptotically uniformly $\rho$-equicontinous in probability then $\{X_\alpha\}$ is asymptotically tight.

Then by another result we saw in class the fact that $\{X_\alpha\}$ is asymptotically tight plus the fact that the finite dimensional marginals converge we obtain the existence of a tight borel probability $L$ on $\ell^\infty(T)$ such that $X_\alpha \Rightarrow L$. By that same result we also have that for every $t_1,...,t_n\in T$ the marginals $L_{t_1,...,t_n}$ have the same distribution as that of $(X(t_1),...,X(t_k))$.

But here is where I get stuck. I don't see how can I get a version of $X$ with $X_\alpha \Rightarrow \tilde{X}$. I know that I can take a random variable, say $Y$ with distribution $L$ but of course it won't be a version of $X$ because they are not even defined on the same probability space.

Site: Academia Stack Exchange
Title: How to ask supervisor for permission to do a tech internship without offending him
Tags: phd, advisor, supervision, internship

Question:
I'm an incoming first year PhD in physics in Canada. Lately I've been thinking about working at a tech company for an internship over the summer sometime during my PhD (maybe the 2nd or 3rd year), in order to earn money and gain experience. I noticed that none of my supervisor's previous students have done internships, so I'm guessing they are a bit frowned upon due to taking time away from thesis research.

I'm wondering what's the best way to ask my supervisor if I can do a tech internship during the PhD? Since my field is AI-adjacent, I'm thinking of framing it as gaining experience that could potentially help with research. Will he get offended? If I tell him I want to do an internship (e.g. at a quant firm or FAANG) he might see me as unserious and not sufficiently committed to research.

P.s. my family is seriously struggling with finances right now, and my secret motivation for the internship is to be able to keep them afloat with the earnings, but I'm unsure whether I should tell this to my supervisor

Answer A:
A supervisor is also a person who advises you on career matters. I see nothing wrong at having a conversation that starts with something like this:

Dr X., I've been thinking about where I want to end up in my career. My goal is to work in industry after graduating, and one of the things that I frequently read is that internships really help with this. What are your thoughts on this matter?

I cannot see anything in such a conversation that would offend anyone. Your adviser may be supportive or not, but it's a matter that can legitimately be discussed between adviser and advisee. In particular, I do not think that your assertion that "I'm guessing they are a bit frowned upon" is well-founded: All you know is that your adviser's previous students didn't do internships, but there are many reasons why they may not have done so, and I don't think you can draw any inferences from the mere fact without knowing more about why.

Answer B:
This is a somewhat orthogonal suggestion. Instead of asking them about a specific sort of thing, ask them what you might do along the way to (a) gain some industry experience and (b) earn a bit of money. Actually, one of these may satisfy so make that clear.

Have a discussion, in which you bring up the internship possibility if they don't.

But make the conversation mutual and see what they suggest. That won't be insulting.

And don't lose track of the fact that completing the degree should be your highest priority.

Title: Neural network (NN) model loss is increasing with epochs
Tags: machine-learning, neural-networks, python, numpy, adam

Question:
I am trying to make a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) using only numpy and other basic libraries. As a first step though, I needed to test the regular NN layers first, so I currently have a regular NN model that I am trying to train on sklearn's california housing dataset. With batch gradient descent I was originally getting an initial decrease in loss, then it would slowly increase, even when the lr was small, so I figured I should implement Adam. After implementing it (or trying to), I get similar behavior, but on a much larger scale. Before, I was only running 200 epochs, and Adam only slightly diverges at that point, but at 1000 it diverges a ton. This is the loss:

loss vs. epochs(goes up over time)

Code to Reproduce:

from model import Model
import numpy as np
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd

import layers.relu as relu
import loss

from sklearn.datasets import fetch_california_housing
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import math

class Layer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.lr = .0001

    def forward(self):
        pass

    def backward(self):
        pass

class ReLu(Layer):

  def forward(self, z):
    self.z = z
    return np.where(self.z >= 0, self.z, -0.1*self.z) # leaky relu

  def backward(self, dLdA, epoch, lr=0.01):
    self.dLdA = dLdA
    return np.where(dLdA >= 0, dLdA, -0.1*dLdA)

class Mse:

    def root_mse(self, y_pred, y):
        #print("y pred shape:", y_pred.shape)
        #print("y actual shape:", y.shape)
        #print(math.sqrt(np.mean(np.sum((y - y_pred) ** 2, 1))))
        return math.sqrt(np.mean(np.sum((y - y_pred) ** 2, 1)))

    def mse(self, y_pred, y):
        return np.mean((1 / y.shape[1] * np.sum(np.square(y_pred - y), 1)))

    def mse_prime(self, y_pred, y):
        #print("y pred shape prime:", y_pred.shape)
        #print("y actual shape prime:", y.shape)
        return (2 * (y_pred - y) / np.prod(y.shape))

class WeightLayer(Layer):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

    def set_optimizer(self, optimizer, *optimizer_args):
        self.optimizer_weights = optimizer(*optimizer_args)
        self.optimizer_biases = optimizer(*optimizer_args)

class FCLayer(WeightLayer):
    def __init__(self, num_nodes):
      # being fed through(batch size)
      self.m = num_nodes  # number of nodes
      self.called_first_time = False
      super().__init__()

    def forward(self, input):
      self.input = input
      #print("input shape", input.shape)
      self.p, self.d, self.n = input.shape  # p is batch size, d is number of dimensions to the data and n is the number of data points

      if not self.called_first_time:
        self.called_first_time = True
        self.x_limit = math.sqrt((2 / (self.n + self.m)))
        self.weights = np.random.uniform(-self.x_limit, self.x_limit, size=(self.m, self.d))  # d by m
        self.biases = np.random.uniform(-self.x_limit, self.x_limit, size=(self.m, 1))

      #print("weights", self.weights)
      #print("biases", self.biases)
      self.z = np.zeros((self.p, self.m, self.n))
      for p in range(self.p):
        self.z[p] = (self.weights @ self.input[p]) + self.biases
      return self.z

    def backward(self, dLdZ, epoch, lr=.00001):
      #print("dLdZ shape", dLdZ.shape)
      self.dLdA = self.weights.T @ dLdZ

      self.dLdW = np.array([dLdZ[i] @ self.input[i].T for i in range(self.input.shape[0])])
      self.dLdW = np.sum(self.dLdW, axis=0)
      # gradients for biases should sum over batch and feature map dims, result shape (m,1)
      self.dLdW0 = np.sum(dLdZ, axis=0)
      # Clip gradients to prevent explosion
      self.dLdW = np.clip(self.dLdW, -1.0, 1.0)
      self.dLdW0 = np.clip(self.dLdW0, -1.0, 1.0)

      #print("dldw", self.dLdW)
      #print("shape of dLdW0, in linear", np.shape(self.dLdW0))
      #print("shape of dLdW, in linear", np.shape(self.dLdW))
      self.weights -= self.optimizer_weights.backward(self.dLdW, epoch)
      self.biases -= self.optimizer_biases.backward(self.dLdW0, epoch)
      return self.dLdA  # d by n

class Adam():
    def __init__(self, lr, beta_one=0.9, beta_two=0.999, epsilon=1e-8):
        self.lr = lr
        self.beta_one = beta_one
        self.beta_two = beta_two
        self.epsilon = epsilon
        self.m = None
        self.v = None

    def backward(self, grad, epoch):
        #print(grad.shape)
        if self.m is None:
            self.m = np.zeros_like(grad)
            self.v = np.zeros_like(grad)

        self.m = self.beta_one * self.m + (1 - self.beta_one) * grad
        self.v = self.beta_two * self.v + (1 - self.beta_two) * np.square(grad)

        m_hat = self.m / (1 - self.beta_one ** epoch)
        v_hat = self.v / (1 - self.beta_two ** epoch)
        #print(self.lr * (m_hat / (np.sqrt(v_hat) + self.epsilon)))
        return self.lr * (m_hat / (np.sqrt(v_hat) + self.epsilon))

class Model:
    def __init__(self, layers: list[Layer], optimizer: Adam, *optimizer_args):
        self.layers = layers
        self.optimizer_type = optimizer
        for layer in self.layers:
            if isinstance(layer, WeightLayer):
                layer.set_optimizer(self.optimizer_type, *optimizer_args)

Title: Changing parameters in Hall-Littlewood functions

Abstract:
We study the transition coefficients $b_{λ,μ}(q,t)$ of the Hall--Littlewood $P$-functions $P_λ(t)$ expanded in the basis $P_μ(q)$. We find a tableaux formula when $λ$ is a hook shape which generalizes term-by-term Lascoux-Schutzenberger's charge formula as well as Macdonald's monomial expansion formula for Hall-Littlewood functions. We conjecture that $b_{λ,μ}(t+1,t)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}[t]$ and prove it when $λ$ is a hook shape, when $λ$ has two-columns and some more simple cases. We prove that $b_{λ,μ}(t+n,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}[t]$ for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$, extending work of Alexandersson, and we record a stability property and some reduction principles.

=
\sum_i c_i(\mu)\,\mathcal O_i ,
$$

where the effects of short-distance physics appear in the Wilson coefficients $c_i(\mu)$, and irrelevant operators are suppressed by powers of $E/\Lambda$ for processes at energy $E \ll \Lambda$.

What confuses me is this:

If the coefficients $c_i(\mu)$ are determined by the UV theory, then the low-energy theory does not seem truly independent of UV physics. It seems more accurate to say that the UV information has been compressed into the coefficients of the allowed operators.

Is the correct interpretation something like the following?

At any fixed desired accuracy in $E/\Lambda$, only finitely many operators are needed.

The detailed UV dynamics affects low-energy observables only through the Wilson coefficients kept at that order.

Therefore many different UV theories can give indistinguishable low-energy predictions up to that accuracy, even though the exact Wilson coefficients still retain some information about the UV theory.

If this is right, what exactly is meant by "UV details decouple"?

For example, in a simple case such as Fermi theory as the low-energy limit of electroweak theory, what information about the $W$ boson has been retained in the low-energy EFT, and what information has been lost or made inaccessible to low-energy experiments?

Site: Math Stack Exchange
Title: How do we get the $3^k$ term in this counting argument?
Tags: combinatorics, intuition, combinatorial-proofs

Question:
I am trying to understand the solution to the following combinatorics problem:

Matt writes a permutation of ${1,2,\ldots,10}$ such that:

The leftmost number is $1$.

The rightmost number is $10$.

Exactly one number (excluding $1$ and $10$) is smaller than both of its immediate neighbors.

The given solution says that the permutation must have the form

$$
1,\ldots,b,\ldots,a,\ldots,10,
$$

where $1<a<b<10$, with the sequence increasing from $1$ to $b$, decreasing from $b$ to $a$, and increasing from $a$ to $10$.

For fixed $a$ and $b$, it then says:

The numbers between $1$ and $a$ must go to the left of $b$, and the numbers between $b$ and $10$ must go to the right of $a$. The numbers between $a$ and $b$ can go in any of the three sections.

I understand why the numbers between $1$ and $a$ and between $b$ and $10$ are forced into particular sections. However, I am having trouble understanding the next step.

If there are $k=b-a-1$ numbers strictly between $a$ and $b$, the solution seems to imply that there are

$$
3^k
$$

possible permutations for fixed $a$ and $b$, because each of these $k$ numbers can be placed in one of the three sections.

My question is: why exactly does choosing one of three sections for each number give $3^k$ distinct permutations?

In particular, I understand the statement "each number has 3 choices," but I am struggling to see why this translates into a product of choices, and why the resulting permutations are uniquely determined once the three sets are chosen.

Also, how does this lead to the final summation

$$
N=\sum_{1<a<b<10}3^{b-a-1}
$$

I am looking for an explanation of the intuition behind the $3^k$ and the summation, rather than just the calculation.

Title: Initial Subcategories via Free Presentations of the Constant Functor

Abstract:
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a small category. We characterize the full initial subcategories of $\mathcal{C}$ as precisely those whose representables give a free presentation of the constant functor $Δ_{\mathcal{C}}\mathbb{K}:\mathcal{C}\to\mathrm{Vect}$. Such a presentation yields a formula for the limit of any functor $\mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Vect}$ as the kernel of a morphism between products of evaluations. When the linearized endomorphism ring of every object is local, we show that a minimal free presentation, whenever one exists, determines the unique minimal full initial subcategory, up to equivalence. Bass's characterization of perfect rings gives a sufficient condition for the existence of such presentations. In particular, every finite category with no nonidentity endomorphisms, such as a finite poset, contains a unique minimal initial full subcategory. In the poset case, our results recover the minimal initial subposet constructed in [BDL27] and [DL26]. When $\mathcal{C}$ is the free category on a finite quiver, we give an explicit construction of its minimal initial full subcategories, show that every such subcategory arises from this construction, and provide algorithms with time-complexity bounds.

Title: STAR-FER: Adaptive Selective Restoration for Edge-Based Low-Resolution Facial Expression Recognition

Abstract:
Variable interaction distances continuously degrade facial resolution in edge-based affective interaction, making low-resolution facial expression recognition (FER) difficult under limited computation. Full-face image or feature restoration incurs substantial overhead, whereas lightweight recognition pipelines may miss local cues that remain discriminative after degradation. We propose STAR-FER, a scale-and-task-adaptive selective restoration framework that balances recognition performance and resource constraints. A lightweight image-scale conditioned Gate jointly predicts a pixel-wise spatial ranking and a continuous restoration budget, then applies exact-support projection to obtain an input-dependent free-form mask. The mask-conditioned restorer retains complete facial context while concentrating sparse restoration and residual insertion on the selected support. Across seven degradation scales from x2 to x8 on the complete RAF-DB test set, STAR-FER achieves 80.92% mean accuracy and 71.64% Macro-F1, improving the low-resolution ResNet-18 baseline by 2.25 and 2.71 percentage points, respectively. It surpasses SR-FER by 1.04 accuracy points while requiring 8.84 GFLOPs, a 54.29% reduction, with 28.01% mean mask coverage, and maintains effective recognition at unseen non-integer scales. These results show that spatial-ranking and continuous-budget driven selective restoration reduces spatial modification and computation while maintaining low-resolution FER performance, offering an efficient path to resource-constrained affective interaction.

Title: Joint optimisation of interim timing and stopping boundaries in group sequential trials

Abstract:
Group sequential designs (GSDs) are common in confirmatory trials, and their efficiency depends jointly on the timing of interim analyses and the shape of stopping boundaries. Most existing approaches optimise one component while holding the other fixed. Joint optimisation over free critical values has been studied for two- and three-stage efficacy-only designs and for tests with binding futility boundaries. Here we jointly optimise the full interim schedule and the boundary shape within the Hwang-Shih-DeCani and Kim-DeMets spending families, minimising the expected sample size under a specified alternative while controlling overall type I and type II error rates. A convex error-spending constraint prevents excessive early type I error spending. On the canonical information scale, the joint optimum depends only on the error rates, number of analyses and spending family, and is invariant to endpoint type and effect size. Without the convexity constraint, the parametric optima reproduced the unrestricted optima of Brittain & Bailey (1993) to within 0.001 in expected inflation factor. For three or more looks the jointly optimal design Pareto-dominated the scheduling-only optimal Pocock design, achieving the same or smaller expected sample size with uniformly smaller maximum sample size. Under a prespecified 1% tolerance, six analyses, five interim plus a final, captured essentially all efficiency attainable with up to seven analyses, reducing expected sample size by 23% and 33% at 80% and 90% power relative to the fixed-sample design. We illustrate the approach by redesigning the CORRECT trial.

Site: Chemistry Stack Exchange
Title: Number of benzenoid structural isomers of C6H3FClBr
Tags: organic-chemistry, isomers

Question:
I am asked to find the number of benzenoid isomers in $\ce{C6H3FClBr}$. This is my approach: There are 6 positions to choose from in a benzene ring, of which I need 3, to place the halogens. Hence, there are $\binom{6}{3}$ ways in which this can be done. Now, a fluorine atom can be placed anywhere in these 3 positions, resulting in the same fluorobenzene molecule. Hence, there is only 1 way to place the F atom. Next, Cl can be placed in two positions, both giving two distinct arrangements (not counting the fact that flipping the ring over may give the same arrangement). Br has only one position, hence only 1 way to place it. Finally, we must account for the fact that flipping the ring over may give the same arrangement in any two arrangements we have calculated till this point. Hence we divide by 2. The resulting value comes out to be: $$\binom{6}{3}\times\frac{2!}{2} = 20.$$ However, the answer key says the answer is 10. Where is my thought process incorrect?

Answer A:
The fact that $\binom{6}{3}$ works here (almost) is a coincidence and would not work in the general case (e.g. $4$ substituents or an 8-membered ring).

If you are going to determine it using combinatorics, it is easier to work from "first principles". There are $6$ places to place $\ce{F}$, $5$ to place $\ce{Cl}$, then $4$ to place $\ce{Br}$, so $120$ possible ways (permutations) to arrange them overall. Then divide by the appropriate numbers to account for the rotations and reflections making most arrangements equivalent.

Answer B:
There are three ways to think about it; you are going along the second way, and it just happened to be the wrong one.

A typical chemist would just look and say: First I place $\ce F$ in any position. Before I place the first substituent, they are all equivalent, so in effect there is just one position to choose from. Then I place $\ce{Cl}$ in ortho-, meta-, or para- position relative to it. Both ortho- and meta- make the remaining 4 positions all distinct, and $\ce{Br}$ can be put in any of them. However, para- is symmetric and only has 2 inequivalent positions for $\ce{Br}$. So, $4+4+2=10$.

The whole approach starting with $\binom63$ is flawed from the start. It implies reasoning along the lines of "I choose one position out of $6$, then one of the remaining $5$, then one of the remaining $4$, then divide by $3!$ because my three chosen positions are all equivalent". There are no $6$ in the first place. As I said above, before our first choice all positions are equivalent. On the other hand, the final $3!$ is not there either, because the chosen three places are not equivalent: one contains $\ce F$, another $\ce{Cl}$, and the third $\ce{Br}$. Luckily, these two mistakes (extra 6 and missing 6) negate each other and we end up with the answer $(20)$ which is almost correct, and becomes exactly correct if we divide by $2$ to account for the reflection symmetry. Indeed, each isomer can exist in two mirror orientations, and (luckily again) none of them is symmetric itself, otherwise simple division by two would not work.

The systematic mathematical way is a lot more involved and requires math (Pólya enumeration theorem) way outside of what is commonly taught to future chemists. Skipping the preliminaries, it goes as follows:

Identify the symmetry group of the unsubstituted molecule (that would be $D_6$, because we ignore the horizontal plane where the whole molecule is located, because if we don't, it will get even more complicated and finally come out the same anyway).

Title: FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D

Abstract:
To accelerate materials discovery, language models must be able to address problems at the research frontier. Yet textbook- and examination-derived benchmarks primarily assess established knowledge, leaving performance on frontier research problems largely untested. We introduce FrontierMat, a benchmark of 330 problems drawn from frontier academic and industrial research in fields including aerospace, semiconductors, embodied intelligence and nuclear fusion. Every problem is validated by leading experimentalists and industry experts in its field. Each problem presents a real study and asks the model to infer a withheld outcome or draw a conclusion from selected experimental evidence. Problems are annotated by functional domain, material system and the scale of the governing mechanism; 130 require cross-scale reasoning. The strongest general-purpose model scores only 53.7%, and on matched problems, cross-scale problems score 8.7 points below single-scale ones. Half of the problems are solved by at most one model, and models fail chiefly by endorsing what is plausible rather than what was observed. A domain-adaptation study with meta-weighted continued pretraining and scale-modular self-distillation raises an open-weight model from 36.7% to 55.4%, matching the strongest proprietary model, with improvements on public materials benchmarks and no decline in aggregate performance on general benchmarks. FrontierMat provides a testbed for measuring progress toward language models that support frontier materials R&D.

Title: The Liouville property for geometric graphs in the plane

Abstract:
We show that every bounded discrete harmonic function with respect to the cotangent Laplacian on a Delaunay triangulation of the Euclidean plane is constant; equivalently, the cotangent-weighted triangulation has the Liouville property. Our main theorem establishes this property for a more general class of connected weighted geometric graphs in the plane. Furthermore, we show that a planar Delaunay triangulation with cotangent weights could be transient but is recurrent if edge lengths are uniformly bounded.

Site: Law Stack Exchange
Title: Does a pardon void the constitutional right to stay silent?
Tags: fifth-amendment, pardon, subpoena, us-senate

Question:
When Dr. Fauci was recently under subpoena to testify before a Senate committee, he repeatedly invoked his right to not be witness against himself under the Fifth Amendment of the constitution:

nor shall [any person] be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself...

This case is somewhat special because the Senate investigation is not a criminal trial; but the Senate has procedural power similar to a criminal court, which is apparently why the Fifth Amendment is principally applicable; at least, I have not heard a principal objection to this.

However, in this specific case Fauci is now held in contempt for not answering. The Senate argues that he invoked the Fifth Amendment unlawfully because he has received a preemptive pardon for at least some of the matters he refused to answer questions about; the argument is that because he cannot be punished for them, he has no right to refuse being a witness in these matters.

I was wondering about that. If the Senate inquiry is procedurally so similar to a criminal trial that the Fifth Amendment can in principle be invoked — would the pardon not protect Fauci from investigations into the pardon period?

Apparently, the Senate does not share this assessment and instead targeted precisely the time period for which Fauci was pardoned, with its powers akin to a criminal court. In this case, since the Senate feels not bound by the pardon: Would Fauci's Fifth Amendment rights not also be unbound from the pardon and be "resurrected"? Either the pardon protects him, or the Fifth; you cannot circumvent both.

Even more broadly, if we assume that the Fifth can principally be invoked in a Senate inquiry: Why would a pardon in this context deprive anybody of their constitutional right to stay silent? If the inquiry bears a great enough similarity to a criminal trial that the Fifth can be in principle invoked then it clearly can also be specifically invoked. There is no wording in the amendment indicating that a pardon would invalidate it, and we are all textualists, aren't we?

In operating systems, a process can create another process via mechanisms such as fork() and exec(). In distributed systems, controllers can create resources such as containers, pods, or virtual machines.

Recently, systems increasingly contain both:

Traditional deterministic computational entities (processes, containers, VMs, services, etc.)

Goal-directed computational entities (agents, LLM-based systems, planners, humans-in-the-loop, etc.)

This creates a more general creation graph:

Hard computation → Hard computation

Process creates process

Controller creates pod

Hard computation → Soft computation

Program starts an agent runtime

Soft computation → Hard computation

Agent provisions infrastructure

Agent launches a job or container

Soft computation → Soft computation

Agent delegates work to specialist agent

I'm looking for the most general theoretical framework that models all of these cases under a single abstraction.

What area of computer science would most naturally study such a model?

I'm not looking for implementation technologies or software frameworks, but rather the underlying theoretical concept or formalism.

Title: System-Level Factors Influencing AGC Cyber-Attack Success and RAS Vulnerability in Multi-Area Grids

Abstract:
Automatic generation control (AGC) stabilizes frequency and scheduled power exchanges among interconnected areas, yet its reliance on communication networks introduces cyber-vulnerabilities. This work examines coordinated AGC cyber-attacks in the presence of remedial action schemes (RAS) and identifies operating conditions under which an attacker can drive grid frequency beyond safe limits while evading RAS. A feedback-based attack policy is used to manipulate AGC signals and steer system frequency toward unsafe trajectories. Then, a large nested-loop parametric sweep---spanning attacked-area inertia relative to its interconnected neighboring area, AGC capacity versus maximum tie-line transfer, AGC update rate, load damping, and bi-directional power transfers---generates over 1.45 million scenarios. These are classified using a decision tree to establish guidelines to distinguish successful from unsuccessful attacks based on frequency deviations. The resulting vulnerability guidelines are validated on a three-area system using phasor-domain simulations with IEEE 9-bus area models, detailed turbine--governor dynamics, and under/over-frequency load and generation shedding. Results show that specific combinations of AGC capacity, inertia distribution, and pre-attack tie-line loading increase the likelihood of successful attacks, offering operators actionable criteria for identifying vulnerable operating conditions.

Title: When AI Investigators Cannot Trust Their Tools: Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification for Cyber Threat Investigation

Abstract:
LLM agents increasingly triage security alerts by combining the outputs of several detection tools, implicitly treating those tools as trustworthy. Unlike prior work on conflicts between a model's knowledge and its context, we study conflicts among the tools themselves: what happens when this machine-generated evidence is conflicting or wrong. On the corrected CIC-IDS2017 dataset, four heterogeneous detectors emit labels and confidences that we corrupt under a threat model varying the number of corrupted tools, the persistence of the corruption, and the confidence attached to wrong outputs. Across open-weight LLMs from 3B to 14B parameters, unverified investigators are fragile: one corrupted detector out of four lowers naive accuracy to .50-.72, three lower every unverified investigator to .13 or less, and honest disagreement alone makes them abstain on up to 63% of flows. We propose Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification (CAV), built from established components: an equal-weight vote that ignores reported confidences, an evidence-conflict gate, and an independent nearest-neighbour trust check that tests the leading candidates. With its prompt frozen before testing, CAV-LLM improves on the naive investigator in every corrupted condition ($p < 0.001$), reaching .84-.88 with three corrupted detectors against at most .08, while calling the LLM on 0.4% of clean traffic. A fixed verification rule is as accurate or better unless most tools are corrupted. When we make the independent channel itself noisy, CAV inherits its errors: it stays ahead when two or more tools are corrupted, but adding the channel as an extra voter is better when at most one is. Verification thus moves trust from the tools to the check, which must be measured and protected in turn.

Lubna Speitan is a British-Palestinian award winning contemporary artist and activist. She is a founding member of the Greenwich Palestine Alliance and a long-standing campaigner for Palestinian rights [ref: ] [ref: GREENWICH PALESTINE ALLIANCE, GREENWICH PALESTINE ALLIANCE]. She has been involved in a legal campaign concerning Greenwich Council's investments and Palestine [ref: Campaigner takes Greenwich Council to court over Israel investments, The Greenwich Wire].

Speitan is based in London and is specialising in Abstracts, Landscapes, Seascapes, Nightscapes and Portraits although she has put her painting career largely on hold for more than two years while undertaking activism [ref: Biography, lubnaspeitan].

== Activism ==

=== Greenwich Palestine Alliance ===
Speitan is a founding member of the Greenwich Palestine Alliance, a London-based grassroots organisation campaigning on Palestinian issues. The organisation has organised political education, demonstrations and campaigns directed at institutions in the Royal Borough of Greenwich [ref: ].

=== Pension-fund campaign ===
In December 2024, Speitan submitted a public question to Greenwich Council concerning support for Palestinian residents affected by the conflict in the Middle East. In 2025 and 2026, Speitan pursued a judicial review backed by the Public Interest Law Centre concerning the investment policy of Greenwich Council’s pension fund. By early 2026, the council conceded that its stance on lacking legal power for divestment was unlawful, leading to a policy review [ref: Greenwich Council concedes pension fund investment policy was “unlawful” following Israel divestment challenge: law centre, www.localgovernmentlawyer.co.uk] [ref: Greenwich Council admits pension investments in Israel are unlawful following legal challenge, Morning Star] [ref: Gaza activist taking Greenwich Council to court claiming it unlawfully invested £60m in Israel, The Jewish Chronicle] [ref: ].

The dispute concerned a clause in Greenwich Council’s Local Government Pension Scheme investment strategy that stated that the council could not exclude investments in order to pursue boycotts, divestment and sanctions against foreign countries and UK defence industries. According to data from the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, Greenwich’s pension fund has invested more than £61.8m in companies with Israeli interests. Following the legal challenge, the council accepted that the relevant provision was legally erroneous and agreed to remove it and consult on its responsible-investment policy [ref: Greenwich Council concedes pension fund investment policy was “unlawful” following Israel divestment challenge: law centre, www.localgovernmentlawyer.co.uk].

Speitan said that the campaign arose partly from her family’s experience in Gaza and the West Bank. In an interview with the Public Interest Law Centre, she described the campaign as an attempt to apply consistent human-rights principles to local-government investment decisions and drew comparisons with local-government divestment campaigns during the South African anti-apartheid movement: "Our own local history proves this: divestment from South Africa was a crucial, tangible step Greenwich council took against apartheid. It showed local government can be a powerful lever for global justice" [ref: ].

=== Art ===
Speitan is a contemporary artist whose work has been exhibited in London. Her website records participation in the FLUX Exhibition in London in 2023, an exhibition involving dozens of contemporary artists [ref: Biography, lubnaspeitan].

In December 2025, she held what her website described as her “final studio exhibition” at Thames-Side Studios in Woolwich. The exhibition presented remaining works from her artistic career, with proceeds intended to support her campaigning through the Greenwich Palestine Alliance and Trade Unionists for Palestine.

Title: Lengths of closed geodesics on random non-compact hyperbolic surfaces

Abstract:
We study the asymptotic distribution of the number of primitive, closed geodesics on Weil-Petersson random hyperbolic surfaces with genus $g$ and $n(g)$ cusps, under various growth rates of $n(g)$ as $g\to\infty$. We prove that the limiting distribution is Poisson with parameter depending explicitly on the limit of $n(g)^2/g$. This work is inspired by that of Mirzakhani and Petri's on closed surfaces and Hide and Thomas when $g$ is fixed. Our proof relies on first order expansions for Weil-Petersson moduli space volumes in the $n(g)/g\to 0$ regime. We also obtain some new existence results for small Laplacian eigenvalues.

Title: A Retrospective-Approximation Interior-Point Method

Abstract:
An algorithm is proposed, analyzed, and tested for solving nonlinearly constrained continuous optimization problem instances wherein the objective function is defined by an expectation over a random variable argument and the constraints include inequalities (and perhaps equalities) involving functions that may be nonconvex. The algorithm combines a retrospective-approximation strategy for handling the objective and an interior-point approach for handling the constraints. In each iteration of an outer loop, the objective is approximated by an empirical average over a set of realizations of the random variable argument and the resulting sampled problem is solved with an interior-point method that allows inexact search-direction computations for computational flexibility. Termination conditions for the interior-point method are tailored for those needed for convergence guarantees by the outer loop. Over the outer loop, the sample set is updated adaptively in such a manner that convergence guarantees for solving the original optimization problem can be assured. The results of numerical experiments are presented, which show that the proposed algorithm can outperform competing methods that have comparable theoretical guarantees.

Title: The lattice of antichains of intervals: Dyck paths, level sets, and sweep dimension

Abstract:
The Clarke-Cormack-Burkowski lattice $\mathcal{E}_n$ is the lattice of antichains of intervals of the chain $\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$, the algebraic structure underlying minimal-interval semantics, a query semantics used in information retrieval. We give an explicit, elementary anti-isomorphism between $\mathcal{E}_n$ minus its top element and the Stanley lattice of Dyck words of semilength $n+1$ (an anti-isomorphism whose existence is implicit in work of Ferrari and Munarini), under which the rank of an antichain is $\binom{n+1}{2}$ minus the area of the associated Dyck word. Hence the rank generating function of $\mathcal{E}_n\setminus\{\top\}$ is the reverse of the Carlitz-Riordan $q$-Catalan polynomial. Using a local limit theorem for the area of random-walk excursions, we confirm unconditionally an asymptotic formula of Takács: the size $λ_n$ of the largest level set of $\mathcal{E}_n$ satisfies $λ_n\simκ\,4^{n+1}/(n+1)^3$, where $κ\approx1.0807$. Finally, for the antichains of intervals of an arbitrary finite poset $P$ we study the sweep dimension, the minimum number of linear orders needed to separate every interval from every element outside it. It equals the Dushnik-Miller dimension of the lattice of convex subsets of $P$, it is the least $k$ for which $P$ maps into $\mathbb{R}^k$ so that every interval is the preimage of an upper orthant, and it lies between $\max(2,w)$ and $2w$, where $w$ is the width of $P$, both bounds being tight. Antichains of intervals embed, preserving joins, into $k$-dimensional staircase regions.

Site: Law Stack Exchange
Title: Would it be fair for a judge to reject submissions because they "appear" AI generated?
Tags: constitutional-law, common-law, human-rights, public-law, procedure-rules

Question:
The rule of law requires access to justice. This usually involves, at the minimum, access to a judicial system. However, some people attempt to abuse this common good. Sovereign citizens, for example, try to clog the judicial system with pseudo-legal documents phrased in apparently legal (but substantively nonsensical) messaging. A major issue for the courts is handling abusive litigants whilst paying due regard to the rights of natural justice (e.g. the duty to give reasons).

A further sub-issue is that it takes far more time to rebut the arguments of sovcits, which often draw upon numerous areas of law (from admiralty to constitutional law, legal history, jurisprudence, and the laws of commerce), than it does for the sovcit to write (or copy and paste) their submissions to be heard by a fair and impartial court. Joe McIntyre has noted that, in some respects, AI (artificial intelligence) or LLM (large language model) text is like sovereign-citizen pseudolaw.

So, my question is, would it be fair and lawful for a judge or judicial system to dismiss submissions on the grounds that they are apparently AI-generated? My question is not so much about specific rules of civil or criminal procedure, but if I were to put it doctrinally:

Suppose that there is a Court System (A) that has had a hell of a problem dealing with LLM-generated submissions, which clog up the system, wasting time and resources, and depriving others of rights of access to justice. These submissions contain fake citations, manifestly wrong arguments, distortions of evidence, and so on. They pose a grave threat to substantive and procedural justice.

As such, Court System A now implements a new internal rule that lawyers cannot submit substantially AI-generated text. All submissions must be written by the lawyer, for the most part, with reasonable exceptions (for example, fixing typos, checking calculations, verifying - not generating! - citations).

A leaves it up to judges C, D, and E to implement this policy accordingly. On the first day after the rule is implemented, each judge throws out cases on the ground of the new rule — C, because of his intuition; D, because an AI-detection software with an n% accuracy said so; and E, who has a degree in linguistics and economics, because he fancies himself a lexical expert, and, applying a set of principles he's gathered from various online resources, rules that, on his interpretation, "a lot of hallmarks of AI use".

As it turns out, all three submissions were by lawyer X, who did not, in fact, violate the policy. He seeks judicial review of Court System A's policies, and of the decisions of C, D, and E. Suppose that leave to seek judicial review is granted. Also suppose that there is no way of verifying for sure whether X had in fact used AI, because, for example, he typed it all in Notepad or some other software that doesn't have a version control history.

The only substantive issues are, thus: Is the policy, and the decisions of the judges, unconstitutional or otherwise unlawful? Suppose the constitutional laws of your preferred jurisdiction.

Title: Strong solvability and its failure for critical SDEs

Abstract:
We revisit the construction of strong solutions to singular SDEs by compactness on Wiener space. For spatially varying diffusion coefficients, assuming sufficiently small form bounds on the drift and diffusion gradient, we use basic energy estimates and an extended compactness criterion for Wiener functionals to construct an approximation-independent stochastic flow of homeomorphisms. Both forward and inverse maps have local Sobolev moment bounds, and the resulting strong solutions are pathwise unique in a class of solutions satisfying a Krylov estimate. We also show that the endpoint critical condition $b\in L^\infty_tL^d_x$, together with $\mathrm{div } b=0$ does not guarantee the existence of a strong solution. For every $d\geq2$, we construct a SDE with a divergence-free drift in this class and an additive Brownian noise, started from the origin, has a weak solution unique in law, but no strong solution. The proof uses logarithmic rescaling to characterize strong solvability by whether the sample measures of an associated stationary diffusion are Dirac masses. Positivity of the top Lyapunov exponent, combined with random SRB theory, rules out this concentration and hence strong solvability.

Title: Pawnshops and Property-Related Crime: Lessons from Interwar Tokyo

Abstract:
Using ward-level panel data for 1927 to 1935 and fixed-effects models, this study examines how pawnshops were related to property-related crime in interwar Tokyo. Accordingly, public pawnshops targeting low-income borrowers are compared with profit-oriented private pawnshops. The results reveal that public lending is negatively associated with theft and positively associated with fraud and extortion, whereas private lending is negatively associated with fraud and extortion as well as embezzlement. A simple monetization exercise shows that offense counts and victim losses can yield different assessments. Overall, the relationship between credit and crime depended on both institutional design and crime type.
